title: Democrats supporting abortion rights won in the midterms, but changes unlikely soon
summary: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs
story: Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government jobs

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.
That’s because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.
Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states’ constitutions to create a right to abortion.

Voters in a dozen states already have passed similar amendments, including two — Nevada and Virginia — this year. Voters in November also kept such protections in Missouri but defeated an initiative to add them to state law in Idaho.

In Georgia, where Democrats gained the House and the governor's office, abortion is banned in most cases after fetal cardiac activity can be detected — around six weeks into pregnancy and before many women realize they’re pregnant.
Josh McLaurin, the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor, is optimistic that one Republican state senator would be willing to join Democrats to repeal that law.
The measure could get at least a vote in the Senate, he said, because Republicans will have a 29-27 majority and may not take a “hyper-partisan approach” to block it.

McLaurin said that voters see the ban as a healthcare issue, especially after a state review board in 2024 found that two women died in Georgia after doctors were hesitant to perform abortions that could have saved their lives.
Still, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms acknowledged that a GOP-held state Senate could be an obstacle.
“If we see a pathway to do something about it this session, then we’re going to take that opportunity," Bottoms said at a news conference. “And it may not be this session.”

After winning the attorney general election in Texas, Democrat Nathan Johnson said he would not sue out-of-state medical providers who prescribe abortion pills via telehealth and ship them to patients in the state as the outgoing attorney general, Republican Ken Paxton, has done. Paxton dropped his suits in November.

Those pills often come from states that seek to protect medical professionals who prescribe them through telehealth and ship them to patients in places with bans. That practice is why the number of abortions has been higher since the fall of Roe. It's also the heart of the current abortion legal battles.
Johnson could also withdraw Texas from a lawsuit challenging federal policy on the abortion pill mifepristone and decide not to defend the state's abortion restrictions against lawsuits.
“It is deeply gutting that now we don’t have Texas to be fighting with the pro-life side on this,” said Kelsey Pritchard, spokesperson for SBA Pro-Life America.

Pritchard and other anti-abortion activists are pushing the Trump administration to make mifepristone harder to get by persuading the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is studying the drug, to bar filling prescriptions through the mail or at pharmacies. The FDA has said it'll have more information by March.
They're also counting on remaining Republican state attorneys general to keep up the fight.

Ohio lawmakers this month passed legislation to bar telehealth prescriptions for mifepristone sent into the state and to reimpose a 24-hour waiting period before obtaining an abortion. It’s not clear whether outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine will sign them into law — or how courts would rule on legal challenges. Voters passed a constitutional amendment protecting abortion access in 2023.

Ingrid Duran, state legislative director at the National Right to Life Committee, said her group will keep pushing measures that Democrats sometimes support — such as supporting ways for women to anonymously and safely give up newborns for adoption. And, she said, it will encourage anti-abortion bills that may not have much of a chance of passing now as a way to build for the future.
“We're not going to give up just because it's going to be more challenging,” she said.

Some congressional Democrats are planning to push forward a measure that would bar states from banning abortion before viability and rescind restrictions that some states have — such as requiring multiple doctor’s visits or ultrasounds.
With a Trump veto expected if it reaches him, the effort would be aimed largely at forcing him to reject a policy that has public opinion on its side.
About 6 in 10 U.S. voters said abortion should be legal in all or most cases, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters in all 50 states.
Associated Press journalists Scott Bauer, Kate Brumback, Marc Levy, Amelia Thomson-DeVeaux and Anna Wilder contributed to this article.

title: A converted shipping container became an unexpected source of mental health help in South Africa
summary: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults
story: In a South African township, a sensory room in a repurposed shipping container was initially designed for young children but has since become a mental health haven for teenagers and adults

JOHANNESBURG -- Sisanda Hani enters a former shipping container at a community center in South Africa, slips off her shoes and plunges into a sea of blue plastic balls. The 40-year-old mother of a teenager with ADHD and epilepsy lets the balls envelop her and screams.
For Hani, that howl is a release.

The shipping container is now a “sensory room” opened in April by youth-focused non-profit Afrika Tikkun in Orange Farm, a low-income township south of Johannesburg. Initially designed for young children with developmental conditions, it surprisingly also became a place of relief for parents and caregivers in a neighborhood where professional therapy is hard to find.
“We had a lot of stress,” Hani told The Associated Press. “No one was asking us how we were doing.”

The room is an assortment of sights and textures. Fairy lights thread through beaded curtains. Foil fish, tiny mirrors, a hammock and a burlap cushion fill the underwater world, with shapes resembling amoebas and coral covering a wall. Outside are balancing logs, sand and water pits, and a swing.
Locals helped design it, making sensory items from recycled materials in workshops led by Afrika Tikkun and its partner, Sensory-Space.

Hani was among those who helped. Caring for her 19-year-old son makes it difficult for the single mother to hold down a job. Even temporary work can be interrupted by a call about a seizure, sending her rushing home. Encounters with people who do not understand his conditions add to her stress.

She initially thought the room was only for children. A social worker encouraged her and other mothers to try it, and she says now she leaves feeling less burdened and better able to talk calmly to her son instead of shouting. She says he also becomes calmer and more playful during visits.
“We bottle it inside, but when you come here, everything comes out,” she said.

Afrika Tikkun describes the space as South Africa’s first community sensory facility. Program participants and their parents can book free sessions. Its usage records list 450 school-going children aged 6 to 18, 67 young adults and 56 parents and caregivers.

Tegan White, an occupational therapist with the program, says the room’s textures, lights, sounds and movement help users explore sensations and regulate their responses. The ball pit, for example, provides full-body contact that can help users sense where their limbs are.
For adults under stress, it offers somewhere to settle without having to explain their feelings.
“It doesn’t require words. Maybe you aren’t ready to talk,” White said.
The room provides sensory activities beyond her appointments, but she stresses that it complements professional care.
“Therapy is absolutely essential. Having access to ongoing intervention is important,” she said.
Annelize Kruger, an independent occupational therapy lecturer at the University of the Free State, says sensory rooms can help children and adults manage distress, although research remains limited.
“Our sensory needs do not disappear as we get older,” she said.

She distinguishes time spent exploring a sensory room from clinical sensory integration therapy, which involves individually tailored activities guided by an occupational therapist. Guidance can help users identify calming strategies to use beyond the room, Kruger said.

But professional care remains difficult to obtain for many in South Africa. In 2023, then-Health Minister Joe Phaahla said fewer than 30% of people with mental health problems in Africa's biggest economy received treatment. The government’s 2023–2030 mental health policy acknowledges staff shortages and uneven services across provinces.
And across Africa, mental health services remain underfunded and fragmented, particularly in underserved communities, according to the World Health Organization.

At the center, teenagers ask to return simply to sit and relax, says disability inclusion manager Bridget Gumede. Some children have shared troubles at school and home, prompting referrals to social workers. Staff admit up to five people at a time for sessions lasting less than 30 minutes.
“I didn’t know that it can do this much,” she said, adding they now need a bigger space.

The container and its sensory contents cost about $4,700 to $5,300, said Lana Roy, who leads Afrika Tikkun’s Disability Inclusion program. The organization has opened another sensory space in Cape Town and hopes to expand further.
Dee Blackie, the designer of the sensory space, says they invite adults to do something they may have left behind: play.
“So it doesn’t matter if you say, well, playing is not for me. When you get into the space, you immediately start playing,” she said.
For Njabulo Ntombela, 19, that play offers relief from worries about finding work and continuing her education. She says she's afraid she will be unable to support her family.

She visits the sensory room once or twice a month when she feels overwhelmed. Before discovering the room, she said she would withdraw and spend the day without speaking to anyone. Afterward, she feels more comfortable approaching others and asking for help.
The ball pit also gives her a chance to experience play she says she missed growing up.
"When I’m here, I feel like I’m back to 7 years old,” she said.
For more on Africa and development: https://apnews.com/hub/africa-pulse

title: CDC director draws doubts from employees and ire from legislators
summary: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation
story: Dr. Erica Schwartz, head of the CDC, is facing scrutiny from House Democrats and calls for her resignation

NEW YORK -- Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.
What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.
She reports to U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.
“She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor.

In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC — including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.
“I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. “Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people.”

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization’s declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.
“I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately,” said U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat.
When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her “a STAR!” on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.
Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president’s agenda.
Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations and retirements.

At her nomination hearing, Schwartz pledged “radical transparency” to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.
“I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments,” she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about 1 in 6 Americans said they believed that “vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps and rubella cause autism” — even though dozens of studies have determined there’s no causal link. Roughly another 1 in 5 said they didn’t know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first “all hands” staff meeting, during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn’t hesitate to disagree with Kennedy — but only privately.
Some say that’s when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

“I don’t have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines,” one CDC health scientist told the AP. “If we’re talking about radical transparency,” it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.
Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: “I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line.”

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz’s salary — even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations — including for measles, the flu and COVID-19.
Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.
But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

“I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration,” said Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “I don’t think we have seen that yet.”
Kennedy continues to back Schwartz. The Health and Human Services Department issued a statement in response to Associated Press queries, quoting Kennedy as saying she had his full support.

“Dr. Schwartz brings the judgment to make hard decisions and the courage to see them through. She is reforming CDC and sharpening its focus on its core mission: protecting Americans from disease,” the statement said.
Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials’ accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.
Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.
Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

“As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports,” according to a statement from Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado and Yvette Clarke of New York.
“We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required,” they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.
Schwartz argued that she was “fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't.”

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what’s going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it’s still too early to judge her.
Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.
Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled “Esther: The Woman Who Didn’t Know Her Place.”

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: “There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day.” She also said DeBerry is on “terminal leave” and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.
None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC’s main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows.
(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as “Officer Stone” during a recent health summit appearance.)

Dr. Tom Frieden, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don’t recall seeing that before.
“It feels like they’re afraid of us,” one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.
A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children’s medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.
The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.
HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.
At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, “and I’m trying to earn that trust every day.”
She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency’s leadership and develop a “strategic hiring plan” for 2027.
CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.
“I think everyone is just exhausted,” one health scientist said. “There’s just a sense that we can’t go on like this anymore.”

title: South Korea confirms its first case of cholera in 10 years
summary: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years
story: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.

The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.

The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not traveled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.

It was the country’s first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.

Cholera spreads mostly through contaminated water and food and can also spread through contact with an infected person’s stool or vomit, according to the agency. Diarrhea is the most common symptom, and severe illness can lead to dehydration or shock that could potentially be fatal if treatment is delayed.

The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases

title: Experts debunk Thanksgiving food myths, from turkey 'coma' to risky leftovers
summary: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
story: Experts say turkey was likely on the table at the first Thanksgiving in 1621, but there's no word on whether anyone took a nap afterward
CONCORD, N.H. -- Was turkey on the table at the first Thanksgiving? Probably. Did anyone take a nap afterward? Unclear.
Among the many myths associated with Thanksgiving is the notion that today's traditional menu harkens back to what the Pilgrims and Wampanoag people actually ate in November 1621.

While no oral history has been passed down by the Native people, Pilgrim Edward Winslow briefly described the three-day feast in a letter to a friend, said Malka Benjamin, director of colonial interpretation and training at the Plimoth Patuxet Museums in Plymouth, Massachusetts.

According to Winslow’s letter — the only surviving record of the celebration — the Wampanoag leader Massasoit provided five deer, while the Pilgrims killed enough fowl in one day to feed the entire colony for nearly a week. He didn’t mention turkey specifically, but it frequently shows up in other firsthand accounts of the time period, Benjamin said.
“I feel very confident saying that it’s highly likely there was turkey on the table, in addition to duck and goose and other kinds of birds,” she said.

The menu also probably featured seafood, she said, along with squash and nasaump, a porridge-like Wampanoag dish made with ground corn and berries. Potatoes? Nope. And while cranberries were available, there was no sugar to turn them into sauce.
Here are some other more modern myths about Thanksgiving food and what experts have to say about them:

Unless you’ve been asleep for the last few decades, you’ve probably heard that tryptophan in turkey makes you sleepy. While the amino acid does spur the creation of feel-good brain chemicals like serotonin and melatonin, there’s not enough of it in turkey to make you nod off, said Kimberly Dong, associate professor of public health at Tufts University School of Medicine. Chicken and beef have similar levels; cheddar cheese has even more.

“What’s happening is that people are eating a lot of carbohydrate-rich foods that are really quickly absorbed into the bloodstream,” she said. That causes a spike in blood glucose levels followed by a rapid drop. It’s that roller coaster that contributes to fatigue, she said, not the “turkey coma.”

Overeating in general also makes you sleepy because blood gets diverted to the gastrointestinal tract to deal with digestion, leaving muscles tired, said Susan Roberts, a professor and nutrition scientist at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth.
“I’m not one of these punitive nutritionists. I think if you have overeaten and you do feel tired, fine, take a nap,” she said. “Enjoy it.”

That said, both Dong and Roberts take issue with the idea that overeating is a given. Skipping breakfast on Thanksgiving might sound smart, but trying to “save” calories for a big dinner usually backfires, Dong said, “because you are so ravenous by the time the food is served.”

Instead, she recommends eating a light breakfast and staying hydrated early in the day. Roberts, meanwhile, suggests a multi-day strategy: eating high fiber foods for two days before Thanksgiving to keep hunger in check.

The experts disagree when it comes to leftovers, however. Dong says setting aside leftovers can counteract the “this is my one chance to eat this” mentality that leads to heaping helpings. But Roberts says hosts should pare back from the start, and that guests who feel they can’t decline leftovers should throw most, if not all, of them away at home.
Willpower doesn’t work when a plate of food is in front of you, she said, because the sights and smells activate the body to receive a big meal.

“A better place to use your willpower is before it ever comes in the house, when you’re still full from the Thanksgiving meal,” she said. “You can throw half or three-quarters of it away now and it’s easy, but if you put it in the fridge, it becomes a whole different matter.”

If you do end up with leftovers, be careful, says Anne Suelzer, a registered dietitian and licensed dietitian with Health Loft. Properly stored leftovers will be safe for three or four days, but don’t rely on your senses to judge.
“The bacteria that make you sick usually don’t change how food looks or smells,” she said.
Leftovers should be refrigerated within two hours, and the clock starts when the food comes out of the oven, not when you’re done eating.
“It helps to start packing things up while people are still at the table,” she said.

title: Scientists report strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes can fend off dengue
summary: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten
story: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten

WASHINGTON -- Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday.

The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.

In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team.
The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

“This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.
The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.
Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy.

How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.

Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.

The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease.
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed to this report.

title: Britain's Princess Catherine reflects on life after cancer diagnosis in a new documentary
summary: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
story: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
LONDON -- Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

“Heal” follows 44-year-old Kate as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. She completed the feat in June to raise money for the cancer charity of the Royal Marsden Hospital, where she was treated.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.

Kate, who is married to the heir to the British throne, announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.
Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.
In the trailer, Kate says cancer changes people profoundly, and “healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”
She adds that “it’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone” and “often, it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

“Heal” will be broadcast by the BBC in Britain on Nov. 29, by NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30, on Australia’s Channel 9 Dec. 1 and Canada’s CTV and Noovo on Dec. 7. Kensington Palace said proceeds from its distribution will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
summary: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted
story: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted

People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer’s disease.

But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer’s, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won’t even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble.

“The community will look like, ’Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they’re gonna leave us hanging,'” said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years.

Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation’s long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation’s medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow.

The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city’s Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer’s and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La’Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study’s field coordinator.

Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer’s? You wonder, do you have dementia?”

Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was “not science,” according to the study’s researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board.
“It wasn’t a Black study or a DEI study,” Wagner said. “It was something that was happening that was real.”

Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July.
While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned.
“It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals,” she said.
Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani’s grant had been terminated for being “not scientific” and “subjective” — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it needed.
“It’s simply brain science research,” she said.

In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words “disparities,” “minority” and “racial.”

Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh’s Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer’s risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants?
“You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it,” she said.

A spokesperson for HHS said “Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump’s directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives.”
This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report.

“It’s unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars,” said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress.
“We’re wasting resources, we’re wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases,” she said.

Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. The study, 15 years in the making, would’ve helped identify participants at a higher risk for Alzheimer’s — and for potential doctor’s visits and care.
Now, Wagner said, the findings are “stuck on a shelf,” and worse, over a decade of trust built with study participants has been breached.
Blair, the study participant, said reinstating trust within their communities will be an uphill battle. “It’s going to take years to reestablish something that was moving pretty good,” he said.

title: UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
summary: Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children
story: Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children

LONDON -- Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children.

Andy Burnham made the announcement Tuesday night on the BBC’s Newsnight program, saying the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts.” An estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed Cold War-era nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans from 1952 to 1967.
“Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish,” Burnham said in a statement.

Veterans claim Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally hid data from blood and urine samples that would demonstrate how they were unwittingly used as test subjects to investigate the impact of nuclear explosions on humans.

Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said in September that he had “inadvertently misled” Parliament in 2018 when he told lawmakers the Ministry of Defense had been unable to locate any information about such blood testing. He later learned that blood samples were taken throughout the military, although veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.
“This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed,” Ellwood wrote in the Guardian.

Britain has no dedicated compensation program for nuclear veterans, unlike the United States. France, which conducted tests in the South Pacific and in Algeria, has also established a compensation program.

The U.K.’s first atmospheric atomic test took place on Oct. 3, 1952, with the detonation of a plutonium implosion device in the Montebello Islands off Western Australia. The blast made Britain the world’s third nuclear-armed nation, after the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
The U.K. eventually set off dozens of nuclear explosions in Australia and ocean territories in the Pacific, including Kiritimati, formerly known as Christmas Island.

Veterans’ groups say military personnel, many of them conscripts, were exposed to nuclear fallout when they were ordered to fly through mushroom clouds or watch the explosions without protective clothing.
Campaigners are convinced there is a link between the tests and health problems that they, and sometimes their children, suffered later in life.

Burnham said the inquiry would be chaired by Bishop James Jones, who previously led the inquiry into the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, when 97 people were killed in the crush of fans at a match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest.
The panel will release an interim report by next October, the 75th anniversary of the first U.K. nuclear weapons test, Burnham said.
Alan Owen, who co-founded the campaign group LABRATS, described Burnham’s announcement as a “fantastic step forward.’’
Owen, whose father participated in a test on Christmas Island in 1962, said it had taken a lot of work “over many, many years” to reach this point.
“The campaigners have been fighting since 1984,” he said. “We’re just the next lot of campaigners that have come through to get it over the line.”

title: Nigeria seizes $220 million worth of meth, arrests 5 Mexican suspects in major bust
summary: Nigeria’s anti-drug agency says it seized at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects in a major operation in the African country's southeast
story: Nigeria’s anti-drug agency says it seized at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects in a major operation in the African country's southeast

ABUJA, Nigeria -- ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — Nigeria’s anti-drug agency on Wednesday announced the seizure of at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and the arrest of five Mexican suspects in a major drug operation in the country's southeast.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said its operatives stormed an industrial-scale laboratory in Enugu state where “Mexican meth specialists” were arrested. The Mexicans were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national before entering the country with forged passports, agency spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.
“A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," Babafemi said.

It is one of the largest seizures this year in a country that has emerged as a hot spot for illegal drugs. A transnational drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans was busted in southwestern Nigeria in May, one of several such operations carried out recently.

The anti-drug agency said the suspects had been under surveillance for weeks. The Mexicans were first denied entry into Nigeria in August, based on intelligence about their alleged plans. A second attempt, crossing over with forged passports from neighboring Benin, was successful, but authorities were alerted to their entry.
Operatives then monitored their movements and activities until Nov. 11, when they were arrested at the Enugu lab, the agency said.

The region of West and Central Africa has become a major hub for global trafficking and manufacturing of illicit drugs because of porous borders and corruption, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

title: Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
summary: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs
story: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs

MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election.

On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living.

The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions, hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little.
These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face.

House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.

Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.
Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

Academics and policymakers trace the origins of the problem to the 2008 financial crash. Home construction plummeted following a building boom that helped fuel the country's housing bubble. Large-scale investors began buying property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation years later.
Both Sánchez and his main opponent, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, have promised to enact measures if elected to financially help first-time home buyers.

That's the share of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 who were still living with their parents in 2025, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute. Almost half of those between 26 and 34 cited an inability to pay rent or buy a home as the reason why.
Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas.
Analysts say the rental supply in these areas has diminished due to a combination of factors, including population growth driven by immigration and tourism.
In cities and holiday hot spots, short-term and tourist accommodations on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com have proliferated, reducing the available rental stock.

That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidized or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.
In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.

“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”
That was the last time Spanish real wages peaked when adjusted for inflation.

Spain’s economy has substantially outgrown the eurozone average since Sánchez took office in 2018, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Spanish economy is expected to expand by an estimated 2.6% this year, more than double the eurozone's projected growth of 1.2%, according to the EU.
Even so, real wages have barely budged.

Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labor force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.

“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”
Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.
That's how much the cost of food increased between 2015 and 2025. While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, other costs have also increased while Sánchez has been in office.
To soften the impact of price rises, his government has at various times reduced value-added taxes (VAT) on food, subsidized energy and provided financial assistance.
Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”

Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticizing Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.
Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.
“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

title: Amnesty calls for independent war crimes probe into Ethiopian shelling in Tigray
summary: Amnesty International called for a war crimes investigation into shelling by Ethiopian troops and an allied militia in Tigray, saying it verified 14 civilian deaths in four attacks
story: Amnesty International called for a war crimes investigation into shelling by Ethiopian troops and an allied militia in Tigray, saying it verified 14 civilian deaths in four attacks

NAIROBI, Kenya -- Shelling of civilian neighborhoods in Tigray by Ethiopian forces and an allied militia should be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said Tuesday, as residents near the Eritrean border described military buildups and fears of another war.
Amnesty said it independently verified 14 civilian deaths in four artillery attacks on Alamata between Sept. 26-28, when Ethiopian forces and the allied Tigray Peace Forces advanced on the city.

It also accused forces allied with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front of endangering civilians by establishing military positions in residential areas and schools. The TPLF rejected those allegations in a written response to Amnesty.
The findings come amid renewed fighting in Tigray and growing fears of a wider confrontation between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea.
Amnesty interviewed residents, including survivors and medical personnel, and analyzed videos, photographs and satellite imagery.
The Ethiopian government and the military have so far not responded to the report by Amnesty. The human rights group said neither the military nor the allied militia had responded before publication.

Berhe Sibagadis, 41, a father of four in Alitena in Tigray’s Irob district, several kilometers from the border with Eritrea, is preparing to move his family further from the border region with neighboring Eritrea.
“I have to save my family, therefore I have to move to the center of Tigray,” he told The Associated Press by phone.
He said Eritrean forces are occupying a part of his local administration inside Ethiopia's borders.
“Eritrean forces committed a crime against our community during the 2020 war, so why should we stay here?” he said.
The 2020-2022 war caused an estimated 500,000 civilian deaths in Tigray from violence, famine and the collapse of health services, according to researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University.
Human rights groups and U.N. experts accused Eritrean troops of wartime abuses. President Isaias Afwerki dismissed the allegations as “a fantasy” in 2023.

Hagos Niguse, another Irob resident, said Eritrean troops are living in his area inside the border of Ethiopia and that he saw them moving tanks and heavy weapons toward the border and digging fortifications.
In Rama, resident Yonas Desta described military movements and drones overhead.
“Both countries are preparing for war and we cannot sleep when we think what could happen tomorrow,” he said.
Hagos and Yonas said TPLF fighters were positioned alongside Eritrean forces. During the 2020-2022 war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia’s army against Tigrayan forces.

Conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, known as ACLED, reported Ethiopian drone attacks on suspected Eritrean positions around Badme on Nov. 12, followed by Eritrean artillery fire and direct clashes.
“The risk of a full-scale military confrontation along the Badme front is now high,” ACLED’s senior analyst for East Africa, Jalale Getachew Birru, said in comments emailed Nov. 17.
ACLED said Eritrean troops reentered Badme around Nov. 15 after withdrawing in October, deploying reinforcements as Ethiopian troops massed nearby.
Badme was a flashpoint in the 1998-2000 border war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which killed about 70,000 people, according to the U.N. peacekeeping mission established afterward.
A 2018 rapprochement helped Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed win the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
Relations have since deteriorated over Ethiopia’s accusations that Eritrea supports Tigrayan rebels, which Eritrea denies, and Abiy’s demands for access to Eritrea’s Red Sea coast.
Fighting resumed in September, following a November 2022 agreement that ended the two-year war in Tigray.
Rahel Kidane, a 35-year-old shopkeeper in Sheraro, spent more than two years with relatives in Axum after fleeing that war. She returned after the peace agreement.
“I live in fear of being displaced again,” she told the AP by telephone. “When will this misery end?”

title: Malaysia Airlines’ parent to buy 10 Boeing Dreamliners, with options for 6 more
summary: Malaysia Airlines' parent company has announced plans to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy
story: Malaysia Airlines' parent company has announced plans to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- Malaysia Airlines’ parent company unveiled plans Wednesday to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy and expansion into Europe.
The 16 are valued at $9.3 billion before discounts, Malaysia Aviation Group President and CEO Captain Nasaruddin A. Bakar said. Airlines typically get steep discounts when they buy in bulk.
He said the new planes would bolster the group's competitiveness and support its expansion into Europe.

The first deliveries of the 787-10 Dreamliners are scheduled to begin in 2032, with the initial 10 aircraft expected by 2035, MAG said in a statement. The wide-body aircraft would gradually replace the group's existing seven Airbus A350s, boosting fuel efficiency and providing greater capacity and operational flexibility, it said.
Nasaruddin said the group currently operates a fleet of about 101 aircraft and expects this to grow to 129 aircraft by 2035, including its cargo operations and low-cost airline Firefly.

The Dreamliners are expected to initially support Malaysia Airlines’ existing network, including services to London and Paris Charles de Gaulle, as well as Asia-Pacific, covering Sydney, Melbourne, Tokyo, Osaka and Seoul, he said.
“As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility,” he added.

title: New Miss Universe's Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
summary: The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose people have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
story: The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose people have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.
“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.
The town of some 39,000 people — named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers — could barely contain itself.
“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.
“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”

Barreto, 27, has one daughter and holds master’s degrees in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the U.S. Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviors.

“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.

The organization began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favor in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.
Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.
Her hometown became known for “Pepino Power,” a volunteer group formed to restore electricity after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in 2017 as a Category 4 storm.
Puerto Rico now has the third-most Miss Universe titles, behind the United States with nine and Venezuela with seven.
Barreto was greeted by thunderous applause at Puerto Rico’s José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum each time she advanced through the competition’s final rounds.

She brought her hands to her face in shock as she was named Miss Universe 2026, beating Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela. Minutes later, she shimmied in celebration to ABBA’s “Dancing Queen.”
And thousands of Puerto Ricans across the U.S. territory danced with her.

“It’s a truly spectacular achievement,” San Sebastián Mayor Eladio Cardona Quiles told The Associated Press. “All the most beautiful women in the universe are there, and she managed to stand out. I’m happy she represented ‘los pepinianos.’”

Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.
Associated Press reporter Berenice Bautista in Mexico City contributed to this report.

title: 29 miners believed trapped by flooding in an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia
summary: Rescuers recovered three bodies Wednesday and searched for 23 other miners believed trapped in a flooded illegal gold mine in Indonesia’s West Java province
story: Rescuers recovered three bodies Wednesday and searched for 23 other miners believed trapped in a flooded illegal gold mine in Indonesia’s West Java province
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Rescuers recovered three bodies Wednesday and searched for 23 other miners believed trapped by flooding more than a day earlier in an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia.
The miners were digging for grains of gold late Monday when heavy rain caused the nearby Ciseureuh River to overflow into a mine shaft in Bogor regency of West Java province.
The shaft, estimated to be about 100 meters (330 feet) deep, is located in a mountainous area south of the capital, Jakarta.

Eleven miners escaped from one section of the excavation before floodwaters filled the shaft, West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said. Local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.
Authorities were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, officials said.

“The problem was that nobody reported it and nobody wanted to report it because the activity was illegal,” said M. Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor disaster mitigation agency.

Rochmawan said police first received reports of trapped miners about 16 hours after the flooding occurred. After an initial assessment by local authorities, firefighters and other agencies, state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.
The search-and-rescue team used submersible water pumps to suck water from the hole and tried to close off openings where groundwater seeped in.
“Water inside the hole has not yet receded and is expected to take a long time to drain,” Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency chief Desiana Kartika Bahari said.
She said high water levels, narrow access, slippery terrain and limited lighting complicated rescue efforts.

The first victim was recovered shortly after midday, followed by two others about an hour later. All three were found dead at depths of 30 to 40 meters (100 to 130 feet), Bahari said. Their identities were not immediately known.
The flooded shaft was near facilities operated by PT Antam’s Pongkor gold mining unit, but the company said the incident occurred at an unauthorized mine and was unrelated to its operations.

Antam said all of its employees were safe and operations continued normally. The company said it has repeatedly shut access to illegal mining sites in the Pongkor area and uses patrols, drones and surveillance cameras to deter unauthorized mining.
“On humanitarian grounds, Antam is supporting search and evacuation efforts,” company spokesperson Wisnu Danandi Haryanto said.
Informal mining operations are common in Indonesia, providing a tenuous livelihood to thousands who labor in conditions with a high risk of serious injury or death.

Landslides, flooding and tunnel collapses are just some of the hazards facing miners. Much of gold ore processing involves highly toxic mercury and cyanide, and workers frequently use little or no protection.

title: Fighting in eastern Congo forces Ebola workers to evacuate, threatening outbreak response
summary: Escalating fighting in eastern Congo has forced health workers to evacuate and blocked roads needed to reach Ebola patients
story: Escalating fighting in eastern Congo has forced health workers to evacuate and blocked roads needed to reach Ebola patients

BUNIA, Congo -- Escalating fighting in eastern Congo has forced Ebola response workers to leave affected areas and disrupted efforts to contain the deadliest outbreak in the country, health officials and humanitarian workers said Wednesday.

The fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, said Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has infected more than 11,700 people and killed more than 5,700 since it was declared in May, according to the latest government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing it requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

The clashes between government forces and the Convention for the Popular Revolution, or CRP, have intensified north of Bunia, the capital of the northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.
“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

WHO temporarily moved its Mongbwalu team and partner staff to Bunia after fighting disrupted road access, Smallwood said. Mongbwalu, a mining town northwest of Bunia, is where the outbreak was first detected in May.
Blocked roads also make it harder to deliver medical supplies, move patients between health facilities and send teams to safely bury Ebola victims, Smallwood said.
Sandrine Buju, a humanitarian worker involved in the Ebola response, said that her team came under gunfire on Monday while returning to Bunia after training community volunteers.
“We were surprised by gunfire about 15 meters (50 feet) from where we were,” she said. “I was very frightened.”
The driver immediately turned around, and the team sought protection at a U.N. peacekeeping base, Buju said. Peacekeepers later escorted them through two areas of fighting toward Bunia.

In neighboring North Kivu province, recent attacks by another armed group had displaced more than 20,000 people, causing health teams to lose track of people who had been in contact with Ebola patients, Smallwood said.
Even before the latest fighting, Congo’s Ebola response faced health worker shortages, delayed payments and attacks on medical personnel, complicating efforts to halt the outbreak.
Some local teams were cautiously returning to work on Wednesday, while WHO’s operations in Bunia continued normally, Smallwood said.

CRP said Tuesday that it was suspending its advance toward Bunia, while Congolese authorities said that government forces had pushed back the rebels. But residents said that the security situation in surrounding communities remained volatile on Wednesday.
Mark Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal.

title: Migration to Spain's Canary Islands breaks day record with nearly 2,000 arrivals
summary: Spanish authorities report nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at the Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a record for a single day
story: Spanish authorities report nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at the Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a record for a single day
BARCELONA, Spain -- Spanish authorities said nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at Spain’s Canary Islands on Tuesday, a record high for migrants reaching the archipelago on a single day.
The islands located off the coast of West Africa saw a surge in arrivals just before Spain holds a national election later this week, when migration will be a major concern for many voters.
Spain’s maritime rescue service said that 1,990 people arrived on 15 different boats as search and rescue vessels accompanied one dinghy after another to the small island of El Hierro.
“Sadly, this is a historic day,” the Canary Islands' regional leader Fernando Clavijo said in an interview with Spanish radio Cadena Ser.
There were around 100 minors among Tuesday’s arrivals, including a four-day-old baby that had been born during the journey, Clavijo said.

The Canary Islands, a tourist hotspot for many Europeans drawn to its year-round mild weather, have for years been a key entry point for migrants desperate to reach Europe. The route is also extremely dangerous with thousands dying in the attempted crossing.

Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. The journeys can last days or weeks, with many boats missing their target and drifting into the open Atlantic.

Over 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with half that total coming in November. The previous single-day record was hit just two weeks before, when 1,400 people arrived at Gran Canaria on Nov. 7.
In June, Pope Leo XIV warned people smugglers that they will face God’s wrath for exploiting the desperation of migrants when the pontiff visited the islands.

Departures from West Africa are seasonal, and November often sees spikes in numbers as many leave before the ocean becomes rough during winter. The seas have been calm recently, which has contributed to the high number of departures.

Most of the boats that arrived on Tuesday were from Senegal and Gambia, Clavijo said. Despite the European Union’s efforts in West Africa to reduce the number of migrants, many believe that leaving is their only option to find work and build a better life.
“The sailing conditions were favorable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores,” Clavijo said.

Clavijo said that El Hierro, the western-most member of the archipelago, with a population of 12,000, could not handle such a large influx of people, many of whom arrived exhausted and in poor condition.

He said that overall he was satisfied with the transfer of adult migrants to mainland Spain, but added that he asked for help from other regions to take in unaccompanied minors who need to be taken care of by authorities.

Spain’s conservative Popular Party is aiming to unseat the ruling Socialist-led central government in Sunday’s elections. To do so, it would likely have to form a government with the far-right Vox party, which is campaigning heavily on expelling migrants and social policies that favor Spaniards over foreigners who have recently arrived.
Without mentioning Vox, Clavijo, who belongs to the regional Canary Coalition party, denounced any attempts to demonize the migrants, calling it “a xenophobic discourse of bad people.”
The Canary Island leader also slammed the recent deal by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to send migrants to Rwanda, calling it “ridiculous.”
“Europe is on the wrong path,” Clavijo said.
___ AP writer Monika Pronczuk contributed from Dakar, Senegal.
