title: Pope Leo laments lack of climate commitments after UN talks end without agreement
summary: Pope Leo XIV has expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement
story: Pope Leo XIV has expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement

VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement, saying that “extreme environmental events linked to the climate crisis are becoming increasingly frequent.”

The pope has embraced defense of the environment in his papacy, taking up one of the core teachings of his predecessor, Pope Francis, whose landmark encyclical Laudato Si (Praised Be) cast care for the planet as an urgent, existential moral concern.

Leo issued an appeal during his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square to “never forget the human face of the climate crisis, which affects the lives of millions of people, strikes entire communities and undermines the prospects of future generations.”
He called for “fundamental changes in behavior, socioeconomic systems and the governance of our societies,” directing his appeal to “the international community and to each individual.”

During his recent trip to Peru, Leo demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, Leo’s No. 2, in a statement to COP31 recalled Leo’s earlier appeal to “bear in mind the human face of the climate crisis,” as a reminder that the talks were not “merely technical … but concern people’s lives.”
The talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

title: Solomon Islands signs treaty with Australia that checks China's influence in the South Pacific
summary: The Solomon Islands is declaring it will never allow a foreign military base on its soil and rejecting a secretive 4-year-old defense deal with China that raised fears of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific country
story: The Solomon Islands is declaring it will never allow a foreign military base on its soil and rejecting a secretive 4-year-old defense deal with China that raised fears of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific country

MELBOURNE, Australia -- The Solomon Islands rejected a secretive 4-year-old defense deal with China that raised fears of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific country and declared Wednesday while signing a treaty with Australia that it would never allow a foreign military base on its soil.

The Solomons’ archipelago is sprawled across the sea route between the United States and Australia, from where U.S. Gen. Douglas MacArthur commanded the Pacific campaign in World War II. U.S. allies fought pivotal battles against Japanese forces on the islands during the war, and the country that today has a population of fewer than 900,000 people remains strategically imperative territory in the U.S. struggle against China for global influence.

The islands' Prime Minister Matthew Wale and his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese signed the bilateral security pact following reports that the Solomons will end its defense treaty with China next year.

The new treaty confirms Australia’s place as the Solomons’ “primary security partner” and states “there will be no foreign military or security base” on the smaller nation 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) northeast of Australia, both prime ministers said in a statement.

The deal is the latest bilateral security pact Australia has struck with Pacific neighbors since Beijing inked a treaty with the Solomons’ previous government in 2022 that created fears the Chinese navy would build a base in the South Pacific.

Since Albanese's government was first elected in late 2022, Australia, a staunch U.S. ally, has been attempting to edge Chinese influence out of the region through bilateral security agreements with countries including Fiji, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

Australia reached a security-linked pact with Papua New Guinea in 2024 that promised Australia's nearest neighbor 600 million Australian dollars ($396 million) over a decade to include a rugby league team in the Australian national competition.

Wale would not confirm or deny news media reports that his government had told Beijing that the security pact with China, which has provided Chinese police trainers to the Solomons’ capital Honiara, would not be renewed when it expires after five years in early 2027.

“Unfortunately there is a non-disclosure clause in the treaty with China,” Wale told reporters in a press conference with Albanese at Australian Parliament House. “So I am unable to talk about that. We have ongoing discussions with China.”
“As you know, Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done. Gone. We don’t want to be there again,” he added.
In Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not directly answer a journalist’s question about whether the Solomons had said it would end the Chinese security pact.

“China always follows the principle of mutual respect and equality in developing relations with the Solomon Islands,” Guo said Tuesday. “There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands."
Albanese said the new bilateral treaty elevated bilateral relations to a “level which has never been seen before and has never been stronger.”
The treaty is broader than security. Australia has agreed to also invest in Solomons’ infrastructure, education, renewable energy and sport.
Oliver Nobetau, Pacific Islands program director at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney think tank, described the treaty as significant and fine-tuned to the Solomons’ priorities.
“It demonstrates that Australia is listening to what the Pacific partners want,” Nobetau told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

title: South Africa's Biovac aims to dramatically increase vaccine production with help from an EU loan
summary: South African pharmaceutical company Biovac says it aims to dramatically increase its vaccine production by the end of 2028 with help from a 75-million euro loan from the European Union's investment bank
story: South African pharmaceutical company Biovac says it aims to dramatically increase its vaccine production by the end of 2028 with help from a 75-million euro loan from the European Union's investment bank

CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- South Africa’s Biovac said Wednesday that a new manufacturing facility aims to dramatically increase African production of vaccines by the end of 2028 to help reduce the continent’s heavy reliance on imported doses.
Africa needs more than 1 billion vaccine doses a year, but only around 1% of them are manufactured on the continent, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Biovac, a public-private pharmaceutical company that's part-owned by the South African government, distributes or does end-stage production for vaccines for polio, tuberculosis, tetanus and other diseases.
It's also seeking regulatory approval to start end-to-end production of an oral cholera vaccine by late 2028, company officials said.

It would be the first cholera vaccine manufactured entirely in Africa and only the second vaccine produced end-to-end on the continent, following a yellow fever vaccine produced by Senegal's Pasteur Institute.

Biovac acquired the base technology for its cholera vaccine from the International Vaccine Institute in South Korea, Biovac CEO Morena Makhoana said. He added that the vaccine is currently undergoing clinical trials and the company expects to have initial safety and efficacy data by June.
Biovac plans to upscale its overall vaccine production by building a new manufacturing facility next to its current base in Cape Town with support from the European Union's investment bank.
The bank has lent Biovac 75 million euros ($82 million) to help finance the new production center and European Investment Bank Vice President Ambroise Fayolle visited Biovac on Wednesday.
“It is important because we believe in science and we believe the benefits can reach beyond vaccine production,” Fayolle said, adding that health resilience should be a global priority.

Biovac chief operations officer Mark MacNaughton said the new facility would give the company the potential to produce around 150 million vaccine doses a year. That would include 30 to 40 million doses of the new cholera vaccine, if it is given regulatory approval, Biovac said.

Cholera, a waterborne bacterial disease, kills thousands of people every year in Africa. A global shortage of cholera vaccines from around 2022 caused the suspension of immunization campaigns in parts of Africa, epitomizing how reliant the continent of more than 1.5 billion is on imported vaccines.
The World Health Organization reported more than 7,000 cholera deaths in Africa last year, the most in more than two decades.
Cholera vaccination campaigns on the continent only restarted this year.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, African governments were left at the back of the vaccine queue and had to scramble to secure doses.

The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Congo, which has killed more than 5,000 people, is another indication of how desperately Africa needs to increase its local vaccine production, health officials have said.
The African Union has set a target for the continent to produce 60% of its vaccines by 2040, though that's seen as a steep challenge.

title: 2 baby meerkats make their debut at Peruvian zoo, spotlighting conservation
summary: A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima to raise awareness about wildlife conservation
story: A private zoo in Peru has introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima to raise awareness about wildlife conservation

LIMA, Peru -- A private zoo in Peru on Wednesday introduced two baby meerkats born in Lima as part of an effort to raise awareness about wildlife conservation and introduce visitors to the African species.
Eduardo Espíritu, a biologist in charge of mammals at NaviFauna, a private zoo and wildlife refuge, said the initiative aims to educate the public about the importance of protecting biodiversity.
Meerkats are small mammals native to southern Africa that dig underground burrows and often stand upright to keep watch for potential threats.
“Meerkats cannot be pets. They are wild animals,” Espíritu said. “We focus on keeping them healthy, and one sign of that is reproduction,” something the zoo has successfully achieved in Lima.
The zoo is home to 15 meerkats, eight of which have been born in Lima since 2025. The other seven arrived from their native Botswana in 2022 through an exchange between zoos, according to NaviFauna.
The species gained widespread popularity through Timon, the meerkat character in Disney’s “The Lion King.”
NaviFauna is a private zoo authorized by Peru’s forestry and wildlife service. It also houses capybaras, macaws and flamingos.

title: Cambodia hosts Chinese military for largest Golden Dragon joint exercise yet
summary: Cambodia and China have started joint military exercises aimed at strengthening cooperation between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia
story: Cambodia and China have started joint military exercises aimed at strengthening cooperation between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- China and Cambodia launched their eighth joint military exercise on Wednesday, seeking to strengthen ties between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia. Cambodian military spokesperson Thong Solimo said the drills are the largest since the exercise began in 2016.
The 15-day Golden Dragon-2026 exercise will end on Dec. 9. Its stated focus is counterterrorism, humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and disaster relief.

The drills are part of Beijing’s broader push to expand its regional influence. Cambodia consistently backs Chinese foreign policy, while Beijing is its most important ally and benefactor. Chinese aid and investment have helped fuel Cambodia’s rapid economic growth in recent decades.

The United States, China’s main rival for influence in the region, has expressed concern over the military ties between Beijing and Phnom Penh. Cambodia suspended its joint Angkor Sentinel exercise with the United States in 2017, after the last drills in 2016. Following efforts by both sides to improve military relations, the exercise is set to resume next February.

Beijing has helped fund an expansion of the Ream Naval Base on Cambodia’s southern coast, raising concerns it could become a strategic outpost for the Chinese navy in the Gulf of Thailand. Cambodia has repeatedly denied any agreement granting China special privileges or the establishment of a foreign military base.

Cambodian leaders have said warships from all friendly countries are welcome to dock at its new upgraded facility, provided they comply with certain conditions. In January this year, the U.S. warship USS Cincinnati arrived at Ream, marking the first time a U.S. Navy warship has docked at the facility since its Chinese-funded renovation was completed in 2025.

According to Cambodia's state broadcaster TVK, three Chinese vessels arrived at Ream earlier this week to take part in the Golden Dragon exercise. The opening ceremony was presided over by Cambodian Defense Minister Tea Seiha and Rear Adm. Liu Sumin, commander of China's Guangzhou Naval Base.

Tea Seiha said the exercise does not aim to threaten or provoke the security of any third country, but is purely for the purpose of strengthening global security and humanitarian relief. Liu Sumin echoed the point, saying through an interpreter that “Its content does not target any third party, nor is it related to the regional situation or any specific security issues.”

title: Bangladesh raises minimum wage for garment workers after weeks of protests
summary: A government-formed wage board in Bangladesh has raised the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers by 36% to 17,000 takas, or $136, from 12,500 takas after weeks of violent protests
story: A government-formed wage board in Bangladesh has raised the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers by 36% to 17,000 takas, or $136, from 12,500 takas after weeks of violent protests

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — Bangladesh raised the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers Wednesday by 36% to 17,000 takas ($136) from 12,500 takas after weeks of violent protests that closed factories and disrupted production as workers demanded the minimum wage be doubled.
The workers took to the streets, fought with police and attacked factories for weeks as they demanded better wages and said higher inflation had made their lives difficult.

The garment industry is Bangladesh’s main sector to earn foreign currency through exports, mostly to the United States and Europe. It represents about 80% of the country’s total exports and directly employs about 4 million workers, mostly women from rural areas.
A government-appointed wage board approved the new wage structure early Wednesday after nearly 12 hours of meetings between workers’ and employers’ representatives.

The six-member board, including two representatives each for workers and employers, approved the new wage structure in a 4-2 vote supporting 17,000 takas as the minimum wage. The other two board members sided with workers’ revised demand for 18,000 takas per month.
The wage board also revised monthly wages for other workers.
It was not immediately clear if the workers would accept the new wage structure.

title: North Korea demands closure of Switzerland's new diplomatic office and orders diplomat to leave
summary: North Korea has demanded the closure of Switzerland’s new diplomatic office in Pyongyang and ordered the senior diplomat heading it to leave the country
story: North Korea has demanded the closure of Switzerland’s new diplomatic office in Pyongyang and ordered the senior diplomat heading it to leave the country

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea on Wednesday demanded the closure of Switzerland’s new diplomatic office in Pyongyang and ordered the senior diplomat heading it to leave the country within 48 hours.

A day earlier, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, threatened to close the office and condemned Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.

The Korean Central News Agency said a senior Foreign Ministry official summoned Astier Sylvain, who heads the Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, and handed him a notice demanding the office’s closure and his departure, in protest of the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp. The report said the ministry declared Sylvain persona non grata.

Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, described the Swiss sanctions as an “open hostile act” and an infringement of the North’s sovereignty in her statement Tuesday. She claimed that the camp in the coastal city of Wonsan supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia but didn’t directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.

North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for aid and military technology transfers. Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he looks to break further out of isolation and position North Korea as part of a united front against Washington.

Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened the diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” KCNA said at the time.

In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities said the facility participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.

The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility. The practical impact of those measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.

Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country. Both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong reportedly attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s.

The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Swiss government had said the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.

The Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said Tuesday the country aimed to “maintain channels of dialogue” despite differences with other governments. “The reopening of the office is independent of our sanctions policy, whether with regard to UN sanctions related to North Korea’s nuclear program or EU sanctions adopted by Switzerland in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine,” it said in the statement to The Associated Press.

title: Kenya cult leader found guilty of new assault and cruelty charges
summary: Jailed Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie has been found guilty of assault and cruelty to children in a new case
story: Jailed Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie has been found guilty of assault and cruelty to children in a new case

NAIROBI, Kenya -- NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Jailed Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie was on Wednesday found guilty of assault and cruelty to children in a new case, following the deaths of more than 400 people who allegedly starved to death after he told his followers to fast until they met Jesus.
Mackenzie, who was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Nov. 7 over the murder of 190 children and one adult, will now be sentenced for the new charges on Dec. 17.
He was charged at a court in the coastal city of Mombasa alongside 11 of his followers, while 24 other people were acquitted.

Principal Magistrate Nelly Chepchirchir emphasized the need to distinguish the parents’ responsibility from the religious beliefs they held, saying religion wasn't an excuse for subjecting children to cruelty.

The six children cited in the case were allegedly required to fast before their parents so they could meet Jesus first. Those who attempted to escape or secretly eat or drink were tied up, beaten and locked up.
Mackenzie is also facing separate radicalization charges, with a judgment expected on Thursday.

He founded the Good News International Church, which operated in the coastal town of Malindi for years before he instructed his followers to relocate to an isolated, vast ranch known as Chakama in 2020.

In 2023, a relative raised the alarm after family members who had moved to the ranch went missing. The concerns prompted authorities to launch investigations and a search operation, which uncovered more than 400 bodies buried in shallow mass graves across the vast property.
Dozens of malnourished members of the church were rescued, with some recounting how Mackenzie had instructed them to fast until death so that they could meet Jesus.
Mackenzie was arrested and charged with murder, cruelty to children and radicalization. He has denied the charges, maintaining that he didn't force anyone to fast.

title: A fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo kills at least 30 people, Egypt’s Health Ministry says
summary: Egypt’s Health Ministry says a fire broke out on a major highway surrounding Cairo, leaving at least 30 people dead
story: Egypt’s Health Ministry says a fire broke out on a major highway surrounding Cairo, leaving at least 30 people dead
CAIRO -- A fire broke out on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, leaving at least 30 people dead, Egypt’s Health Ministry said.

The cause of the blaze was not immediately known. The ministry said that in addition to those killed, at least 15 people were injured in the fire on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading amongst the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement.
Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the 15 injured were taken to nearby hospital and that he would head to the scene himself.
He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a massive multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

title: Pope creates new Vatican initiative to coordinate church's prison ministry in sign it's a priority
summary: Pope Leo XIV has launched a new global initiative to coordinate the Catholic Church’s spiritual care for inmates
story: Pope Leo XIV has launched a new global initiative to coordinate the Catholic Church’s spiritual care for inmates

ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV, who has followed Pope Francis in making prison ministry a priority, created a new global initiative on Wednesday to coordinate the Catholic Church’s spiritual care for inmates.

Leo named the archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Ignacio García Cuerva, as the first coordinator of the service for prisoners’ pastoral care. The new entity reports to the Vatican’s development and charity office.

Just a few weeks ago, García Cuerva welcomed Leo to the Devoto Prison in Buenos Aires on the last day of the pontiff’s visit to Argentina. Francis had ministered at Devoto for years as archbishop, and went on to schedule prison visits throughout his pontificate during his foreign trips and even while in Rome.

Leo has followed suit, visiting inmates at a notorious prison in Equatorial Guinea and then in Buenos Aires. The message has been to encourage inmates to have hope, and to show they are still beloved children of God. In Buenos Aires, Leo urged the inmates to see their time behind bars as a chance for redemption and reconciliation.
Prison ministry is an important tenet of the Catholic faith, following the Biblical mandate “I was in prison, and you came to me.”

The Vatican’s new prison service aims to help the church at the parish, diocesan and national levels develop and coordinate pastoral care for inmates. The service aims to promote prison ministry globally and help local churches develop programs. It also aims to train workers and help them communicate with civil authorities to arrange prison visits and ministry.

title: Hungary’s Magyar says he will visit Ukraine in a sign of mending relations
summary: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar plans to visit Ukraine soon, signaling improved relations between the two countries
story: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar plans to visit Ukraine soon, signaling improved relations between the two countries

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Monday that he will soon travel to Ukraine in a sign that the icy relations between the two neighboring countries, pushed to the breaking point by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, are improving.

Magyar's planned visit to the embattled country comes after Kyiv passed a law in October — long demanded by Hungary’s government — that expanded language rights for a Hungarian ethnic minority in western Ukraine.

Speaking to lawmakers on Monday, Magyar did not announce a date for his visit, but said it would take place in the western Ukrainian region of Zakarpattia, home to tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians. It will be the first visit to the region by a Hungarian head of government since 2015.
Magyar denounced Russian strikes that hit the mountainous region last week and said he would travel there “soon ... to personally deliver the support of the motherland to our Hungarian brethren.”

Before Magyar and his Tisza party won a landslide election in April, Hungary's government under Orbán pursued a hostile approach to Ukraine, repeatedly blocking aid to Kyiv and holding up European Union sanctions against Russia, all while maintaining cordial ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Orbán's government had also depicted Ukraine as a threat to Hungary's security, and cast President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an enemy, using his likeness in taxpayer-funded political campaigns.

Since taking office, Magyar's government has taken a markedly different approach, expressing solidarity with Ukraine and designating Russia a national security threat. In an interview last month with The Associated Press, Magyar said he saw “a chance to open a new chapter in Ukrainian-Hungarian relations.”

On Monday, Magyar expressed his sympathy “to the Hungarians of Zakarpattia and to the entire Ukrainian people, who for nearly five years have been waging a superhuman struggle for their mere survival.”

“I want to make clear what every well-meaning person in the world knows: that Russia is the aggressor and Ukraine, the Ukrainian people, are the victims,” he said. “We stand by our Hungarian compatriots in Zakarpattia and for the Ukrainian people who have come under attack, even if someone in Moscow doesn't like it.”
Magyar also said he would attend negotiations later this week on the EU's next seven-year budget, but that Hungary would insist that the bloc's financial support for Ukraine be handled separately.

title: North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
summary: North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
story: North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.

Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.

Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.

Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.

Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.

“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.

It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.

The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.

Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.

The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”

Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.

During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO’s 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.

“Canada is also on track to meet NATO’s new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal,” he said in a statement.
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.

The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO’s 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.

The criticism follows a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts U.S. military officials’ participation in Canadian think tank and social events. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

Wesley Wark, a Canadian national security expert and former government adviser, titled his Monday newsletter “Pentagon Pete strikes again,” calling the criticism “insulting and infuriating.” He suggested Washington was discounting Canada’s NATO deployment in Latvia and its support for Ukraine.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby paused a U.S.-Canada defense advisory board established in 1940, accusing Ottawa of failing to make credible progress on its military commitments.
The Pentagon said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%.

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. His government plans to buy up to 12 replacements.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new 5% target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.”

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025. The forum’s president, Peter Van Praagh, previously served as a senior adviser to a Conservative government in Canada.

Before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Van Praagh warned that Trump might undermine the results if Republicans suffered major losses. If those efforts succeeded, he said, it would mean “the end of the United States as we know it.”
Speaking at the Halifax forum Saturday, Rounds said Hegseth’s directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

title: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to travel to Russia to fight against Ukraine
summary: A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine
story: A Zimbabwean man has been convicted in South Africa of trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine

JOHANNESBURG -- A Zimbabwean man was convicted and sentenced on Tuesday for trying to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine after being arrested in South Africa with eight others earlier this month.
Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison, suspended for five years, and he is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.
He told a South African court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.
Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia.

His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors. He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training.
The law also applies to foreign nationals.
Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.
He said he entered South Africa legally on Nov. 4 and stayed in accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.
He was arrested at O.R. Tambo International Airport on Nov. 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.

“He agreed and offered to serve as a member of the armed forces of the Russian Federation in return for remuneration. He knew that the Russian Federation was engaged in an ongoing armed conflict with Ukraine and that the military service he intended to render would be performed in the context of that armed conflict,” his lawyer told the court.
Zimbabwe is among several African countries where Russia has been recruiting fighters for its war against Ukraine. Others include South Africa, Kenya, Botswana and Ghana.
Zimbabwean authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others.
The government said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.

An investigation by Code for Africa, a nonprofit data journalism and technology organization, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits. South Africa’s Institute for Security Studies cited the findings.

Kenya’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.

South Africa has helped repatriate some citizens it said were lured into the conflict and police investigated allegations that Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla, a daughter of former South African President Jacob Zuma, helped lure 17 South African men to fight for Russia under promises of security training.
She denied wrongdoing and resigned from Parliament in November 2025 following the allegations.
A tenth suspect who is a Botswana national also appeared in court on Tuesday on similar charges.

title: Houthi rebels close in on Aden as Yemeni forces dig in behind a fortified line
summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced close to Yemen's government seat in Aden
story: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced close to Yemen's government seat in Aden

Iran-backed Houthi rebels have advanced to within about 60 kilometers (about 40 miles) of the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the southern city of Aden, but the forces fighting them have set up a fortified line to defend the city, a military official said Tuesday.

Iran reiterated Tuesday that it would not hold talks with the United States to end their conflict unless several conditions are met. It also said three oil tankers had struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire despite U.S. aerial protection.
Meanwhile, at least nine Palestinians were killed in several Israeli strikes in Gaza, local officials said.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.

The Houthis' advance toward Aden has come after forces allied with the government withdrew from areas on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their grip on territory around the crucial waterway.

Col. Majed al-Nuzaily, spokesman for the Yemeni army, said the forces that withdrew from the western coast are now stationed north and west of Aden “on a defense line built to stop the Houthi advance," as the rebels come within 60 kilometers of the city.
“Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out,” he said during a virtual briefing.

Speaking in the same briefing, Yemeni foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman called for the United States and other Western countries to support the Yemeni coast guard in its efforts to intercept smuggled weapons to the Houthis, as well as provide training to Yemeni forces fighting the rebels on the ground.
“The Houthis are a terrorist organization. They threaten Yemenis first, and then every nation whose ships cross the Red Sea,” he said.
Yemen’s Interior Ministry said Tuesday that shelling of areas in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen killed three civilians, including a child, and wounded two other children, citing local police.
The ministry, which is aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government, blamed the Houthis for the attack.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen continue to trade accusations that civilians in their respective territories have been targeted in recent hostilities.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said Tuesday that 11 people were injured when one of the towers in the financial district of the Saudi capital Riyadh came under what it described as a “terrorist attack.”
It was the second incident targeting the capital’s financial district in less than a week. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The Houthis have in the past claimed responsibility for attacks on Riyadh, including last week’s strike. The Houthis have said their attacks are in response to Saudi strikes in Yemen.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said Tuesday that the kingdom won’t “tolerate any infringement” of its sovereignty and would “defend its resources with all our strength and resolve.”

Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Tuesday that Tehran wouldn't negotiate with the U.S. "until Iran’s seven conditions are met,” according to Iranian state television.

Iranian authorities haven't publicly disclosed those conditions, but Iranian state media have said they include the lifting of sanctions, the ending of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and the release of seized Iranian assets.
He also warned that Iran would “shift the geographical scope of the conflict should the enemy make a mistake.”
The naval arm of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said the three oil tankers struck the naval mines because they were “in violation of regulations” regarding passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guard’s navy said in a post on Telegram Monday that the strait “is not a place to test unauthorized routes or to disregard maritime warnings.”
It said the tankers were “engulfed in flames” after hitting the mines despite being under U.S. aerial escort.

At least nine people were killed in four Israeli strikes Monday night and Tuesday morning, officials in Gaza said. Among those killed was a senior security official in the Hamas-run government’s Interior Ministry.

The ministry said Na’im Abu Nahl, director-general of its internal security service, was killed in a strike west of Gaza City on Tuesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the killing and said Israel would continue targeting Hamas security forces.

Hospital officials across Gaza reported at least eight other deaths in the four strikes, including a child killed in an airstrike in central Gaza on Tuesday and three police officers killed in Khan Younis.

Israel’s military did not immediately respond to questions about the strike that killed the officers. Since last year’s ceasefire, Israel has repeatedly targeted police stations in Hamas-controlled areas of Gaza, viewing them as instruments of the group’s rule.
Hamas maintains that police are needed to preserve order amid persistent shortages and instability.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in the three-year Israel-Hamas war, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains casualty records regarded as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts, but does not distinguish between civilians and militants.
Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus, AlJoud from Beirut and Metz from Jerusalem.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Indonesian rescuers race to find 34 missing workers after a deadly candy factory fire
summary: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
story: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesian rescuers searched Monday for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta.

Saturday’s fire broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province. Firefighters battled flames for about 14 hours before largely containing the blaze tearing through the three-story building.

About 300 workers were inside the factory when the fire erupted, officials said. Of those, 63 were believed to have been in the hardest-hit area, mostly on the second floor where the flames originated from a cooling unit.

Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, or Basarnas, did not immediately offer a death toll, but said they collected human remains in 24 body bags for identification through forensic examination.
Meanwhile, rescuers saved 29 workers, five of whom were hospitalized, and continue to search for the missing.

More than 500 rescue personnel, including soldiers, police, Indonesian Red Cross personnel, and volunteers, joined the emergency response, according to Basarnas, to locate the victims within an area of about 2,000 square meters (21,527 square feet), while anxious relatives awaited news.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to more than 40 countries worldwide.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
summary: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street
story: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street
HONG KONG -- World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street.
U.S. futures slipped and oil prices also fell.
Relief over Nvidia’s decision to restore Jensen Huang as its CEO has been tempered by questions over the chipmaker's corporate governance and President Donald Trump’s influence.
In early European trading, Germany’s DAX was up 0.1% to 25,046.66. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 1% to 8,120.72, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.5% to 10,515.74.
The future for the S&P 500 was 0.8% lower, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%.
In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5% as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. sank 3.6%. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10%.
In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.2% to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9%. SK Hynix plummeted 11.1%.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8% to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8% and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2%.
The Hang Seng in Hong Kong slipped 1.1% to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined 2% to 3,476.47, falling to its lowest level in more than a year.
The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged 0.4% lower to 8,692.40. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9% from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates.
India’s Sensex rose 1.5%.

On Tuesday, stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower after a surge the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy.
The S&P 500 fell 0.5% to its eighth loss in the last nine days. The Nasdaq composite shed 1.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.9%.
They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month.

The surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO, announced Monday, does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry. But it does not settle deeper concerns such as whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to justify massive investments in data centers.

High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers.
Nvidia fell 5.9% a day after soaring 31.5% to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts.

And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5% to drop below $83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype.

Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 2.4% to $88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between $72 and $114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Early Wednesday, Brent was down 1.5% to $87.43 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 1.8% to $80.56 per barrel.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.42 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. The euro slid to $1.0944 from $1.0966.

title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate eases to 7.21%, not far from 2026 high
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month
The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. fell to 7.21% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Wednesday. One year ago, it was at 6.23%.
The weekly average rate has been above 7% since late September. As recently as Oct. 15, it was at 7.4%, its highest level in nearly three years.

Elevated mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also eased this week. That average rate fell to 6.54% from 6.66% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.51%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.
That yield was at 4.81% at midday on the bond market Wednesday.
Mortgage rates have been marching higher overall since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher.

The upward march in mortgage rates this year has weighed on home sales, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged.

Data pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September.
While the Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans.

title: Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
summary: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died
story: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died
Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry's most iconic families and later took over the NFL's Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101.
The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given.
Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford's grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014.

Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp.

The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.”
The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later.

“Martha was special," NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. "She cared so deeply about her family, the players, their fans, and the city of Detroit. She was committed to making the Lions - and the game of football - better. Martha and her husband, William Clay Ford, led the franchise with dignity and integrity. We will miss her kindness and sweet sense of humor. We extend our deepest condolences to her children, the entire Ford family, and the Lions’ organization.”
Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year.

Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage — looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” — and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history.

Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison.

Martha and William Clay Ford had three daughters and a son. Their son, William Clay Ford Jr., is the current executive chairman of Ford Motor Co.. In 2001, Bridgestone/Firestone and Ford severed their nearly 100-year relationship because of a dispute over a series of deadly tire failures on the Ford Explorer.
Sheila Ford Hamp is the Lions’ principal owner and chairman.

William Clay Ford’s first full season leading the Lions was in 1964, seven years after they won an NFL title. Since that 1957 championship, the franchise has won playoff games in 1992 and 2023 and has not played in the Super Bowl.

Although Martha Ford kept a low profile, the shakeup in the middle of the 2015 season was a sign that she was more than willing to bring about change in an effort to reverse the team’s fortunes. Then-coach Jim Caldwell said she was very much a presence within the organization.

“I think visible ownership is great, and Mrs. Ford does it extremely well,” Caldwell said in 2015. “She’s there before games and she’s there after games, and I think guys enjoy that part of it. She comes to practice and things of that nature, so it’s been fun.”
Even at 101, she attended games, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month.

Martha Ford also made an impact in the Detroit community. She was an officer on the board for Detroit Lions Charities and on the board of the Henry Ford Health System. Martha and William Clay Ford were credited with helping establish the Maplegrove Center, a substance abuse treatment facility in West Bloomfield.
In 2017, Forbes estimated Martha Ford’s net worth at more than $1.4 billion. She survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren, and 17 great-grandchildren.
See AP’s full NFL coverage here

title: Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
summary: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs
story: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs

MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election.

On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living.

The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions, hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little.
These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face.

House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.

Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.
Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

Academics and policymakers trace the origins of the problem to the 2008 financial crash. Home construction plummeted following a building boom that helped fuel the country's housing bubble. Large-scale investors began buying property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation years later.
Both Sánchez and his main opponent, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, have promised to enact measures if elected to financially help first-time home buyers.

That's the share of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 who were still living with their parents in 2025, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute. Almost half of those between 26 and 34 cited an inability to pay rent or buy a home as the reason why.
Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas.
Analysts say the rental supply in these areas has diminished due to a combination of factors, including population growth driven by immigration and tourism.
In cities and holiday hot spots, short-term and tourist accommodations on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com have proliferated, reducing the available rental stock.

That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidized or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.
In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.

“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”
That was the last time Spanish real wages peaked when adjusted for inflation.

Spain’s economy has substantially outgrown the eurozone average since Sánchez took office in 2018, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Spanish economy is expected to expand by an estimated 2.6% this year, more than double the eurozone's projected growth of 1.2%, according to the EU.
Even so, real wages have barely budged.

Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labor force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.

“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”
Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.
That's how much the cost of food increased between 2015 and 2025. While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, other costs have also increased while Sánchez has been in office.
To soften the impact of price rises, his government has at various times reduced value-added taxes (VAT) on food, subsidized energy and provided financial assistance.
Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”

Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticizing Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.
Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.
“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

title: How major US stock indexes fared Wednesday 11/25/2026
