title: Eurostar cancels Paris-London trains after staff go on unannounced strike
summary: Eurostar has canceled several trains between Paris and London due to an unannounced strike by some staff
story: Eurostar has canceled several trains between Paris and London due to an unannounced strike by some staff
PARIS -- Several Eurostar trains between Paris and London scheduled for Wednesday are being canceled because of a strike by some Paris-based staff that the company said it was notified of overnight.
Eurostar advised travelers to postpone their journeys and warned of possible disruption on other routes.

“Regrettably, Eurostar customers travelling between Paris and London today are being impacted by industrial action which the company was notified of overnight," the company said in a statement. “Unfortunately, this is causing some cancellations to services. Other routes are not directly affected but may see some knock-on impact.”

The striking staff include train drivers and managers based in Paris, Eurostar said. It advised customers whose trains had been canceled not to go to the station, saying they could rebook for another date or receive a full refund.
“Discussions are ongoing with the union and the company remains open and willing to engage in constructive dialogue,” Eurostar said.
Eurostar operates passenger trains linking London with Paris and other European destinations.

title: Malaysia Airlines’ parent to buy 10 Boeing Dreamliners, with options for 6 more
summary: Malaysia Airlines' parent company has announced plans to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy
story: Malaysia Airlines' parent company has announced plans to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- Malaysia Airlines’ parent company unveiled plans Wednesday to buy 10 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft, with options for six more, as part of its fleet modernization strategy and expansion into Europe.
The 16 are valued at $9.3 billion before discounts, Malaysia Aviation Group President and CEO Captain Nasaruddin A. Bakar said. Airlines typically get steep discounts when they buy in bulk.
He said the new planes would bolster the group's competitiveness and support its expansion into Europe.

The first deliveries of the 787-10 Dreamliners are scheduled to begin in 2032, with the initial 10 aircraft expected by 2035, MAG said in a statement. The wide-body aircraft would gradually replace the group's existing seven Airbus A350s, boosting fuel efficiency and providing greater capacity and operational flexibility, it said.
Nasaruddin said the group currently operates a fleet of about 101 aircraft and expects this to grow to 129 aircraft by 2035, including its cargo operations and low-cost airline Firefly.

The Dreamliners are expected to initially support Malaysia Airlines’ existing network, including services to London and Paris Charles de Gaulle, as well as Asia-Pacific, covering Sydney, Melbourne, Tokyo, Osaka and Seoul, he said.
“As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility,” he added.

title: Australia set to pass digital duty of care law, fines up to 5% of global revenue
summary: Australia is set to create new online safety laws that would make tech giants potentially liable for multibillion dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms
story: Australia is set to create new online safety laws that would make tech giants potentially liable for multibillion dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms

MELBOURNE, Australia -- The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.
The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

“We can’t cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.

Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.
Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.

“Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits,” Shoebridge said in a statement.
The Senate will likely pass the bill on Wednesday and the House of Representatives, where the government holds a majority, would pass it into law before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday.
The Greens' amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million) to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration expressed “serious concerns” in a submission in September to a parliamentary committee examining the draft law. U.S. concerns included how Australia would designate what constitutes “foreseeable harm.”
U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said he had conveyed his government’s objections to the amended legislation to Wells on Tuesday.
“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.
“As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors,” he added.
Wells said of their conversation: “There are points of difference and we’re ironing them out.”

The conservative opposition Liberal Party shares U.S. concerns that the bill empowers government ministers and the nation's online safety watchdog to judge what was harmful. Opposition lawmakers oppose the legislation.
“This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression,” senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters.
The Greens' amendments would also give people a legal right to sue social media companies in Australian courts for harms suffered online.
It follows Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest having to go to U.S. courts to sue Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission. The case is not yet resolved.

In October, a U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.

Australia's bill would also let social media users opt out of algorithms that send them content and empower Australia’s online safety watchdog to remove apps and websites that fabricate naked images from genuine images of people.

It would also require protections for children against content that promotes eating disorders, hostile ideas about women, pornography, crime or dangerous stunts, or causes serious mental health distress.
Lisa Given, an information sciences expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, described the draft legislation as “very good” and largely in line with European laws.

“It’ll be very interesting to see what happens now globally,” Given said. “I’ve always been of the view that if countries can band together and put through similar legislation, collectively we have a better chance of actually pushing Big Tech to make real changes in terms of the design of their systems.”

title: US consumer confidence soars as election uncertainty ends, gas prices fall
summary: Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainy ended
story: Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainy ended
WASHINGTON -- Americans’ confidence in the economy jumped this month as gas prices continued their steady decline and election-related uncertainty ended.

The Conference Board said Tuesday that its consumer confidence index soared to 103.3 this month, from a reading of 91.9 in October. It’s the second straight increase after the index fell in September to its lowest level since April 2014, even lower than during the pandemic.
Consumer confidence is closely linked to gas prices, and the Conference Board also said Americans see the job market improving.

The improvement could signal a pickup in consumer spending in the months ahead, though Americans have been spending at a solid pace this year even as consumer surveys have been lackluster. Economists say the surveys are not as reliable a measure of consumers' behavior as they have been in the past.

title: Small US trucking firms scramble to survive mounting diesel costs
summary: High diesel prices have put pressure on small U.S. trucking businesses
story: High diesel prices have put pressure on small U.S. trucking businesses

NEW YORK -- When diesel prices topped $4 a gallon early in the U.S.-Iran war, Kevin Otto thought he could manage by telling his Minnesota trucking company's 16 drivers to slow down. He estimated that traveling at 65 miles per hour would allow Otto Transfer's fleet of flatbeds to squeeze two-tenths of a mile more from every gallon and save him $7,000 per truck.

Instead, prices kept climbing. After diesel surpassed $6 a gallon in September, Otto added a fuel surcharge to every job for the first time. He based the surcharge on the government's weekly Midwest diesel average, beginning at 5% and eventually raising it to 12.5%.
“To me, it’s drastic, but it’s the only way to survive," said Otto, who took over the 80-year-old company from his parents in 2002.

High diesel prices this year have put new pressure on the small businesses that make up most of the nation's motor carriers. The war drove up one of their largest and least avoidable daily expenses just as the highly fragmented U.S. trucking industry showed tentative signs of recovery from a yearslong slump marked by weak demand and depressed rates.

Small trucking companies usually have fewer financial buffers against surging fuel prices than their larger competitors. Big fleets typically have greater cash reserves, often buy diesel at bulk discounts and tend to negotiate long-term contracts with adjustable fuel surcharges. Many smaller operators negotiate rates one load at a time and must absorb higher pump prices while waiting three to four weeks for spot rates to catch up, freight data provider DAT Freight & Analytics said.
Even when a rate includes a separate line item for fuel, carriers may wait 30 to 90 days to be paid.

“Those lags in the rates catching up to fuel are even more challenging if you’ve got to put food on the table and you don’t have a large company that’s helping carry over that difference,” Alex Leslie, senior research associate at the American Transportation Research Institute, said.

On-highway diesel reached a record national average of $6.53 in September, according to the Energy Information Administration. The price was $5.94 a gallon for the week of Nov. 16, about 56% more than before the war, EIA said. Gasoline averaged $3.81, about 30% higher.

Getting goods hauled around the U.S. and Canada costs substantially more than it did a year ago. Spot rates paid by freight brokers for individual loads were 44% to 48% higher in September, depending on the type of trailer, according to DAT. The company estimated that diesel costs accounted for at least two-fifths of the year-over-year increase.

The rest of the increase didn't necessarily translate into profit. Insurance, maintenance, equipment, tolls and other expenses were going up as the industry began to emerge from the lows of a “freight recession,” the American Transportation Research Institute said.

The average cost of operating a truck reached a record $2.34 per mile in 2025, a 3.4% increase from the year before, while nonfuel costs rose 4.2%, the industry research organization reported in July.

Profit margins were also exceptionally thin last year. Truckload and refrigerated carriers reported average operating margins of less than 1%, while flatbed carriers averaged a 0.5% operating loss, according to ATRI.

The downturn started in early 2022, when a pandemic-era surge in freight demand faded and too many trucks were left chasing fewer loads. Industry data suggest that a shrinking supply of trucks, rather than a renewed boom in shipments, is contributing to this year’s higher freight rates, obscuring how strained many trucking businesses are.

At October’s average diesel price, a tractor-trailer that gets six miles per gallon would have used $521 worth of fuel traveling 500 miles a day, compared with $310 in February, DAT calculated. Yet monthly freight volumes were lower for all three major trailer types than a year earlier, the company said.

“Demand actually hasn’t increased that much, and the market for the last few years has been quite depressed,” Adam Parish, director of trucking procurement at supply chain management company Flexport, said. “And so there’s been a lot of pricing pressure from customers.”

Wes Oberman’s company in Huntingdon, Tennessee, works with 14 drivers who own their tractor-trailers but operate under Oberman Logistics’ federal motor-carrier authority as they haul steel and consumer goods across the South.

The owner-operators handle jobs at individually negotiated flat rates and buy diesel on the road with company discount cards. They are allocated 85% of each load’s gross revenue, from which Oberman deducts their fuel purchases and fixed expenses.

As diesel consumed more of each load's revenue, he became pickier about the jobs he accepted. Sometimes that's meant waiting a day for a better-paying load or one requiring fewer “deadhead” miles, when the truck travels empty between jobs.
“We just got to keep trucking, as they say, save every penny we can and just weather the storm until this diesel crisis goes away,” Oberman said.

President Donald Trump sought to ease the pressure in October by directing the Internal Revenue Service to suspend federal penalties and reporting requirements through Dec. 31 for using dyed diesel on highways. Federal excise-tax payments were deferred, but state taxes and restrictions can still apply.
The restricted diesel normally is reserved for tax-exempt off-road uses such as farming. The fuel is dyed red to make improper use easier for law enforcement to spot.

David McKinney, the owner of McKinney & Sons Transfer in Lexington, Alabama, called the dyed diesel plan “absurd.” He doubted it would provide meaningful relief for small trucking companies. After selling two trucks in September to preserve cash, he worried that residual dye in the tanks of his company's remaining 15 trucks could expose him to fines after the temporary policy expires.
The IRS is considering a grace period.

McKinney, who has been in the trucking business for 30 years, has a fueling station at his shop so he pays less for diesel than he would if his drivers filled up at truck stops. Yet given the complicated calculus of trucking, his company is only breaking even, he said.

“Our bottom line is: For the past four months, we have survived. We have not profited any money,” McKinney said. “Rates need to be higher, but the trucking business is so competitive, it keeps it down."
In Delano, Minnesota, Otto worries his new surcharge will cost him customers. He previously adjusted his freight rates only once a year, but his long-term clients have accepted the added charge.

Otto usually gives the drivers who haul utility poles around the country for his company a bonus at the end of the year, but since his costs have risen so much, he isn’t sure if he is going to be able to do that this year.

EIA expects diesel prices to ease next year as more Middle East oil production outside Iran recovers. But the agency raised its 2027 forecast by 54 cents in November, to an average of $5.03 a gallon, citing continued constraints on global refined-fuel supplies. It warned that shipping disruptions could still produce short-term price swings.
“It’s a five-alarm fire, absolutely,” Otto said. “It is unsustainable, and I fear that it will only get worse.”

title: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi, founders after Kalshi halts trading there
summary: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise
story: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi's decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.

The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance." Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.
“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court.
The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on Dec. 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case.

Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown's office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling.

Utah's felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. In a separate case, Brown's office is still asking a state court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah.

Kalshi, the nation's largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission wouldn't immediately stop Utah's attempts to shut it down there.
A Kalshi spokesperson called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi" but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah.

Kalshi didn’t close open positions or void contracts when it blocked any new positions from being taken in Utah. It also let Utah traders close out their open positions and withdraw their funds, Kalshi said.

Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 42 other states have opposed that view.

Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending at the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which declined to halt Utah’s regulatory enforcement during Kalshi’s appeal.
Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi.
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Crowdstrike to acquire Zscaler in $44B deal that would create a cybersecurity giant
summary: CrowdStrike is acquiring cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion
story: CrowdStrike is acquiring cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion

CrowdStrike is buying cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion, the companies said Monday, in a major acquisition that combines two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest names.

The all-stock deal arrives after a string of high-profile hacks hit banks, supermarket fridges and crypto platforms, forcing the White House to shake up its cybersecurity leadership and raising alarms with officials around the world.
Cybersecurity experts have warned that artificial intelligence is being used to turbocharge cyberattacks by making it quicker and easier to find software flaws.
“Security used to be about keeping the adversary out," George Kurtz, CEO of Austin, Texas-based Crowdstrike, said in a statement. “Today, safety is required to let AI in.”
Reports of advanced artificial intelligence models deploying agents working on their own to break into other organizations have also raised alarms.
“In the AI era, Zero Trust security has become non-negotiable, and AI agents are rapidly becoming the new weakest link," Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said.

Crowdstrike's focus has been on so-called endpoint security, with services to protect laptops, mobile devices and desktop computers. Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler, meanwhile, specializes in cloud-based network protection.
Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 shares of Crowdstrike for each Zscaler share they own, under the deal's terms, which represent a 34% premium to Zscaler's closing price on Friday.
Shares of CrowdStrike tumbled more than 7% before the opening bell Monday. Shares of Zscaler rose 20%.
Existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84.1% of the combined company, while existing Zscaler shareholders will hold the remaining 15.9%.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler were already working together in a partnership that included 2,000 shared customers. The deal would expand the combined company's market by more than $185 billion by 2029.
The transaction is expected to close in the second half of Crowdstrike's fiscal 2028 year, which begins in February.

title: Federal agency boosts size of most single-family loans the government can guarantee to $855,400
summary: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices
story: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices
The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices.
Beginning next year, mortgage buyers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be able to acquire loans of up to $855,400 on single-family homes in most of the country, the agency said Tuesday.
The new conforming loan limit amounts to a roughly 2.7% increase from its 2026 level.
FHFA oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which buy home loans from banks and other lenders, guaranteeing them against default. The loans are then bundled into securities sold to investors.
But FHFA sets limits to the size of the loans that Fannie and Freddie can buy. Such loans are known as conforming loans, while mortgages above the conforming loan limit are known as jumbo loans.
FHFA adjusts the limits of a conforming loan annually to reflect changes in U.S. home values, which have been rising nationally, albeit more slowly.

Rising mortgage rates have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged.
The FHFA’s latest House Price Index shows that, on average, U.S. home prices increased about 2.7% in the July-September quarter compared to a year earlier.

The 2027 single-family home conforming loan limit will apply to most of the country, though the FHFA allows higher loan limits for certain states, such as Alaska and Hawaii, and in counties where the local median home value is more than double the conforming loan limit.
For example, the conforming loan limit in 2027 for single-family homes in Los Angeles County will be $1,283,100, while in New York County it will be $1,224,750.

title: Honda recalling more than 810,000 vehicles due to airbag inflator issue
summary: Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture
story: Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture
Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles because their airbag inflators may rupture.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said that the recall includes 810,592 Honda Civic vehicles with model years 2012 to 2013, Honda CR-V vehicles with model years 2012 to 2013, Honda Accord 2013 models and Acura ILX and RDX vehicles with model year 2013.

The NHTSA said that the vehicles have certain Takata front and passenger air bag inflators. The inflators may rupture due to propellant degradation occurring after long-term exposure to high absolute humidity and high temperature variation.
If an inflator ruptures, it could result in sharp metal fragments hitting a driver or other vehicle occupant and result in serious injury or death.
Tens of millions of Takata airbags have been recalled, one of the largest ever product recalls.

Dealers will replace the front driver or passenger air bag inflator for free. Interim letters notifying owners of the safety risk are expected to be mailed Dec. 18. Additional letters will be sent once the final remedy is available.

Owners may contact Honda’s customer service at 1-888-234-2138 for more information. Individuals may also contact the NHTSA vehicle safety hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the agency's website at www.nhtsa.gov.

title: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
summary: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming
story: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming

ANTALYA, Turkey -- Work crews boxed up the venue for this year’s United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations.”

In the lead-up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
“No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be,” said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.
Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the pavilions, where countries showcased innovations and hosted panels, workers were seen packing up electronics and boxing up belongings on Saturday.
The hallways, previously bustling with tens of thousands of participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos by deserted pavilions.

“COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.

Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year’s heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly.

Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.

“Every year there seems to be a greater discontent, a mistrust and frustration for civil society, indigenous people and countries that are more climate vulnerable,” said Tuvalu's Minister of Environment Maina Talia, during a Saturday press conference.
“I am still holding the line, trying to be very optimistic until we see the text," he said.
The United States, a major polluter and the world’s largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks.
The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan “you are killing the future” interrupted official proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting: “You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait.”

The Global South isn’t a geographical term, but a reference to developing countries in general. As the protester was escorted out by security, he shouted: “You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now."
The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said “let’s try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks.

“Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it’s nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here, watching the negotiations,” said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.
“We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on,” he said.

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Tammy Webber contributed from Fenton, Michigan.

title: Iran strikes 3 tankers as it shows off missile launchers, and other Mideast news
summary: Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility
story: Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility
Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States and Israel accelerates once more.
Meanwhile, in the Gaza Strip, an Israeli airstrike hit a truck carrying food, killing three men, the head of Shifa Hospital said. The Israeli military said that it struck Islamic Jihad militants.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.

Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher that it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles.

The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory.
The location of the missile site wasn't revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter statements from Washington that the U.S. has destroyed the missile program.
During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, said that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly."

Separately, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday that Tehran remained in contact with mediators from Qatar who visited Iran on Friday to explore “whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy.”
At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.

The U.K. military’s maritime security center said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. There were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported.
There was no immediate comment from Iran on the center’s report.

The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels.

Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.
An Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food in Gaza City’s Tel al-Hawa district on Saturday, killing three men, Mohamed Abu Selmiya, the director of Shifa Hospital, told The Associated Press.

Videos circulating online showed a pickup truck reduced to twisted metal with boxes of cooked rice torn open in the back. It wasn't immediately known where the food was being taken or whether it was connected to an aid organization. Most of Gaza's more than 2 million people are homeless and dependent on food distributions by the United Nations and other aid groups.

The Israeli military said later Saturday that it had struck Islamic Jihad militants who were traveling in a vehicle used to transport food and logistical supplies to fellow militants. The vehicle wasn't visibly marked as belonging to a humanitarian aid organization, the military said.

One of the men had been fired from such an organization after Israel's military notified it of his militant role, a military official said on condition of anonymity in line with military regulations. The men were targeted because they had “advanced attacks” against Israel's military and civilians in recent weeks, the military added.

Since a ceasefire deal with Hamas came into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes have killed more than 1,650 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn't distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll, but says women and children make up around half the dead.

In a Saturday address to mark Lebanon's independence day, President Joseph Aoun said that the country faced two “fundamental obstacles”: Israel’s occupation and “foreign interference in our affairs — specifically by certain influential elements within the Iranian regime.”
Aoun said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon, but defended the two countries’ first direct talks in decades, saying “diplomacy is not surrender.”

He said: “The era of weapons outside state control has come to an end” — a reference to Iran-backed Hezbollah militants, who began firing on Israel right after the start of the Iran war. The group has refused to hand over its weapons while Israel is occupying parts of southern Lebanon.
Sally Abou AlJoud reported from Beirut, and Wafaa Shurafa from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses
story: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses

NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it.
“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.
She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”

And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”
If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.
Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.
It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.
The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage
“The funny part," she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

title: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
summary: Climate talks in Turkey failed to reach an overarching agreement.
story: Climate talks in Turkey failed to reach an overarching agreement.

ANTALYA, Turkey -- Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations, but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.

The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.

Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.
For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”
Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

title: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned
summary: Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day
story: Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day

ANTALYA, Turkey -- This year's U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators still debating how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects.
Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft.
Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding.
Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, said they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday.

Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year's disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding.
If phasing out fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa.

In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.
“The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.”

In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

“There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!”
One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

But the final draft doesn't spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push.

“At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa.
The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change.
Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time.
Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text's draft.

“We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey's Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said.

“Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere," said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.”

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don't emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change.
They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need.

The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft's previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually.
Many of the world's most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year's talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter.
It's richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it's hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room.
Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker.

“Disappointment is rife," said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.
“Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said.
Delgado reported from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report from Fenton, Michigan.

title: Issue with automation system causes Delta flight delays in Atlanta
summary: An issue with Delta Air Lines’ weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide
story: An issue with Delta Air Lines’ weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide
ATLANTA -- An issue with Delta Air Lines' weight and balance automation system was causing flight delays Sunday at its hub in Atlanta and nationwide.

Delta said in a statement that its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they continued to work to restore automation. The delays come as Americans begin traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday this week.
The Federal Aviation Administration said on X that Delta was working to resolve the issues, and that the delays weren't related to any FAA air traffic systems.

Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights.
As of midday Sunday, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 48% of Delta's flights were delayed.
FlightAware said that 38% of flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — Delta’s hub — were delayed while about 36% of flights destined for the airport were delayed.

title: Tarik Skubal and New York Mets finalize $450 million, 9-year contract, record for a pitcher
summary: Tarik Skubal, a two-time Cy Young Award winner, has finalized a record $450 million, nine-year contract with the New York Mets
story: Tarik Skubal, a two-time Cy Young Award winner, has finalized a record $450 million, nine-year contract with the New York Mets

NEW YORK -- Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was this offseason’s top free agent, finalized his $450 million, nine-year contract with the New York Mets on Wednesday in a record deal for a pitcher.
Skubal's contract includes $30 million in deferred money: $5 million of his $45 million signing bonus and $25 million in salaries payable from 2038-46.
His signing bonus, which is protected from a possible lockout, calls for $40 million to be paid this coming March 1, $3 million on July 1, 2037, and $2 million on July 1, 2038.
New York defers $2,777,777.78 a year of his salaries. That money will be paid in a $1 million installment on July 1 in 2038 and $3 million each July 1 from 2039-46.

Skubal’s deal, averaging $50 million annually, topped the previous high total for a pitcher, Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s $325 million, 12-year contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers that started in 2024. The previous high for a pitcher’s average annual value was $43.33 million for Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander with the Mets.

“Tarik is an ace, and we are thrilled that he will be a Met for years to come,” Mets owners Steve and Alex Cohen said in a statement. “He is an impressive competitor who has distinguished himself with his talent, drive and leadership."
Skubal received the fourth-largest deal among all baseball players, trailing Juan Soto’s $765 million, Shohei Ohtani’s $700 million and Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s $500 million.
Skubal’s agreement includes a full no-trade clause.

“Acquiring an elite starting pitcher in the prime of his career is rarely an option,” Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns said in a statement. “Tarik has established himself as one of the best pitchers of our generation. Adding Tarik to our existing group of emerging, homegrown young starters creates a rotation that we believe can fuel success for years to come."

Skubal joins a Mets team that finished last in the NL East at 74-88 despite owner Steve Cohen bankrolling baseball’s second-highest luxury tax payroll at $366 million. New York’s starters had a 4.47 ERA, ranking 23rd in the majors. Skubal will top a rotation featuring youngsters Nolan McLean and Christian Scott, with veterans Sean Manaea and Kodai Senga also under contract.
New York’s 2026 payroll is $108 million above Major League Baseball’s proposed salary cap figure for 2028.
A two-time All-Star left-hander who turned 30 on Friday, Skubal is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA in 88 starts over the last four seasons, striking out 655 and walking 95 in 546 innings.
Skubal had a $32 million salary this year after winning a record amount in salary arbitration.

Skubal was 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts this year for Detroit and the Los Angeles Dodgers, who acquired him on Aug. 2 for three prospects: right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith, and outfielder Zyhir Hope. Skubal didn’t pitch for the Tigers between April 29 and June 13 because of surgery to remove a loose body in his pitching elbow. Dodgers head team physician Dr. Neal ElAttrache used a NanoNeedle scope 2.0 to perform the procedure, designed to speed recovery.

Skubal was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA in a pair of postseason starts for the Dodgers. He beat Atlanta in a Division Series opener and lost Game 1 of the NL Championship Series against Milwaukee, allowing two runs over five innings in a 2-1 defeat. The Brewers went on to sweep the two-time defending World Series champions.

He averaged 96.8 mph with his four-seam fastball this year, down from 97.6 mph in 2025, when he won his second straight AL Cy Young Award. He threw 38% four-seamers this year, 25.6% changeups, 17.5% sinkers, 13.9% sliders and 5% curveballs.
Skubal is 66-44 with a 3.02 ERA in 160 starts and three relief appearances over seven major league seasons with 1,075 strikeouts over 925 1/3 innings.

title: Bruno Fernandes scores bizarre Man United goal as shot hits divot he made moments earlier
summary: It was perhaps the unlikeliest assist Bruno Fernandes has ever produced
story: It was perhaps the unlikeliest assist Bruno Fernandes has ever produced
MANCHESTER, England -- It was perhaps the unlikeliest assist Bruno Fernandes has ever produced.
But it proved pivotal for the Portuguese playmaker and Manchester United in the Champions League on Wednesday.
With the score 1-1 against Sporting Lisbon, Fernandes unwittingly provided an assist for himself at Estádio José Alvalade.

Chasing the ball down in the second half, Fernandes dug his heel in the turf inside the Sporting penalty area. When the home team failed to play its way out of defense, United managed to turn the ball over and when it came to Fernandes outside the box he let fly with a speculative effort.
His shot lacked any real power and looked like rolling harmlessly into the hands of Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira.
That was until it hit the divot Fernandes had left moments earlier, causing the ball to suddenly shoot up into the air and over the head of Pereira.
United's captain ran away in celebration, with his teammates likely unaware that it was a goal very much of his own making.
The former Sporting icon had also scored from the penalty spot just two minutes earlier.
His two goals put United on the verge of victory until keeper Senne Lammens' late blunder allowed Luis Suárez to equalize to earn Sporting a 2-2 draw.

“Mistakes are part of football, and from that you get goals,” Fernandes told TNT Sports. "But obviously it’s not an individual sport, so everyone has to take the blame for everything we do good and everything we do bad.

“I think the main thing and the most important thing is that we understand that we need to be in this together in the good and the bad moments, and it’s not going to change the belief we have in each other.”

story: Matteo Berrettini and Andrea Vavassori have won a decisive doubles match to help three-time defending champion Italy beat South Korea 2-1 to advance to the semifinals at the Davis Cup Final 8

title: Malen continues scoring streak as Roma ends PSG's winning run with 2-2 draw in Champions League
summary: Roma striker Donyell Malen has continued his prolific scoring form to end Paris Saint-Germain’s winning run
story: Roma striker Donyell Malen has continued his prolific scoring form to end Paris Saint-Germain’s winning run

PARIS -- Roma striker Donyell Malen continued his prolific scoring form to end Paris Saint-Germain's winning run, blasting in a 78th-minute penalty to earn a 2-2 draw at the Champions League title holder on Wednesday.
Coach Luis Enrique's PSG had previously won 12 straight games and not dropped points since losing at home to Monaco on Sept. 4.
Malen hit four goals in a 5-1 win at Parma on Saturday and Serie A's leading scorer caused PSG's defense problems when he came on midway through the second half.

The way he took the penalty underlined his confidence, deploying a two-step run-up before sending goalkeeper Matvei Safonov the wrong way for his 17th goal in 16 games this season, including five in the Champions League.
Referee Glenn Nyberg awarded the penalty after checking VAR and seeing that Vitinha had blocked a shot from left winger Matías Soulé with his arm.
PSG had star forwards Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia  out injured, but Ousmane Dembélé came off the bench to put PSG ahead in the 62nd.
Defender Mario Hermoso scored for Roma early on and central defender Illia Zabarnyi made it 1-1 with a header in the 31st.

title: Krivas scores 31, grabs 17 rebounds as No. 8 Arizona tops Ole Miss 84-73 for Maui Invitational title
summary: Motiejus Krivas scored 31 points and grabbed 17 rebounds, and No. 8 Arizona rallied from a seven-point halftime deficit to defeat Ole Miss 84-73 on Wednesday and win the Maui Invitational championship
story: Motiejus Krivas scored 31 points and grabbed 17 rebounds, and No. 8 Arizona rallied from a seven-point halftime deficit to defeat Ole Miss 84-73 on Wednesday and win the Maui Invitational championship

MAUI, Hawaii -- Motiejus Krivas had 31 points and 17 rebounds to help No. 8 Arizona rally from a seven-point halftime deficit and beat Ole Miss 84-73 on Wednesday and win the Maui Invitational championship.
Krivas shot 11 of 13 from the floor and made nine free throws to lead the Wildcats (7-1), who outscored Ole Miss 51-33 in the second half.
Ivan Kharchenkov finished with 18 points, six rebounds and five assists for Arizona, while Caleb Holt had 14 points and seven rebounds. J.J. Mandaquit added 11 points and five assists.
AJ Clark led Ole Miss (6-1) with 17 points, while Ilias Kamardine, Corey Stephenson and Ben Henshall each scored 12 points. Sebastian Trouet added seven.
The Rebels built a 13-point lead late in the first half before settling for a 40-33 halftime advantage.
Arizona opened the second half by chipping away at the deficit, with Kharchenkov scoring six consecutive points for the Wildcats to pull them within 44-41.

The Wildcats shot 58.3% from the floor, including 68.2% in the second half, and finished 8 of 17 from 3-point range. Kharchenkov accounted for half of Arizona’s 3-pointers, going 4 of 5 from beyond the arc.
The Rebels shot 42.4% from the floor, including 7 of 19 from long distance.
Arizona overcame 16 turnovers that led to 16 points for Ole Miss by outrebounding the Rebels 39-27 and outscoring them 38-32 in the paint.
The Wildcats won their fourth Maui Invitational championship and second under coach Tommy Lloyd.
Arizona: Hosts New Orleans on Tuesday
Ole Miss: Visits Virginia Tech on Tuesday

title: No. 20 LSU moves to 7-0, rallies to beat Arizona State 94-92 in 2OT
summary: Donovan Dent scored 20 points to go with 12 assists, and undefeated and 20th-ranked LSU rallied from a 12-point deficit to beat Arizona State 94-92 in double-overtime on Wednesday in the Acrisure Series
story: Donovan Dent scored 20 points to go with 12 assists, and undefeated and 20th-ranked LSU rallied from a 12-point deficit to beat Arizona State 94-92 in double-overtime on Wednesday in the Acrisure Series

PALM SPRINGS, Calif. -- Donovan Dent scored 20 points to go with 12 assists, and undefeated and 20th-ranked LSU rallied from a 12-point deficit to beat Arizona State 94-92 in double-overtime on Wednesday in the Acrisure Series.
Michael Ruzic's dunk gave LSU a 93-92 lead with 33.3 seconds left. Paulius Murauskas missed a 3-pointer for Arizona State on the ensuing series before Skyy Clark sealed it from the free-throw line.
Ruzic finished with 17 points and 11 rebounds for LSU (7-0). Clark, Mo Dioubate and Abdi Bashir Jr. scored 12 points apiece.
Murauskas scored 27 points but was 0 of 6 from 3-point range for Arizona State (5-1). Joel Foxwell hit six 3s and scored 25 points for the Sun Devils. Dillan Shaw added 19 points and 14 rebounds.

Arizona State led 66-54 but LSU answered with 20-5 run to take its first lead of the second half, 74-71 with 4:15 left. Dent and Dioubate scored four points apiece, and Clark and Bashir each hit a 3 during the stretch.
Murauskas made a pair of free throws to tie it 76-all with 39 seconds to play. Clark missed a 3-pointer on the ensuing possession to force the first overtime.
Foxwell and Shaw scored 14 points apiece as the Sun Devils shot 57% and made seven 3s to build a 43-38 halftime lead. LSU shot 39.5% in the half and made 5 of 10 from long range.
ASU beat LSU in overtime in the 2007 Maui Invitational and the Sun Devils won the third-place game of the 2009 Preseason NIT in the previous matchups between the teams.
The Acrisure Series continues Thursday with Arizona State facing South Carolina and LSU playing SMU.

title: USWNT embarks on Women's World Cup qualification at the CONCACAF W Championship
summary: The pursuit of a fifth Women’s World Cup title begins in earnest for the U.S. national team on Friday
story: The pursuit of a fifth Women’s World Cup title begins in earnest for the U.S. national team on Friday
The pursuit of a fifth Women's World Cup title begins in earnest for the U.S. national team on Friday.
The United States will play El Salvador in the quarterfinals of the CONCACAF W Championship, which serves as the confederation’s qualifying tournament for next year’s World Cup in Brazil.
Win, and the United States is World Cup-bound. And while the world's No. 2-ranked team shouldn't have trouble against No. 78 El Salvador, nothing is guaranteed.

“I’ll be leaning on our experienced players. They know how to do this, and they’ve been with us the longest to be able to deliver that," U.S. coach Emma Hayes said. "And I think the less experienced players have had a good body of work in the last couple of years. So we know what we need to do. We need to just make sure we come into camp with really clear minds about those things. Focus on the only game in front of us.”

The United States has won four World Cups, most recently in 2019. The team had a disappointing finish in the 2023 tournament when they were eliminated in the round of 16 by Sweden. El Salvador has never played in a World Cup.

The United States, the defending W Championship winner, most recently played a pair of matches on home soil against defending World Cup champion Spain, losing the first 2-0 before playing to a 2-2 draw in the second.

But the U.S. squad will be without one of its biggest stars for qualifying. Trinity Rodman was injured in last weekend's National Women's Soccer League championship game. While the team characterized it as a minor shoulder injury, Rodman was replaced on the 23-player roster for the tournament by Jaedyn Shaw.
After El Salvador lost back-to-back matches to Paraguay in the October window, coach Eric Acuna sparked controversy when he publicly disparaged his team and called out individual players.
His comments were condemned by the nation's soccer federation, which said any statement that “discredits, belittles or publicly exposes in a derogatory manner” is unacceptable.
“Wearing the El Salvador jersey deserves respect, both in victory and in difficult times,” the federation's statement said.
All four of the winners from the quarterfinals of the tournament this weekend will earn direct spots in the Women's World Cup.
Jamaica plays Costa Rica in the opening match Friday in Mansfield, Texas, following by the United States' game against El Salvador. Then on Saturday, Canada plays Panama and Mexico meets Haiti.

In addition to a spot in the World Cup, Canada is vying for 2028 Olympic berth. The top three finishers in the W Championship qualify for the Los Angeles Games. Should the United States be among the top finishers, the berth will include the fourth-place team because the U.S. has qualified as host.
Canada's best finish in the World Cup was fourth place in 2003. The team made it to the quarterfinals of the 2015 edition, which Canada hosted.
Ranked No. 9 by FIFA, Canada's squad features Chelsea defender Kadeisha Buchanan and Arsenal striker Olivia Smith. Also included were five players from the domestic Northern Super League.
Panama, ranked No. 45, hopes for a second World Cup appearance. In 2023, the squad was eliminated in the group stage.
The team's top scorer with 23 goals is captain Marta Cox, who plays professionally in Turkey.

The Jamaican squad is ranked No. 40 but features one of the world's most dynamic players in Khadija “Bunny” Shaw, who plays for Manchester City and was one of the three finalists for the Ballon d'Or. Shaw leads the national team with 49 goals in 67 appearances.
The Reggae Girlz have earned berths in the past two World Cups and advanced to the round of 16 in 2023.
Costa Rica, ranked No. 41, made the World Cup field in 2015 and 2023, but were eliminated in the group stage both times. The team was a surprise runner-up in the 2014 CONCACAF W Championship.
Jamaica and Costa Rica will be guaranteed spots as hosts for the 2031 World Cup, along with the United States and Mexico.
Mexico, ranked No. 28 in the world, missed out on the last two World Cups. But the team has been on the rise, in part because of the growth of a domestic professional league, Liga MX Femenil.

Veteran Charlyn Corral, who plays in the domestic league for Pachuca, was recently awarded the Gerd Müller Trophy for best forward and goalscorer at the Ballon d'Or ceremonies. Corral has scored 53 goals in 89 games for Mexico since 2008.

Haiti, ranked No. 48, is led by former U.S. coach Pia Sundhage, who took over in February. The team's first World Cup appearance came in 2023, after upsetting Mexico in the group stage of the 2022 W Championship and then winning a spot via the intercontinental playoff, where they beat Senegal and Chile.

title: No. 2 Virginia beats Marquette 60-54 after 90-minute delay due to a leaky roof in Bahamas
summary: Johann Grunloh scored 14 points, Elijah Gertrude made a key 3-pointer with 2:32 remaining and No. 2 Virginia beat Marquette 60-54 on Wednesday in the opening game of the Battle 4 Atlantis that was delayed for over 90 minutes due to leaky roof at Imperi...
story: Johann Grunloh scored 14 points, Elijah Gertrude made a key 3-pointer with 2:32 remaining and No. 2 Virginia beat Marquette 60-54 on Wednesday in the opening game of the Battle 4 Atlantis that was delayed for over 90 minutes due to leaky roof at Imperi...

NASSAU, Bahamas -- Johann Grunloh scored 14 points, Elijah Gertrude made a key 3-pointer with 2:32 remaining and No. 2 Virginia beat Marquette 60-54 on Wednesday in the opening game of the Battle 4 Atlantis that was delayed for over 90 minutes due to leaky roof at Imperial Arena.

The teams were warming up after halftime before the second half was put on hold as event staff dealt with a leak in the roof at the arena, a converted ballroom that has hosted basketball games and concerts for years at the Atlantis resort.

The 1-hour, 35-minute break did not seem to affect the teams in the opening 3:04 as they combined to score 19 points. But then the teams missed 17 straight shots combined before Grunloh's 3-pointer ending the drought to give Virginia a 38-35 lead with 10:52 left.

Gertrude's 3-pointer from the corner, off a nice drive and pass by Sam Lewis, gave Virginia the only double-digit lead of the second half at 58-48. Lewis also had a putback with 22.2 seconds left to seal it.

Nolan Adekunle added 13 points, and Thijs De Ridder and Lewis each had 10 for Virginia (9-0), which entered averaging 92.4 points per game. De Ridder picked up his fifth foul with 4:49 left in the second half and played just 25 minutes.

Marquette (4-3), in its first appearance at the event, did not have a double-digit scorer until Sananda Fru completed a three-point play with 4:03 remaining to pull within 51-48 and reach 12 individual points. Royce Parham added 11.

Virginia led 25-23 at the break after scoring the final 12 points of the half, capped by back-to-back 3-pointers by De Ridder. Earlier in the half, Marquette scored 16 straight points to take a 21-11 lead with 5:53 remaining, but the Golden Eagles only scored two more points before the break.
Virginia went nearly 10 minutes without scoring in the first half and then had a six-minute drought in the second.
Both teams play their second game at the Battle 4 Atlantis on Friday. Virginia faces Xavier and Marquette plays Texas A&M.
