The controversial plan raised concerns from the public, environmental organizations and medical groups over the potential impacts of the blast's anticipated lead dust plume.
According to the Army's latest guidance, the surface deposition of the explosive material's hazardous dust and materials may cover a 148 square-mile zone outside of the plant.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said in an X post after the explosion that "initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained."
The detonation comes eight months after the Army said it discovered that the explosive bomb-making material had become unstable.

Due to the risks of an accidental, uncontrolled detonation in packing and moving the stockpile, the Army said it determined that the safest way to dispose of the degraded lead azide was to destroy it in place.
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said that months of research determined there was no other way to safely get rid of the barrels.
"Inaction is no longer an option," Shirley said during a press conference on Tuesday.

The Army worked with experts to mitigate the effects of detonating nearly 9,700 pounds of the toxic and volatile substance, including using a waterwall, foam barriers and gel blocks to contain the explosion, according to acting Army Secretary Adam Telle.

Though mitigation efforts will be in place, a public advisory released by the Army on Tuesday recommended that Middletown residents and those in surrounding areas evacuate their homes ahead of the blast "out of an abundance of caution."
Those who evacuate will be updated by phone once the all-clear has been given, the advisory said.

The Environmental Protection Agency will be monitoring levels of lead, a neurotoxin, in the area "for as long as it takes that we have the comfort that the levels are back to safe levels," Tom Croci, the associate administrator for national security and operations coordination at the EPA, told reporters Tuesday.
Lead azide is the primary explosive used to detonate munitions, such as grenades and artillery shells.
The planned detonation of the degraded stockpile was originally scheduled for Friday, but the Army postponed it twice amid public concerns and a legal challenge.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter filed an emergency motion on Thursday arguing that the detonation could spread lead dust across a large area, potentially reaching communities more than 100 miles from the plant.

In an order filed late Thursday night, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted an administrative stay of the permit while the federal appeals court considered the emergency request to formally halt the detonation.
President Donald Trump said Monday that he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this long term problem," but left the decision to the appeals court and incoming Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand.
The federal appeals court ultimately denied the emergency motion and lifted the administrative stay, allowing the operation to proceed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide. However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place," the opinion stated.

The two environmental groups said they would not attempt to further block the detonation following Monday's decision, but pushed the federal government to remain transparent about the operation with the public.
Sand, a Democrat, deferred to the Trump administration on moving forward with the federal operation while also calling for greater transparency.
The governor-elect said in a statement after the blast that he was grateful.
"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," Sand said in an X post Wednesday.

"Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared. There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did. And any Iowans who have been impacted in any way must be taken care of fully, right away," he added.
The Army said Wednesday morning will "allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) activated an emergency response to assist with the Iowa detonation, the agency said Tuesday.

The CDC said it is supporting Iowa's health department to help protect people from potential lead and air pollution exposure, as well as activating a team with expertise in toxicology, communication and public health emergency response.
Ahead of the detonation, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster emergency proclamation for several counties to activate the "disaster response and recovery aspects" of the detonation.
Illinois and Missouri were also bracing for potential impacts, though officials in both states said they expected them to be minimal.

Reynolds' office said Tuesday up to 100 federally activated Iowa National Guard soldiers would assist with evacuation efforts, including outreach to approximately 150 households identified by local and federal authorities.

Federal officials recommended that residents in the impacted area -- in particular pregnant women, children under the age of six and those with a chronic illness -- evacuate due to the potential lead exposure.
Some Middletown residents taped up their windows and garage doors to protect from the blast and dust plume and could be seen evacuating with their families ahead of the planned detonation.
Alec Patterson told ABC News ahead of the detonation that he and his pregnant wife were planning to leave.
"We just want to do everything we can to make sure that she's safe and the baby is safe," he said.
"It's terrifying," Patterson said, adding, "The lead dust stuff is the biggest concern, I think for everybody."
ABC News' Steve Beynon and Mason Leib contributed to this report.

title: Trump admin proposes new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners
summary: A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
story: A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and some European Union countries, marking the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

"We're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on CNBC Wednesday morning.

President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his economic policy, but has suffered significant defeats in court -- including the Supreme Court's move earlier this year to invalidate most of the global tariffs his administration imposed. Tariffs were also a key issue in the midterm elections, during which Republicans suffered major losses as Democrats took back control of both chambers of Congress.

The administration says the new levies would be enforced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, where the U.S. is permitted to respond accordingly if it determines that other countries are participating in unfair trade practices that harm the U.S.

The USTR conducted a series of investigations into countries’ trade practices, announcing on Wednesday that they have determined "the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce." The USTR said its investigations into Norway and Mexico are ongoing.
These proposed tariffs will replace Trump's other levies that the Supreme Court invalidated in their ruling.

A senior administration official clarified that these tariffs are not "blanket" tariffs and that they are "targeted" to each specific country. They are also not expected to stack on top of existing duties, except for China.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tariff on China, but threatened to double it to 40% if China does not abide by the agreed-upon trade truce as talks continue, according to a senior administration official. The new tariffs would be added on top of preexisting 25% forced tech transfer tariffs.
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun reacted to the news of the proposed tariffs in a press conference on Wednesday.

"Our position on handling China-U.S. economic and trade issues is consistent and clear. Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests. Relevant issues should be resolved through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit," Jiakun said.
This comes just a week after Trump visited China for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

China is among the several countries that have objected to tariffs under the Trump administration. A senior administration official said all of the countries have been informed of these new proposed tariffs, including China, and added that they do not expect retaliatory action.

There is no immediate impact of this announcement as a public comment period would be required to first take place, with the administration eyeing January as the earliest target date to fulfill such requirements.

"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now," Greer said on CNBC.
Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden said in a statement that the proposed tariffs are "not the solution."

"Only weeks after Americans overwhelmingly voted against his high tariffs and higher prices agenda, he’s back with another round. This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses," Wyden, a Democrat, said.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, blasted the proposed tariffs.

"The bad actor here is China, and instead of addressing the problem, Trump continues to let them dictate the terms while alienating our allies and passing the costs onto American families, with little benefit for American workers," he wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.
Separately, the U.S. is also considering modifying Brazil tariffs by increasing taxes on sugar and aircraft products.
"Today’s proposed modification would provide greater leverage to obtain the elimination of Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices," Greer said in a statement on Wednesday.

Greer's statement argued that imposing an "additional, specific tariff” on Brazil sugar imports as well as a 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports “is intended to help bring Brazil to the table" over what the U.S. perceives to be trade practice violations.
That action also would not be immediate, as the USTR says it will hold a hearing about Brazil's proposed tariff changes on Jan. 14.

title: Iran live updates: Trump says war 'funded' through January, Houthis claim new attacks
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: Trump said regime change in Tehran was "never a criteria" for U.S. success.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines
7:02 AM ESTHouthis claim fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia2:55 AM ESTTrump says Iran war 'funded' through JanuaryNov 24, 2026, 11:49 AM ESTUS investigating whether Iran is behind tanker cyberattacks
7:02 AM ESTHouthis claim fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia
2:55 AM ESTTrump says Iran war 'funded' through January
Nov 24, 2026, 11:49 AM ESTUS investigating whether Iran is behind tanker cyberattacks
Renewed Yemen fighting displaces 364,000, UN official says

Renewed fighting in Yemen's civil war has forced more than 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands over the past week, the United Nations' humanitarian chief said in a statement Wednesday after he arrived in the port city of Aden in the south of the country.

"Fighting, insecurity and heavy restrictions along key supply routes are preventing families from accessing the food and medicine they need to survive," UN Under Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher said, noting that half of Yemen's population needs aid. "Millions are hungry," he added.
Fletcher also called on the Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release our detained UN colleagues and other humanitarians."
"Our work and our people must be protected," he said.

Since 2014, Yemen's internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government -- now based in Aden -- has been fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis, which occupy the capital Sana'a. The conflict has become a widening front in the regional war involving Iran that began in February.
-ABC News' Morgan Winsor
Houthis claim fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia
A military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said on Wednesday that the group launched new strikes targeting the financial district in Riyadh and a key Saudi oil refinery.
In a video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the operation against the financial district in Riyadh "caused extensive damage."
The Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province was also targeted, causing "fires to break out there," Saree said.
Early on Wednesday morning, a Saudi military spokesman said four drones had been intercepted in Ras Tanura and "a number of fragments fell as a result of the interception, with no casualties."
Satellite images showed black smoke above the Ras Tanura oil refinery on Wednesday.
-ABC News' Nasser Atta and Othon Leyva
Trump says Iran war 'funded' through January
President Donald Trump said the ongoing war with Iran is "funded" through January, when Democrats take control of Congress and could reign in his authority to authorize the conflict.
In an interview with the New York Post conducted in the Oval Office on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said the incoming Democratic majority will "take a total win and make it a loss."

Trump again touted the U.S. military success against Iran. "Their navy's gone, their air force is gone, their anti-aircraft, everything's gone. Their leaders are gone. I mean, if [Democrats] do that, they'll just take a win and make it a loss," Trump said.
When pressed on whether his timeframe to freely launch renewed strikes is narrowing, Trump reportedly said he finds it "hard to believe" that Democrats would stop the war.
"I don't know how they could do that politically, because we have a win. We can put that war to bed anytime we want," Trump said, according to the Post.

Israel's goal of ending the Islamic Republic is "probably doable," Trump also said, but told the Post that regime change is not his goal. "I just don't want them to have a nuclear weapon. I was never for or against regime change, that was never a criteria for me," Trump said.
Trump also addressed an Iranian announcement this week that it would be suing the U.S. for compensation for an airstrike on a school.

"Well, I want compensation for the people that they've killed, which is far more because they've killed, first of all, they killed 75,000 protesters in the last seven months. But they've killed our people for years," Trump replied, according to the Post.
"The USS Cole, they've killed many, many hundreds of Americans. So if they want to play the compensation game, we win," the president said.
-ABC News' Isabella Murray
US investigating whether Iran is behind tanker cyberattacks
The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is behind a series of cyberattacks that targeted energy tankers, according to multiple officials.
At least 50 ships are believed to have been attacked, with some receiving bomb threats that purported to say the ship was to be detonated.
The U.S. has identified Iran as the prime suspect, but are also investigating whether Russia could also be the suspect. The threats are believed to scare boats into not traversing overseas.
The Coast Guard has helped thwart all of the cyber attacks, according to officials.
They've also posted a warning on their website telling tankers to patch their systems, prior to a cyber event occurring.

"Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterway," according to a Coast Guard spokesperson.
Earlier this year, two boats headed to Texas were boarded by U.S. Coast Guard teams after it was discovered that cyber incidents occurred onboard.

title: Treasury's financial crimes agency says it's investigating 'cybersecurity incident'
summary: The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes.
story: The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," and has taken some systems offline as a precaution, according to an alert posted on its site.
The agency handles sensitive information and reports about financial crimes including money laundering, trafficking and terrorism financing.
The agency posted an alert on the site where banks and financial institutions can report suspicious activities.
"As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline," the alert read. "The BSA E-Filing website remains operational; however, some services may be temporarily unavailable."
ABC News has reached out for comment.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Melania Trump reunites seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children with families
summary: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families
story: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families

WASHINGTON -- First lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of kids in these wartime reunifications to 43, the White House announced Wednesday.

It's the latest example of the first lady taking modest yet tangible interventions to address Russia's war in Ukraine, which started nearly five years ago. Her husband, President Donald Trump, had vowed to broker a quick end to the conflict but has said it's been harder than he expected.

“Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war," the first lady said in a statement shared first with The Associated Press.
“As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately," she said.

Melania Trump said the reunification of these nine children with their families took place with the “full cooperation” of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. No additional information about the children was made available.
The first lady has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
The work began in August 2025, when she had the Republican president hand-deliver a letter that called for peace in Ukraine to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska.

After a year, she had helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives after they had been separated because of the war, and she has said she has a “direct channel” with the leaders of the warring countries.

Then in October, she helped negotiate a six-day ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Earlier this month, she hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to mark that milestone.

The local ceasefire in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During the pause in the war, some 800 people were able to leave the city while food, water and other humanitarian aid were delivered to help those who stayed.
Follow the AP's coverage of first lady Melania Trump at https://apnews.com/hub/melania-trump.

title: 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization'
summary: A D.C. magistrate judge has issued a scathing written order ripping the Trump administration for what he described as the blatant "weaponization" of law enforcement.
story: Judge Zia Faruqui blasted charges that were brought in the Hunter Biden probe.

The D.C. magistrate judge who earlier this month dismissed a criminal case against two former FBI agents accused of lying to Congress about past investigations of Hunter Biden issued a scathing written order Tuesday again ripping the Trump administration for what he described as the blatant "weaponization" of federal law enforcement powers.

"For years, the administration has treated the weaponization of law enforcement like a horror movie villain coming for them. Now the threat is finally real," Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said. "Only the call is coming from inside the house -- the White House."

In a hearing two days before the midterm elections, Faruqui ruled that the criminal complaint prosecutors brought against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides failed to establish probable cause that they purposely misled Congress -- an unusual move given the low evidentiary bar required.

"What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," Faruqui said in the hearing, which he used to summarize testimony about the high-level interventions by senior DOJ officials and FBI Director Kash Patel in pushing for the case.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In Tuesday's written ruling summarizing his decision, Faruqui described the case as just one among a series of politicized prosecutions brought by the D.C. U.S. attorney's office during the second Trump administration.

"This case is not a one-off mistake. This court has seen a line of botched, politicized cases where the government has rushed to charge cases, only to have them fall apart," Judge Faruqui wrote. "The Department of Justice still lists 'Independence and Impartiality' first among its values, stating it 'work[s] each day to earn the public's trust by following the facts and the law wherever they may lead, without prejudice or improper influence.' This prosecution is a betrayal of these values."

"The slapdash prosecution of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides in response to a public command from the President demonstrates a lack of independence and impartiality from the political desires of the Administration," Faruqui said. "Moreover, the rampant errors and misstatements stemming from the slapdash nature of this investigation and prosecution further undercuts public confidence in the work of the Department of Justice."

"If a high-profile case like this is so poorly executed, what can the public expect in the run-of-the-mill case with far less resources and oversight? The erosion of public confidence in the Department of Justice further harms public safety," the judge wrote.

title: Groups push back on Trump administration changes to historical monument
summary: Two Philadelphia groups filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration over the removal of panels at the slavery memorial at the President’s House site.
story: The site is where President George Washington lived and enslaved nine people.
Two Philadelphia groups filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration over the removal of the interpretative panels at the slavery memorial at the historic President's House site.

The memorial marks the site is where President George Washington lived for most of his presidency -- from 1790 to 1797 -- and where he enslaved nine people. It was born out of a community campaign and established in 2010 to tell their stories.

The lawsuit was filed on Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania by Avenging the Ancestors Coalition (ATAC) -- a group that fought for years for the memorial to be established -- and The Black Journey, which runs the African American Walking Tour of Philadelphia.

"Right now is where we fight the good fight. What you have here is based on mythology. What you have here is based on half-truth," ATAC founder Michael Coard said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit. "What you have here is based on lies and nothing but lies."

The lawsuit names the National Park Service, the Department of the Interior (which oversees NPS), Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and acting NPS Director Jessie Bowron as defendants. Neither the Interior Department nor NPS immediately responded to ABC News' requests for comment.

Coard, who reflected on his years-long battle to fight for this memorial in a July interview with ABC News, accused the Trump administration of attempting to sanitize the brutality of slavery and downplaying the Founding Father's role in it.

He pointed to language contained in the new panels that focuses on Washington's "discomfort" with slavery and language that suggests people enslaved at the President's House received more favorable treatment than those enslaved elsewhere.

The complaint argues that the removal of the panels and the changes at the memorial that were made by the Trump administration violate the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act.

"NPS's actions are part of a coordinated effort by the Trump administration, not only to distort the past and manufacture an alternative narrative of the history of the United States, but also to disparage and denigrate the stories and history of Black people in this country," the lawsuit alleges.
This is the second federal lawsuit that was filed seeking to stop the Trump administration from making changes to the interpretive materials at the memorial.

The first lawsuit, filed by the city of Philadelphia and backed by Coard's group, was ultimately unsuccessful after a federal appeals court in July cleared the way for the Trump administration to replace the exhibit panels.

The Interior Department claimed that the content was "divisive" and "disparages" Washington. The court determined that the new panels installed by the Trump administration at the site were historically "accurate."

The White House did not provide specific examples of panels that they took issue with, but appeared to dispute the focus and tone of the exhibit. President Donald Trump asserted in the past on social media that institutions "across the country" focus too much on "how bad slavery was," instead of focusing about the "success" and "brightness" of the country.
The changes at the slavery memorials stem from orders outlined in Trump's March 2025 executive order, "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History."
The order called for the removal of "negative" and "divisive" materials from national parks and content that "disparages" Americans, living or dead.
"What we want to make sure we do is to restore the truth," Coard said. "What [President Trump] has done at this site created a dangerous precedent."

title: Trump awards Medal of Freedom to former NYC Mayor Rudy Giuliani
summary: Trump pardoned Giuliani last year.
story: Trump pardoned Giuliani last year.
President Donald Trump awarded the Medal of Freedom to former Mayor of New York City Rudy Giuliani at the White House on Tuesday.
Giuliani said in a statement after the ceremony that he was "honored and humbled" to receive the Medal of Freedom from Trump.

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit,'" Giuliani wrote. "I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me -- particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together."
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said that Trump recognized Giuliani with the highest civilian honor for his "lifetime of service to the American people."

Wales described Giuliani as a "dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," going on to reference his efforts to root out crime in New York City and his leadership in the aftermath of 9/11.
The White House press pool was not invited to cover the ceremony.
Following the White House event, Giuliani’s son, Andrew Giuliani, briefly addressed reporters on the White House North Lawn, saying his father’s Medal of Freedom ceremony was "incredibly special."
"To see your father receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom is an unbelievable honor. It’s tough to describe," Andrew Giuliani said.
Last year, Trump announced his plans to present Giuliani with the Medal of Freedom, after Giuliani suffered injuries in a car accident.

"As President of the United States of America, I am pleased to announce that Rudy Giuliani, the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot, will receive THE PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM, our Country’s highest civilian honor," Trump said on Sept. 1, 2025.
Trump pardoned Giuliani last year for his alleged involvement in attempts to overturn the 2020 election.

Giuliani served as the president’s personal lawyer and was disbarred in two jurisdictions in 2024 over "false and misleading" statements on the 2020 election. Voting machine company Dominion settled its $1.3 billion defamation lawsuit against Giuliani over false allegations surrounding the 2020 presidential election.
Trump's pardon was largely symbolic as Giuliani -- along with others Trump pardoned at the time -- were not facing federal charges, and Trump does not have the ability to pardon states charges.

In his second term, Trump posthumously awarded the Medal of Freedom to conservative activist Charlie Kirk and 9/11 hero Welles Crowther. He has also announced plans to present the award to neurosurgeon and former Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Ben Carson, Team USA Hockey goalie Connor Hellebuyck, and baseball player Roger Clemens, a White House official confirmed.

title: Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of last year
summary: President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
story: His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.

His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.

"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia, saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC.
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S&P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation.
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.

title: Trump granted new chance to potentially erase his hush money case
summary: An appeals court is giving President Trump a new chance to move his criminal hush money case into federal court, where he could then attempt to overturn his conviction.
story: Trump is seeking to move the criminal case into federal court.

A federal appeals court is giving President Donald Trump a new chance to move his criminal hush money case into federal court, where he could then attempt to overturn his conviction on grounds of presidential immunity.

The late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein decided in August that Trump could not move the case into federal court, two years after a jury in Manhattan convicted him on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to a hush payment to adult actress Stormy Daniels.
On Monday, a three-judge panel of the Second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals disagreed.

"First, the district court erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case after a federal officer defendant has been convicted," the panel said. "Second, the district court erred in holding that Defendant-Appellant failed to show 'good cause' to justify granting him leave to file a second notice of removal."
The ruling allows Trump, for a third time, to argue the hush money case rightfully belongs in federal court, where he would be able to argue he is immune from prosecution.
Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, previously decided that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity."

The appellate court's two-page ruling asked that "no further proceedings occur in the state courts" while Trump's petition is pending, effectively pausing Trump's traditional appeal of his conviction through the state appellate courts.

In May 2024, in between his two presidential terms, Trump became the first president in American history to be criminally convicted after Manhattan prosecutors alleged that he engaged in a "scheme" to boost his chances during the 2016 presidential election through a series of hush money payments to Daniels, then falsified New York business records to cover up that alleged criminal conduct. He denied all wrongdoing.

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, he was sentenced to an unconditional discharge and later made his lead defense attorney from the trial, Todd Blanche, the attorney general of the United States.

title: They want to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan die but the Army won’t let them
summary: Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in gunfire at Fort Hood in 2009. 'It's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she said.
story: The Army is limiting witnesses to victims' survivors and those who were wounded.

Julia Wilson was nine months pregnant when she found herself caught in the gunfire at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. She had just returned from lunch and was shutting off her truck when she heard gunshots and watched a soldier nearby collapse after being struck by a bullet.

A civilian human resources employee at the base, Wilson repeatedly sounded her truck alarm, hoping to distract the gunman from shooting her colleagues, and called 911. As she ducked across the seats of her truck, she counted at least a dozen bullets flying in her direction.
"'I'm never going to see the face of my child. I'm never gonna hold him' -- it's crazy how quickly things run through your brain," she told ABC News.
She and her baby were unharmed.

Now, 17 years later, Wilson wants to witness the execution of the man who could have killed her. But the Pentagon has denied her request to attend the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 31 others. Nidal is set to die by firing squad at the same Army base where he carried out the attack.

Wilson is among multiple survivors of the massacre who say the Pentagon has denied their requests to witness Hasan's execution, despite assurances that victims and their families would be permitted to attend. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at one time said it would be livestreamed, though that plan was overturned by President Donald Trump.

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, who was then an Army major, opened fire inside a medical processing building at Fort Hood in a rampage he described as a jihad in protest of U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Dozens of other soldiers and civilian employees, including Wilson, Dr. Kathy Platoni and Dr. C. Alan Hopewell, were caught in the attack.

All three had hoped to attend the execution, saying they wanted to be there for the friends and colleagues they lost and that watching the Army carry out Nidal's sentence might bring them some measure of relief after 17 years.

Though none were struck by gunfire, all three witnessed the attack firsthand and said they continue to live with its psychological toll. They say that they are appealing the Army's decision to Department of Defense officials and raising the issue with lawmakers.
The Defense Department did not respond to ABC News' questions about who is allowed to attend.

Wilson called the Army's decision an "institutional betrayal," arguing that its interpretation of its rules effectively dismisses the trauma experienced by those who survived the shooting but weren't hit by gunfire.

The Army's rules on who can witness an execution are relatively broad. They outline that prison staff, the condemned prisoner's attorney and family, and victims of the crimes that led to the death sentence may attend. Hasan was convicted of numerous charges of murder, premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

But the regulations also give the Army discretion to invite additional witnesses, including victims who might not meet the narrower definition of victims. Army rules also require the presence of at least two journalists, effectively as third-party witnesses, a common practice in civilian executions.
Army officials cited security concerns and limited space at the execution site in restricting attendance, correspondence reviewed by ABC News shows.
"The fact that I don't meet the category doesn't change the reality of what I experienced with my unborn child," Wilson said. "I continue to hear the screaming and smell the blood."

Platoni, a retired Army colonel and former chief psychologist for the Army Reserve, was undergoing routine medical processing ahead of a deployment to Afghanistan in an adjacent building when Hasan opened fire. She said she had never met Hasan but would have been his supervisor in Afghanistan.

Military bases can be heavily guarded at their gates while remaining relatively open once someone is inside, particularly someone in uniform. Troops carrying out ordinary duties outside combat zones do not carry weapons. Security falls largely to military and civilian police, who patrol installations.

Platoni, who tended to the wounded in the aftermath of the attack, argued that the Army is applying an unnecessarily narrow interpretation of its own regulations, which authorize victims of offenses punishable by death, including attempted offenses, to witness an execution.
"I've never been this angry in my life that they're doing this to us and telling us we weren't victims because we didn't take a bullet to the brain," she said.
Hopewell, then an Army major who oversaw the outpatient psychiatry clinic at Fort Hood and was Hasan's supervisor, was inside the facility when Hasan tried to force his way in during the shooting.
Armed with an FN-5.7 pistol equipped with a laser sight and a 20-round magazine and carrying a .357 Magnum revolver as a backup, Hasan moved through the halls, shouting for doors to be opened.
Hopewell and his colleagues had barricaded themselves inside a room just before Hasan reached them. Unable to force his way in, he screamed in frustration, Hopewell recalled.
"I was about two feet away from him when he was trying to smash into my clinic to kill me," Hopewell said. "You can't go through something like this and have it not affect you."

Hopewell said he was initially ambivalent about witnessing Hasan's final moments. But Sgt. Kimberly Munley, who was shot three times, asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution. Hopewell had received communications from Army officials inviting him to attend but they subsequently rescinded that invitation.
"Since I was one of the senior officers, I feel it's my duty to represent the families and the victims and my clinic staff," Hopewell said.

For Platoni, attending the execution is not just about watching Hasan die but also supporting the people who survived his attack and the families who lost loved ones. Five soldiers in her unit were killed in the shooting and she still wears a hero bracelet that bears their names to commemorate them.

"It would mean that I could be there to support my fellow soldiers that were wounded and did survive. It would mean that I might be able to, as I did during the court martial, be there to support the families, and I want to witness this so that I know he's gone from the Earth," she said. "So I want to see justice served in some way. But all we've encountered is injustices, one after the other."
All three survivors say they have struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder since the shooting.

Wilson described years of living with a heightened sense of danger, even in otherwise ordinary situations. She said that she has grappled with depression and struggled to hold down a job due to difficulty with concentrating.
"You're constantly looking over your shoulder. You're constantly scanning for threats," Wilson said.

The decision to exclude them from Hasan's execution has compounded a longstanding frustration among the three survivors, who say the Pentagon has repeatedly failed to support those whose lives were upended by the massacre.
For Wilson, witnessing the execution would offer a "smithereen of closure and justice," after 17 years. She said she wants Hasan to see her one final time and recognize that she survived his attack.

"I need him to read from my eyes that you tried to victimize me, but I survived you, and you have destroyed my life and many other people's lives," she said. "And maybe, just maybe, with you ending here -- maybe my life might be able to start somewhat again."

title: Airline glitches, storms could make for a messy Thanksgiving travel week
summary: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday
story: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.
No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.
“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said.
As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s mid-section, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day and reach Maine by Friday, he said.

The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).
The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.
“This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”

Rainy and windy weather also was expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.
Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state and northwestern Pennsylvania.

“Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
summary: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding
story: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.”
It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.”
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency's abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.”
Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said.

title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
summary: The Trump administration has given SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space
story: The Trump administration has given SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk’s rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million “orbital compute modules” (forming a data center constellation called “Starmind”) would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing “the full power of the sun.”

“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move “opens a bold new frontier.”

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least “one authorized space station” by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers “a fantasy."
“It’s not going to happen,” he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun’s energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are “basic physical limits” to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.
He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

“You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions,” said Becker, noting such crashes could create “a cloud of debris” in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a “substantial number” of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites “serves the public interest” — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and “the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.”

“The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that “these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky.”
Becker echoed that sentiment. “It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye,” he said.
Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’ requests for further comment Wednesday.

title: Trump heads to Arizona next week for a high-stakes expansion of TSMC's computer chip factories
summary: President Donald Trump plans to visit Arizona next week to speak at the groundbreaking of a new computer chip foundry for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The company has been expanding aggressively in the Phoenix area, manufacturing chips for ma...
story: President Donald Trump plans to visit Arizona next week to speak at the groundbreaking of a new computer chip foundry for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. The company has been expanding aggressively in the Phoenix area, manufacturing chips for ma...

WEST PALM BEACH, Florida -- President Donald Trump, who has staked his economic policy on growth in the artificial intelligence sector, will travel to Arizona on Dec. 4 to speak at the groundbreaking for a new Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. computer chip foundry, according to both the White House and the Taiwan-based company.

The trip will come at the end of a week where AI comes under the microscope in Washington in the aftermath of Trump intervening to get his ally Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. Huang is slated to testify at a Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3 and will face questions about how his company has been selling its chips abroad — and his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Beijing has denied it.

TSMC has expanded aggressively in the Phoenix, Arizona, area, using its U.S. facilities to manufacture chips for tech companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, and Qualcomm. Trump is attending the start of construction on the fifth phase of TSMC's expansion in Arizona.
TSMC in July announced plans to spend another $100 billion on expanding its manufacturing capacity in the United States, bringing its total pledged investment in American chipmaking to $265 billion.

The size of the investment has grown as the development of artificial intelligence has stimulated demand for more computer chips, at the same time as Taiwan's dominance in chipmaking has led countries including the U.S. to address supply chain vulnerabilities by producing more domestically.

While Trump has sought to promote the investments as a function of his tariffs, the company began construction in Arizona during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden. The bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by Biden, also helped to provide some financial support for the project.

The White House said the expansion would enable the creation of 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the wider community. The site currently accounts for more than 12,000 construction jobs.

title: Vance says Jensen Huang won't need a pardon as scrutiny of Nvidia scandal builds in Washington
summary: Vice President JD Vance is downplaying the possibility that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could need a pardon from President Donald Trump
story: Vice President JD Vance is downplaying the possibility that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could need a pardon from President Donald Trump

WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio -- Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday played down the possibility that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could need a presidential pardon just days before the executive of the AI giant is expected to appear before a congressional committee.

Vance told reporters that Justice Department officials and “multiple officials in our national security apparatus” have confirmed that Huang is “under no investigation.” The vice president made the remarks after having a Thanksgiving Eve meal with troops at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

The Nvidia CEO resigned earlier this month after acknowledging extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. He was reinstated 11 days later at the urging of President Donald Trump.

“I don’t think he needs a pardon at all,” Vance said. “I haven’t seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that’s up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him.”
The comments from Vance came after Trump told the New York Post on Tuesday that pardoning Huang is “always an option,” but that he did not think it would be necessary.

Trump also told the Post he doesn't want Huang to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights under the U.S. Constitution to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution when he appears before lawmakers. Pleading the Fifth allows a person to refuse to answer questions or provide testimonial evidence if doing so could reasonably expose them to criminal prosecution.

Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview with a trio of panels on Dec. 1, including the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs committees, and the Select Committee on China. Then on Dec. 3, Huang is expected to appear at a public hearing of the Senate Banking Committee.
The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.
Nvidia and the White House are also facing scrutiny about Trump's relationship with Huang, a close adviser to the president on artificial intelligence issues.

The president has repeatedly welcomed Huang to the White House and earlier this year invited him aboard Air Force One for a state visit to China. The New York Times has reported that Trump had previously been briefed on intelligence concerns about the Nvidia CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. U.S. officials suspected that she was working with China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has denied it.

Congressional staffers from the House and Senate Intelligence Committees and representing chamber leaders received a classified briefing on Tuesday about the matter from intelligence officials, according to two people familiar with the matter who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Officials from the CIA, FBI, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence were among those on hand for the briefing, one of the people said.
“We don’t try people in the court of public opinion. We don’t try people based on anonymously sourced stories in the New York Times, we try people based on evidence,” Vance told reporters.
Trump, meanwhile, has taken credit for pressing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said that his administration assured the company's officials that Huang did not present a national security risk.

The president has staked the nation’s economic growth on artificial intelligence, and worried Huang’s ouster was tanking the stock market. Trump also saw Huang's ouster as risking putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for dominance in the field if Huang, widely seen by backers and critics as a generational talent in AI, were to be poached by a Chinese firm.

The president earlier this week said Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were among administration officials he enlisted to make the case to Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang.

White House officials deemed Vance, who worked in Silicon Valley before jumping into politics, as having the stature to serve as an effective emissary in helping Nvidia board members overcome their reservations, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Madhani reported from Washington. AP writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

title: King tides, strong waves destroy part of Pacifica pier as officials warn of flooding
summary: King tides combined with powerful waves have destroyed part of a pier in Northern California
story: King tides combined with powerful waves have destroyed part of a pier in Northern California

SAN FRANCISCO -- SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — King tides combined with powerful waves destroyed part of a pier in Northern California on Wednesday, and officials warned more beachfront homes are at risk of flooding.

A video showed a massive wave tearing down a portion of the pier in the city of Pacifica and slamming it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped, 1,140 feet-long (350 meters-long) pier in the summer after finding cracks in the structure.
Beachfront homes in the city south of San Francisco began flooding this week as king tides, the highest tides of the year, arrived in the area.

North of San Francisco, Marin County officials issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach, saying large waves expected through the afternoon could send water and debris into roads and homes.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Pacific Coast and bay shorelines along San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay through 4 p.m. Wednesday. It also issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area for Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 meters), about two to three stories high, could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.
“Rising tides will bring water and waves farther up the beach than normal, restricting escape from beaches and coastal area,” the weather service said.

King tides occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.
High tides have already flooded several communities this week along California’s coast.

In the Bay Area, some homes and streets in the coastal Marin County cities of Mill Valley, Larkspur, Sausalito and Corte Madera flooded. Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff’s office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where most of the buildings flooded.

title: FACT FOCUS: Maps online falsely claim to show the path of fallout from Iowa lead azide detonation
summary: Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout from the Army's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa have spread on social media
story: Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout from the Army's controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa have spread on social media
Maps falsely claiming to show the projected fallout of a controlled detonation of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday spread widely on social media in advance of the blast.

One showed lead dust spreading throughout the Midwest and Southeast. Another had it reaching Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan and Ohio. In a third, the contamination enveloped the entire East Coast and in another it expanded in all directions, moving as far south as New Orleans and north toward Montana.

But none of these maps are accurate. The U.S. Army, which conducted the blast, released updated maps early Wednesday morning that include a much more contained area. They predicted that winds would blow the plume, potentially containing toxic lead dust, southwest from the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and into nearby Missouri.
Here's a closer look at the facts.
CLAIM: Toxic lead dust from a controlled detonation of lead azide will spread far beyond Iowa and Missouri, according to maps of the projected fallout.

THE FACTS: This is false. Official maps published by the U.S. Army projected the plume heading from southwest Iowa as far as northern Missouri. In some cases, social media users misrepresented maps that showed unrelated data.

Those in charge of the detonation called it a success. All of the lead azide was successfully destroyed, said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who led the Army operation. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency air monitors detected no lead in the air around the ammunition plant in Middletown, about 200 miles (300 kilometers) west of Chicago.

Still, it’s unclear yet whether the plume carried any toxic lead toward the homes and farms in its path. Lead is a heavy metal that’s not safe at any level and is especially dangerous to children and pregnant women. Government agencies plan to do more testing in the days and weeks ahead. Independent researchers also intend to do extensive environmental testing on water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds.

One map misrepresented on social media shows the Midwest with colored bands expanding from an orange center on the border of Missouri and Illinois. It has nothing to do with the lead azide detonation. The map, which was created with the College of DuPage's weather prediction modeling tool, shows snowfall accumulation predicted for Friday. It is labeled as such in the top-left corner.

On another map, skinny blue lines cover states in many different regions. But the lines represent Mississippi River tributaries, not the path of the plume. A map published by the EPA shows a similar tributary structure, as does one from the conservation nonprofit American Rivers.

The Army took steps to mitigate the spread of the plume. The hazardous materials were surrounded by concrete and sand barriers two stories high. Additional “blast barriers” were set up around the two bunkers where the 68 barrels of lead azide were detonated. Ballistic gels, foams and more than 100,000 gallons (380,000 liters) of water were intended to absorb the lead dust. A video of the site released by the Army before the detonation showed a bunker encased by an earth berm and sand-filled blocks.

Following two loud booms around 9 a.m. local time, a pair of wispy white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating, according to an Associated Press report. The Army attributed the smoke to the foam.

Environmental groups had filed a lawsuit to halt the detonation, but a court ruling on Monday put it back on track. A federal appeals court found the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.
Find AP Fact Checks here: https://apnews.com/APFactCheck.

title: Nvidia CEO's comeback fuels debate over misogyny and impunity for the rich and powerful
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's reinstatement despite allegations of misconduct is raising concerns about a culture of impunity for the rich and powerful
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's reinstatement despite allegations of misconduct is raising concerns about a culture of impunity for the rich and powerful

NEW YORK -- Just over a year ago, the chief executive officer of an Ohio tech company was forced to resign when he was caught on video embracing an employee at a Coldplay concert. The CEO of McDonald's was among several pushed out over a consensual relationship at the height of the #MeToo movement.
Now the stunning reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang despite similar allegations of sexual misconduct is fueling fears of a resurgence of impunity for the rich and powerful.

Huang resigned from Nvidia after he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and following reports that he was involved with a second woman who was his subordinate. Huang has acknowledged that he violated the company's code of conduct, which warns against personal relationships that may create conflicts of interest.

But in an extraordinary turnaround following a pressure campaign from Huang's tech allies and President Donald Trump, Nvidia's board voted unanimously Monday to reinstate him. The board said it had received assurances from the U.S. government that Huang was not a national security concern, but there was no mention of the sexual misconduct allegations at the center of the scandal.
Trump, however, did address Huang’s personal conduct
The president, who has a history of marital infidelity and has faced allegations of sexual assault he says are false, predicted the scandal would only help Huang's reputation.
“Sex sells, fellas,” Trump declared in an interview on CNBC.

He also posted a doctored image of Huang raising a red bra in triumph, a pose that parodied a famous photograph of Trump himself moments after he survived a 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request by The Associated Press for comment Wednesday.

Trump’s response reinforces the impression “that there is a class of men who see violence against women, coercion of women as a currency of power,” said Cheyenne Hunt, an attorney who founded the advocacy group Reckoning Action after her role in bringing to light the sexual assault allegations that brought down Democratic Sen. Eric Swalwell and Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner.
“This sends a horrible message to men everywhere that it's open season on their direct reports,” Hunt said.

Randall Peterson, a professor of organizational behavior at the London Business School, said the #MeToo movement had reinforced the idea that company leaders who engage in relationships with subordinates “are in serious trouble because you cannot rule out coercion. You just cannot.”
Peterson said the messaging now is that “you are at risk, as in the days before #MeToo.”
“I’m sad about that,” he said. “I thought we had moved on from that.”

Huang, for his part, apologized to his employees a day after returning to Nvidia, saying he had made mistakes and was in daily therapy, according to a livestreamed meeting reviewed by The New York Times. He also warned that his reinstatement didn't mean other employees could violate the company's code of conduct, saying that “sometimes, it’s appropriate to forgive” and “sometimes it’s not.”

He also addressed a report by The Times about his management style that included publicly berating and threatening violence against employees. He acknowledged he had sometimes gone too far and promised that the company’s human resources department would henceforth collect feedback about his conduct.
The saga, however, has “made very clear that Huang is untouchable,” said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado Boulder law professor who specializes in corporate and securities law.
“It suggests that if you’ve had a certain amount of success, then you should be able to get away with pretty much whatever you want,” Lipton said.
That’s especially true in the male-dominated tech industry, she added, citing Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg’s comment last year that corporate culture needed more “masculine energy.”
The Nvidia scandal has brought scrutiny to the independence of its 10-member board and a corporate culture centered around hero-worshiping its celebrity CEO.

Thousands of people, including former and current employees, had signed a petition calling for Huang's return. Nvidia's collapsing stock had fueled fears that the AI bubble would pop and, for Huang supporters, bolstered their argument that his vision, connections and deal-making skills were indispensable to the entire industry.

Nvidia's shares rocketed up 31.5% upon his reinstatement on Monday — although they have since fallen — and employees chanted Huang’s name as he returned to headquarters. The company did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

Freada Kapor Klein, an investor and activist in equity and access issues around tech, said Nvidia and other successful tech startups “become cult-like. And people get addicted almost to being part of this inside powerful club."

While America has a history of industries idolizing big names like Henry Ford or Andrew Carnegie, tech culture adds to that by “glorifying geniuses. And so there is something extra special about technological prowess, more than or on top of just business success,” Klein said.

Women make up just 21% of Nvidia’s global workforce and an even smaller share of its managers and leaders, according to the company’s latest sustainability report, which touts its efforts to achieve gender pay parity as well as establish employee resource groups for women and other groups, and family-supporting policies such as generous paid parental leave.
The company's code of conduct, meanwhile, says employees “must report” suspected violations and offers extensive guidelines and reassurances about protection against retaliation.

Huang's triumphant return, however, is exactly the sort of outcome that silences victims of sexual misconduct, said Fatima Goss Graves, president and CEO of the National Women’s Law Center, which runs the Time’s Up Legal Defense Fund, a program to support workers facing sexual harassment.

Still, she said the legacy of the #MeToo movement continues to inspire women to speak out about sexual harassment and misconduct, adding that public scandals like the one at Nvidia sometimes provoke outrage that leads to an uptick in complaints to Time's Up and other organizations.

Goss Graves noted that on the same day Huang was reinstated, Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California resigned from Congress after the House Ethics Committee released a report finding “substantial evidence” that he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer and subjected the staffer to unwanted sexual contact, the latest in a string of lawmakers or candidates brought down by misconduct allegations in recent months.
Meanwhile, Trump’s role in getting Huang’s job back drew immediate bipartisan fire and the CEO is expected to testify next week before the Senate Banking Committee.
“What comes next really matters," Goss Graves said. "If everybody shrugs their shoulders and says some people are too important to be held accountable, then we will have a problem.”
