title: Judge halts order for Georgia's Fulton County to give 2020 election records to state election board
summary: A judge has paused an order for Georgia's Fulton County to hand over digital copies of ballots and other records from the 2020 election to the State Election Board
story: A judge has paused an order for Georgia's Fulton County to hand over digital copies of ballots and other records from the 2020 election to the State Election Board

ATLANTA -- A judge on Wednesday put on hold an order instructing Georgia's Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other records from the 2020 election that were seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board.

Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe on Tuesday had ordered county election officials to deliver the records to the board by 5 p.m. Wednesday. But after county election officials filed a notice of appeal, she granted the county's request to halt her order while the appeal is pending.

The FBI served a search warrant at the Fulton County elections hub on Jan. 28 seeking records related to the 2020 election, leaving with hundreds of boxes containing ballots and other records. The county unsuccessfully sought to have a judge order the return of the records, but the federal government did provide the county with what it said was a digital copy of the records that were taken.

A majority of the State Election Board aligned with President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to reopen a case alleging wrongdoing by Fulton County during the 2020 election. The board in November 2024 served subpoenas on the county seeking records related to that election.

The overwhelmingly Democratic county, which includes most of the city of Atlanta, has been a target of Trump and his allies since he narrowly lost the presidential election in Georgia to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. Trump has insisted without evidence that widespread voter fraud in the county cost him victory in the state. Multiple courts and state and federal officials have found no evidence of fraud that would have altered the outcome.

County election officials asked a judge to quash the subpoenas from the State Election Board. Fulton County Superior Court Judge Robert McBurney in December 2025 declined, finding that the board's inquiries “fell squarely within the SEB’s authority.” He ruled that the state board would have to bear the costs of producing the records it was seeking, and a hearing on that matter was pending when the FBI seized the county’s records. As a result of the seizure, McBurney put the case on hold.
Ellerbe, who took over the case this year, held a hearing on the matter in October before issuing her order Tuesday.

title: A timeline of key events in Kilmar Ábrego García's fight with the Trump administration
summary: Kilmar Ábrego García has been a focal point in the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies
story: Kilmar Ábrego García has been a focal point in the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies

Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.

In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Here is a timeline of key events:
Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.
Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.
Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.
The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.
In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.
Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.
ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.

Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.
Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.
A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.
A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.
A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution."
The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.

Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.
Ábrego García lands at Madrid’s international airport. He doesn't speak to reporters but raises a fist as he enters a van.

title: What's closed on Thanksgiving and when stores reopen on Black Friday
summary: Thanksgiving is for diet busters
story: Thanksgiving is for diet busters
Thanksgiving is for diet busters. Black Friday is for doorbusters.
Most big U.S. retailers will be closed on Thanksgiving Day. But they plan to open early the following day, Black Friday, as the holiday gift-buying season shifts into high gear.
Here are the holiday schedules for selected services and stores on Thursday and Friday:
Federal government offices, post offices and courts are closed on Thanksgiving but open the following day.

The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are closed Thursday. Both reopen on Friday for a shortened trading day, wrapping up at 1 p.m. EST. Banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, said local branches will be closed on Thanksgiving but ATMs and mobile banking will be available. Banks reopen on Friday.

Standard FedEx and UPS pickup and delivery services will not be available on Thanksgiving, although some critical services will be offered at certain locations. Both FedEx and UPS will operate as usual on Friday.

Check local grocery store listings online. Many major supermarket chains, including Kroger, Albertsons, Safeway and Sprouts, have reduced Thanksgiving Day hours. Whole Foods also will be open but individual locations may close early. All Trader Joe’s, Aldi and Publix stores will be closed. Hy-Vee will be open from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m. only for customers picking up premade holiday meals.
Walmart will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Target will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Dollar General stores in most states will be open on Thanksgiving from 7 a.m. – 8 p.m.
Costco will be closed on Thanksgiving but will reopen on Friday. Executive members get in starting at 9 a.m. Doors open to other members at 10 a.m.
Best Buy will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will open at 6 a.m. on Friday.
Macy’s will be closed on Thanksgiving but stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. on Friday.
Kohl’s will be closed on Thanksgiving but will be open from 5 a.m. to midnight on Friday.

Walgreens said its nearly 8,000 stores will be open on Thanksgiving, with pharmacies operating in about half. Most locations will be open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and 24-hour locations will remain open around the clock.

title: US travelers facing long airport lines, bad weather in the run up to Thanksgiving
summary: Thanksgiving travel is in full swing, with airline and road traffic ramping up across the U.S. But travelers in many spots are facing weather challenges, including rain on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section and coastal flooding in the West
story: Thanksgiving travel is in full swing, with airline and road traffic ramping up across the U.S. But travelers in many spots are facing weather challenges, including rain on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section and coastal flooding in the West

Airline and road traffic are ramping up even more on the eve of Thanksgiving on one of the busiest travel days in the U.S., with rain storms expected on the East Coast, snow in the nation's mid-section, coastal flooding in the West and lingering worries about technology failures.

Travelers at some airports took to social media to report long security-check lines on Wednesday morning. Some of the longest wait times were 81 minutes at Miami International Airport and around 40 minutes at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey and Portland International Airport in Oregon, according to the Transportation Security Administration.
The TSA expected to screen about 17.6 million passengers between Tuesday and Monday.

Terri Zimmerman said she waited in the security line at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport for nearly an hour early Wednesday morning before boarding a flight to Tallahassee to see relatives for the holiday.

“I was just surprised when we walked in to see that kind of line,” said Zimmerman, 71, a retiree from Deerfield Beach, Florida. "It was 5 a.m. in the morning. I thought we’d be like the first flight out and there wouldn’t be anybody there, but the place was packed.”
Zimmerman and scores of other South Florida travelers trudged through heavy rains that sparked concerns about more flooding in the Sunshine State.

AAA projected that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) between Tuesday and Monday, including nearly 73 million on the roads and nearly 6 million in the air. Another 2.6 million people were expected to take buses, trains and cruises.
The flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 31 flight cancelations and more than 1,100 delays in the U.S. on Wednesday morning.

For Tracy VanLeuven Miller, an early morning flight out of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Atlanta did the trick Wednesday. It was the first time she had ever flown to see family for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. She sailed through baggage check and the TSA in less than 10 minutes, adding online, “Now I’m ready for a Mimosa!”

“As a military spouse (now retired), my family always traveled by car due to affordability,” she told The Associated Press via social media. “I decided to try air travel this year after a long, grueling road trip last year from northern Virginia to Atlanta. Since I’m traveling solo this year, I decided to fly, using points to absorb some of the crazy expensive plane ticket.”
For people on the road, bad weather was shaping up to be a challenge in parts of the country.

A major storm developing along the Eastern Seaboard could bring heavy rain, coastal flooding, high winds and power outages to the Carolinas on Wednesday and the northern Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving, the National Weather Service said. Wind gusts could hit 50 mph (80 kph) along the Interstate 95 corridor. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.
Heavy rain was falling Wednesday morning in parts of Florida, the Carolinas, Mississippi and western Washington state.
Winter storm warnings and watches were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois, with up to 9 inches (23 centimeters) of snow expected in the St. Louis area.
And king tides were continuing on the West Coast, with coastal flood warnings issued from Southern California to the San Francisco area to the Oregon and Washington coasts.

Travelers were also hoping to avoid new tech and system failures like the ones that upended airlines this month, including the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years caused by a Federal Aviation Administration network malfunction. Within the past week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed.

title: What is lead azide? A look at the chemical being detonated at an Iowa Army base
summary: The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide at an Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
story: The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide at an Iowa Army Ammunition Plant
The U.S. Army has detonated a dangerous and degraded stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday.
Here's what to know about lead azide, and why local officials and scientists have some concerns about potential health and environmental effects from the explosion.
Lead azide, which typically appears as a white or colorless crystalline powder or needlelike crystals, is a highly sensitive chemical compound containing lead and nitrogen.
The compound is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, and historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives, such as TNT.
It is sensitive to shock, heat, impact and friction, and may explode when dry. With temperature changes and time, lead azide can form unstable, larger crystals that are even more sensitive.
The decades-old lead azide supply in Iowa was crystallizing, posing the risk of spontaneous detonation.
Broken down, lead is a toxic heavy metal that can harm the brain, nervous system, kidneys, heart and other organs. Lead exposure also causes developmental damage.

As lead exposure can pose both immediate risks and longer health and environmental hazards, officials and researchers are questioning the levels of lead that might be in the air and nearby land and water sources, impacting residents, crops, cattle and wildlife after the detonation.
The military stopped using lead azide in the 1980s because of its hazards.
The Army says safety preparations ahead of Wednesday's detonation included barriers around the blast zone to reduce the spread of the resulting plume, along with ballistic gels to absorb lead dust.
Alexa St. John is an Associated Press climate reporter. Follow her on X: @alexa_stjohn. Reach her at ast.john@ap.org.

title: Vance is set to serve up turkey to Air Force troops at an Ohio base pitched as Space Academy home
summary: Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are planning to visit Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio
story: Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are planning to visit Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio

DAYTON, Ohio -- DAYTON, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children are visiting Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, where they plan to serve a Thanksgiving meal to troops on Wednesday and join them for lunch.

The family plans to spend the holiday in the state, Vance's office said. The base in southwest Ohio is about 60 miles (97 kilometers) from their home in Cincinnati and close to where Vance was born. In tow for the trip: Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; Mirabel, 4; and four-month-old Alec.

The visit comes just days after Ohio’s congressional delegation, led by Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, a friend and former Senate colleague of Vance, made a push for the Trump administration to locate the U.S. Space Academy close to the technologically advanced Wright-Patterson complex.

"What West Point is to the Army and Annapolis is to the Navy, Wright Field should be to the United States Space Force,” Moreno wrote in a letter co-signed by GOP Sen. Jon Husted and all 15 of Ohio’s U.S. representatives.

title: Inflation remains uncomfortably high despite a retreat in gas prices as challenges mount for the Fed
summary: A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington
story: A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington
WASHINGTON -- A key inflation gauge remained high last month even as gas prices cooled in a sign that elevated costs remain a challenge for the Federal Reserve and elected officials in Washington.

The Commerce Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. On a monthly basis, consumer prices climbed 0.3% from September to October, down from a 0.6% increase the previous month.

The stubbornly elevated price figures come as the economy is expanding at a healthy pace, driven by strong consumer spending and surging business investment as large tech firms splurge on building out AI infrastructure. Consumer spending has been resilient even as persistent inflation raises the costs of many necessities and has soured most Americans on the economy. Yet much of the spending is driven by upper-income households, and there are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending.

Gas prices rose just 0.8% last month, according to the department, after surging 9.2% in September. Food prices, however, jumped 0.4% from September to October, the biggest monthly increase since April.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core inflation accelerated to 3.3% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.1% in September. On a monthly basis, core prices rose 0.3% for the third month in a row.

The yearly core figure is now at its highest level in three years and above the Fed's target of 2%, which will likely intensify concerns among Fed officials that inflation is getting worse and further rate hikes are necessary.

Also Wednesday, the government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3% annual rate, the fastest in three years.
Consumer spending jumped 4.2% in the third quarter, while business investment soared 16.1%, lifted by big gains in spending on equipment and intellectual property products such as software.

“Taken together, the data reinforce the Fed’s latest assessment that growth in economic activity is ‘strong,’ meaning more must be done to bring inflation down,” Bradley Saunders, an economist at Capital Economics, a consulting firm, wrote.

The Fed combats inflation by lifting its key interest rate, which over time can raise borrowing costs for cars, homes and credit cards. By discouraging borrowing and spending, the Fed seeks to cool the economy and inflation.

Many officials have signaled that they support raising the Fed's short-term rate, and economists expect an increase at its next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Solid economic growth and still-high inflation suggest that the Fed's key rate isn't yet high enough to cool price increases.
In October, the government also reported that incomes jumped 0.7%, before adjusting for inflation, a healthy gain after prices rose faster than incomes in the previous month.

In another report, the number of people applying for unemployment benefits dropped 13,000 to just 189,000, a very low figure by historical standards and evidence that layoffs are low and companies are mostly holding onto their workers.

title: US plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
summary: President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
story: President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.

The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.

The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
Like China, Vietnam also faces a 20% rate, pending finalization of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday. The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10% to 18%.

The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

China has pushed back consistently on U.S. tariffs. On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. “The so-called overcapacity is a false narrative, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”

The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
AP writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: As GLP-1 use grows, patients and doctors rethink Thanksgiving dinner
summary: Thanksgiving can be a challenge for those on weight loss medications like GLP-1s, but it doesn't have to derail progress
story: Thanksgiving can be a challenge for those on weight loss medications like GLP-1s, but it doesn't have to derail progress

WASHINGTON -- For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed weight loss medications known as GLP-1s, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1s. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

“I can’t sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I’ll still be able to sample everything, but I just can’t overdo it,” said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1s, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans’ approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1s part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1s will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan, suggests the over-indulgence associated with the holiday could diminish over time.
“I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Some people who use GLP-1s feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.
Doctors say people who are just starting their weight loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

“Thanksgiving doesn’t have to be off-limits,” said John Horlander, a Louisville, Kentucky, gastroenterologist. “The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated and recognizing warning signs.
"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday.”

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1s as “a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic.” More than 100 million American adults are obese, according to the latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.
In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight loss drugs Zepbound and Wegovy.

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1s as a result of the Trump administration’s actions. The agency wants to expand access to GLP-1 treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years — 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June 2026. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from two years ago.

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.
Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.
“We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other’s eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating “usually isn’t a great relationship strengthener,” she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.
Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, “Is that all you’re going to eat?”
“Leave that phrase off the table. We’ve spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy,” she said.
Babak Orandi, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health, said, “There’s a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don’t want to lose that.”
Patients, Orandi said, should focus “a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance” during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last four years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.
But as someone who has been on a weight loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.
“We still have to eat," she said. "Just don’t worry about it so much.”

title: Melania Trump reunites seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children with families
summary: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families
story: The White House says Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families

WASHINGTON -- First lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of kids in these wartime reunifications to 43, the White House announced Wednesday.

It's the latest example of the first lady taking modest yet tangible interventions to address Russia's war in Ukraine, which started nearly five years ago. Her husband, President Donald Trump, had vowed to broker a quick end to the conflict but has said it's been harder than he expected.

“Children in this region of the world, like children everywhere, cannot possibly understand why geography and government have put them into the horrors of war," the first lady said in a statement shared first with The Associated Press.
“As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately," she said.

Melania Trump said the reunification of these nine children with their families took place with the “full cooperation” of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. No additional information about the children was made available.
The first lady has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
The work began in August 2025, when she had the Republican president hand-deliver a letter that called for peace in Ukraine to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska.

After a year, she had helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives after they had been separated because of the war, and she has said she has a “direct channel” with the leaders of the warring countries.

Then in October, she helped negotiate a six-day ceasefire for the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Earlier this month, she hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House to mark that milestone.

The local ceasefire in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During the pause in the war, some 800 people were able to leave the city while food, water and other humanitarian aid were delivered to help those who stayed.
Follow the AP's coverage of first lady Melania Trump at https://apnews.com/hub/melania-trump.

title: Pentagon hires conservative contractors to audit military base schools
summary: The Defense Department continues to revamp its schools for military families to align with conservative education ideals
story: The Defense Department continues to revamp its schools for military families to align with conservative education ideals

WASHINGTON -- The Defense Department is continuing to revamp the schools it operates for military families to meet conservative education ideals — auditing curriculum and policies in all schools and piloting a so-called “classical” physical education course at two U.S. campuses.

The Department of Defense Education Activity operates about 160 schools across 11 countries, educating roughly 70,000 students who are children of active-duty military or civilian service members. Under the leadership of Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has sought to use the schools as models for the broader Republican education agenda. Those goals include restrictions on instruction about race and gender, along with an emphasis on patriotic values and classical learning.
Now, the agency has begun issuing contracts to companies well-connected to conservative ideals, with no outside competition.

In October, the department approved a contract for a curriculum audit, saying it was complying with an executive order from President Donald Trump aimed at limiting how schools teach about race and gender. It awarded the $5.7 million contract to American Education Solutions, without seeking other bids. The firm was founded by Jordan Adams, whose past work involved consulting with conservative-led school boards in Pennsylvania and Texas to overhaul curriculum.

Separately, the department awarded a contract for just over $100,000 to Iliad Athletics to pilot a classical physical education program. Classical education broadly focuses on critical thinking, citizenship and, often, writers from ancient Greece, Rome and other Western civilizations. Inspired by traditional Greek athletics, the P.E. course will include running, jumping, climbing, carrying and throwing, Iliad Athletics said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense Education Activity said the agency regularly reviews its academic programs and makes improvements. The audit will review "curriculum, instruction, and professional learning, helping ensure these areas remain rigorous, effective, and aligned with the needs of students and educators,” the department said in a statement.

But two employees of the Pentagon's education division, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution, said a system-wide review by a consultant is without precedent. Typically, schools work with a national accreditor to evaluate and develop standards for subjects.

On its website, American Education Solutions advertises a curriculum adoption, analysis and development service. It criticizes curricula used in American schools, saying they are “content-light, employ pedagogical practices not supported by the science of learning, and eschew the patriotic civic role of public education.”
The company also offers an audit to ensure schools “Do No Harm."

“The intellectual and character formation of children is a serious responsibility for school systems,” the website says. “As with medicine, the first requirement is to do no harm — both pedagogically and with respect to parents as first educators. AES reviews school systems to ensure this is the case.”
In a statement, the Pentagon lauded the approach, saying it “preserves effective practices while identifying opportunities for thoughtful improvement."
AES did not respond to questions and said the company does not “share work for past, current or pending clients without authorization.”

The new classical P.E. course will be offered at LeJeune High School in North Carolina and Quantico Middle High School in Virginia. In a statement announcing the partnership with the military, Iliad Athletics described the course as focused on functional physical fitness rather than introducing students to sports.
In addition to physical activity, the course includes a “character development program," which highlights a weekly virtue and gives examples of historical figures who lived it out.
As with the auditing contract, Iliad's hire did not involve competitive bids. Instead, the Pentagon said the company was the only one that could meet its requirements at the time.
Patrick Whalen, CEO of Iliad Athletics, said in an email he was not aware of any other programs like the one the company offers.
In a statement, a Pentagon official said no company receives preferential treatment.

“The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity,” the statement said. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

Hegseth has a longtime interest in classical education, especially in a version of the teaching style that incorporates Christian history and virtues. As defense secretary, he has pushed to advance those views.

U.S. military academies now accept the Classic Learning Test, a college entrance exam that positions itself as a classical alternative to the SAT. In September, defense schools announced they would give 100 vouchers to students to take the CLT. This month, the agency announced the test would be widely available to students as a college readiness assessment.

This summer, schools operated by the department announced they would begin offering a new online course on Western Civilization, using a text that some scholars said presents a misleading portrait of historical events. In particular, the book often portrays Western civilization and Christianity as one and the same, and it selectively highlights details to frame Islam as a violent threat to both.

The course's textbook includes suggested lesson plans developed in partnership with Hillsdale College, a conservative Christian school in Michigan that has also developed influential materials for K-12 schools.
The new Pentagon contractors have ties to Hillsdale, too.

Adams, the consultant, graduated from Hillsdale and worked in K-12 curriculum development for the college, including on the Trump-aligned 1776 Project, a free curriculum for schools that was created in response to what the college described as “the weaponization of history.” The content has been criticized for downplaying slavery and for describing the Jamestown colony as a failed communist project.
Whalen, the Iliad Athletics CEO, previously worked in the college president’s office.

Along with the curriculum changes, leadership at the military's education system has also been overhauled. The schools are now led by Matthew Kirby, who was promoted from his former position as the system's Americas regional director. Kirby is the founder and former CEO of Liberty Classical Schools, an Atlanta-based network of charter schools.

Early in Trump's second administration, Defense schools also removed books from libraries that covered topics like race, gender and democracy. The ACLU filed a lawsuit and was partially successful in overturning the book bans at a handful of schools.

The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org.

title: The US Army will be detonating a 5-ton stockpile of lead azide in Iowa. Here's what to know
summary: The U.S. Army says it's taking numerous precautions as it prepares to detonate 5 tons of degraded and dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa
story: The U.S. Army says it's taking numerous precautions as it prepares to detonate 5 tons of degraded and dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa

The U.S. Army is planning to detonate 5 tons of degraded and dangerous lead azide in southeastern Iowa Wednesday in what military officials say is an unprecedented effort to prevent a spontaneous, uncontrolled explosion at the site.

While authorities say a host of safety measures will be in place to limit the plume of lead particles that will drift from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, public concerns remain about the potential health and environmental effects.

The Army says the lead azide, which is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, is degrading. Crystallization inside the containers increases the risk of an explosion as the outside temperature changes, especially when it's below freezing.
The ammunition plant is in Middletown, not far from the Mississippi River and the Illinois and Missouri state lines.
Here's what to know about the planned explosion:

Lead azide is a highly sensitive compound including lead and nitrogen that historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives. The military moved away from using lead azide because of its hazards and officials have said it is no longer needed for munitions production.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can harm the brain, nervous system and other organs.

Production of lead azide increased sharply during the Vietnam era, especially for use in gravel mines, according to the Army's emergency application to detonate the Iowa stockpiles. Mass production began declining in the early 1980s and eventually ceased, the application said.
The 68 barrels of lead azide set for detonation in Iowa, transferred there in 2009 from an Army facility in Texas, are the nation’s entire stockpile of the compound, the Army said.

Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, said in a court filing that the Army will use a combination of C-4 explosives, explosive charges and diesel fuel to blow up the stockpile. The diesel will be used to enhance the consumption of the lead azide, and the charges are intended to direct the blast effects downward, Teller said.
The lead azide is stored at the Iowa site in reinforced structures, known as magazines.
The Army and other federal agencies placed sand barriers about two stories high around the magazines along with walls consisting of four 16,000-gallon (60,000-liter) water tanks.

Special screening to contain the lead has been installed. A 2-foot (61-centimeter) layer of foam that will flood the area is meant to dissipate the blast and capture particles that blow off the stockpiles, Army officials said. The ground above and surrounding the storage magazines will be saturated with water before and during the detonation to reduce particle dispersal.

The Army planned extensive drone surveillance of lead levels before and after the detonation to see if the levels rise and to identify areas that may need cleanup. Officials expect to contain most of the blast particles at the site.
During the last lead azide detonation by the Army in Colorado in 1977, no mitigation measures were used and 75% of the lead particulate remained at the site, officials said.
The plume likely will head southwest and away from nearby Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people.
Wednesday's forecast for the area calls for winds of 5 to 10 mph (8 to 16 kph), blowing to the southwest, according to the National Weather Service.

There were no mandatory evacuations as of Tuesday. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said it is supporting the recommended relocation of all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding areas beginning Tuesday.

The recommended evacuation zone is a 5-mile (8-kilometer) cone that extends southwest of the Iowa plant. An emergency notification sent to cellphones Tuesday morning told people up to 20 miles (32 kilometers) away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration.”

Government officials said support will be provided to people who choose to leave the area, including transportation, short-term lodging and food, water and other supplies. People who evacuate will be notified when it's safe to return.

Environmentalists who sued last week to stop the detonation said in court filings that there is no safe exposure level for lead, which is especially harmful to children. Lead has been shown to permanently damage children's brains and development.
They said lead also is harmful to adults and has been linked to heart, kidney and liver disease as well as reproductive harm, cognitive decline and cancer.
The environmentalists said the Army's own modeling showed that a large amount of farmland in the area as well as waterways could be contaminated with lead dust from the detonation.

“Once lead dust is dispersed, there is no undoing the harm,” one filing stated. “Lead persists in the environment and spreads easily between media. Lead dust in the air will not just disappear once it settles to the ground—people, cattle, chickens and wildlife will continue to face exposures to lead from soil, water runoff, and deposition into waterbodies.”
Federal officials said they are taking precautions to keep people safe. Recommendations include cleaning outdoor surfaces, including areas children have touched.

“The team overseeing this operation conducted extensive safety and environmental reviews, analyzed potential blast impacts, practiced the planned detonation procedures, and put safety zones, monitoring systems, and emergency-response plans in place,” the Army said.

title: Inside Rikers Island as jail staff cooks 6,000 lbs. of turkey for Thanksgiving
summary: Workers at New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail are cooking thousands of pounds of turkey to serve to inmates for Thanksgiving
story: Workers at New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail are cooking thousands of pounds of turkey to serve to inmates for Thanksgiving
NEW YORK -- How do you cook more than 6,000 pounds of turkey in time for Thanksgiving at one of the nation’s largest jails? Get a few days' head start and plenty of ovens.

Preparations began in earnest at New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail earlier this week as batches of turkey roasts were loaded into tall ovens lined up in a cavernous, industrial-grade kitchen.

Julet Thompson Pitt, a senior cook, was among the staff switching gears to Thanksgiving preparations Monday morning as soon as the day’s lunches were finished and sent off to housing units across the more than 400-acre complex. The kitchen staff turns out more than 20,000 meals per day.
“It’s always a joyous time for us, as you can see, everyone puts the effort in to get it done,” she said as she launched into a flurry of activity.

Thompson Pitt worked her way down a line of 10-pound boneless roasts, generously slathering each with a dark marinade of spices, including dried sage, thyme, garlic and onion powder mixed with browning sauce.
The seasoned meat slabs are then loaded on tray carts and placed in a fridge for about a day to soak up the flavor before going into an oven, she said.
Thompson Pitt opened one of the tall ovens and revealed a batch of finished roasts, their skins lightly browned after cooking for about three hours.
The turkeys are then set out to cool before being transferred back to a walk-in fridge to await slicing.

On the other side of the ovens, just past a row of massive, stainless steel caldrons, another set of cooks were using deli-style meat slicers to carve the turkey meat into the tender slabs, taking care to set aside any scraps and juices in a large bin nearby.
“That’s what we use to make the gravy,” Thompson Pitt said. “There’s no turkey without a gravy.”

The essential sauce is one of the few things that will be cooked on the holiday itself, she said. The turkey and other meal components will mostly be finished by Wednesday, as many of the staffers will be off on Thanksgiving.
On Thursday, each inmate will be apportioned 4 ounces of meat — roughly a slice or two, according to dietitian Christinne Caylan-Linstromberg.
They’ll also get a serving of familiar Thanksgiving fixings — green beans, yams, stuffing and cranberry sauce — as well as a slice of carrot cake for dessert.

For those with other dietary needs, there are options, including a plant-based protein for vegetarians and a kosher pound cake, she added. All told, the staff will make about 10,000 Thanksgiving lunches.
Some might begrudge inmates being given such niceties, especially at Rikers, which has been plagued for years by violence, overcrowding and mismanagement.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced last week a sweeping plan to shutter the antiquated jail by 2032 — 100 years after it first opened — as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027. The jail currently houses about 6,700 people, most of them awaiting trial or serving out shorter sentences.

But Capt. Marc Allen Lorquet, a veteran corrections officer who oversees kitchen operations, says a familiar meal — along with time watching some of the day’s football games on TV — goes a long way in maintaining order in the unruly lockup.

“Thanksgiving is like the one day on the calendar they look forward to,” he said. “It’s one of the easier days to work because everybody gets what they’re supposed to. So securitywise, it’s definitely a benefit to have.”
Jessus Bailey, an inmate who works in the kitchen, said he didn’t expect a holiday meal as he awaits trial on multiple counts of robbery.
“This is a new experience for me,” he said. “I’m definitely gonna enjoy this meal. This is my first time away from my family.”
Like other inmates on kitchen detail, the 44-year-old is focused on cleaning duties and doesn’t do any cooking, which is reserved for the staff.
“It’s pretty hard work, but I enjoy it. I get to learn different things,” Bailey said. “I learned how to work a buffer. I learned how to properly clean the kettles and really sanitize a kitchen.”
As for Thompson Pitt, she’ll be with family for the holiday.
But the native of Jamaica, who has worked at Rikers for 11 years, won’t be cooking, and it certainly won’t be turkey that’s served by her mom, she said.
“All this turkey?” Thompson Pitt said. “I’m done looking at turkey.”

title: Alaska ends voter data agreement with Justice Department, which had been searching for noncitizens
summary: A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections says she has ended an agreement in which the state shared its detailed voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for removal
story: A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections says she has ended an agreement in which the state shared its detailed voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for removal

JUNEAU, Alaska -- A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections said she has ended an agreement under which the state shared its voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for possible removal.

No voters were removed as a result of the agreement signed last December, and the Justice Department since then had not identified “any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the office of outgoing Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said.

Dahlstrom said she notified the Justice Department that Alaska was terminating the agreement, effective Monday. That's also when Alaska officials announced that the results of the Nov. 3 general election, in which Democrats flipped a U.S. Senate seat and the governor's office, had been certified.

The Alaska Division of Elections directed the department to destroy the confidential voter information the state provided, Dahlstrom's office said in a statement released late Monday. A Justice Department spokesperson on Tuesday said the agency would send a formal response to the state.

The federal government's demand for detailed state voter information was part of a broader effort throughout the midterm election cycle to promote the idea that scores of noncitizens were on state voter rolls and potentially casting ballots illegally. In fact, years of research, state investigations and the Justice Department's own record of arrests showed the issue to be extremely rare.

The Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for not complying with its demands to provide detailed voter registration data or other election-related records, with 28 of those lawsuits dismissed by courts, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. The department entered a settlement agreement with Oklahoma and dismissed its case with that state, the group said.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states to provide voter lists that included information such as driver’s license and partial Social Security numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Alaska and Texas also signed data-sharing agreements with the Justice Department, in which it outlined plans for its own analysis of voter files, its plans to flag voter list issues and directions for removing voters deemed ineligible.

Voting and civil rights groups sued Alaska elections officials earlier this year, alleging that sharing the state’s full voter registration list violated the Alaska Constitution and that terms of the agreement violated due process rights. That case is still pending.
ACLU Voting Rights Project, one of the organizations involved in representing the groups, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dahlstrom said the Division of Elections “entered the agreement in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners as permitted under Alaska law. The circumstances have now changed, the election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”

She said Alaska "has strong list-maintenance procedures and will continue to protect both the accuracy of its voter rolls and the rights of eligible Alaska voters.” Her office said terminating the agreement “does not constitute an acknowledgment of wrongdoing by the Division of Elections."

Alaska state Sen. Bill Wielechowski, a Democrat and critic of the state's decision to hand over voter information, said Tuesday he believed the motivation for ending the agreement was to try to “make the lawsuit go away” before the administration of Alaska’s new governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, “could settle or produce discovery.”
He said he wants Kreiss-Tomkins’ administration to look into the circumstances surrounding the decision. Wielechowski also questioned the impact of the demand to delete the records.
Kreiss-Tomkins and his lieutenant governor, independent Zac Johnson, take office Dec. 7.
