title: Records: Government, judge debated constitutional implications of searching Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
summary: A magistrate judge who authorized a search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents has ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search
story: A magistrate judge who authorized a search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents has ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search

WASHINGTON -- A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar 's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday.

The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress’ private residence for a criminal investigation.

The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated.

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the “Speech or Debate Clause” implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures.
Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.
“That logic does not hold,” the magistrate wrote.

Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any Speech or Debate Clause material before agents carried out the search.

Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. She hasn’t been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing.

Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the Oct. 12 search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. He ruled after over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to access the records.

Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government’s investigation. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.
An attorney for Omar didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.
Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.

title: Pacific Coast king tides could break decades-old records and flood communities
summary: High tides along the Pacific Coast could break records and flood low-lying areas, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week
story: High tides along the Pacific Coast could break records and flood low-lying areas, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week
SAN FRANCISCO -- High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach 2.6 feet (0.8 meters) above normal Tuesday before peaking Wednesday at 2.8 feet (0.9 meters) above normal, said Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.

The Bay Area’s highest recorded tide reached 2.9 feet (0.9 meters) above normal in San Francisco on Jan. 27, 1983, he said. San Francisco's famed Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded during heavy rain last week, is again at risk of flooding.

King tides, the highest tides of the year, occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.
The weather service issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area on Wednesday, when breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 meters) could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.
“Remain out of the water and stay off of jetties, piers, and rocks. Never turn your back to the ocean!” the agency said in a social media post.
Heavy rain forecast for Tuesday evening into Wednesday could worsen street flooding.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, who urged people over the weekend to consider avoiding holiday travel because of an “extremely serious” situation, later said the forecast had improved somewhat.

“As you make plans for Thanksgiving, keep the weather in mind. Check conditions before traveling, and avoid unnecessary trips when roads are flooded or winds are strong,” he wrote on social media on Monday.

Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff’s office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where some buildings flooded on Monday, saying people needed to leave by Tuesday morning.

“The tides are expected to be higher by Tuesday, and the southerly winds will have been blowing for 24 hours by then, and so that will push the storm surge even higher,” said Matthew Kidwell, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Humboldt County.

National Weather Service offices in Portland and Seattle warned of coastal flooding through Friday. The most significant flooding could occur Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day as several weather systems bring strong winds and rising surf coinciding with high tides.
Waves can sweep people off rocks or knock them off their feet and pull them into the ocean, the agency warned.

Washington State Ferries has canceled several sailings because of high tides. About 300,000 people are expected to use the ferry system over the holiday weekend, and extreme tides could disrupt their trips.
Heavy snow in the mountains could slow holiday travel over passes, especially along Interstate 90 east of Seattle.

In South Florida, king tides are expected to cause coastal flooding from Palm Beach to Miami. Water levels could remain elevated for several hours before and after high tide Wednesday and Thursday mornings.
A storm arriving Tuesday night could increase the risk of flooding if it moves over land, the National Weather Service said.
Many South Florida communities were just beginning to dry out after slow-moving storms dumped more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) of rain less than a week earlier.

The St. Johns River has been above flood stage near Cocoa since Nov. 2. Last week, it broke a record set in 1953. The river is forecast to remain at least 2 feet (0.6 meters) above flood stage, according to the weather service.
Associated Press writers Martha Bellisle in Seattle and John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia, contributed.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO’s 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.

“Canada is also on track to meet NATO’s new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal,” he said in a statement.
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.

The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO’s 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.

The criticism follows a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts U.S. military officials’ participation in Canadian think tank and social events. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

Wesley Wark, a Canadian national security expert and former government adviser, titled his Monday newsletter “Pentagon Pete strikes again,” calling the criticism “insulting and infuriating.” He suggested Washington was discounting Canada’s NATO deployment in Latvia and its support for Ukraine.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby paused a U.S.-Canada defense advisory board established in 1940, accusing Ottawa of failing to make credible progress on its military commitments.
The Pentagon said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%.

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. His government plans to buy up to 12 replacements.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new 5% target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.”

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025. The forum’s president, Peter Van Praagh, previously served as a senior adviser to a Conservative government in Canada.

Before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Van Praagh warned that Trump might undermine the results if Republicans suffered major losses. If those efforts succeeded, he said, it would mean “the end of the United States as we know it.”
Speaking at the Halifax forum Saturday, Rounds said Hegseth’s directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.

title: How to make holiday travel less of an expensive hassle and get home safely
summary: The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start
story: The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start
The busiest week of the year for U.S. travel is getting off to a bumpy start.

Technology failures — including one earlier this month that led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years — are rattling air travelers. Bad weather is swirling around San Francisco and the East Coast.
“You start to get a little anxious,” said Debra Birnbaum, a journalist who lives in Los Angeles.
Birnbaum grew up in New York and planned to fly there Tuesday for Thanksgiving. She said she’s not an alarmist, but she still doesn’t feel like she fully understands the reasons for the ground stop.
“I wish the government had done a better job of explaining what happened and why,” she said. “If I could drive, I would drive.”

But driving has its own hassles. While gas prices have fallen over the last two months, Monday's national average of $3.64 per gallon for regular gasoline was still 18.5% higher than last year, according to AAA. Diesel, at $5.82 per gallon, was 54% higher than a year ago.
Here are some tips for easing travel headaches over the holiday season:
Motor club AAA predicted that 81.5 million people will travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) from home between Tuesday and the Monday after Thanksgiving. Ninety percent of them will travel by car.

Inrix, a transportation data provider, said that Tuesday and Wednesday would likely be the busiest days on U.S. roads, while next Sunday and Monday are busy as people return home. Major metro areas like New York, Washington, Los Angeles and Boston could see more than double their normal traffic congestion, Inrix said.

Motorists should consider hitting the road in the morning to avoid the heaviest congestion, Inrix said. The worst times for traffic will be in the afternoon and early evening, the company said. Another option, if time permits, is driving on Thanksgiving Day, when congestion is expected to be minimal.

U.S. gasoline prices are close to the Thanksgiving record of $3.56 per gallon, which was set in 2022, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which tracks gas prices across the country.
“It’s still going to be one of the most expensive Thanksgiving Days that we’ve seen," De Haan said.

There is wide disparity in what stations are charging, he said, because some have been quicker to lower prices as the cost of oil drops. Some states, like Ohio, Georgia, Indiana and North Carolina, have also suspended their gas taxes, he said.
De Haan recommended that motorists use apps to check gas prices in their neighborhood and along their routes. He said other cost- and gas-saving measures include:
— Joining wholesale clubs and loyalty programs that offer lower gas prices.
— Using cruise control, which can decrease the amount of gas used during trips.
— Not exceeding 70 mph (113 kph).
— Traveling at off-peak times to avoid traffic jams.
— Removing items in vehicles to reduce their weight.
Think about the weather and emergency situations you might encounter, like traffic pileups in dense fog, as you put together an emergency kit for your vehicle.

The National Safety Council, a training and consulting organization, said drivers should check their emergency vehicle supplies every six months and replace expired items. Here are some items the group recommends:
— Mechanical: A properly inflated spare tire, wheel wrench, tripod jack, jumper cables, multipurpose utility tool, flashlight with extra batteries, duct tape
— First aid: Gauze, tape, bandages, antibiotic ointment, aspirin, non-latex gloves, scissors, thermometer, tweezers, instant cold compress
— Food: Drinking water and nonperishable, high-energy foods like nuts, dried fruit and hard candy
— Weather: Rain poncho, snow brush, shovel, warm clothing, cat litter for traction, windshield washer fluid
— Miscellaneous: Compass, reflective vest, fire extinguisher, cellphone charger

The Transportation Security Administration said it’s preparing to screen 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30. More than 3 million people are expected to travel by air on Sunday alone.

The agency recommends arriving at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights to allow sufficient time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop and security screening.

It also reminds travelers that containers with more than 3.4 ounces of liquids or spreads — think mayonnaise or chip dip — must be packed in checked bags. That includes cranberry sauce, gravy, maple syrup and canned fruit or vegetables. Holiday pies, meats and solid casseroles can be brought as carry-on items, the TSA said.

U.S. airfare prices have reached a 10-year high as airlines account for jet fuel cost increases in the wake of the U.S. war with Iran, according to travel booking site Hopper. As of late October, available flights for the Thanksgiving period cost 39% more than last year, while searches for flights around Christmas showed prices were up 40%, to an average of $466 for a roundtrip ticket, the company said.

To save money, consider shifting your itinerary by a day or two if you have the flexibility, Hopper's lead economist, Hayley Berg, advised. Flying on Thanksgiving Day and returning the following Monday or Tuesday can be hundreds of dollars cheaper than flying on Wednesday and Sunday, for example. Leaving the Monday or Tuesday before Christmas instead of the weekend before can also save money.

Berg also recommends considering different airlines and airports. This is the first holiday season since Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May, leaving consumers with one less ultra-low-cost option. But a handful of budget carriers, including Frontier and Allegiant, are still in business. Just factor in those airlines' extra charges for bags and seat assignments when comparing prices.
“If you’re going on a vacation rather than home for the holidays, shop around,” Berg said. “There might be deals from your local airport that you haven’t considered before.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat reported from Las Vegas. Dave Collins contributed from Hartford, Connecticut.

title: Beloved drive-thru worker on making a year's salary on last day of work
summary: When Sighle Williams decided to retire from Mac's Drive Thru after 37 years, she never could have expected the send-off she received, which is the focus of a new Netflix documentary.
story: Sighle Williams keeps it simple.
"I just like to treat people the way I like to be treated," she told "CBS Mornings."

So when Williams, who'd spent her 37-year career making people smile at Mac's Drive Thru in Gainesville, Florida, was approached about having a documentary made about her last day, she was excited but a bit skeptical.
That short film, called "One Last Order," premieres on Netflix Tuesday and has already garnered awards from the Aspen Shortfest, Nantucket Film Festival, Miami Film Festival and more.

The movie documents Williams' final day on the job, but it also shows the side of Williams that her beloved customers didn't see, like how she raised five girls — her sister and niece's children — as her own. The film shares how she lived in a house for a while with no running water or electricity.
"I just did what I needed to do, I knew I needed to make sure they were straight, and I needed to make sure I went to work," she said.
When she went to work, she made everyone feel like she was glad to see them. She remembered people's orders.

On her last day at Mac's, her boss decided that every dollar made would go back into Williams' pocket as a retirement bonus. Community members lined up around the block and waited for up to four hours to say goodbye and give Williams one final order.
The whole thing made her feel on "top of the world," she told "CBS Mornings."

"I didn't even eat all day, I didn't go to the restroom all day," Williams said, "I was just so -- I wanted to acknowledge everybody and thank everybody for coming out, you know, sharing the love with me on my last day."
She ended up making a year's salary on that final day, but won't reveal how much she made.
"I don't want nobody to feel no type of way because, you know, I'm hamburgers and fries," she said.
Now that she's been retired for a couple of years, Williams has some time for herself.
"I'm traveling, I'm ready to go," she said. "With the film fests, I've been going to different places and enjoying myself."
When asked about where her drive comes from, she said, "Just be kind. Just be patient and, you know, don't take everything so serious."

title: Don Toliver concert in U.K. evacuated due to mystery substance
summary: Some 12,000 fans of American rapper Don Toliver had to evacuate his concert in Manchester, England, after a noxious substance spread through the arena.
story: More than 12,000 people were evacuated from an arena in northern England Sunday night after the crowd at American rapper Don Toliver's concert suddenly started screaming, choking and coughing when a powerful smell spread through the venue.
Police said the Co-op Live arena in Manchester was evacuated at about 10 p.m. (5 p.m. Eastern).
There's been speculation online that the mysterious substance that spread through the air in the arena was tear gas, but authorities have not confirmed that.
Don Toliver, who is set to end a world tour with a Tuesday night show in London, left the stage in Manchester and police declared it a major incident.
One person was hospitalized and dozens were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms according to the local ambulance service.
The arena was being fully decontaminated as a precaution, the emergency medical service said.
Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News newspaper that he was in the audience standing section when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said the lights came on as Toliver left the stage, but that everyone remained in the venue for almost an hour before an announcement asking people to make their way out was heard over the loudspeaker.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker told reporters.
The venue opened in 2024 and is only about 2 miles from the Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in 2017 by a suicide bomber who blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert.

title: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"
summary: For the award-winning star of "Monk," food had always been an integral part of family. And now he's teamed with daughter Josie Adams to write a food memoir: "We Thought They'd Never Leave," the story of their family reunions - and their recipes.
story: He was a detective with a quirk in "Monk," and played an alien opposite the "Men in Black." But if you really want to feel the soul of Tony Shalhoub, this character might be it: the stubborn chef Primo in "Big Night," his 1996 film with Stanley Tucci about food, family and … even more food.

Shalhoub is himself an investor in a New York City restaurant, Massara, where he invited us last week to break bread with his daughter, Josie Adams. The act of breaking bread, he said, is very important: "It's part of the family tradition, really. Having bread at the center of the table, it's how we were formed."
He's even made a TV series, "Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread," about different types of bread from different places.

For him and his family, the passion for food can be traced back to a time when there wasn't any. Shalhoub's father, Joseph, was born in war-torn Lebanon. Orphaned at a young age, he faced hunger and food shortages as a child. "A lot of his early memories were about that hunger," he said, "so that ties into our current family situation and our appreciation for and devotion to preparing food and feeding each other."
The Shalhoubs settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, and by the time Tony came along in 1953, there were a lot of mouths to feed; he was one of ten children.

The family was close, and stayed that way. Every summer, the entire extended Shalhoub clan – more than 50 in all – gathers in Wisconsin for a reunion. It's a week of big, homecooked meals and intense family bonding. And when the party's over, everyone gets a traditional Shalhoub family send-off: "At the end of the week," Tony said, "as people are loading up their cars, everyone else who's remaining gathers in a line in the drive and raises their hands," and a chorus cries out: "We thought they'd never leave!"
"We Thought They'd Never Leave" became the title of a book Shalhoub co-wrote with Josie, the story of their family and its recipes.

She actually started it during the pandemic, when both of her parents (Tony and actor Brooke Adams) were sick with COVID, and she feared that their memories and recipes would be lost forever. So, she gave them both journals to write it all down. "My dad was like, 'Do you think we're going to die? Why are you giving us this right now?'" Josie said. "He's like, 'I'm better now!' So I said, 'OK, well, will you maybe work on this cookbook with me? I'd like to do the family cookbook for real.' And he said yes."

Shalhoub and his wife raised two daughters in Los Angeles as he navigated the feast-or-famine life of a Hollywood actor. But for every Emmy-winning success like "Monk," there were lesser roles. "Sometimes there were jobs that I did that were just for the money," he said. "Do I regret doing those jobs? Not really. I mean, maybe one or two, but sometimes you just got to eat."
In 2016 he said he wanted to take a break from screen acting, move to New York, and just do live theater. He won a Tony Award for best lead actor in a musical for "The Band's Visit."
But then he got a job offer that was irresistible. As family patriarch Abe Weissman in "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel," Shalhoub won his fifth Emmy.

In real life, Shalhoub has been married to Brooke Adams for 34 years, and he actually does a lot of the cooking at home. Josie said, "Yeah, you cook for Mom a lot. Every morning my dad wakes up before my mom and makes her a cappuccino and brings it to her in bed. Every single morning."
"Except when I'm not there!" he laughed.
And that's the Shalhoub family's love language: cooking and serving each other, whether it's one loved one, or a crowd of 50.

Josie said, "It's really easy to send a text and say, 'I love you, thinking about you.' But it's a lot harder to do something for someone else. And that's what this whole reunion is about: getting together and showing the people that you love, that you love them."

title: Kwame Onwuachi's culinary journey
summary: The New York Times named the award-winning chef's Tatiana the best restaurant in the city two years in a row. Kwame Onwuachi discusses his Afro-Caribbean menu, and his path to becoming one of today's brightest culinary stars.
story: New York City's famed Lincoln Center is a dream destination for ballerinas, baritones, and one award-winning chef. As a youngster, Kwame Onwuachi sat on the steps in the plaza, taking a break from selling candy on the subway. "I never thought that one day ... I would have my sister's name on the side of the building," he said.

Onwuachi's restaurant Tatiana, located right on the renowned plaza, is one of the hardest reservations to book. The New York Times named Tatiana the best restaurant in New York City two years in a row; Time magazine put Onwuachi on their list of Most Influential People; and the James Beard Foundation gave him the Rising Star Award.

For Onuwuachi, now 37, he's just cooking what he knows. Asked to characterize the food he makes, he replied, "I would say Afro-Caribbean. The technical term is African people who came through the Caribbean. You're going to see a couple different things from these different regions, but they're all tied together. Jambalaya and joloff rice, gumbo and okra stew, right? Barbecue and suya. Like, these things are connected."
Onwuachi's love of food started early. He grew up in the Bronx. His mother was a caterer, his father an architect.

Asked his first memory of food, Onwuachi said, "Oh man, I remember very, very vividly being on my grandmother's hip, and her putting this piece of bread, this thin bread with, like, this electric, almost like a muted electric green sauce into my mouth. And it was curry goat with roti. And I remember the explosion of flavors. It was very vivid."

As a teenager, he found himself working a variety of jobs, but always had an appetite for the kitchen. He enrolled at the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park, New York. On a return visit, he said, "It's always feels good to be back here. So many memories, so many, like, defining moments for me, like truly becoming like a leader – that happened here."

He's a star there now, mentoring students at the school that gave him direction and purpose, when he was one of the few Black students in his class. "I think there was two of us in my class," he said. Asked how it made him feel, he said, "I'm a chef, for God sakes! I took it out on the lobsters.

"I focused on my studies at the end of the day," he said. "It's reflective of the industry, too, in the fine dining sense. There's not a lot of people of color in that. I didn't focus on this, but I knew I wanted to use my platform to help amplify my culture."

Onwuachi has a lot on his plate. Over the past decade, he's been everywhere from bookshelves to competing on shows like "Top Chef." He now has three restaurants, including Dogon in Washington, D.C., and his latest, Maroon, which opened last April on the Las Vegas Strip.

For Kwame Onuwachi, success never gets stale. And we witnessed him receive Maroon's first big review last month, when the Los Angeles Times called his restaurant "the best steakhouse in Las Vegas, and beyond."
But the chef says he's cooking up more than just food.
"I think if a dish tells a story, it has a soul," Onuwachi said. "You're not just cooking for perfect seasoning, you're cooking to share something with someone."

title: Princess Kate announces she's in remission from cancer
summary: Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.
story: Catherine, the Princess of Wales, said Tuesday her cancer is in remission, about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.

"It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery," she said in her post on Instagram after visiting the Royal Marsden Hospital in London. "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
The princess had announced last March that cancer was discovered following an abdominal surgery and she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy.

In September, she said she had finished chemotherapy. She spoke about receiving the cancer treatment during her visit Tuesday. "It's really tough,'' she said, according to the Associated Press. "It's such a shock."

Kate spoke with patient Katherine Field about the chemotherapy port that's used to deliver the treatment, saying, "I got so attached to it," and joking that she was almost reluctant to have it removed, according to the AP.
On social media Tuesday, Kate said she visited the hospital to thank the staff "for looking after me so well during the past year."

"My heartfelt thanks goes to all those who have quietly walked alongside William and me as we have navigated everything," she said, referring to her husband, the Prince of Wales. "We couldn't have asked for more. The care and advice we have received throughout my time as a patient has been exceptional."
Kensington Palace also announced that she and William have become patrons of the hospital.

"My hope is, that by supporting groundbreaking research and clinical excellence, as well as promoting patient and family wellbeing, we might save many more lives, and transform the experience of all those impacted by cancer," Kate said on social media.

Since 2007, William has held the role of the hospital's president. His mother, Princess Diana, also held that position, according to the palace. The hospital is known as a world-leading cancer center with three sites in London.
Kate spoke with other patients as well as doctors and nurses during Tuesday's visit, according to Britain's Press Association news agency.
"The body is amazing at telling us 'you need to take time out,'" she said after learning about a man's diagnosis.
She also talked about receiving her cancer diagnosis, according to the news agency.

"It's the uncertainty of that initial diagnosis," she said. "It's such a wealth of information. Understanding the diagnosis, it's a massive amount of information to take on as a patient. Having that continuity, in the clinical setting and outside in the home setting, is so important."

title: Book excerpt: "We Thought They'd Never Leave" by Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams
summary: The Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor and his daughter collaborate on a book featuring reflections on food and extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor Tony Shalhoub's new book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family" (written with daughter Josie Adams, and published by Gallery Books), offers reflections on food and his extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Tracy Smith's interview with Tony Shalhoub and Josie Adams on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 22!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Origin Story
What kind of lunatic family willingly gathers fifty-plus people in one place for seven days straight with no catered food, no outside help, and no exit strategy? Mine.

Every July, we converge in Wisconsin like salmon returning to spawn. Only with more card games, more garlic, and slightly less grace. Outsiders never believe it when I explain it to them. Nearly all my relatives, across four generations, cooking every meal from scratch, cleaning up the fallout, negotiating sleeping arrangements, and arguing over who's on the hook for Tuesday breakfast. No, we don't get paid. Yes, we do it every year. And the most bewildered question I'm always asked is ... Why?!

I used to respond with logistics. I'd explain how each family takes a night to cook, how we rotate the duties—head chef, sous chef, cleanup crew—as if we were on a ship, alone at sea with no port in sight. I'd describe how the menu is posted months in advance, how someone inevitably forgets the garlic, how someone else then inevitably overbuys the garlic, how someone else altogether inevitably burns the garlic, and how, miraculously, it all gets eaten anyway.

I'd outline the sleeping arrangements: the cousins packed in bunk beds like sardines, the uncles snoring in recliners, the blow-up mattresses that never survive the week. But logistics only explain how it works, not why it works. And that's the real question, isn't it? Because if you drill down, this reunion is objectively insane. Most sane people spend their summers escaping family obligations—jetting off to beaches, renting cabins far away from their in-laws, finding any excuse to avoid the awkward conversations and mismatched expectations that come with extended kin. We, on the other hand, run toward them—voluntarily spending seven days each summer marinating in each other's quirks, grievances, and toum sauce.

Truth is, a reunion should not be confused with a vacation. It's work. It's heavy lifting—sometimes literally, when you're carrying cases of tomatoes up the steps or hauling coolers of ice across the lawn. It's emotional labor, too: smoothing over past grudges, refereeing card games, and determining which conversations are "on the table" and which are simply "tabled."

Which is why, to explain why we do this, to understand this ritual of ours—the chopping and bickering and feeding of too many people until the table groans—I need to go back a hundred years, to another table on another continent, where the question wasn't how to make food for fifty, but whether there would be bread enough for one.

title: Brits are having less sex, but watching a lot of porn, survey finds
summary: A third of Brits aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, a landmark survey finds, though most acknowledge sexting and watching pornography.
story: London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.

The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.

Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.

Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.

"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."

One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."

Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."

Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.

"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: U.S.-based firms helping China access Nvidia's most advanced chips
summary: It's not just Megaspeed. A CBS News investigation reveals that at least two California-based Nvidia customers have Chinese ownership — giving the U.S. adversary potential access to Nvidia's most advanced technology.
story: Nvidia is selling its most cutting-edge chips to at least two companies that are U.S.-based, but are actually controlled by Chinese-owned firms, raising fresh questions about efforts to keep sensitive technology away from the nation's rivals, a CBS News investigation found.

One of the chip giant's "preferred partners" is a California company owned by a Chinese firm whose chief executive is a graduate of a Chinese military university, records show. Another California company was renamed after its Chinese-owned parent company was blacklisted.
Some of these U.S.-based, Chinese-owned firms have then leased or sold the advanced chips, used for artificial intelligence, to other companies in Southeast Asia, records show.

The world of computer chip exports is murky — and labyrinthine chains of custody have made it even more difficult to determine just how many of the most sensitive Nvidia chips are being exploited by China, experts told CBS News.

"It is a wake-up call for accountability, for properly resourcing the enforcement bodies, and for every leading private-sector tech company to map where it is exposed," said Mishel Kondi, a senior analyst at C4ADS, which specializes in using public data, from corporate filings to satellite imagery, to uncover sanctions violations and smuggling.

C4ADS, a Washington-based global security nonprofit also known as the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, examined corporate filings and other company ownership data at the request of CBS News. This story is based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an investigation of Nvidia's corporate relationships dating back to 2023 — long before its CEO Jensen Huang and his behemoth chip company dominated the news cycle.

That explosive saga began 27 days ago when the news broke that Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang — a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion, and Beijing denies she is a spy. The company she ran, Megaspeed, a cloud computing company based in Singapore, is under investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.

But Megaspeed, national security and trade experts say, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the transfer of Nvidia chips to China. And elected officials are now asking questions like: How are Nvidia's chips getting to China? And what did Jensen Huang and his colleagues know about it?

"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement this week.
California company, Chinese owners
Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year. The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.
What is not allowed — and is under strict export controls — are the sales of Nvidia's most technologically advanced chips, which are powering the AI revolution.
But recent reporting, including from CBS News, has shown some of the highest end chips, called Blackwells, have made it into Chinese hands.
The circuitous trail traveled by Nvidia chips quickly gets muddy.

Take RiCloud AI, a data center company based in San Jose, California. RiCloud AI appears on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners" in the U.S., affording it preferential access to sales of high-end computer chips used for advanced AI models.
These are classified as American sales, according to Nvidia's public filings — with the chips going to RiCloud AI, Inc., a U.S. company.
But RiCloud AI's parent company is Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited. That company is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu is also CEO of a related RiCloud company in California.

And Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, was previously chairman of data firm Global Switch Holdings, which was dropped as a data center provider by Australia's Department of Defense in June 2024 over national security concerns.
The U.S. government has not accused RiCloud and Yuxing of any wrongdoing.

By December 2025, just 10 weeks after it was incorporated, RiCloud AI had secured its partner status with Nvidia and has since become a "preferred" cloud partner, giving the company priority access to advanced chips, Nvidia's software and technical support. Nvidia has not responded to questions about what background checks it conducted before awarding the privileged status to RiCloud AI.

An examination of RiCloud AI's clients suggests that some seem like unorthodox customers for such high-powered technology. This year, for example, it signed a $120 million deal to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to a company in Taiwan that was primarily known for selling whisky.

Agencia Comercial Spirits was a small whisky importer with $609,000 in net income in 2025 when it listed on the Nasdaq as an AI company. This year it has made commitments for AI data center-related deals totaling between $488 and $598 million, after Li was appointed as chairman.

Agencia did not respond to a request for comment. In a February press release announcing its pivot into data centers, Agencia said the move was "part of a broader review of strategic opportunities outside its core whisky business."
Blacklisted owners
Then there is California company Aivres, which is currently listed on Nvidia's website as an "elite" compute partner — the highest tier of relationship with the chip giant.

Aivres used to be called Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. But when Inspur group firms in China were added to a federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk to the U.S. in March 2023, the California subsidiary changed its name and today still maintains its close relationship with Nvidia. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist.

Aivres, which produces data center servers housing Nvidia chips, exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, according to a New York Times analysis of trade records published two months ago.
Some $3 billion of those exports were for computers containing Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, the Times reported.
The Aivres chips then went to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani — providing cloud AI services to Chinese firms Alibaba and ByteDance, according to the Times.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm where Jensen Huang paramour Alice Huang was a top executive, was blacklisted by the U.S. government this week, in the wake of the scandal. The company denies any wrongdoing.

The Pentagon put Alibaba on a blacklist in June, claiming it used advanced chips to help the Chinese military. The company denies it and sued the government over the blacklisting, winning a preliminary injunction last month.
The servers owned by Inspur — Aivres' parent company — are used in China by the country's military, according to the U.S. government. Aivres did not respond to requests for comment.
Selling to suspected smugglers
Another of Nvidia's elite U.S. partners has surfaced in a recent $300 million chip smuggling case, though it has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Earlier this year, a California businessman named Greg Lui was indicted for allegedly smuggling export-controlled chips to China via Malaysia and Singapore in 2023 and 2024. He has pleaded not guilty.
Records reviewed by CBS News link Lui to 2CRSi, an Nvidia elite partner in the U.S. that is a branch of a French-owned company making AI data servers.

Lui's indictment says his company bought 100 H100 servers — which required a license to export — worth more than $22 million from an unnamed manufacturer. 2CRSi's website lists his firm, Topmost Corp., as an "authorized partner," while his company website said he is an "authorized reseller of … 2CRSi."
The indictment does not accuse Nvidia of having any knowledge of the arrangement.

2CRSi said in a letter to shareholders this month that it received a grand jury subpoena from the federal prosecutor's office in Los Angeles about "a customer that we ourselves had reported to the authorities." It has not been accused of wrongdoing.
The company's U.S. revenue fell from $201 million to $4.7 million this year.
In addition to 2CRSi, Lui listed California firm Super Micro Computer, Inc. as one of his customers.
In March, the Justice Department accused Super Micro's co-founder of a scheme to smuggle $2.5 billion worth of servers to Chinese customers via a Southeast Asian company.

The co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw has denied the charges. His alleged "fixer" pleaded guilty in a deal with prosecutors last month. The company says those involved "no longer have any relationship with Supermicro" and its current executives had no knowledge of the alleged smuggling.
Accounting changes

Nvidia used to publish the regional breakdown of its chip sales based on the customer's billing location. That data showed that in 2024, nearly half of its chip sales were billed to the U.S., 18% to Singapore and 13% to China.

Last November, the company switched to using the customer's headquarters as its location. This bookkeeping change revealed that an extra $7.9 billion of customers' bills were actually from firms headquartered in China in 2024.
In 2025, U.S.-headquartered customers made up 69% of Nvidia sales, while China was cut to 9%.
Nvidia's public filings say "the end customer and shipping location may be different from our customers' headquarters location."
CBS News' findings suggest Nvidia's changes to the way it published these sales figures may make the locations of its customers less clear.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, who is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is poised to investigate whether companies are circumventing the bans on sales of chips to China, and into alleged Chinese espionage connected to Nvidia.

Kondi told CBS News that she believes the investigation of chip sales "matters beyond the news cycle because it exposes export control violations and potential economic espionage, and shows how Beijing ties intelligence work to its industrial plans, pursuing self-reliance while still reaching for foreign technology where it lacks parity."

title: Stocks turn volatile as Jensen Huang rebound rally fades
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell more than 1,000 points in early trading before clawing back most of the losses.
story: Stocks swung wildly on Wednesday, plunging in early trading before paring losses by the close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 1,000 points early in the session, but regained ground to close down 148 points, or 0.6%, at 23,586.  The S&P 500 fell 0.2% on the day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%.

Stocks have slumped in recent weeks amid concerns surrounding the health of the artificial intelligence sector. Shares of Anthropic, the AI lab that staged the largest initial stock offering in history last week, declined 7.6% to $75.66, below its IPO price of $83 per share.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the AI sector can justify the enormous investment in data centers. Compounding those fears just before the Thanksgiving holiday are the Trump administration's plans to raise tariffs on China and other major trading partners.

"At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn't look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year," Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in an email.

With Democrats set to control Congress next year and winning many state-level seats, AI companies may face more headwinds as lawmakers push back against data center construction, according to investment adviser Capital Economics. Even before the midterm elections, investors were increasingly questioning the finances of AI companies, it added.

Investors are also bracing for the impact of more interest rate hikes starting in December, with expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs to counter rising inflation. That could make it more difficult for businesses, including AI companies, to borrow money to fuel growth.

title: Most Polymarket users lost money betting on the U.S. midterms
summary: More than half of Polymarket accounts lost money betting on the U.S. midterm elections, according to one analysis.
story: Prediction market companies tout themselves as a place where anyone can make a quick buck. Don't bet on it, recent data suggests.

Take the U.S. midterm elections, which generated ample business for prediction market platforms as users wagered on who would win congressional races nationwide. And a few people did, in fact, clean up — very few.

On Polymarket, the top 1% of accounts took home 91% of the profits from midterm bets, totaling roughly $23 million, according to research this week from the Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC), a nonprofit advocacy group focused on corporate and financial corruption. The bottom 99% of traders lost a total of $15 million.
Of the nearly 82,000 accounts that the group analyzed, more than half lost money on Polymarket's midterm-focused markets.

"At a time [when] affordability was a major issue at the ballot box, average traders handed over their cash to an elite few, including many professional and automated traders," ACDC said in its study.
According to Polymarket, 95% of the markets on its platform accurately predicted the outcome of this year's midterm elections.

"Prediction markets have become an important source of real-time election information as they bring together the knowledge and insights of informed participants to show the public how likely different outcomes are," a Polymarket spokesperson said in an email to CBS News. "Polymarket continues to be a destination for timely, accurate information that anyone can follow as events unfold, whether they trade or not."

According to the Pew Research Center, Polymarket and rival prediction market Kalshi hosted a combined 34,000 contracts related to the midterms, up from 2,300 in 2024. The midterms generated $2.7 billion in trading volume on the platforms, compared with $8.5 billion during the 2024 presidential and congressional elections, Pew found.
Other recent data point to the challenge of winning money on prediction markets.

Findings released by the New York City Council on Tuesday show that, from Jan. 1 to Aug. 11, New York City residents who traded on Kalshi lost a total of $17.6 million. So-called institutional traders on the platform won $210 million over the same period.

On Wall Street, institutional investors generally refer to financial firms, market makers and other pros who invest money on behalf of their clients. In Kalshi's case, it also encapsulates retail traders, solo forecasters and two-person teams that use LLCs for tax or business purposes, according to Elisabeth Diana, a spokesperson for the prediction market.
"Most winning traders [are] labeled as 'institutional' even though they are often 'individuals,'" she said in an email, adding, "These are not Wall Street institutions."
Diana also said that, as in other financial markets, a trader's skill level matters.

"Traders who get better at forecasting can earn more, and their trades make the market more efficient," she said. "Individuals do worse day trading on the stock markets than professionals. The only difference here is that prediction markets give more people an opportunity to be a 'professional.'"

title: FCC approves SpaceX plan for 1 million data center satellites
summary: In an X post on Wednesday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the satellites will be a "great asset to America and the world."
story: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday greenlit SpaceX's request to put 1 million satellites in space that will create orbital data centers, bringing CEO Elon Musk closer to his goal of harnessing the sun to generate computing power.
"Today, in a historic first, the FCC approved SpaceX's request for 1 million satellites (orbital compute modules) to create data centers in space," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a post on X.
Musk responded by saying, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
SpaceX's satellites will conduct telemetry, tracking and command operations, and will connect with other satellites, including those in SpaceX's Starlink system, the FCC said in a February filing.

SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to put data centers in space in January. In its application, it said  that deploying data centers in space would be the "first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization," referring to a threshold Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev proposed at which a civilization could tap the entire energy output of its star.

When it filed its initial public offering in May, SpaceX said that orbital data centers would be able to handle intense demand from the AI sector and generate energy more efficiently than land-based facilities, which have become a flashpoint across the U.S.

Thousands of data centers are being built, sparking backlash from communities who argue the facilities will transform their cities, create unwanted noise and drive up electricity and water use. In the midterms, American voters approved dozens of proposals aimed at restricting data centers.
In its IPO filing, SpaceX said it expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028.

title: Why are investors freaking out even as the U.S. economy surges?
summary: The economy is sending mixed signals, with growth jumping while stocks gyrate. Here's what economists say is going on.
story: The U.S. economy is racing ahead, with new data showing that the country's gross domestic product rose at a blistering 4.3% pace in the third quarter. So why are investors hitting the panic button, causing stocks to swing wildly and bruising your 401(k) plan?

The answer boils down to the relationship among inflation, interest rates and the Federal Reserve, along with mounting concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence boom could turn to bust.

Stocks on Wednesday show just how brittle investor sentiment is at the moment. Leading indexes plunged more than 1,000 points in morning activity, only to claw back much of those losses in afternoon trading. Where stocks go next, nobody knows.
The S&P 500 index is now about 8% lower than its most recent high on Oct. 6, putting it close to a correction, or a decline of more than 10% from its recent peak.

Also on Wednesday, the Bureau of Economic Analysis sharply raised its estimate for third-quarter growth from its previous forecast of 3.4%. That growth is being fueled by steady consumer spending and surging business investment, with large tech firms splurging on building out data centers and other infrastructure required to power AI.

Americans benefit when the economy is growing, fueling consumer spending and hiring. But heady growth can also have a downside — especially when, as in the current moment, inflation is already running hot.

"In the simplest possible words, the economy is overheated, with demand exceeding supply.  The consequence is a blowout of the trade deficit and inflation," HFE chief economist Carl B. Weinberg said in a research note.
The link between AI and inflation

Although inflation earlier in the year was largely driven by rising energy costs, more recent signals suggest that strong economic growth, fueled by heavy AI spending, is now the main factor driving up prices. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee said last week that trillions in spending on data centers are contributing to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation.
Newly released inflation data showed consumer prices rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September.

Meanwhile, the admixture of high inflation and heady economic growth virtually cements a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike at its December meeting, and possibly additional hikes in early 2027, according to economists.
Rate hikes and the stock market

The specter of rate hikes is weighing on the stock market, as higher borrowing costs could create hurdles for AI and other tech companies seeking to expand their computing capacity. And households, already stretched thin by rising inflation, could face higher costs for everything from credit cards to mortgages — a headwind for consumer spending.

"Households face renewed inflation pressures, diminished saving capacity and higher borrowing costs, while elevated interest rates are raising the cost of investment and financing across the economy," EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said in an email.

Investors are also questioning whether the huge investments by AI companies will pay off, given the massive losses recorded by many of the big AI labs. Anthropic, which last week recorded the largest initial stock offering in history, lost a startling $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026. It plans to spend nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

"But the critical thing AI may never be able to do is make profits high enough to justify its declining, but still stratospheric valuations," Boston University economist Laurence Kotlikoff said in a Wednesday blog post.
What's the outlook for stocks?
Some investors and economists say that investors should brace for more downside, at least in the near term.

"As investors saw last week, pessimism can build quickly and suddenly take the wheel of market momentum," said Anthony Saglimbene, Ameriprise chief market strategist, in a research note. "And fear tends to feed on itself at these readings, as falling stock prices become the evidence that justifies more selling across the market."

Experts advise against making snap decisions during a market downturn, such as selling stocks, as it can lead to losses that are tough to recover from. For instance, investors who sold in previous downturns may have missed the sharp market gains that have often followed.
Despite investors' fears, the economy remains strong, helping shore up corporate growth, noted Doug Beath, global equity strategist at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"We expect solid economic and earnings growth in 2027 to support our year-end S&P 500 target of 8,700," he said.

title: Trump administration to issue new tariffs on China, EU and others
summary: The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on goods from other major economies.
story: The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.

The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.

In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.

Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.

Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
Tariffs unpopular with voters, small businesses

In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.

Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.

The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.

"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."

title: How people use AI agents to handle annoying tasks and save money
summary: Shrugging off fears of AI, some consumers say the technology is simplifying their lives and helping them save money.
story: Count Megan Roszak, a busy executive coach, business founder and mother of 11-year-old twins, among the recent converts to artificial intelligence as a tool for helping run her life.

The San Francisco, California, resident explained to CBS News how she uses an AI agent, Fo, from the agent platform Wajo, to process and return online purchases. She also recently used it to book an appointment with her electric company, which she said saved her multiple phone calls and about 40 minutes.

"I am a full-time working mom. Making returns to Poshmark and Etsy are things that I would let go of and drop in the past because it's going to be annoying," Roszak said. "Now, I just put Fo on the case, and I got $250 back."

Companies ranging from Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI to hundreds of smaller developers are rolling out AI agents designed to handle tedious tasks, such as returning products, and also to comb through people's email inboxes for unclaimed refunds and other money they may be owed.

More broadly, AI proponents say the technology can help consumers reckon with the "annoyance economy," or what advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative describes in a recent report as the "time, fees and irritation" involved in dealing with a host of menial tasks.

Those tasks, such as handling customer service, scheduling appointments and canceling subscriptions, cost Americans $165 billion per year in wasted time, fees and other surcharges for routine transactions, according to Groundwork.
A cure for annoyance?

Used wisely, AI agents can reduce the friction companies depend on to pocket forgotten fees and payments, according to Stanford University economist Neale Mahoney, an author of Groundwork's report on the so-called annoyance economy.
Kevin Newman, another Fo user, estimates the agent has saved him roughly 2,800 hours he would otherwise have spent generating advertising leads for his small business and on personal tasks.

The agent also sifted through his email to turn up multiple gift cards he had earned for testing products and found unclaimed funds he was owed from his former residences, including a $60 claim from a settlement with Time Warner, Newman said.

Fo can summon a person to finish the job when necessary, with Wajo assistants on call who can work with agents when, for example, an institution doesn't have a website, or it blocks agents, according to the company.

Wajo founder Shivani Poddar told CBS News that people use Fo for a wide range of pesky tasks, including booking plane tickets, tracking down lost luggage with airlines or negotiating healthcare costs.
"These are complex negotiations, and these systems are still very hybrid," she said, highlighting the importance of having a human on call when necessary.

Meta also touts its Muse agent's money-saving capabilities. For example, in the "ideas" section of the app, which suggests financial management uses, Meta recommends using Muse to "Get back money that's already yours" by checking state databases for owed amounts. The agent offers to file refund claims and also to "cancel those random subscriptions you forgot about."
Businesses vs. agents

Businesses that count on consumers giving up on claiming refunds or fighting junk fees aren't taking such tactics lying down, with some websites and financial institutions blocking AI agents. Amazon, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase & Co. are among the businesses that have banned the bots from conducting transactions on behalf of consumers.
"More firms are blocking agents because they're making it difficult to increase their revenue. They're like a superpower for consumers, so companies have an incentive to block it," Mahoney said.

Concerns also swirl about agents accessing users' sensitive data, including payment information, and about their incentives. For example, Lindsay Owens, founder and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News that companies could be steering users toward products and services from which they earn commissions, to pad their own bottom lines.
