title: Paperwork, not work, causing enrollees to lose Medicaid in Nebraska
summary: Data from the months after Nebraska's early rollout of new Medicaid work mandates offers a look at the challenges enrollees in other states could face.
story: When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Trump's sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.
Many also watched the Cornhusker State's experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.
On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.

They'll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don't meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don't comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren't working.
Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.

"The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans' chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.

Democrats' massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they'll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they're fully enforced.
The basics

Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.

But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.

The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called "medically frail."
It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.

On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data.

Nebraska's Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn't have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News.
About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented.
But the state data also shows some troubling issues.
For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules.

Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. "It's not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size," he said.
Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state's outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said.
The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF. Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage.

"This is definitely a red-flag warning," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. "The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling."
Navigating the new requirements

Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn't understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed.

"I want to make sure I send in everything they need," said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer.
She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job.

Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times.
One challenge in evaluating Nebraska's implementation is that the state, as of mid-November, had released data only through August.
State officials said this summer that they would post an online dashboard with various performance metrics to improve public transparency. That hasn't happened yet.

"We have seen a lot of negative effects so far," said Sarah Maresh, program director at Nebraska Appleseed, a nonprofit social justice advocacy group. "Every person that goes without coverage is a problem."
She worries that people are being deterred from applying to Medicaid because of the policy.
Brunssen, the interim Medicaid director, defended his state's performance.

"We are experiencing what we expected," he said in an October interview at a National Association of Medicaid Directors conference in Maryland. "The vast majority of people newly applying, or for those going through redetermination, are getting coverage or retaining coverage."

Yet, Brunssen noted, it's still early. Fewer than 25% of Medicaid enrollees subject to the work requirement have had to prove they meet the new rules to retain coverage. The rest won't be completed until next summer, he said.

The state's Department of Health and Human Services, which operates its Medicaid program, has used various methods to inform enrollees about the new rules, such as letters, emails, texts, and messages in an online portal, Brunssen said.
"Most Medicaid enrollees know about the new rules," he said, attributing awareness to community partners and managed-care companies that helped get the word out.
"I feel like we've done everything in our power to communicate what was coming," he said.
Brunssen noted the state has taken advantage of a federal option to let enrollees self-attest that they meet exemptions. All declarations must be truthful, or enrollees could face perjury charges.
Self-attestation is as easy as checking a box on an online form. No supporting documents are required. That's made it easier for people to comply, Brunssen said.
The state has also exempted people living in three counties with high unemployment rates and in two counties declared federal disaster areas because of weather events, he said.
"Our goal is to make sure people who are eligible get or retain coverage," Brunssen said.
Some enrollees say the state could do more to make the process easier.

Chalandria James, 37, of Omaha was worried about whether she still had Medicaid coverage after she tried to renew in July but did not hear back from the state, despite repeated calls. Unsure of her coverage status, she canceled a doctor's appointment to check her blood pressure. It took until September, and a multi-hour visit to the state agency office, for her to find out she still had Medicaid and was exempt from the work requirement because she had a child under 14 years old.
"It was nerve-racking not knowing," said James, a community health worker and doula.
In Nebraska, about 37% of enrollees met the work requirement while 61% qualified for an exemption — with the most common reasons being medical frailty or caregiving.

Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families, said Nebraska's experience shows the work rules do little to promote work, since most who can are already working. "This policy punishes low-income people by subjecting them to serious, often insurmountable, hurdles," she said.

Even with data showing the large majority of enrollees working or meeting an exemption, Brunssen said the new requirements still are a good idea. "Part of being a good, healthy person does involve engagement with the community," he said, "and we think there is value in the work we are doing in this space."

title: 5 questions Nvidia still faces after bringing back Jensen Huang
summary: Despite Jensen Huang's shock return as Nvidia's CEO, experts say it's anything but business as usual for the chipmaker.
story: Jensen Huang's first task in returning to lead Nvidia after resigning last week under a cloud will be to deal with the fallout from his stunning exit and even more surprising reprieve.

Following his reinstatement by the company's board, some lawmakers are calling for investigations into President Trump's role in the billionaire entrepreneur's return and whether Nvidia skirted export rules meant to prevent its advanced chips from reaching China. And while Huang may be viewed as key to Nvidia's success, his return raises a thicket of legal and operational problems, according to financial and governance experts.

"Three tests will now decide how strongly it builds from here: how its leadership sits with Washington, how it handles China and how long AI spending keeps growing at this speed,"  said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory firm, in an email.
Here are five critical questions facing Nvidia as Huang retakes the helm.
Did Nvidia compromise U.S. national security?

One of Nvidia's major customers, Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, employed a Chinese businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is also alleged to have smuggled Nvidia's advanced chips into China and provided remote access to the technology in violation of U.S. export controls.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear on Dec. 1- 2 in closed-door interviews before multiple congressional panels to discuss the company's ties to China. Huang is also scheduled to appear on Dec. 3 at a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on U.S. export rules and global AI competition.

"The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the Republican chairs of the House committees who will interview Huang and Teter said on Monday.
Will Nvidia's board face legal issues?

The board's decision to reinstate Huang is likely to set off a flurry of shareholder lawsuits over questions including whether Nvidia failed to disclose the spying allegations earlier and whether the company was aware of Megaspeed's links to China, according to Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware.

Shareholders could also challenge Huang and Nvidia over their failure to disclose his personal relationships with subordinates at the company, which appears to violate the chipmaker's code of conduct. Earlier this month, Nvidia was sued by shareholders for allegedly failing to disclose information about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive (no relation).
"There's just a whole range of things that they can bring actions," Elson said.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment about whether it will continue pursuing an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence.
Will Nvidia face new U.S. export restrictions?
Nvidia is expected to come under increased scrutiny and face greater regulatory hurdles in selling chips to China and companies in Southeast Asia.
"There will definitely be tighter restrictions, and any dealings directly with China will be the government's primary focus," StoneX equity research analyst Cody Acree told CBS News.

Huang has long lobbied U.S. officials to permit Nvidia to sell its most advanced chips to China, with an eye toward growing its market. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department moved to curb sales of U.S. chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.

"Going forward, they'll be subject to more export controls so that their chips don't end up in China and data centers in Asia," Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment firm D.A. Davidson, told CBS News. "In that way, Nvidia's market has shrunk, and that business will go away."
Can Huang ease investor fears about an AI bust?

Investors cheered Huang's return partly because it suggests that Nvidia will continue in its role as the de facto "bank of AI," providing financing for companies that buy its chips and otherwise fueling the sector's growth. Huang helped arrange deals such as Nvidia's investment in OpenAI. Through such circular financing, Nvidia invests vast sums in AI companies, which then flow back to the chipmaker through chip purchases.

"Nvidia is more than just a chipmaker — it's heavily involved in the broader AI ecosystem by financing other companies," Capital Economics senior economist James Reilly told CBS News. "Having Jensen back reassures investors that those relationships and that financing will continue."
Still, Huang's return doesn't erase concerns about the sector's debt-fueled spending, or whether AI companies will ever turn a profit and deliver returns to investors.
"There are growing concerns as to whether all of this AI investment will generate the revenue it needs long-term to make it worthwhile," Reilly said. "Those hurdles are very demanding."
What is Nvidia's succession plan?
Developing a succession plan to replace Huang will be the first item on the board's agenda, Elson, a prominent governance expert, told CBS News.

When Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, he had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that allowed him to wield enormous power. However, his departure made it clear that the company had no succession plan should Huang be unable to lead.
As a result, Elson expects Nvidia to hire an outside consultant to help forge a plan for who might succeed Huang.
Such "key man" risk isn't unique to Nvidia, Acree noted.

"You have other high-profile CEOs at the helm of large companies, but that's the nature of Silicon Valley, unfortunately," he said, pointing to Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX's Elon Musk. "There is no way to address that risk entirely or make it go away, but boards will be more sensitive to that in the future."

title: Shein to pay $100 million to settle claims it deceived customers
summary: The Singapore fast-fashion company misled millions of U.S. consumers about its products and policies, FTC alleges.
story: Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.

The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.

"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.

Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint.

The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.

A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.

Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.

title: Wendy's "pricing scheme" inflated menu prices, lawsuit alleges
summary: In a proposed class action, a California resident alleges that Wendy's conspired with its franchisees to set and raise menu prices.
story: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges that Wendy's engaged in a pricing scheme that reduced competition across its restaurants, driving up costs for customers.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in a Maryland district court, accuses the burger chain of conspiring with independently owned franchisees to set and raise prices at its U.S. locations over a six-year period between 2016 and 2022. Wendy's collected "competitively sensitive information" from franchisee locations, including transaction data, to coordinate prices, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by Andy Garcia, a California resident and longtime Wendy's customer, according to the suit. He alleges that Wendy's engaged in "anticompetitive conduct" that resulted in artificially high prices, causing him to pay more than he otherwise would have.
Garcia also sued NCR Voyix, a software company that provides Aloha POS, a point-of-sale system used by Wendy's.

"By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers," Blake Hunter Yagman, the lawyer representing Garcia and founding partner of Yagman PLLC, a class-action law firm headquartered in New York, said in an email.

"This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher — and Wendy's owes [it to] its consumers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing," Yagman added.

Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As of September, Wendy's had 432 company-owned restaurants and 6,762 franchisees across the U.S., according to the company's most recent regulatory filing.

In 2024, Wendy's raised concerns after saying it would test Uber-style pricing. Also known as dynamic pricing, that approach allows companies to set prices based on real-time market conditions and other factors such as weather.
Other restaurants have also faced scrutiny over their pricing practices. Last month, a consumer sued McDonald's over the use of an AI tool that recommends dynamic pricing.

title: "We're racing towards huge dangers," AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio says
summary: As one of the "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, Yoshua Bengio helped bring generative AI into the world. Now he worries society isn't ready for what's coming.
story: Yoshua Bengio is the most professionally cited scientist alive, and the most cited computer scientist of all time. He's informally known as one of the three "godfathers" of artificial intelligence, along with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun, for his foundational work on the deep neural networks that power today's AI models.
In short, Bengio helped usher AI into the world — a technology now being integrated into our schools, our search bars, our smartphones and our wars.
Yet despite being one of the principal minds behind AI, the University of Montreal professor is now urgently calling for a slowdown in its development and a renewed focus on using AI safely.

LawZero, the nonprofit where Bengio is co-president and scientific director, strives to develop AI that is "designed to be trustworthy and safe" — effectively a dissent from the models being released by Anthropic and OpenAI. Bengio wants companies, governments and AI lab employees to stop developing ever more capable AI systems.

What led to such a dramatic turnaround for one of the world's most prominent AI researchers? Bengio spoke with CBS News about AI risks, regrets and responsibility. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

CBS News: You're considered one of the people most responsible for the early advancement of deep learning, and you're the most cited scientist in the world because of your work in AI. How do you feel about your past work today?

Yoshua Bengio: I feel like I learned a lot. It was exciting. But I should have seen some of the most serious risks earlier. And I think, like most humans, I was focused on the good side of my work. And not enough on the potential consequences.
What was the original goal of your early work on deep learning or AI?

I was trying to understand intelligence and do it in a way that was sufficiently abstract to help us understand human intelligence, animal intelligence and build intelligent machines. That was a very exciting research goal, with the hypothesis that there could be a few simple principles — think of the laws of physics for the physical world — that could explain intelligence.
Do you feel like that goal has been accomplished since then?
Beyond our expectations. There are still people who are in denial, but it's very clear that we have been making very rapid progress towards machines that are intelligent.
Have your personal views on what intelligence actually is changed over time?

It has been refined, but I haven't made a U-turn about the nature of intelligence. In the last few years, I've focused on how it can go wrong, in the sense that intelligence can be in the service of goals that are not ethical.
You've now shifted to advocating for AI safety — that's a markedly different focus than your earlier research. Can you explain that shift?

I was spending a lot of my brain cycles on two things. One was understanding how we can make AI more intelligent, and the other was how to apply AI to fields like medicine or handling the climate crisis, education and so on. I made a big pivot to orient my research to how we can make AI safe because the capabilities, the intelligence, can be in the service of really, really bad goals — whether in the hands of humans with those bad goals or the AI itself.
And as the intelligence of those systems grows, the risks of the very dangerous use of that intelligence grow as well.

Anthropic recently became the first AI lab to go public, turning many of its employees into millionaires and even billionaires. At the same time, these researchers acknowledge they might be building the equivalent of a doomsday device. What should AI researchers think about as they develop new models?

They should try to look honestly at their work, its consequences and at what is the best use of their time to be aligned with their values. If they care about humanity and democracy, I think they should reconsider what they're doing now.

What we've seen in the past few years, and especially since the summer, is that the companies don't really know how to deal with the misalignment problem — in other words, with building AIs that do things that are bad for us.

The risk is growing with capability. I don't think society is even ready. Even if we were to solve this problem — to deal with the existence of machines that are greatly superior to humans —we're racing in a direction that is dangerous. And even the people working in AI safety in those companies, in some ways, are contributing to this.

Many experts think that more powerful AI models far surpassing human intelligence, including in areas like creativity where people excel, will arrive sooner rather than later. Do you agree with that general timeline, and if so, how should we respond to such advancements?

My perception of when things could go wrong has certainly shifted towards earlier than, say, I was anticipating before the Hugging Face incident, and even earlier with the Mythos cyber capabilities. We are moving faster towards more and more capable systems, and we're moving faster towards systems that we don't know how to control.

Because of this, in my own work at LawZero, we have shifted our research program to aim for shorter-term goals that could have an impact earlier — to show that there is a different way of training AIs that will not almost systematically lead to reward hacking. In other words, systems that prefer to cheat and try to hide it rather than do the things we are asking.
What would a more honest AI look like?

I'm going to use an analogy. Right now, the way we're training AIs is like how you would try to teach drivers on the highway to not go over the speed limit. They get rewards when they get to their destination faster. And we're trying to control their bad behavior by putting detectors on the highway.

So what happens? Well, first, drivers are going to try to figure out where the detectors are. They're going to slow down only where the detectors are. And we're already seeing that in AI. In other words, when the AI knows that it's being tested, it behaves well. And if they're really smart, those drivers might even hack the detectors themselves.

Now let's imagine a different kind of way of building the drivers. Imagine a human driver who is in the same situation with the detectors, and they want to get to their destination. But they believe God is watching them, and there is nothing they can do to hide what they do from God. Well, they're going to behave well.
How can society prepare itself for what seems like an inevitable future in which AI is a feature of ordinary life?

The short-term urgency is to stop this crazy advance toward more and more capable systems that we're not sure how to control. It's not just inside the companies. The models can be leaked. The methods can be copied. There are many risks, and they all come from having machines that are very, very intelligent and can do things we didn't know how to do before.

So there's urgency in stopping this. And the place where it's most acute is in the compute resources that are used to train the next generations. Right now, the majority of compute resources are going into training future machines, rather than actually using what we have for the benefit of society. And those new models are bringing more and more danger because intelligence gives power, and that power can be misused.

What is the right way of pacing the frontier, of slowing down? And what kind of regulation and oversight is needed? I think that's an interesting discussion, and we should have it. But it's not going to happen until people understand we're racing towards huge dangers.
What do you think ordinary people who don't work in government or at artificial intelligence companies should do to make a positive impact on AI?

People need to understand this is much more serious than they would typically believe. That's the first thing. The second thing is: Don't fall into desperation and powerlessness, because we can change the future. We still have agency. We can change society. We're in a democracy, where governments can actually do something about all this.

But it's going to take enough people to ask for it, and demand it. And for that, they need to understand their life is at stake, children's lives are at stake, democracy is at stake, peace and stability are at stake. People need to understand that the stakes here are comparable to a war. It's not yet in front of us, but it's coming, and we need to prepare.
I've got a kid, and I know you have children and grandchildren. Do you feel positive about the future despite the dangers posed by AI?

For sure. I'm an optimist by nature. Here is the flip side of all the scary stuff. Humans, when they see danger, can pivot quickly. Think about how quickly we reacted to the pandemic. We didn't wait for an international agreement that would take a decade — we just acted and coordinated.

Because of the risks, I think that we might end up in a much better world, where there is no war anymore. Because we can't afford that kind of risk when there are AIs that can be used to kill everyone, or a large number of people.

I also think democracy is going to have to be much more robust, because the temptation to abuse the power that AI will provide is going to be so great that the only way around it is to have incredibly strong institutions.

So we may end up in a much better world, and that's in addition to, of course, all the scientific advances that AI can bring. But it's not going to happen if we're blind collectively to the current trajectories' risks.

If we were to solve the alignment problem, which is what I'm trying to do as a scientist, we still have to make sure humans don't use very powerful AIs — maybe even superintelligent AI's — against each other in the search for wealth, power and for reasons of hatred. All the bad things that humans are capable of. And I don't think our society is ready for this.

title: Huang's return at Nvidia puts spotlight on chipmaker's board
summary: Nvidia directors' decision to rehire Jensen Huang shows a "lack of courage," according to one prominent governance expert.
story: Nvidia's stunning about-face on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO undermines the credibility of its board of directors and raises questions about its commitment to enforcing the company's own rules, according to corporate governance experts.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12  after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. In announcing its decision to rehire Huang, the company's board said it had concluded that reinstating him "poses no national security risk," citing input it had received from senior U.S. officials.

Yet in reversing itself, Nvidia is undermining its own corporate code of conduct and could expose the company to potential legal liability, Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, told CBS News.
"It shows a weakness, and I think, frankly, a lack of courage to stand behind the correct decision they made to suggest he resign. That was the right decision," he said.

Nvidia's code of conduct stipulates that personal relationships can create a conflict of interest and instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."
"A company culture that allows this sort of stuff to occur ultimately will kill the company itself,"  Elson said.

Nvidia's board members were not originally planning to reinstate Huang as CEO, a source familiar with their thinking told CBS News last week. More than 10,000 employees, about one-fourth of the company's workforce, signed a petition to "bring Jensen back."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In announcing Huang's return, Nvidia Board Chairman Harvey Jones said the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
Bowing to political pressure?

Technology industry leaders and President Trump celebrated Huang's return. Investors also cheered the return of the man who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and whom many view as synonymous with the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector. The company's stock price surged more than 31% on Monday, quickly bolstering its market value by $1 trillion.

At the same time, the move drew swift condemnation from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who said the board's decision could put America's national security at risk by undermining efforts to strengthen chip export controls to China.

Despite Nvidia's stock market gain on Monday, governance experts said Nvidia directors failed to live up to their fiduciary duty to act in the best interest of shareholders, including ensuring the company's long-term value.

"They are there for the difficult times. They are the shareholders' fiduciary and lifeboat pick to navigate through a crisis," said Betsy Atkins, who has served on dozens of private and public company boards. "That's their job — deliberate and make the right business judgment."

President Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia's board and convinced directors to reinstate Huang, raising questions about whether the board may have bowed to political pressure.

Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, said Mr. Trump's move put Nvidia directors in a difficult position, given the U.S. government's importance as a stakeholder in the company.
"I don't know whether any board would have been able to say no to the president," he told CBS News.
Nvidia's 10-person board, which includes the former president of Taco Bell and a former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs, was lacking in critical ways even before bringing Huang back, Rajgopal added.
"I don't see a whole lot of expertise in, say, export controls, chip architecture, or foundry supply chain," he said.

Several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, such as former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook. But it's rare for a CEO to exit under a cloud only for the board to swiftly bring them back.

The only other high-profile case cited by experts was in 2023, when OpenAI's board decided to rehire CEO Sam Altman just days after pushing him out over questions about his ability to lead the AI startup.

Huang's reinstatement is noteworthy given allegations that he violated Nvidia's code of conduct at least twice, Elson said. Huang allegedly had a relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence has linked to China's Ministry of State Security. At the time, Alice Huang was an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore data center Megaspeed.

The Trump administration on Monday formally restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips. Megaspeed has been accused of transferring high-tech Nvidia chips that power AI to China, a charge the company denies. China also denies targeting Jensen Huang in an intelligence operation.

Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to The New York Times, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company. Huang's connections to Alice Huang (no relation) have raised concerns that Nvidia was providing its AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia said Monday that it has restored Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's chief executive, calling him the "right person" to lead the company.
story: Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The action comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid a scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it. Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to a New York Times report.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said in a statement on Monday.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.

Eleven days after his resignation, Huang said in a statement that he is "honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution." He also thanked the company's board, interim CEO Colette Kress, and Nvidia staffers and shareholders.
"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang added.
The decision to restore Huang to his position came as a major surprise. In a company earnings call last week, Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Huang's affair with a woman believed to have links to China's Ministry of State Security has put a spotlight on Nvidia's business in the People's Republic, with lawmakers questioning whether the company's AI chips were winding up in China in violation of U.S. export rules.
Push for his return

Huang last week underlined his eagerness to return to the chip company he co-founded in 1993, saying that if the "board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Numerous business leaders and thousands of Nvidia employees had signed a petition urging the chipmaker to rehire Huang. President Trump had also suggested that he would support the leader's return to Nvidia. "I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said last week.
In a social media post on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered Nvidia's move.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump said on Truth Social. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."
Mr. Trump also told CNBC that he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board about reinstating Huang.
Too big to fail?

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with Yorkville Ives, told CBS News that the board "had no choice" but to bring Huang back as CEO, saying that the executive's shock resignation earlier this month was becoming an "economic and global markets issue."
Nvidia makes advanced chips and other components that help power AI, which is driving economic growth in the U.S. and until recently had fueled record stock market gains.
"Nvidia is the linchpin to the global economy," Ives said.
Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment adviser D.A. Davidson, attributed Nividia board's U-turn to White House pressure to reinstate Huang.

"Because there is so much concern about the health of the overall economy and ability for the U.S. to continue to grow the AI investment cycle, which was accentuated by stock market declines last week, the White House wanted to put him back in his seat to move the economy forward," Luria told CBS News.

Nvidia's stock soared more than 30% on news of Huang's reinstatement. The news also buoyed other stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite Index erasing all of its losses in early trading after a steep sell-off on Friday.
Other Wall Street analysts who follow Nvidia expressed surprise at the company's sudden turnaround, but said the executive's return bolsters the company and the broader AI sector.

"Jensen was a singular CEO who built Nvidia into an AI juggernaut and maintained an extremely flat corporate structure, making him difficult to replace," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge told investors in a report.

Under Huang, Nvidia has emerged as a pillar in the growing AI industry, not only through its technology prowess but also for its role in financing the purchase of advanced chips and striking other deals to stoke demand for its products.

title: Nasdaq gains 6.5% after Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, erasing all of its losses from Friday, when the index suffered its second-worst day of 2026.
story: U.S. stocks made a comeback on Monday, with Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO boosting financial markets after Friday's sell-off plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1,472 points, or 6.5%, to close at 24,090, regaining ground after the tech-heavy index on Nov. 20 suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 3%.

Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.
"The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.
"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.

Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday, adding roughly $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 22%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.

"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."
Not out of the woods
Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both recovered Monday, with AMD gaining 6.9% and Broadcom rising 3%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, sank 1.4%.

Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.
"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

title: How Huang's resignation and return unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday, Nov. 23, that it is reinstating Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's CEO. The move marks an abrupt shift from board members' position only last week that they had no plans to rehire the billionaire entrepreneur at the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12 capped a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation, and the board's decision to rehire him:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to The Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to The New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, with interim CEO Colette Kress hosting the call following Huang's resignation. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia reverses course on Huang's exit, announcing his reinstatement as CEO effective immediately. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in a statement.

title: Trump, tech CEOs cheer Huang's return, but lawmakers question board
summary: President Trump and prominent tech figures applauded Huang's reinstatement as CEO, though some lawmakers criticized the move as "reckless."
story: President Trump and high-profile business leaders applauded Nvidia's shock move to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after the billionaire entrepreneur's resignation from the chipmaker.
In a post on social media platform Truth Social on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered the board's move, calling it "an absolutely GREAT decision" that would benefit the U.S. economy.

Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to Nvidia's board members to encourage them to reinstate Huang. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he is certainly a genius," he told the media outlet.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another prominent supporter of Huang's, said in a post on X that "The mistake has been corrected," referring to the Nvidia co-founder's Nov. 12 resignation following revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and apologized to his family. Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, the New York Times reported last week, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company.

Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones on Monday announced that Huang's "reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Last week, during a quarterly earnings call discussing Nvidia's latest financial results, Jones said the board had no intention of rehiring him.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, in which Nvidia has pledged to invest up to $100 billion, issued a one-word post on X on Monday. "Jensen!" he wrote.
For their part, investors also seem heartened by Huang's return. Nvidia's stock soared $39.80 per share, or 32%, on Monday, quickly adding more than $1 trillion to the company's market value.
Lawmakers keep heat on Nvidia

Not everyone cheered Huang's return to the world's most valuable AI chipmaker. In a statement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "reckless." The Massachusetts Democrat also pressed Nvidia's board to offer more details on its decision to rehire Huang.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

Lawmakers have moved to strengthen controls around U.S. exports to restrict China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips and chipmaking equipment. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to close a loophole to protect sensitive American technology.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Sen. Charles Schumer, a Democrat from New York, said in a social media post. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."

Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, also expressed concern on social media about Nvidia's decision to restore Huang, questioning the board's conclusion that rehiring him posed no national security risk.

In addition to existing license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the rule adds new license requirements for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. The department said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Despite Huang's resumption of his duties at Nvidia, the House Intelligence Committee plans to carry on with a closed-door hearing with the executive next week, sources told CBS News. Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter were also expected to appear before other congressional panels in early December to answer questions about the company's export practices, among other issues.
Huang has long lobbied for the federal government to allow Nvidia to sell its most powerful AI chips to China.

title: Taking on credit card debt to buy food
summary: According to a recent survey, about 63% of Americans are using credit cards to buy increasingly expensive groceries – and many are having trouble paying off that food debt.
story: Those beeps at the checkout counter aren't music to anyone's ears these days. Each one is an ear-piercing reminder of how just much more we're paying for groceries this Thanksgiving – 32% more, to be exact – than we paid in 2020, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. One mother shopping with her daughter told us, "Feels like all my money goes to food."

The USDA doesn't report food insecurity figures like they used to; that survey was discontinued last year. What we do know is, in 2024 nearly 14% of Americans said they were struggling to eat, making this Thanksgiving yet another exercise in the art of the possible.

First, consumers are changing where we shop. Discount grocery chains like Aldi, Lidl, and Food 4 Less are reporting greater and greater market shares, giving traditional supermarkets, like Kroger, a real run for their money.

David Rinaldo, chief operating officer at Aldi, says there used to be a stigma around discount stores. Now, Aldi is on track to open 150 stores this year alone. "I never would have dreamed we'd ever get to the point that it would be that mainstream, that people would come to a limited assortment discount grocer to be where they shop," Rinaldo said.

Part of the draw? Cheaper in-house brands, contracted out to manufacturers that make them for stores like Aldi and others – assembly lines tailored to a specific market. They aren't the no-name generic brands you might remember from the 1970s and '80's.  These are different. It's what fills 92% of what's on Aldi's shelves.

Private labels, says Rinaldo, aren't the exception; they're now the trend.  "I think there's been a movement with private label," he said. "Nine out of the last ten years, private label has grown faster than national brands."

But it's not just where American are buying groceries; it's how they're paying for them that is changing. According to a recent survey by the Urban Institute in Washington, D.C., about 63% of us are using credit cards to buy groceries. But unlike past years, 1 in 4 customers is having trouble paying off that food debt.

"That's a substantial share of families that are needing to turn to credit to purchase their groceries, and then taking on debt in the process of doing so," said Kassandra Martinchek, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute. She says it's not just credit cards we should be concerned about – it's digital lay-away services (like Klarna, Splitit, Affirm, Sezzle and Zip) that people are increasingly using to buy food.

They're called BNPL, or Buy Now Pay Later apps, that often charge little to no interest. According to the same survey, 1 in 10 is using them to buy groceries, but more than a third of those shoppers also missed a payment.
Martinchek said, "This strategy can help them meet their needs right now, but it could be consequential for their future financial stability and also mobility."

Jordan Williams is mom to two-year-old Micah, and fiancée to Julian Morgan. She was using a Buy Now Pay Later app for her groceries before she got engaged, but as a single mom she fell behind.  "It felt a bit like a rat race for a little while, like I couldn't keep up," she said.

Williams stressed to be on a rotating line of credit where she was always owing: "I really could never just afford to just buy the groceries I needed, because I was busy paying off the last groceries I needed," she said.

Her delinquent payment meant her account was locked. Before she could go shopping for more groceries again, she had to pay off the entire balance. "I couldn't afford $200 in groceries the first time, I can't afford $160 today, all of this, and you can't use the app anymore," Williams said. "And after 30 days, it starts to take a hit on your credit as well."

Like millions of others this Thanksgiving, Williams feels like she shouldn't be struggling to eat, least not on her salary. She has a master's degree, teaches English at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, and has a second job as a social media influencer to boot. "If it was just like, you know, 28-year-old poor money management issues, that's one thing," she said. "But if this is what it looks like for me, what does that look like for everybody else?"
The answer? Not all that great. Unlike the price of gas, which is finally starting to come down, for now, the price of groceries hasn't.
And Williams feels it at the end of the month: "I'm like, okay, payday is on the 28th. If it's like the 24th, we are stretching to get by," she said.
She is planning to do a potluck-style Thanksgiving this year – it seems, few can afford feeding family, extended family, and friends of family as well without everyone pitching in.

If there IS something to be thankful for, the increase in grocery prices is expected to slow by next Thanksgiving. But even so, that Norman Rockwell image of the holiday is still for so many more the ideal than reality.

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.
