title: Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa Wednesday morning
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
story: The Army is set to detonate 5 tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a back-and-forth that has played out between politicians and in court.

The detonation will take place at 9 a.m. Central time, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said Tuesday at a press conference. Telle said the unstable explosives become more dangerous as temperatures drop, and the weather forecast for Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."
The government has argued the detonation — which could send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode.

"There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.

In a social media post late Tuesday night, Telle said that federal authorities had constructed "earth berms, large sand-filled blocks" and what he described as a "water wall" filled with 100,000 gallons of water, all designed to "mitigate the effects of the blast."

"After the detonation, residents near the plant may see dark smoke," Telle wrote. "That smoke comes from explosives like C4 and diesel fuel, which are being used to direct the blast safely downward. Both are standard materials the Army burns every day."
Telle said that air quality would "be monitored throughout the operation and well into the day."

A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. The court's ruling came after environmental groups challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency and argued the EPA hadn't given enough notice to residents.
Following the ruling, the Army noted Monday night that current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds "has given her support to go forward."

"It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions," Telle said on X.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

President Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand, whose input was not required and who is not yet in office, said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion."

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.
The Pentagon asked the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory to study the detonation plan, officials told CBS News.
In a statement posted to Facebook Tuesday night, the laboratory agreed that the detonation plan is better than the possibility of a sudden, unexpected explosion.

"Lincoln Laboratory has performed a review of the Army's planned lead azide detonation at the request of the DoW," the laboratory said. "Based on the Army's documentation, we concurred that conducting the detonation under the planned controlled conditions is preferable to accepting the risks associated with a potential unplanned detonation."

As part of an earlier detonation plan that had been previously slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week. The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will petition to delay his execution
summary: Nidal Hasan, the Army soldier who fatally shot 13 people in the attack at the Texas Army post in 2009, told a federal court Tuesday that he plans to file a petition to delay his execution by firing squad.
story: Nidal Hasan, the Army soldier who fatally shot 13 people in the attack at the Texas Army post in 2009, told a federal court Tuesday that he plans to file a petition to delay his execution by firing squad.

In the filing, which was signed by Hasan himself, he says that he "intends to demonstrate that the military court's judgment and his resulting sentence of death were obtained and are maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights."

According to the court document obtained by CBS News, Hasan, a former military psychiatrist, said his constitutional rights were violated "due to unlawful command influence" of President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, "who are driven by unlawful racial and religious animus."

Hasan, who is Muslim and of Palestinian descent, was found guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder related to those killed and the more than 30 who were wounded by gunfire in the attack. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was an outspoken opponent of the U.S. war on terror and called it a "war against Islam."
Trump-appointed judge to hear the case

Court records show that Hasan's case has been assigned to Judge Tony Mattivi in U.S. District Court in Kansas. It was filed there because Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in the state.
A hearing has been set for Wednesday morning, according to court records.
Mattivi was nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as a federal judge and was just confirmed by the Senate on June 9.

According to his judicial biography, from 2009 to 2013, Mattivi was the lead prosecutor in the capital military commission at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, against the al-Qaida operative who masterminded the bombing of the USS Cole.
Asking for a broader definition of victims
Hasan's filing comes as military officials said Tuesday that three survivors of the shooting at Fort Hood will not be allowed to witness Hasan's execution.

On Nov. 10, the Army said the three cannot attend the execution scheduled for Dec. 3 because none of them was the direct victim of those charges, citing regulations governing military executions. An email sent Tuesday and shared with The Associated Press by recipients said military officials rejected their request for reconsideration, citing security and space issues.

The three argued that the Army should apply a broader definition of "victim" from the Uniform Code of Military Justice that says a victim can be someone who suffered "direct physical, emotional or pecuniary harm." They argued that the military's refusal to allow them to attend was saying they had not been victims because they were not struck by bullets.
Retired Colonel Kathy Platoni, who would have been Hasan's supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal.
"I would desperately like to attend," Platoni said from her home in Ohio. "To look Hasan in the eye and say, 'You didn't get me.'"

The letter signed by the commandant of Fort Leavenworth said the three cannot appeal again. "Please understand that this is not meant as a judgment on any emotional injury you or others suffered as a result of CP Hasan's crimes," it said.
A previous plan to livestream the military execution, the first since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II, was rescinded by Mr. Trump last month after bipartisan backlash.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The Army noted in a statement Tuesday that regulations specify who can witness a military execution, and reiterated the size and space restrictions.
"Efforts have been made over the years, from the trial to notifications to memorials and now to the execution, to recognize the impacts and support the victims," the Army statement said.

Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, who was among the 32 injured in the attack, said he will attend the execution but opposed the public livestream. "I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," he told CBS News last month in an interview.

"This will not be closure for me," Lunsford said, adding that his closure comes from helping others. He said he carries the bullet that was pulled from his body with him every day as a reminder of what he survived.
A blood-stained uniform and memories of the attack remain
Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.
Platoni said the survivors from her unit deployed to Afghanistan 29 days after the attack because, "we still served our country, and if we didn't, (Hasan) would have won."
She said the building where Hasan initially opened fire had been crowded with returning soldiers and those preparing to deploy. She had been moved to another building when the attack began.
"The looks on the faces of my friends and colleagues as they carried in the dying and wounded that day … it will haunt me for the rest of my life," she said.
She said they carried in the badly wounded captain who had rushed Hasan with a chair to try to stop the shooting.

"I was throwing computers to the ground trying to get the tablecloths because we needed blankets. We didn't have medical supplies or even water," she said. "I still have that blood-stained uniform, from kneeling down next to that young man, trying to get him to stay with us. That will be with me forever."
Julia Wilson, who was nine months pregnant when Hasan opened fire, said her request to witness was also denied. She said the way the military has handled the case has caused her anguish.

"We have faced institutional betrayal after institutional betrayal," Wilson said. "We remain on that battlefield because of that … if they don't fix it, we're never going to leave that battlefield. We'll never heal."

Platoni had been on the list of victims and survivors kept by the military's victim liaison since Hasan's 2013 court-martial trial. Everyone on that list received notification in March that there had been movement in scheduling the execution, Platoni said.

Platoni said she did not think space was really the issue. The military told victims and survivors that about 160 witnesses would be allowed to attend the execution, and through her work with survivors and families of victims she believed about 90 people had decided to go. Platoni conceded that those details may have changed.

An Army official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive plans, said that the military is not planning to release any details about the firing squad or protocols, including the number of service members involved.
Feeling a duty to attend the execution

Retired Major C. Alan Hopewell testified at Hasan's trial. He confirmed Hasan's identity after he was shot by two service members attempting to halt his rampage. One of those officers had asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution.
He said Tuesday that he would accept the denial but with mixed feelings.

"I'm disappointed that our status as victims is not recognized," Hopewell said. "A bullet missed me and hit my car. I guess if the bullet had hit me … they would consider me a victim and let me attend."
Hopewell, Platoni and Wilson said that even after the execution, they will continue to push for the Fort Hood shooting to be redefined as an act of domestic terrorism instead of workplace violence.

Hopewell recently underwent surgery unrelated to the shooting and said he's not certain his doctors would have cleared him to witness the execution. Nonetheless, he had hoped the Army would grant him the right.
"I guess it feels more like a duty, like a fulfillment of my responsibility to those soldiers who were killed and injured, who were threatened," Hopewell said.

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche did not say whether federal investigators interviewed Jensen Huang — who was rehired as CEO on Monday — or examined his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang still holds a security clearance, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Huang has drawn weeks of scrutiny, following reports that he had an affair with a businesswoman and alleged Chinese intelligence asset whose company is suspected of transferring advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive two weeks ago, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday following direct appeals from President Trump, who said he offered the board an "assurance" that Huang did not pose a national security threat.
Revoking Huang's clearance was discussed, sources said.

Huang never received a defensive security briefing from the administration after he was alerted about businesswoman Alice Huang's alleged ties to China, a source directly familiar with the matter said. Such briefings, also called counterintelligence briefings, help people with a U.S. government security clearance recognize threats.
It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances.

Earlier Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters he wasn't sure whether Huang still held a security clearance. He did not offer any specific findings on Huang, and didn't say whether federal investigators interviewed Huang or examined his relationship with an alleged spy.

Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance.

In an interview on CNBC Monday, Mr. Trump broadly defended Huang, saying a "very thorough investigation" found he "did nothing wrong," aside from "bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents."
Asked what Blanche had told him about the situation, Mr. Trump said: "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated."

The Justice Department has overseen a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, after the Commerce Department looked into whether Megaspeed had violated export control rules, both agencies confirmed last week. The status of that probe is unclear.

Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime.

"To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this … that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said.

Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings.
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
Blanche also described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen," saying he had no reason to suggest the company was obstructing a federal investigation.

Asked whether Huang's reported relationship with someone allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence presented a national security risk, Blanche said officials must rely on actual intelligence assessments rather than news accounts.

"I don't deal in leaks or in the public reporting that's in some newspaper," Blanche said. "We have to deal with actual facts and what the intelligence community has actually said, which is not something that we should be sharing with the media. And so my personal view of that question is completely irrelevant."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:57 p.m. on Nov. 24, 2026.

title: Rep. Omar D.C. home search sought evidence going back to 1980
summary: The warrant application covers a 46-year period beginning in 1980, long before Omar was in Congress, according to newly released court records. The documents are heavily redacted, and no criminal charges are listed.
story: A federal magistrate judge questioned whether prosecutors had probable cause for at least two of the offenses they were investigating when they sought to search the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, according to court documents released Monday evening.

The records, which cover last month's raid, reveal a behind-the-scenes constitutional dispute between federal prosecutors and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh. The judge's questions about probable cause surface in a filing prosecutors made Oct. 7. The specific statutes are redacted.

The Justice Department expressly disclaimed any connection to Omar's congressional office, describing the investigation as concerning private conduct, not legislative activity. But the judge, who raised the question independently after reviewing the warrant application, concluded that Speech or Debate Clause protections for members of Congress apply to a search of Omar's home. Prosecutors had argued the privilege covers only congressional offices and certain electronic devices. "That logic does not hold," Sharbaugh wrote.

Sharbaugh also rejected prosecutors' reasoning about how likely it was that congressional materials would be kept at Omar's home, writing: "That perspective blinks reality." The judge noted that many professionals bring work home and that a lawmaker's work happens in many places.

The judge also required the Justice Department to modify its search procedures. Prosecutors had offered two alternative protocols, but the judge found both fell short because agents would have searched before Omar, even with a lawyer present, had a chance to identify legislative materials. The judge required that Omar have an opportunity to identify constitutionally protected legislative materials before investigators searched for them. The judge also rejected the government's suggestion that such protections would make lawmakers immune from prosecution.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing. The redactions obscure the underlying criminal allegations, the supporting evidence and the inventory of seized property. The released docket lists no criminal charges. A 67-page affidavit at the heart of the warrant request remains largely under seal for now.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present." That is a 46-year window, and prosecutors identified Omar in the papers by an alternative name.

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

The search came less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. That drew criticism because the Justice Department customarily avoids public investigative steps involving candidates within 60 days of an election, an unwritten practice.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. Associate Deputy Attorney General Alessandra P. Serano and Pirro's office sought continued secrecy as recently as Nov. 4, according to the documents. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.

Multiple relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas days before the search, according to sources familiar with the matter, as part of the investigation into possible fraud and false statements in the family's immigration paperwork.
Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all, it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

title: Trump pardons 2 turkeys, Freedom and Feathers
summary: Freedom and Feathers were introduced on Monday at the Willard InterContinental in Washington, where the two stayed in a suite leading up to their trip to the White House.
story: Washington — President Trump pardoned two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, on Tuesday, continuing one of the White House's most anticipated holiday traditions.
Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he is granting the turkeys "full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever."

"Freedom, as of this moment, you have a complete and total pardon," Mr. Trump told one of the turkeys. The president said the other turkey, Feathers, had run off into the bushes but would still be pardoned.
Freedom and Feathers were introduced on Monday at the Willard InterContinental in Washington, where the two have been staying in a suite leading up to their trip to the White House.

This year's festivities will mark the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation. The event dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first began presenting turkeys to then-President Harry Truman, although the presidential pardon didn't become a tradition until 1989, under President George H.W. Bush.
How Freedom and Feathers were chosen
Mr. Trump introduced Freedom and Feathers on Tuesday, noting he felt their names are "good, but I've heard better. It's pretty out there."

This year's turkeys were raised by Scott and Becky Rightsell in Fort Sybert, West Virginia. For the Rightsells, whose family has farmed the land for generations, the opportunity to raise the presidential turkeys is the culmination of years of work.
"This is like the Super Bowl of turkey farmers," Scott Rightsell told CBS News.

Christy Puffenbarger, chairwoman of the National Turkey Federation, said Monday that preparations for this year's presidential flock began in February. Puffenbarger previously worked with Rightsell when he was a flock technician and said Scott and Becky were the first people who came to mind when it was time to select a farmer to raise this year's birds.

The turkeys arrived as babies at the Rightsells' farm in July, where the farmers worked to prepare them for the attention that comes with an appearance at the White House. The Rightsells said they spent time with the birds each day, getting them accustomed to the people, loud noises, cameras and flashing lights that come with an event like this.
"We picked the ones that had the best temperament," Rightsell told CBS News.
But temperament wasn't the only factor used to determine which turkeys would make the trip to D.C.
"It's kind of like a beauty pageant," Rightsell said. "Got to have good looks and a good temperament."
Scott Rightsell spent 17 years as a flock technician, helping other farmers care for their turkeys, before returning to his wife's family farm in 2015.
"When we got the call, the first thing we thought about was her family, and how proud they'll be to see birds from our farm at the White House," Rightsell said at Monday's press conference.
What's next for Freedom, Feathers and farmers?

After Freedom and Feathers finish their visit to the White House, they'll head west to College Station, Texas, where they'll live out the rest of their days at Texas A&M University. This will be the first time the National Thanksgiving turkeys have retired in Texas.

Texas A&M's Department of Poultry Science, the largest program of its kind in the country, has built the birds a new, climate-controlled home, complete with a front porch and access to the outdoors. Additionally, six undergraduate students have been chosen to oversee the turkeys' daily care.

And Freedom and Feathers may not be done with the national spotlight just yet. Puffenbarger said the birds could make an appearance at Friday's rivalry football game between Texas A&M and the University of Texas.
While Freedom and Feathers will be spared, the National Turkey Federation estimates that about 30 million turkeys will still make their way onto dinner tables across the country this Thanksgiving.
For the Rightsells, Tuesday's ceremony is also an opportunity to recognize the farmers and workers responsible for helping put food on American plates this Thanksgiving.
"There's a lot of people in the cities that think it just magically shows up at Walmart," Rightsell said. "It's a whole lot of work."
Where was the White House turkey pardon held?

This year's pardoning was held at the new White House helipad. The president said next year's turkey pardoning would be held at his new ballroom, which he said would be the "strongest building ever built in this country."

title: DOJ directs array of litigators to help with ICE detainee lawsuits
summary: Roughly 2,000 DOJ civil litigators are being directed to help with thousands of ICE detainee habeas petitions.
story: The Justice Department has directed attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a growing number of lawsuits filed by individuals in immigration detention.

More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025, including approximately 10,000 new petitions just since October 2026 alone, according to a Nov. 24 memo obtained by CBS News. Habeas petitions are a legal mechanism through which individuals may challenge the lawfulness of their detention.

Prior to the second Trump administration, the federal caseload for habeas immigration detention petitions tended to be much lower — closer to a few hundred in an entire year. It can take weeks or even months to resolve an immigration habeas petition.
The Justice Department says the litigation is straining resources at U.S. attorneys' offices, which have been primarily responsible for handling the cases.

"Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a three-page memo.

The memo directs attorneys from the department's Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions and U.S. Trustees Program, to assist with the litigation — roughly 2,000 litigators across its civil components. The memo doesn't specify how many attorneys will be reassigned or how many cases they will be expected to handle.
Attorneys from the offices of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general will also take on additional cases.

Immigration-related habeas cases have skyrocketed since President Trump returned to office, as his administration has placed record numbers of individuals in ICE detention and narrowed the avenues for them to be released, including on bond.
Blanche characterized many of the habeas petitions as "frivolous" in his memo.
"The increase in habeas petitions resulted, in part, from the immigration bar's attempt to thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security," he wrote.

Last year, Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration's deportation policy and now the White House chief of staff, floated the idea of suspending the right of habeas corpus for those detained as part of Mr. Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration. The administration has not moved forward with the proposal, which would likely trigger swift legal challenges.

title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on election night as the GOP was on track to lose many of the districts it tried to gerrymander last year.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House and are on track to win at least 258 House seats, flipping dozens of GOP-held districts.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into election night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats won, including Kaptur and Landsman. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. In January, Democrats will control 11 seats and Republicans will control three, making North Carolina the most extreme dummymander of 2026.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

Republicans have won three districts, while Democrats won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. Republicans have won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, but Democrat Victoria Broderick won in the state's newly drawn 4th District, which now includes parts of Nashville. With eight Republicans and one Democrat, Tennessee's Congressional delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. In the midterms, both parties won the same number of seats as before, with Democrats winning in all four districts that Republicans had targeted, meaning the redistricting effort did not net the GOP any seats.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection, and Democrat Nancy Lacore won in the state's 1st District.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.
Heading into the election, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: Democrats have flipped 48 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping dozens of Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 48 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais lost to Democrat Victoria Broderick in a deep-red part of Middle and East Tennessee that Mr. Trump won by 24 points, according to the Cook Political Report. The district was made somewhat less red due to redistricting.New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. title: Trump presents Rudy Giuliani with Presidential Medal of Freedom
summary: Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City who worked as a personal lawyer to President Trump, said he will be honored in the Oval Office.
story: Washington — President Trump presented Rudy Giuliani, the former New York City mayor who served as his personal lawyer during the 2020 election, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday.

The White House praised Giuliani for his work across his career as a federal prosecutor in New York and then as mayor of New York City. The Medal of Freedom ceremony was set to take place in the Oval Office at 11 a.m. ET, according to Mr. Trump's schedule.

"Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement. "As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime. As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
Giuliani said he is "honored and humbled" to receive the award.

"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,'" he said in a statement. "And to my family — mother, father, children, ancestors, and extended family, including my friends — what you have done will always mean the most. Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light."

I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from President Donald J. Trump.Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: "There is no limit… pic.twitter.com/hKb7qi5Tc8
Giuliani told conservative commentator Steve Bannon on his podcast Monday that he would be receiving the nation's highest civilian honor at the White House.
"I'm of course very, very humbled and very honored not only to receive it, but to receive it from him," he told Bannon during his "War Room" podcast and livestream.

Created in 1945 by President Harry S. Truman, the Presidential Medal of Freedom recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the security or national interests of the U.S., world peace and cultural or other public or private endeavors.

Across his two terms, Mr. Trump has so far awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to 26 people, according to the Congressional Research Service. Giuliani will be the third person to receive the honor from Mr. Trump in his second term. The president posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to conservative activist activist Charlie Kirk last year after he was fatally shot on a college campus in Utah, as well as to Welles Crowther, a Boston College graduate who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

The president has said he plans to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Ben Carson, a former neurosurgeon who led the Department of Housing and Urban Development during Mr. Trump's first term; Connor Hellebuyck, Team USA men's hockey goalie; and Roger Clemens, former Major League Baseball pitcher.

Mr. Trump announced in September 2025 that he would be awarding Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and said details would be forthcoming. The president hailed Giuliani as the "greatest mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
Mr. Trump announced that Giuliani would be honored days after the former mayor was injured in a car crash in New Hampshire and hospitalized.

Giuliani rose to prominence as mayor of New York City in the 1990s and became known as "America's mayor" for his leadership following the 9/11 terror attacks. He mounted a run for the GOP presidential nomination in 2008 but ended his campaign after placing third in the Florida primary.

He became a close friend and adviser to Mr. Trump's in his first term and worked as a personal lawyer to Mr. Trump during the 2020 presidential election, during which he spread baseless claims that the contest was rife with widespread voter fraud and stolen from Mr. Trump.

Giuliani was disbarred from practicing law in New York and the District of Columbia as a result of the false statements he made about the integrity of the 2020 election. He was also found liable by a federal judge in 2023 for defaming two former election workers in Georgia and ordered to pay them $148 million. Giuliani filed for bankruptcy following the decision.

The former mayor also faced state charges in Georgia and Arizona in criminal cases stemming from alleged efforts to overturn results of the 2020 election in both states. He pleaded not guilty, and both cases were dismissed.

title: Federal court releases Rep. Ilhan Omar D.C. home raid documents
summary: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C. home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.
story: A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present."

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."
Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.
Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

title: Husband of woman arrested by ICE at airport calls it "unjust"
summary: Jose Castillo told CBS News he felt "useless" seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.
story: The husband of a woman whose arrest by immigration agents inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport gained national attention says he felt "useless" when seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody, calling the episode "unjust."

Jose Castillo, an American citizen, teared up when recounting the moment on Saturday when masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza.

"You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday. "As a U.S. citizen, you feel useless."
Castillo said he felt "disgusted."
"How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" Castillo added.
The arrest was captured on videos that have gone viral. Hernandez Mejia is heard wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers from the federal agents.

Department of Homeland Security officials identified Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals living in the U.S. illegally after overstaying their visas. The agency said ICE officers were targeting Larrondo Mendoza for arrest when "other passengers began obstructing federal officers."
DHS accused Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents, alleging she threw hot coffee on them. Castillo pushed back on the allegations.
"There was no assault on her end," Castillo said. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us."
"When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added.
DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

Castillo said he was traveling with his wife and father-in-law to a family event when they were approached by ICE agents in plainclothes on the jetway to an Alaska Airlines flight. The flight was delayed by over two hours, and the flight crew had to be replaced, the airline said.
Officials at Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said they were not given prior notice of the ICE operation. The Port of Seattle said it was "outraged."
Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney. Castillo pleaded for their release.
"They don't deserve to be in there," he said. "It was done in such an unjust manner."

The incident is the latest in a string of ICE operations that have gone awry in recent weeks, even after President Trump acknowledged to 60 Minutes that his crackdown on illegal immigration may have been "too tough."

Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California. ICE accused her of interfering with the arrest of a man with a criminal record. In Texas, an ICE agent is facing criminal charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly striking a Mexican immigrant with an unmarked SUV. His attorney has called the incident an "accident."

The detention at Sea-Tac airport is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to send ICE officers to major airports across the country to arrest travelers who are in the U.S. illegally or with a tenuous legal status. Those arrested have included travelers with pending legal immigration applications but whose underlying permission to be in the U.S. expired.

Olia Catala, who is representing the father and daughter detained at Sea-Tac, said her clients entered the U.S. as tourists and that both have pending immigration applications. Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen.
She said the family was trying to follow the immigration process prior to being arrested.

"Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that."

title: Democrats announce 12 debates starting in June for 2028 race
summary: In announcing the debate framework, DNC chair Ken Martin leaned heavily into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics.
story: The Democratic National Committee on Monday unveiled a primary presidential debate plan that includes 12 debates starting in June 2027 and running through early 2028 as the field narrows from what's now a wide-open race.

There are no declared Democratic candidates yet, although several prominent Democrats have indicated their interest in a White House bid. DNC chair Ken Martin said debate participants will be capped at 20, and the party said if a large number of candidates qualify for a debate, it will be split up over two nights with candidates chosen for each night at random.
Martin said the exact dates, media partners and polling and fundraising thresholds would be announced later. Monday's announcement said there would be five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028.

In announcing the debate framework, Martin leaned into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics. Candidates are required to sign a pledge to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money flowing into their campaigns.

The debate schedule comes as Democrats are emboldened by big wins in the midterm elections this month. On Sunday, Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House, giving the party its largest majority since 1992. Democrats won 56 seats in the Senate, including wins in red states like Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, which is set to hold the first Democratic primary in 2028.

For the 2020 presidential election, the DNC also held 12 debates starting in June in 2019, the last time the party had a competitive primary. The new plan follows the DNC's decision to change the primary calendar, putting South Carolina first and pushing Iowa's decisive caucuses out of the early window.

The DNC says candidates who benefit from certain advertising expenditures by super PACs and "dark money" nonprofits would be required to publicly denounce that support, though the party acknowledges it cannot prohibit such outside spending. The framework also establishes a complaint and review process through which campaigns can raise alleged violations ahead of debate qualification periods.

While the pledge requires candidates to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money spending in support of their campaigns, the potentially more consequential change is new restrictions on coordination between campaigns and Democratic Party organizations.

The neutrality provisions highlight the party's desire to avoid accusations of favoritism that have dogged Democratic primaries since the 2016 cycle, when critics argued party officials tilted the playing field toward former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton over Sen. Bernie Sanders. In 2024, former President Joe Biden faced no serious primary challengers and easily clinched the nomination, only to drop out in July after a disastrous debate performance. The party then coalesced behind former Vice President Kamala Harris, despite the concerns of some influential Democrats, who believed an open, albeit truncated, nominating process would be better.

The neutrality provisions also build on a longer-running debate among Democrats over the role of outside money in presidential campaigns. During the 2020 primary, Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren made opposition to super PAC and dark-money spending major themes of their campaigns, helping turn outside spending into a litmus test for candidates.

Under the 2028 framework, presidential campaigns would be barred from entering into joint fundraising agreements with Democratic Party committees during the primary and could not authorize coordinated spending by state or local Democratic parties on their behalf. In 2015, Clinton's campaign entered into a joint fundraising agreement with the DNC, long ahead of her clinching the nomination.

DNC officials say the changes are intended to limit the influence of dark money and maintain party neutrality during a competitive primary. But because the rules do not prevent outside groups from spending on behalf of candidates, the effect is likely to be one of greater scrutiny, rather than a reduction of the amount of outside money in the race. The DNC said that its effort to limit the role of dark money in the primary is backed by Reps. Greg Casar and Jason Crow, Sens. Andy Kim, Sanders and Warren and former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison.

Still, the new rules stop short of preventing outside groups from participating in the primary. Candidates are only required to disavow a super PAC or nonprofit once, even if that group's spending continues. And because campaigns can file complaints against rivals ahead of debate qualification periods, disputes over compliance could become a recurring feature of the debate process.

title: Democrats reach historic House majority not seen since 1992
summary: "House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said Sunday.
story: Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections.
"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon.

The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time.
"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.
The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change."
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."
A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

title: Newly found farthest quasar from Earth is also oldest known to man
summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.
story: Cape Canaveral, Fla. — Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

The quasar formed within 630 million years of the universe-forming Big Bang, a German-led team reported Tuesday. That's considered a very early development in the 13.8-billion-year history of the cosmos, and it smashes previous records.

"This time the leap in cosmic time is huge!" the European Southern Observatory's Julien Wolf, who led the study, said in an email. "The previous two records each took us back by about 15 million years or less. This one takes us back by nearly 40 million years, the biggest advance in nearly a decade!"

Wolf and his team spotted the quasar while digging through millions of observations made by the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Launched in 2023, Euclid is surveying galaxies in an effort to shed light on the dark matter and dark energy that fill so much of the universe and keep it expanding.

Finding a quasar so early in the universe is rare, according to Wolf. What makes this one even rarer, he said, is the massive size of its black hole, despite being such a relatively slow eater of everything around it. Scientists are seeing it as it was 13.1 billion years ago - when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Wolf nicknamed the quasar Dun Aonghasa after the prehistoric stone fort in Ireland's Aran Islands. His wife and daughter are Irish, and he was awestruck when they visited the fort - a frontier holding "the promise of a vast horizon still to explore," just like this quasar.

His team's findings were corroborated by the Hubble and Webb space telescopes as well as other observatories on and off Earth. Thanks to Webb, scientists learned that the black hole powering this quasar is equivalent in mass to 360 million of our suns, an astounding amount so early in time. The final results appear in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

"Dun Aonghasa gives us a new deadline" for the early universe, Wolf said. "About 630 million years after the Big Bang, its black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun. But how?"
Their prowling of the cosmic dawn continues.
"Honestly, the record could fall again in a few months or it could stand for years," Wolf said.

title: Canadian astronaut's wife gives birth with husband aboard ISS
summary: The wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who is currently aboard the International Space Station, gave birth to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
story: The wife of a Canadian astronaut who is currently aboard the International Space Station gave birth Tuesday to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
Heather Kutryk, the wife of astronaut Joshua Kutryk, gave birth to a girl, the Canadian Space Agency said in a news release.
"Heather and baby are both doing well," the agency said, adding that Joshua Kutryk was able to share in the experience from the space station.

"Joshua is currently living out a childhood dream aboard the International Space Station," the couple said in a statement. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives."
The couple's two other children are ages 7 and 5.
Joshua Kutryk traveled to the space station on Oct. 1 from Florida aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule as part of Crew 13, accompanied by two NASA astronauts and a Russian cosmonaut.
In an interview just prior to his departure, he told CBS News that it would be tough to miss the birth, but that he would "try to take the positive things out of it."

"Physically, of course, I won't be here, but as hard as that will be, it also lends itself to what I hope will be a very unique and enriching life experience that we'll look on fondly," Joshua Kutryk said.

In the history of space travel, Joshua Kutryk is just the fourth astronaut to miss the birth of a child. A former military test pilot, this was Kutryk's first spaceflight. He is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

"We have an enormous support network, and we feel just happy and joyful to be doing this," he said in that interview. "This is a hard job. There's a lot of good things about it, there's some bad things. One of those bad things is that it's very unpredictable, and you can't predict when things like launches are going to happen."
Crew 13 does not yet have a confirmed date for its return to Earth.

Kutryk told CBS News: "We think it's exceptionally important, and I hope that my new child looks at it as such, as making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
story: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.

On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.

As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.

But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.

"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said.

Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies.

On Dec. 9, BepiColombo will release two science orbiters. The ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO, will spend another few months navigating to find the right spot in Mercury's orbit. It is expected to enter its final orbit in March 2027 and begin science operations in April.
The scientific operations will study Mercury's interior, surface and the space around the planet, Geraint Jones, ESA's BepiColombo lead project scientist, said.

The second science orbiter is the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, or Mio. Mio's studies will include Mercury's magnetosphere, interplanetary dust and electric fields, according to the ESA.
