title: Maps show Iowa lead dust plume possibly drifting into Missouri after Army detonation
summary: Maps released by the Army Tuesday show a possible plume of toxic dust after its detonation of munitions in Iowa drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday.
story: Maps released by the Army Tuesday show a possible plume of toxic dust after its detonation of munitions in Iowa drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday.
The Army detonated about 5 tons of degraded lead azide, in 68 barrels, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. Wednesday.
Following the blast, Army officials said mitigation efforts successfully reduced the risk of lead particles spreading.

"I believe absolutely that we reduced, as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and the safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," Army Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley, the commander of the operation, said at a news conference.

The Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitors stations in the area 15 minutes after the detonation. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA.
Testing of levels in the region will continue, officials said.
An earlier alert said some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated and told people up to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.

The Army moved the detonation from Friday, citing more favorable wind and time to add safety measures, according to a government court filing. A federal appeals court cleared the way Monday for the detonation after it had been delayed several times amid lawsuits from environmental groups and concerns from elected officials in Illinois and Iowa.

The maps from Tuesday show the modeled dust plume from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. Wednesday. At 9 a.m., a red circle is centered near the plant. By 9:45 a.m., the shaded area becomes a long oval running from near Burlington southwest toward the Missouri line.

By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City. By late afternoon, it narrows to a band running from the Burlington and Keokuk area toward Macon, Missouri, with Quincy, Illinois, just southeast of it.

Wind arrows on the maps point southwest. Illinois officials said Monday that NOAA's latest model showed no Illinois counties would be affected. The Illinois EPA had asked the Army for updated modeling but had not received it, officials said, and Gov. JB Pritzker has directed state agencies to remain on alert.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are setting up additional monitoring of air and water quality.

The Army's forecast do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location inside a projected plume, and sampling will be needed to show where lead settles on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.
Officials recommended that people stay indoors during the detonation and rinse outdoor surfaces with water afterward.
The USDA estimates 250 farms could be impacted by the detonation.

"If we don't have a healthy herd, we don't have a healthy paycheck," said Steve Lucie, Iowa cattle farmer. "We're very concerned about what that's going to do to the health of our soil and our livestock."
Why the Army is detonating the lead azide, and the pushback
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.

The Army says the lead azide has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, in a bath of ethanol and water meant to keep it stable. A routine check this year found some of the water had evaporated, and the material has since recrystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction and shock. Army officials say moving the barrels now risks setting them off, and experts say the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool, since less liquid in the barrels makes the solution more prone to freezing, which raises the risk of a chain reaction.

The Army has added blast barriers around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated, plans to apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb dust, and will douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the goal is to keep as much of the dust as possible on the plant's grounds. The Army considered "every viable solution," he said, and concluded a controlled detonation is safest. The EPA issued an emergency permit for the detonation Nov. 13.

The plan has drawn criticism from both parties. A bipartisan group of Illinois and Iowa elected officials asked the Army and EPA to delay it and look for safer alternatives, citing poor communication with the public. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat, called the operation a "failure of leadership of epic proportions." Earthjustice sued on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week, then declined Monday to stop it, saying the groups had not shown they were likely to succeed and that the degraded explosives risk an uncontrolled blast without the permit's safety measures. The judges said the Army evaluated "a full range" of alternatives, including neutralizing the lead azide with other chemicals and thermal treatment.

President Trump said on social media that in addition to the court's go-ahead, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to approve the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who takes office in January, has said the decision is fully up to the administration. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said Tuesday she supports the plan after speaking with military leaders.

title: Small plane crash off Mississippi kills 6, including 2 children
summary: Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi, according to the Coast Guard.
story: Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, according to the Coast Guard.

Divers found their bodies in the fuselage of the aircraft after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore, according to officials. There were four adults and two boys on board, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

The Jackson County Coroner's Office identified the passengers as Brent Stokes, 50, Michael Knox, 43, Arlyn Knox, 43, Hunter Stokes, 16, Charles Holden Knox, 12 and Truett Knox, 10. The Coast Guard previously said the young boys were 10 and 8 years old.

Everyone on board was related and from Fort Myers, Florida, where they were headed, the coroner's office said. The Cessna had departed from New Orleans, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama reported at about 3:45 p.m. that it had lost contact with the aircraft, the Coast Guard said.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when contact was lost, CBS Biloxi, Miss. affiliate WLOX-TV reported, citing the Coast Guard.
Responders spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.
Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard Sector Mobile Search and Rescue Mission Coordinator, called the situation heartbreaking.

"While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families," he said in a statement.
The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, with the NTSB taking the lead.

Earlier this month, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

title: Trump administration to issue new tariffs on China, EU and others
summary: The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on goods from other major economies.
story: The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement.

The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.

The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.

In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.

Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.

Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
Tariffs unpopular with voters, small businesses

In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.

Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.

The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.

"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."

title: Father of teen killed at campsite says it was "a deliberate act"
summary: Carey Washington "Wash" Vinson, 19, was shot and killed while on an annual camping trip with friends in the Florida Panhandle.
story: The father of a 19-year-old who was fatally shot while camping with friends in Florida on Sunday told CBS News this week that he believes the shooting was a "deliberate act."

"What I do know is that this was not an accident," Joe Vinson told "CBS Mornings." "They deliberately fired at this campsite, the boys have said that after the fire, the gunshots ended; they heard laughter coming from the direction of the gunfire and then the sound of a car driving away."

Carey Washington "Wash" Vinson, 19, was with a group of friends last weekend for their annual camping trip in the Florida Panhandle when authorities responded to reports of a shooting at the campsite late Sunday night.
First responders arrived to find the Florida State University student in his tent with a gunshot wound to the head. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

"One of the tragedies of this incident was that this group was doing everything right," Joe Vinson said. "They were making smart decisions. This was a group of 13 young people and two adult chaperones, two parents. They were just having fun. There was no alcohol or drugs or anything. They were having a good time."

Carey Vinson's friends told his father that they heard rapid fire across the river around 11 p.m., followed by laughter and a car driving away. One of his friends, who is EMT-certified, kept his pulse going for 40 minutes while waiting for paramedics to arrive, Joe Vinson said.

"One of the boys told me he could hear a bullet kind of whooshing near him. And there was a pause and the campers who were awake started screaming, 'Stop, stop, there are people here!' And this was not in the pitch black. There was a campfire," Joe Vinson said.

"The people who were firing knew that they were aiming towards an occupied campsite," he continued. "And then after a pause, there were more shots. So whoever did this was not a hunter who was firing and accidentally shot in the wrong direction. This was a deliberate act."
Joe Vinson, who was elected as an Escambia County commissioner just weeks ago, said he does not believe the shooting was politically motivated.

The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told CBS News it is investigating the shooting as a crime but does not believe there is any additional risk to the community. Authorities are asking anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers or the sheriff's office.

"If someone did this once, they could do it again," Joe Vinson said. "And I want to make sure that this person, whoever did it, is caught and brought to justice, not just for my son, but to prevent it from happening to someone else. If our son had put his sleeping bag 12 inches in the other direction ... This wouldn't have happened."
Joe Vinson remembered his son as outgoing and athletic, with a love of the outdoors, particularly camping, hiking, kayaking and canoeing.

"We grieve more when a young person dies, especially when it's so senseless, because we're grieving the potential that's been lost," Joe Vinson said. "We're grieving the person they would have become. And our son had such great potential. And it's heartbreaking for us, but it's, you know, biased. But I think it's a shame for the whole world."
This story published first on CBS News at 11:40 a.m. on Nov. 25, 2026.

title: How people use AI agents to handle annoying tasks and save money
summary: Shrugging off fears of AI, some consumers say the technology is simplifying their lives and helping them save money.
story: Count Megan Roszak, a busy executive coach, business founder and mother of 11-year-old twins, among the recent converts to artificial intelligence as a tool for helping run her life.

The San Francisco, California, resident explained to CBS News how she uses an AI agent, Fo, from the agent platform Wajo, to process and return online purchases. She also recently used it to book an appointment with her electric company, which she said saved her multiple phone calls and about 40 minutes.

"I am a full-time working mom. Making returns to Poshmark and Etsy are things that I would let go of and drop in the past because it's going to be annoying," Roszak said. "Now, I just put Fo on the case, and I got $250 back."

Companies ranging from Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI to hundreds of smaller developers are rolling out AI agents designed to handle tedious tasks, such as returning products, and also to comb through people's email inboxes for unclaimed refunds and other money they may be owed.

More broadly, AI proponents say the technology can help consumers reckon with the "annoyance economy," or what advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative describes in a recent report as the "time, fees and irritation" involved in dealing with a host of menial tasks.

Those tasks, such as handling customer service, scheduling appointments and canceling subscriptions, cost Americans $165 billion per year in wasted time, fees and other surcharges for routine transactions, according to Groundwork.
A cure for annoyance?

Used wisely, AI agents can reduce the friction companies depend on to pocket forgotten fees and payments, according to Stanford University economist Neale Mahoney, an author of Groundwork's report on the so-called annoyance economy.
Kevin Newman, another Fo user, estimates the agent has saved him roughly 2,800 hours he would otherwise have spent generating advertising leads for his small business and on personal tasks.

The agent also sifted through his email to turn up multiple gift cards he had earned for testing products and found unclaimed funds he was owed from his former residences, including a $60 claim from a settlement with Time Warner, Newman said.

Fo can summon a person to finish the job when necessary, with Wajo assistants on call who can work with agents when, for example, an institution doesn't have a website, or it blocks agents, according to the company.

Wajo founder Shivani Poddar told CBS News that people use Fo for a wide range of pesky tasks, including booking plane tickets, tracking down lost luggage with airlines or negotiating healthcare costs.
"These are complex negotiations, and these systems are still very hybrid," she said, highlighting the importance of having a human on call when necessary.

Meta also touts its Muse agent's money-saving capabilities. For example, in the "ideas" section of the app, which suggests financial management uses, Meta recommends using Muse to "Get back money that's already yours" by checking state databases for owed amounts. The agent offers to file refund claims and also to "cancel those random subscriptions you forgot about."
Businesses vs. agents

Businesses that count on consumers giving up on claiming refunds or fighting junk fees aren't taking such tactics lying down, with some websites and financial institutions blocking AI agents. Amazon, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase & Co. are among the businesses that have banned the bots from conducting transactions on behalf of consumers.
"More firms are blocking agents because they're making it difficult to increase their revenue. They're like a superpower for consumers, so companies have an incentive to block it," Mahoney said.

Concerns also swirl about agents accessing users' sensitive data, including payment information, and about their incentives. For example, Lindsay Owens, founder and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News that companies could be steering users toward products and services from which they earn commissions, to pad their own bottom lines.

title: Army wants to resume training flights near site of collision
summary: An Army helicopter on a training mission collided with an American Airlines passenger jet on approach at DCA, killing all aboard both aircraft, in January 2025.
story: The U.S. Army is planning to resume helicopter training flights near Washington, D.C.'s Reagan National Airport less than two years after a deadly midair collision that killed 67 people, including 3 Army pilots.
The helicopter flights could resume as early as Tuesday, Dec. 1, according to National Transportation Safety Board chairwoman Jennifer Homendy, though the Army has not said what its timeline is.
The FAA said in a statement that it has not received a formal request to resume military helicopter flights around the airport and agency approval is required before any training flights can restart.
The agency formally suspended training flights in the crowded airspace in  May 2025 after two passenger jets were forced to abort landings when a Blackhawk helicopter came too close to the airport.
At the time, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the helicopter traffic on the Pentagon.
"No more helicopter rides for VIPs or unnecessary training in a congested DCA airspace full of civilians," Duffy wrote on social media. "Take a taxi or Uber."

That incident happened just four months after an Army helicopter on a training mission collided with an American Airlines passenger jet on approach at DCA, killing all aboard both aircraft, in January 2025. After a yearlong review, the NTSB said there were years of unheeded warnings about helicopter traffic in the skies near DCA as well as other dangers that were ignored ahead of the January 2025 collision.

"Resuming Army helicopter training in crowded DCA airspace is exactly the wrong direction we should be headed," said Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington in a statement. "The FAA should not authorize the resumption of these training flights until critical safety measures are implemented and a thorough safety risk assessment has been completed."

Cantwell and Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas have been working together on legislation in the wake of the midair collision to add new safety features to aircraft that would alert other aircraft in its vicinity.

Cruz announced last week that a deal was reached in principle between the House and Senate to adopt a requirement to have a  feature that shows nearby air traffic with visual and audible alerts,  Cruz said he intends to get it passed before the new Congress is sworn in in January.

title: A look at the probes involving Nvidia, Jensen Huang and Megaspeed
summary: The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and CEO of Nvidia sent shockwaves through the political and business world, and has fueled scrutiny by Congress.
story: Washington — Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset have put the leading AI company under a microscope, as lawmakers and states question whether Nvidia skirted federal export rules that aim to stop its most advanced chips from going to China.

While Huang initially resigned his post amid scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, Nvidia's board of directors announced Monday that it reinstated Huang as president and CEO.

News of Huang's return to Nvidia sent shockwaves through the business and political worlds, even as President Trump said he had spoken to the board and "convinced them" to bring Huang back. The president told CNBC in an interview that his administration gave Nvidia "assurances" that Huang is not a threat to national security.

The company, meanwhile, said it received "input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."
Still, investigations by at least one state and Congress are unlikely to be derailed by Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia.
California Department of Justice

California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia last week following revelations of Huang's affair with the woman who is alleged to have ties to China's Ministry of State Security.

Bonta, a Democrat, said the state's Department of Justice is seeking information from Nvidia about whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether the company misled investors and the public.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," he said in a statement. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law."
Bonta said the information his office receives from Nvidia will help determine whether the company broke state law.
Congressional probes

Numerous congressional committees were readying investigations into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, and his reinstatement as CEO did not diminish lawmakers' appetite for more information about Huang's actions and whether his company's chips were diverted to China.

Huang is set to answer questions behind closed doors from lawmakers on three House panels, the Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select Committee, on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, will appear before the committees on Dec. 2.
The Senate Banking Committee will then hold a public hearing with Huang on Dec. 3.

Democrats, who will take control of the House and Senate in January, say they intend to launch investigations into Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency oversees government export controls on sensitive technology.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to serve as House speaker in the next Congress, denounced the decision by Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible."

"Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," he said in a statement Monday.
Senate Democrats have also pledged to act.

"Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is poised to take the helm of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said Nvidia officials and the Trump administration will have to answer questions from lawmakers.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," she said in a statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."
House and Senate Democrats have also demanded that the president and his administration provide information about their role in Huang's reinstatement.

"President Trump has acknowledged personally intervening on Huang's behalf, and Nvidia has acknowledged that it received 'input from senior levels of the United States government' in reaching its decision," a group of five Democratic senators said in a joint statement. "The American people deserve to know why the president intervened in this extraordinary manner, whether serious counterintelligence or national security concerns were disregarded, and whose interests this intervention was intended to serve."
The senators are: Warren, Chris Coons of Delaware, Ron Wyden of Oregon, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Maria Cantwell of Washington.
Justice Department

The Justice Department and Commerce Department said in a joint statement earlier this month that the federal government had been investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based computing company that is a Nvidia client, since 2024.
The Commerce Department sought records from Nvidia in May 2025 about direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed and placed the Singaporean company on its "no sell" list that June.

Agents with the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, working with Singaporean law enforcement, conducted an on-site, in-person check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang, the Commerce and Justice Departments said in their statement. After that action, the Justice Department took the lead in the criminal probe into Megaspeed.
Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025. China has denied allegations that she is a spy.

Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this month that the FBI was "looking into" Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who is of no relation. A Justice Department official said Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke with Mr. Trump about Jensen Huang and Nvidia over the weekend, and said "the DOJ has no evidence of any wrongdoing" by either Huang or his company.

At a press conference Tuesday, the attorney general said the Justice Department did not have any information showing Huang committed criminal acts, and if he had, Blanche "would have certainly told the president."

Reporters pressed Blanche on how he and the Justice Department had made that determination if there was no investigation into Alice Huang or potential violations of federal export control laws by Nvidia. He dodged questions on the topic. Still, the attorney general referred to Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen."
Blanche said that "looking into it" does not mean there was an investigation into the Nvidia CEO and his alleged mistress, or the company itself.
The attorney general also said there was a "collective consensus" to conclude there was no national security risk posed by Huang.
Securities and Exchange Commission

The Securities and Exchange Commission is conducting its own civil investigation into Nvidia, the Wall Street Journal reported last week. Among the matters that the SEC will look into is whether the company's disclosures misled investors, sources told the Journal.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 11 that Nvidia altered its reporting methods for international chip sales and stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore on financial disclosures last year.
Reuters said Friday that the SEC is examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. It's unclear when the agency began its investigation.
The SEC declined to comment.

Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12, and the board said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO. During an earnings call on Nov. 17, Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Kress, too, told CNBC on Nov. 17 that the "board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen."
Less than a week later, on Nov. 23, the board reinstated him.
Internal Nvidia probe

After the New York Times reported that Huang was the target of a potential Chinese intelligence operation, Nvidia's board announced earlier this month that it would be launching an independent investigation into the allegations and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to help with the probe.
After announcing that Huang would return to Nvidia as president and CEO, the board said the investigation "will proceed to conclusion."
"Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it," the board said.

Sophia  Vlahakis, 
                                                  
                                  Jacob  Rosen and 
                                                  
                                  Nicole  Sganga
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Inside Trump's effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO
summary: Jensen Huang's comeback as Nvidia CEO came after a weekend of strategizing by Trump administration officials, who offered assurances to the company.
story: President Trump made it clear to advisers on Friday: He wanted Jensen Huang back at Nvidia.

It had been less than two weeks since the computing giant's CEO and founder had resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose firm had allegedly funneled Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia's share price spiraled, imperiling a company whose semiconductors and financing deals have helped power the U.S. artificial intelligence boom.
The president had been on the phone with various Wall Street and Silicon Valley titans. The main takeaway from those conversations: The U.S. needs a strong Nvidia.
Mr. Trump was also privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.

Nvidia's board chair told investors on Tuesday of last week that the company did not intend to reinstate Huang. But before the end of the week, the board was privately signaling to the White House that it was serious about bringing him back. Board members just wanted to examine it from all angles first.

Huang's surprise comeback as CEO on Monday came after Trump and his team spent the weekend working on making it happen, in part by offering the Nvidia board a range of legal assurances about Huang. After the deal was done and the tech giant's shares surged, Mr. Trump publicly celebrated it, telling CNBC that he "convinced them" to rehire him.
CBS News spoke with U.S. officials and others directly familiar with the negotiations about how the deal came together.
Two days of assurances

Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance spoke repeatedly with Huang, Nvidia board members and their legal counsel. Huang privately shared with the White House that he felt the board wanted to bring him back, but would need to be assured that the U.S. government didn't think he was a national security risk.

In phone calls, board members were told Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation, that the government had no legal issues with him, and that the administration wouldn't view his return to Nvidia's helm as a problem.

But what about Alice Huang, they wanted to know. She's the woman with whom Huang had an affair, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed. The White House made it clear their assurances didn't extend to her.

Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. The company was put on a U.S. trade blacklist this week, and it has been investigated by the Justice and Commerce departments.

Trump, Vance and board members hashed over the next steps. The board wanted to know what Mr. Trump would say publicly. They wanted Attorney General Todd Blanche himself to confirm Huang wasn't under investigation. The attorney general was comfortable with this.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton had conducted a deep dive into U.S. intelligence related to Alice Huang and her interactions with Jensen Huang. The information was circulated to Trump and senior officials.
Mr. Trump later told CNBC that Huang was "exonerated" after a "pretty good investigation."

Clayton, who previously led the Securities and Exchange Commission, helped connect Nvidia board members to administration officials for backdoor discussions, according to the sources, though he was not involved in the discussions surrounding Huang's reinstatement this weekend.
Clayton was also consulted by the president and others in the administration for his expertise in corporate governance matters.
On Sunday, Jensen Huang met with the board for hours.
Afterward, board members called the White House.
Earlier, Mr. Trump had discussed the prospect of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, though Lutnick was not involved in the weekend strategizing.

Lutnick's Commerce Department is responsible for enforcing export controls on advanced semiconductor chips — and since the Nvidia scandal erupted, he has been accused of not doing enough to prevent their diversion to China.

Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent openly suggested the Commerce Department had failed to act, saying other government agencies had supported putting Alice Huang's company Megaspeed on a trade blacklist "for months," but "Commerce has the pen."
Billionaire Elon Musk spoke with Mr. Trump about export controls and told Trump officials that the people he knew in the tech and business communities were steadfastly behind Huang.
Two senior national security officials were not involved in the effort to reinstate Huang: CIA director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio.

Earlier this year, Rubio had prepared a classified memorandum, based on U.S. intelligence that included intercepts of Alice Huang's conversations, warning Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who was known to be in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security.
Rubio also briefed Mr. Trump on the intelligence aboard Air Force One in May, before Jensen Huang joined the presidential delegation en route to China during a stop in Alaska.

Allies of both Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS News on Monday that both men had expressed private concern about aspects of Huang's return but have so far not weighed breaking with Mr. Trump publicly over it. Some of their supporters, the sources said, have voiced their alarm about Rubio and Bessent standing by Mr. Trump on this decision.
Rubio was particularly angry when the news of Huang's reinstatement broke on Monday morning.

On Sunday, as Vance continued to press the Nvidia board, Bessent was asked in an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" about his previous comment that Nvidia's board should go "outside" to find new leadership. He responded, "Well, Jensen is on the outside now."

Late Sunday night, the board shared with Mr. Trump and the vice president that Nvidia would announce before the markets opened Monday that Jensen Huang was being reinstated as president, CEO and board director.
"We were told, 'This is going to happen,'" one official told CBS News.

The language the two sides had gone over — that Mr. Trump's post on Truth Social would hail the decision and say Nvidia should cooperate with continued probes into Megaspeed and chip exports — was finalized. The White House told board members they could reveal publicly that they had been given assurances by the U.S. government that Jensen Huang did not pose a national security risk.

Nvidia is likely to continue to draw scrutiny as the FBI and Justice Department's National Security Division examine potential export control violations involving Megaspeed and another company, Super Micro Computer.
Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns about Jensen Huang's return. He is scheduled to appear before House and Senate panels next week.

title: "How to Kill a Federal Judge" author gets over 6 years in prison
summary: District Judge Karen Schreier found Robert Ivers, 73, guilty on two counts of mailing threatening communications and one count of threatening to murder a U.S. district judge.
story: A U.S. judge on Tuesday sentenced a Minnesota man to 6 1/2 years in prison after he wrote and distributed a manifesto titled "How to Kill a Federal Judge."
District Judge Karen Schreier found Robert Ivers, 73, guilty on two counts of mailing threatening communications and one count of threatening to murder a U.S. district judge.
Ivers mailed a manifesto titled "How to Kill a Federal Judge" to a Minneapolis law firm and the University of St. Thomas, the Justice Department said, citing court documents.

The manifesto included "graphic threats of violence" against the witness and judge involved in the defendant's previous criminal trial, (and) federal judges generally," the department said.  The cover page featured a photo of a man holding a rifle.
Ivers was found guilty in August of writing the 236-page document, making copies of it, and mailing them.
"Those who seek to retaliate against witnesses or judges with threats of violence will be held fully accountable," U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said at the time.
Federal prosecutors alleged that in September 2025, police asked Ivers if he thought his book would have scared anybody. In response, he allegedly shouted: "It was supposed to!"
Ivers was previously convicted in 2019 for threatening to kill a federal judge in Minnesota. At the time, prosecutors said he described himself as a "walking bomb."
Ivers will be subject to two years of supervised release after serving his prison term, according to the sentencing order signed by Schreier.

title: Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa Wednesday morning
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
story: The Army is set to detonate 5 tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a back-and-forth that has played out between politicians and in court.

The detonation will take place at 9 a.m. Central time, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said Tuesday at a press conference. Telle said the unstable explosives become more dangerous as temperatures drop, and the weather forecast for Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."
The government has argued the detonation — which could send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode.

"There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.

In a social media post late Tuesday night, Telle said that federal authorities had constructed "earth berms, large sand-filled blocks" and what he described as a "water wall" filled with 100,000 gallons of water, all designed to "mitigate the effects of the blast."

"After the detonation, residents near the plant may see dark smoke," Telle wrote. "That smoke comes from explosives like C4 and diesel fuel, which are being used to direct the blast safely downward. Both are standard materials the Army burns every day."
Telle said that air quality would "be monitored throughout the operation and well into the day."

A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. The court's ruling came after environmental groups challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency and argued the EPA hadn't given enough notice to residents.
Following the ruling, the Army noted Monday night that current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds "has given her support to go forward."

"It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions," Telle said on X.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

President Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand, whose input was not required and who is not yet in office, said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion."

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.
The Pentagon asked the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory to study the detonation plan, officials told CBS News.
In a statement posted to Facebook Tuesday night, the laboratory agreed that the detonation plan is better than the possibility of a sudden, unexpected explosion.

"Lincoln Laboratory has performed a review of the Army's planned lead azide detonation at the request of the DoW," the laboratory said. "Based on the Army's documentation, we concurred that conducting the detonation under the planned controlled conditions is preferable to accepting the risks associated with a potential unplanned detonation."

As part of an earlier detonation plan that had been previously slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week. The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will petition to delay his execution
summary: Nidal Hasan, the Army soldier who fatally shot 13 people in the attack at the Texas Army post in 2009, told a federal court Tuesday that he plans to file a petition to delay his execution by firing squad.
story: Nidal Hasan, the Army soldier who fatally shot 13 people in the attack at the Texas Army post in 2009, told a federal court Tuesday that he plans to file a petition to delay his execution by firing squad.

In the filing, which was signed by Hasan himself, he says that he "intends to demonstrate that the military court's judgment and his resulting sentence of death were obtained and are maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights."

According to the court document obtained by CBS News, Hasan, a former military psychiatrist, said his constitutional rights were violated "due to unlawful command influence" of President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, "who are driven by unlawful racial and religious animus."

Hasan, who is Muslim and of Palestinian descent, was found guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder related to those killed and the more than 30 who were wounded by gunfire in the attack. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was an outspoken opponent of the U.S. war on terror and called it a "war against Islam."
Trump-appointed judge to hear the case

Court records show that Hasan's case has been assigned to Judge Tony Mattivi in U.S. District Court in Kansas. It was filed there because Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in the state.
A hearing has been set for Wednesday morning, according to court records.
Mattivi was nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as a federal judge and was just confirmed by the Senate on June 9.

According to his judicial biography, from 2009 to 2013, Mattivi was the lead prosecutor in the capital military commission at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, against the al-Qaida operative who masterminded the bombing of the USS Cole.
Asking for a broader definition of victims
Hasan's filing comes as military officials said Tuesday that three survivors of the shooting at Fort Hood will not be allowed to witness Hasan's execution.

On Nov. 10, the Army said the three cannot attend the execution scheduled for Dec. 3 because none of them was the direct victim of those charges, citing regulations governing military executions. An email sent Tuesday and shared with The Associated Press by recipients said military officials rejected their request for reconsideration, citing security and space issues.

The three argued that the Army should apply a broader definition of "victim" from the Uniform Code of Military Justice that says a victim can be someone who suffered "direct physical, emotional or pecuniary harm." They argued that the military's refusal to allow them to attend was saying they had not been victims because they were not struck by bullets.
Retired Colonel Kathy Platoni, who would have been Hasan's supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal.
"I would desperately like to attend," Platoni said from her home in Ohio. "To look Hasan in the eye and say, 'You didn't get me.'"

The letter signed by the commandant of Fort Leavenworth said the three cannot appeal again. "Please understand that this is not meant as a judgment on any emotional injury you or others suffered as a result of CP Hasan's crimes," it said.
A previous plan to livestream the military execution, the first since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II, was rescinded by Mr. Trump last month after bipartisan backlash.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The Army noted in a statement Tuesday that regulations specify who can witness a military execution, and reiterated the size and space restrictions.
"Efforts have been made over the years, from the trial to notifications to memorials and now to the execution, to recognize the impacts and support the victims," the Army statement said.

Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, who was among the 32 injured in the attack, said he will attend the execution but opposed the public livestream. "I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," he told CBS News last month in an interview.

"This will not be closure for me," Lunsford said, adding that his closure comes from helping others. He said he carries the bullet that was pulled from his body with him every day as a reminder of what he survived.
A blood-stained uniform and memories of the attack remain
Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.
Platoni said the survivors from her unit deployed to Afghanistan 29 days after the attack because, "we still served our country, and if we didn't, (Hasan) would have won."
She said the building where Hasan initially opened fire had been crowded with returning soldiers and those preparing to deploy. She had been moved to another building when the attack began.
"The looks on the faces of my friends and colleagues as they carried in the dying and wounded that day … it will haunt me for the rest of my life," she said.
She said they carried in the badly wounded captain who had rushed Hasan with a chair to try to stop the shooting.

"I was throwing computers to the ground trying to get the tablecloths because we needed blankets. We didn't have medical supplies or even water," she said. "I still have that blood-stained uniform, from kneeling down next to that young man, trying to get him to stay with us. That will be with me forever."
Julia Wilson, who was nine months pregnant when Hasan opened fire, said her request to witness was also denied. She said the way the military has handled the case has caused her anguish.

"We have faced institutional betrayal after institutional betrayal," Wilson said. "We remain on that battlefield because of that … if they don't fix it, we're never going to leave that battlefield. We'll never heal."

Platoni had been on the list of victims and survivors kept by the military's victim liaison since Hasan's 2013 court-martial trial. Everyone on that list received notification in March that there had been movement in scheduling the execution, Platoni said.

Platoni said she did not think space was really the issue. The military told victims and survivors that about 160 witnesses would be allowed to attend the execution, and through her work with survivors and families of victims she believed about 90 people had decided to go. Platoni conceded that those details may have changed.

An Army official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive plans, said that the military is not planning to release any details about the firing squad or protocols, including the number of service members involved.
Feeling a duty to attend the execution

Retired Major C. Alan Hopewell testified at Hasan's trial. He confirmed Hasan's identity after he was shot by two service members attempting to halt his rampage. One of those officers had asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution.
He said Tuesday that he would accept the denial but with mixed feelings.

"I'm disappointed that our status as victims is not recognized," Hopewell said. "A bullet missed me and hit my car. I guess if the bullet had hit me … they would consider me a victim and let me attend."
Hopewell, Platoni and Wilson said that even after the execution, they will continue to push for the Fort Hood shooting to be redefined as an act of domestic terrorism instead of workplace violence.

Hopewell recently underwent surgery unrelated to the shooting and said he's not certain his doctors would have cleared him to witness the execution. Nonetheless, he had hoped the Army would grant him the right.
"I guess it feels more like a duty, like a fulfillment of my responsibility to those soldiers who were killed and injured, who were threatened," Hopewell said.

Texas

title: Wendy's "pricing scheme" inflated menu prices, lawsuit alleges
summary: In a proposed class action, a California resident alleges that Wendy's conspired with its franchisees to set and raise menu prices.
story: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges that Wendy's engaged in a pricing scheme that reduced competition across its restaurants, driving up costs for customers.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in a Maryland district court, accuses the burger chain of conspiring with independently owned franchisees to set and raise prices at its U.S. locations over a six-year period between 2016 and 2022. Wendy's collected "competitively sensitive information" from franchisee locations, including transaction data, to coordinate prices, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed by Andy Garcia, a California resident and longtime Wendy's customer, according to the suit. He alleges that Wendy's engaged in "anticompetitive conduct" that resulted in artificially high prices, causing him to pay more than he otherwise would have.
Garcia also sued NCR Voyix, a software company that provides Aloha POS, a point-of-sale system used by Wendy's.

"By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers," Blake Hunter Yagman, the lawyer representing Garcia and founding partner of Yagman PLLC, a class-action law firm headquartered in New York, said in an email.

"This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher — and Wendy's owes [it to] its consumers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing," Yagman added.

Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. As of September, Wendy's had 432 company-owned restaurants and 6,762 franchisees across the U.S., according to the company's most recent regulatory filing.

In 2024, Wendy's raised concerns after saying it would test Uber-style pricing. Also known as dynamic pricing, that approach allows companies to set prices based on real-time market conditions and other factors such as weather.
Other restaurants have also faced scrutiny over their pricing practices. Last month, a consumer sued McDonald's over the use of an AI tool that recommends dynamic pricing.

title: Leaked data shows 490,000 Russian forces have died in Ukraine war
summary: Russian government data obtained by pro-Ukraine hackers and analyzed by the BBC indicates that Russia has lost at least 490,334 soldiers during its war on Ukraine.
story: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.

A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.

The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.
In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence.

"Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.

The Kremlin has not publicly revealed the Russian death toll from the war. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said for the first time in February that his country's losses stood at 55,000. That figure has not been independently corroborated, however, and the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank estimated as many as 150,000 Ukrainian fatalities up to June 2026.

The BBC also reported that the leaked data shows 65% of 18- to 24-year-olds in Russia who died in 2025 were casualties of the war. For Russians aged 25-34 last year, the number was 59%, making the war the main cause of death for young Russian adults last year, according to the data.

When asked about the various reports surfacing from the data leak, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Defense Ministry of the Russian Federation."
"I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he said.

title: "Narco sub" seized in Atlantic but no drugs found on board
summary: The operation was carried out in cooperation with the Colombian navy and the U.S. Joint Interagency Task Force South.
story: The French navy intercepted a semi-submersible craft suspected of involvement in drug trafficking in the Atlantic Ocean, a prosecutor said Wednesday, days after stopping a similar "narco sub" carrying several tons of cocaine.
"The semi-submersible was flying no flag and was suspected of being involved in drug trafficking" when French forces intercepted it on November 17, said organized crime prosecutor Vanessa Perree.
No drugs were found but "the vessel's location, lack of flag, its clandestine nature and items discovered onboard" led to the arrest of two crew members, she added.
The operation was carried out in cooperation with the Colombian navy and the U.S. Joint Interagency Task Force South.
The vessel's seizure "deals a serious blow to the drug traffickers' logistics." said Perree.
Catherine Vautrin, the country's armed forces minister, hailed the operation in a social media post, which included images of the vessel.

"The French armed forces are maintaining their efforts in the fight against drug trafficking networks," she wrote on X.  "With this intervention by the Armed Forces in the French Antilles, an entire criminal network and its associated logistics have been disrupted."
Narco subs, which cannot go fully underwater, are popular among international drug traffickers as they can sometimes elude detection by law enforcement.

It was the second interception of a semi-submersible in recent weeks by Caribbean-based French forces, she said. On November 12, the French navy seized nearly 330 pounds of cocaine from a similar craft, and the armed forces released a video of the interception.

Les armées françaises ne relâchent pas l'effort dans la lutte contre les réseaux de narcotrafiquants. Pour la deuxième fois en novembre, la @MarineNationale a intercepté une embarcation semi-submersible suspecte en océan Atlantique, permettant le placement en garde à vue de… pic.twitter.com/TcyEPbNzce
The rest of the cargo, amounting to several tons, sank along with the semi-submersible, authorities said at the time.
Four Colombians were arrested during that operation and face charges including "unauthorized importation of narcotics committed by an organized gang."
They have been remanded in custody, said Perree.
The two separate investigations are being overseen by the national organized crime prosecutor's office, she added.
Manned semisubmersibles built in clandestine jungle shipyards have been used for decades to ferry cocaine north from Colombia, the world's biggest cocaine producer, to Central America or Mexico.
But in recent years, they have been sailing much farther afield, crossing the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

In January, Portuguese authorities seized a record haul of cocaine from a semi-submersible craft intercepted off the Azores archipelago before the vessel sank. In March 2025, Portuguese officers confiscated nearly 6.5 tons of cocaine from a semi-submersible vessel in the same region.
In January 2025, a "narco sub" broke in two pieces as a fishing boat was towing it to a port in northwestern Spain.

title: Titanic postcard sent days before doomed voyage sells for pricey sum
summary: A postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail.
story: A rare postcard from a Titanic crew member that features the famed ocean liner and was sent less than a week before its doomed voyage in 1912 sold at auction for over $41,000, according to a U.K. auction house.

The postcard from Jack Phillips, the Titanic's chief radio officer, was postmarked April 6, 1912, four days before the ill-fated ship set sail on its maiden voyage across the Atlantic from Southampton, England, for New York City.
Phillips, who turned 25 on the ship, sent the postcard to his sister, Elsie Phillips, according to auction house Henry Aldridge and Son Ltd.
"Thanks very much for your letter. Having glorious weather, went to Cowes yesterday. Will write later before we sail. Love all, Jack," Phillips wrote on the back of the postcard.
The front features a picture of the Titanic at Southampton in southern England. The auction house said the postcard was in "very good to fine condition, with some light soiling and toning."
According to the auction house, the postcard sold for 32,000 British pounds, or around $41,800. With taxes and fees, the final cost was 40,000 pounds, or around $52,300.
During the trans-Atlantic crossing, on the night of April 14, 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg and eventually sank, killing over 1,500 people.
As the Titanic was filling with water, Phillips stayed at his post and tried to get other ships to come to the rescue of the ocean liner's approximately 2,200 passengers and crew.
According to the auction house, Phillips abandoned ship when the water reached his station, and he ultimately died from exposure to the severe cold on an overturned collapsible lifeboat.
The ship's junior wireless officer, Harold Bride, hailed Phillips for his efforts, calling him "the man who saved us all," according to the auction house.

Bride and Phillips, who also handled messages for passengers, received multiple iceberg warnings from other ships during the voyage and sent most of them along to the bridge. On the night the Titanic struck the iceberg, one warning about an ice field from another ship, the Mesaba, didn't make it to the bridge.

title: Serbia government wants to limit reality TV, adopt 4-day work week
summary: Serbia's Student List party, which recently ousted the country's Russia-aligned strongman leader, wants to restrict reality TV.
story: Serbia's newly elected, student-led but still leaderless government wants to restrict the amount of reality television aired in the country to just 45 minutes per day, and to make it only available after 11 p.m. on terrestrial TV channels.
The Student List party ousted Serbia's longtime strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic, an ally of Russia's Vladimir Putin, in an October election, promising to end corruption in the Balkan nation.

Subscription channels would still be allowed to carry reality shows, according to the party's plans, published on its website. The party also wants to ban all live reality show broadcasts on the terrestrial channels, and repeats or additional coverage of the shows would count toward the 45-minute maximum.
Broadcasters would be compelled to interrupt reality shows if there is any violence, hate speech, or threats.
Paid channels would not be subject to the restrictions under the plans.

The Student List says it sees reality TV as emblematic of a violent culture espoused under Vucic's authoritarian government. Serbian news channels were long seen as favoring the regime in their coverage.
The Student List, which is deliberately free of hierarchy and has no leader, is still very much getting to grips with the job of governing the country after its election victory.

The new administration is targeting better working conditions and curbs on what it sees as the corrosive influence of reality programming. It also announced plans to institute a 4-day work week in Serbia.

"We will limit overtime to eight hours a week and total daily working time to 12 hours," according to the party's website. "Employers who choose to will be able to introduce a four-day working week, with 32 full-time hours, while keeping employee salaries unchanged."

The Student List has also set out to reset Serbia's foreign policy — most notably by moving the country away from Russia and potentially holding a referendum on seeking membership in the European Union.

In a first speech to the EU by any of its members, newly-elected Student List lawmaker Aleksandar Baucal said on Nov. 12 that the party would intensify efforts to meet the EU's interim accession criteria.

"The European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market," he said.
The party does not plan to completely oppose Moscow, however, and says it wants to maintain bilateral relations.
It also wants to stop Serbia's arms trade with Israel.

title: High-quality medieval armor discovered in shipwreck that sank in 1495
summary: The ship, known as "Griffin" or "Gribshunden," was the warship of Denmark's 15th-century leader King Hans.
story: Maritime archaeologists have found pieces of high-quality medieval armor found among the wreckage of a 500-year-old Danish warship, an international team of researchers revealed on Tuesday.

The ship, known as "Griffin" or "Gribshunden," was the warship of Denmark's 15th-century leader King Hans. The ship was also used for diplomatic expeditions. In 1495, there was an explosion that led to the ship catching fire and sinking while anchored north of Sweden's Stora Ekö Island. The wreck was discovered in the 1970s.

In the decades since, the ship has been the subject of frequent study. The latest discovery of the chain mail armor was made by team of experts from the United Kingdom's University of Southampton and Swedish institutions Södertörn University and Stockholm University, who have been conducting joint expeditions of the wreck since 2019.

The team's archaeologists and hydrographic survey specialists were using advanced robotic survey technology and 3-D photogrammetric imaging to make detailed archaeological records of the wreckage when they found the armor fragments, according to a news release from the University of Southampton.

The chain mail armor is made of copper-alloy, the university said. It was found while documenting an ammunition-tool chest just below the ship's forecastle, which was an elevated fighting platform at the front of the vessel.

Military gear may have been stored in the area, said Dr. Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, a visiting fellow at the University of Southampton's Centre for Maritime Archaeology, in the news release. German mercenaries, known as Landsknechts, were aboard the ship when it sank in 1495, Pacheco-Ruiz said.
"It was truly an amazing find!" Pacheco-Ruiz said in the news release.

Rolf Fabricius Warming, a Southampton alumnus and current Ph.D. researcher at Stockholm University, said that this kind of armor could be used for "extended periods," aided by repairs or being reused by other soldiers. The fragments "may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

Analyzing the manufacturing and composition of the armor pieces may reveal more about the origin of the armor, Warming said. Other weaponry-related artifacts aboard the ship were also sampled to undergo further analysis. The researchers will also study the structural elements of the forecastle and other features of the ship to determine how weapons and equipment were stored on the ship, and how military personnel lived and worked while aboard the vessel.

Also undergoing analysis are lead objects found during earlier research expeditions. Those items may be related to molds used to manufacture ammunition, the university said. Samples of lead and other materials were taken from the tool chest for further study.
The wreck is "partly disintegrated," but its remaining pieces "very well preserved."

"The ship is an important piece of the puzzle in the 'military revolution at sea' in the Early Modern Period, in which the primary tactics shifted from hand-to-hand combat to  heavy naval artillery fire," Warming said in 2024, adding that the ship is comparable to other preserved wrecks including the Mars and the Vasa, which has been on display in Stockholm, Sweden since the 1960s after being salvaged from the ocean floor.

title: Brits are having less sex, but watching a lot of porn, survey finds
summary: A third of Brits aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, a landmark survey finds, though most acknowledge sexting and watching pornography.
story: London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.

The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.

Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.

Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.

"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."

One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."

Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."

Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.

"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.
