title: Security forces storm scene, end Colombia supermarket siege
summary: Security forces stormed a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena, ending a day-long siege, with the nation's president saying all hostages were rescued and one captor was killed.
story: Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held hostage had been rescued and one captor killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to have been held by armed men.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a video posted on social media.
Shortly after midnight, a police helicopter hovered low over the shopping center as security forces massed outside the supermarket, AFP reporters saw.
Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of the roughly 30 people initially held had been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.
De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and a sidearm while brandishing a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success.
"We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively," he said, lauding the operation as "absolutely flawless."
The president said one hostage-taker had been killed.
Cartagena's mayor said all the hostages were "safe and sound" and would reunite with their families before undergoing medical checks.
Hostage takers were "caught off guard"
The siege gripped Cartagena, one of Colombia's main tourist draws — a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship visits.
Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.
"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told AFP earlier in the standoff. "He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared on social media appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear carrying long guns alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.
De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping -- no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted armored vehicle robbery at the shopping center.
According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly $2 million, two armored vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles northeast of Cartagena.
AFP couldn't independently verify those reports.

The Rafael Nunez airport in Cartagena resumed landings after a brief suspension of about 45 minutes so the armed forces could use one of its runways in connection with the incident. the Reuters news agency reported.
The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas and a series of attacks across the country.
Despite the deal that ended the region's largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organizations still fight for control of parts of the country.
Late Monday, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a "terrorist attack" on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several southwestern departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

title: NATO allies anxious as war spreads beyond Ukraine, Russia borders
summary: As Ukraine attacks Russian ships in far-flung waters, some NATO nations are voicing increasing anxiety over the war's spread to new regions.
story: Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.

Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."

"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."
A "need for stability in our near areas"

Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.

The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.

Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base.

"The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.
Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air.

"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."

The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.
Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems.

"Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."

The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives.
"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do"

While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression.

"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet."
Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet —   hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.
Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters.

"The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it."
"Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean said, meanwhile, that Ukraine's "successful effort to expand the map of its war with Russia is bound to cause tension with partners, both in Washington and in NATO countries who feel their security is threatened by Ukranian operations near their territory. But Ukraine can no longer rely on Washington's support, which negates the leverage Washington once had over Kyiv's decision-making."

While European support for Kyiv is "more robust," MacLean added, "the Ukrainians — with some justice — feel as though they are fighting a war on behalf of many of NATO's eastern members, and so feel like they have some running room to impose pain on Russia, even in ways that its NATO partners might sometimes find uncomfortable."

title: Prince William and Kate's country home broken into, 2 arrested
summary: Two men were arrested over a suspected burglary at the U.K. royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of Prince William and Catherine, police said.
story: Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of William and Catherine, the Prince and Princess of Wales, U.K. police said.

Police responded to reports of "suspicious activity" at Anmer Hall on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in eastern England Monday at about 6 p.m., Norfolk police said. William and Catherine and the rest of their family weren't present at the time, the police said.

The police said Wednesday that Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They were due in court later Wednesday.
]Police dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the property and make the arrests, officials said.
Kensington Palace told CBS News it wouldn't comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from Queen Elizabeth II. It is used as a country residence on weekends. William and his family spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, which they have described as their "forever home."
The reported break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street.
Catherine recently opened up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

"Heal" follows the 44-year-old royal as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

title: Canadian astronaut's wife gives birth with husband aboard ISS
summary: The wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who is currently aboard the International Space Station, gave birth to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
story: The wife of a Canadian astronaut who is currently aboard the International Space Station gave birth Tuesday to the couple's third child, Canadian officials announced.
Heather Kutryk, the wife of astronaut Joshua Kutryk, gave birth to a girl, the Canadian Space Agency said in a news release.
"Heather and baby are both doing well," the agency said, adding that Joshua Kutryk was able to share in the experience from the space station.

"Joshua is currently living out a childhood dream aboard the International Space Station," the couple said in a statement. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives."
The couple's two other children are ages 7 and 5.
Joshua Kutryk traveled to the space station on Oct. 1 from Florida aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule as part of Crew 13, accompanied by two NASA astronauts and a Russian cosmonaut.
In an interview just prior to his departure, he told CBS News that it would be tough to miss the birth, but that he would "try to take the positive things out of it."

"Physically, of course, I won't be here, but as hard as that will be, it also lends itself to what I hope will be a very unique and enriching life experience that we'll look on fondly," Joshua Kutryk said.

In the history of space travel, Joshua Kutryk is just the fourth astronaut to miss the birth of a child. A former military test pilot, this was Kutryk's first spaceflight. He is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

"We have an enormous support network, and we feel just happy and joyful to be doing this," he said in that interview. "This is a hard job. There's a lot of good things about it, there's some bad things. One of those bad things is that it's very unpredictable, and you can't predict when things like launches are going to happen."
Crew 13 does not yet have a confirmed date for its return to Earth.

Kutryk told CBS News: "We think it's exceptionally important, and I hope that my new child looks at it as such, as making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

title: China launches first foreign astronaut to its space station
summary: China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts, sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.
story: China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.

The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.

While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.

Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23, which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

title: Man on cruise ship goes overboard off Bahamas, search underway
summary: The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.
story: Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.
The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.

The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said.

The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captain's announcement obtained by CBS News.
Christian Bunse, a passenger aboard the ship, told CBS Miami, "People got quiet when they heard it, because they heard his name again."
Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.

The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard.
"We are coordinating with the cruise and will have a vessel on scene," said a spokesperson for the Royal Bahamas Defence Force.
Royal Caribbean said its care team is providing "support and assistance to the guest's loved ones."

A woman fell from her balcony on the Allure of the Seas on a Taylor Swift-themed cruise in October 2024. Dulcie White's family alleged in a lawsuit that Royal Caribbean's unlimited drink package encouraged overconsumption, and that crew members ignored clear warning signs before the fatal fall. Her body was never recovered. The case remains ongoing.

title: Armed men take hostages at supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia
summary: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
story: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday, Colombian police said.

Initially, they were holding around 30 hostages, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. As of Sunday night, they had released 10 of the hostages, including five elderly women, the president and Colombian police said. There was no immediate word on their conditions or the conditions of those still being held.
De la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of an Exito supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena's airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in a social media post that operations were slowly returning to normal.

title: Top Denmark court upholds "non-Western" evictions law
summary: Denmark's Supreme Court has upheld a law that lets authorities limit the number of "non-Western" residents who can live in a public housing development.
story: Denmark's Supreme Court upheld on Monday a controversial law intended to eliminate ethnic enclaves in public housing, or "ghettos," as the government calls them, by giving authorities the ability to limit the number of "non-Western" immigrants and their descendants who can live in any particular housing development.
The court ruled that the eviction in 2022 of residents from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej, a housing development in the city of Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, did not constitute ethnic discrimination.

The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. It has attracted both international condemnation and admiration from politicians in other countries that seek to emulate Denmark's approach to immigration and integration.

Under the legislation, residential areas with at least 1,000 inhabitants, where more than 50% of residents are immigrants or descendants of immigrants from "non-Western" countries, and which meet certain socioeconomic criteria relating to employment rates, income levels, education attainment, and crime, can be subject to redevelopment requirements.

Housing developments designated as "transformation areas" are required to reduce the proportion of public family housing to no more than 40% by 2030. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.

Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The classification is based on a person's country of origin rather than their citizenship, which means even Danish citizens born and raised in Denmark can be classified as non-Western if both of their parents immigrated from non-Western countries.

The seven families evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej argued in their case that the distinction between Western and non-Western origins was effectively a proxy for ethnicity, and thus amounts to illegal discrimination based on race. The Supreme Court concluded that the distinction was based on nationality and country of birth rather than ethnicity, however, noting that both categories encompassed a wide range of ethnic groups and that people of the same ethnicity could fall into either category.

The court's ruling followed a decision last December by the European Union's highest court, which found that the Danish legislation could constitute discrimination on the grounds of ethnic origin, but the EU court left it to Denmark's courts to make the final determination.
Anders Svendsen, Chief Legal Officer for Denmark's national tenants' organization, LLO, told CBS News the organization didn't expect the Supreme Court to rule the way it did.
"We were slightly surprised, considering what the EU court had come up with previously last December," he said.
The organization estimates that several thousand homes have been demolished under the legislation already.

"A lot of people are still quite concerned, because they don't know if they're going to be next," Svendsen said. "This regulation has been quite unpopular among the renters in the public sector, but it has been quite popular in the population at large."

The LLO said it recognized the government's desire to promote social cohesion, but it questioned whether demolishing homes and reducing the availability of affordable housing was a proportionate response.
"We disagree, because it sees public housing as a problem to be solved and less public housing is seen as the cure," Svendsen told CBS News.
Joachim B. Olsen, a former Danish lawmaker who is now the opinion editor for the Danish newspaper B.T., was not surprised by Monday's ruling.

"Legislation is thoroughly vetted by the Department of Justice to make sure that it is in accordance with the constitution and Denmark's international obligations before it is presented to parliament," he told CBS News.
Olsen rejected the suggestion that the distinction between Western and non-Western origin was a proxy for race, arguing that it was based on cultural background.
"It is important to understand that the provisions in the 'ghetto law' apply to anyone living in the area designated as a 'ghetto,' no matter ethnicity or citizenship," he said.
Olsen argued that the policy had been broadly successful. According to Danish government figures, the number of neighborhoods officially classified as ghettos fell from 29 in 2018, to five in 2025.
"Incomes in these areas have risen. Employment is up. So is the educational level," he said. "Overall, I would say that positives outnumber the negatives."
Denmark's influence on European immigration policy
Denmark has become a model for some other European governments as they look at ways to tighten immigration restrictions and address public concerns over the integration of immigrant communities.

While demands for tougher immigration policy in many European nations have been driven predominantly by right-wing populist parties, Denmark's restrictive approach has been championed by its center-left Social Democratic Party, led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Frederiksen has been outspoken about her desire to preserve Danish culture and her opposition to a concept of multiculturalism in which all cultures are afforded equal standing in the country.

"We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe," Frederiksen said last week on the B.T. newspaper's podcast, Borgerlig Tabloid. "Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture."
Britain's government cited Denmark's policies earlier this year as it changed its own rules on people granted asylum in the U.K.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, announcing a new policy in March under which people granted asylum will have that status subject to regular review, said the "reset in Britain's asylum offer" had been "inspired by Denmark's success."
Denmark has also been at the forefront of efforts to establish "return hubs" — deportation centers outside Europe.

Last week, Denmark joined Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing plans to establish a "return hub" in Rwanda for migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in Europe, but who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

title: Iranian women praise singer lashed for not wearing a hijab
summary: Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times for the crime of "outraging public decency" after she livestreamed a concert without her hair covered.
story: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without the head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.

Ahmadi was dealt the corporal punishment for her chosen attire during a livestreamed concert in 2024, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Etemad on Monday. But Iranian women who spoke with CBS News on Tuesday said she was punished not for breaking the rule, but for daring to publicly defy the country's repressive regime — defiance that has made her "a symbol of resistance."

Ahmadi's lawyer told Etemad that the singer and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom, as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
The court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency," citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran.
In addition to the 74 lashes, Ahmadi and eight members of her team were also sentenced to a two-year ban on travel out of the country and a two-year ban on all "artistic activity."

Ahmadi performed her concert in the Dayr-Gachin Caravanserai, an ancient site along the Silk Road route in Iran. It included themes of nationalism and popular uprising, and saw her openly flout both the Islamic Republic's dress code and a long-standing ban on women singing in public.
"I feel as though I have been flogged"
Ahmadi's punishment has reverberated across the country as her performance did two years ago.

"When it comes to her flogging, I feel deep pain," Marjan, a 41-year-old optician from Karaj, a city northwest of Tehran, told CBS News on Tuesday. "I feel as though I have been flogged for doing what I want."
"This is something which is much deeper than just sympathy or solidarity," she said. "We Iranian women identify with her in a deeper psychological sense."
Marjan, who declined to give her full name, called Ahmadi "a symbol of resistance."

"She was an icon when she performed in that concert, and now, after she received those lashes. Both are acts of resistance," said Marjan, who spoke with CBS News over the phone. "The regime is not afraid of women who sing, they are afraid of people who courageously carry out that which they prohibit."

This "is not the punishment of an artist, it is the punishment of a person who made use of their most fundamental rights of freedom of speech and creative expression," agreed Tehran resident Thoraya, 32.

"No state has ownership over the voices of their citizens. Singing is not a crime," she told CBS News, also in a phone interview. "No state power can precondition artistic expression on political obedience. I feel solidarity with Parastoo, but it's human solidarity first and foremost, not political."
"I'm not taking her place or speaking for her," she said, "but her right to wear what she wants, pursue her artistic life, is something I see as my right, too."

title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
summary: BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018.
story: A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.

On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.

As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.

But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.

"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

Despite the error and the incomplete maneuver, ESA scientists were eventually able to confirm that BepiColombo had locked onto Mercury's orbit. It took six hours from the time the maneuver started to confirm that it had been successful, the ESA said.

Over the next few weeks, the spacecraft will continue to make small thruster burns to gradually adjust its orbit around Mercury. Each movement will be adapted by BepiColombo's flight dynamics team using the spacecraft's actual trajectory. This will allow BepiColombo to enter the "optimum point" in orbit. The ESA compared it to "braking a car at just the right moment" to find the "sweet spot." Conducting multiple maneuvers also allows the craft to maximize its fuel supplies.

On Dec. 9, BepiColombo will release two science orbiters. The ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, or MPO, will spend another few months navigating to find the right spot in Mercury's orbit. It is expected to enter its final orbit in March 2027 and begin science operations in April.
The scientific operations will study Mercury's interior, surface and the space around the planet, Geraint Jones, ESA's BepiColombo lead project scientist, said.

The second science orbiter is the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, or Mio. Mio's studies will include Mercury's magnetosphere, interplanetary dust and electric fields, according to the ESA.

title: Cold case murder mystery solved 58 years after girl found dead
summary: Canadian police say they've solved a teen girl's mysterious murder case, nearly six decades after she was found dead.
story: Canadian police say they've solved a girl's mysterious murder case, nearly six decades after she was found dead.

Using modern forensic and DNA tests, investigators were finally able to identify the man responsible for killing Jacqueline "Jackie" Dunleavy in 1968, according to Canada's London Police Service. Dunleavy was 16 at the time of her death.

Her killer was identified as Michael Joseph Moore, then 25, who couldn't be charged in Dunleavy's murder because he died in 2018. When she was killed, police say Moore had recently moved to London, a city in the southern part of Ontario, near the U.S. border, after emigrating from Ireland.

At a news conference held this week to announce the murder had been solved, London Police Chief Thai Truong described Dunleavy as "a daughter, a sister, a friend, and a young girl who had her entire life ahead of her" when she was killed. Her father was also a London police officer, the police chief said.

Dunleavy was last seen leaving the London convenience store where she worked on Jan. 9, 1968, according to police.  Less than two hours after her shift ended, Dunleavy's body was found by three young people on the grounds of a school several miles away. Emergency responders pronounced her dead at the scene. Strangulation was later ruled the cause of her death, police said, although Dunleavy had also suffered a head injury.

A homicide probe conducted at the time never led investigators to a suspect, but subsequent generations of officers went on to review the case in the years that followed. Their latest review incorporated advanced DNA testing and forensic genetic genealogy, which is an investigative technique that uses relatives' DNA to solve cold cases.
In this case, the Texas-based lab Othram, Inc. used the suspect's DNA to identify his distant genetic relatives. Those connections eventually led investigators back to Moore.

"Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison," said Mike Budzyn, a London police detective and the lead investigator on Dunleavy's case, in a statement.
Budzyn added that investigators were confident Moore committed the murder.

"Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met," he said. "Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie's murder."
Anyone with information about Moore has been asked to contact London police.

title: New details emerge about U.S. involvement in drug lord's capture
summary: The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.
story: The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.

The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro" illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.

President Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.
"This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces" of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.
The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.

The weekend detention of the capo triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.

The FBI had placed Chapo Isidro on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. On Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department called him a senior leader of the Sinaloa cartel, which it calls "one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities."

Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of "very important intelligence sharing" with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores' location in Guasave.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

In the week leading up to Meza Flores' capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law.

On Monday, Mexico's prosecutors' office announced that it had formally charged Meza Flores and two other alleged cartel members with illegal possession of firearms and possession of methamphetamine with the intent to sell, adding that the three were flown to Mexico City over the weekend following their capture.

Authorities also highlighted that the U.S. has an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.
His capture, which was captured on video, was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region.
The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.

Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as "Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.

The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho."
While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight against crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire.

In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa.

title: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude images sent to media
summary: Gisèle Pelicot, who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and 50 other men, says she's been "once again humiliated."
story: Gisèle Pelicot, the French woman who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday that she had been "once again humiliated" after nude photos and videos of her were sent to media outlets to promote a book that she said is dismissive of her husband's crimes.
Pelicot, 73, told France's BFMTV that she will take legal action against the publisher, Tinard, and the author of the book, French psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris.

The book criticizes the concept of coercive control and questions whether Pelicot was really a victim, suggesting she could have been complicit in her husband's actions despite her having been surreptitiously drugged for years.

"I am deeply shocked that images relating to my most intimate life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot said in a statement to the French broadcaster, adding: "Above all, I refuse to have my story rewritten by implying that I was complicit in what I suffered."

"Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed, and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial wasn't enough," she said. "I fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."

Pelicot became a global symbol of resilience in 2024 when she waived her right to anonymity in her then-husband Dominique's trial. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison for his abuse — and for inviting 50 other men to join him in raping his wife while she was incapacitated repeatedly over the course of a decade.

"How can you imagine that your husband is drugging you? It's unthinkable — impossible," she told CBS News in February. "In fact, I was manipulated for about 10 years. Because he was looking me in the eyes every day while knowing he was poisoning me. But I never saw that. I saw a kind, caring man."
She said she waived her anonymity during the trial to show that "shame has to change sides," from victims to perpetrators.

On its website, the publisher Tinard said it had offered "our sincerest apologies" to Pelicot and that it would not be reprinting the book after 280 copies already printed are sold. It said "no images of rape or pornographic videos were leaked to the press."

It is not clear where the publisher got the nude images of Pelicot. In her statements to French media, Pelicot did not question their authenticity. She also did not confirm or deny a report by the French weekly news outlet Le Canard Enchaîne, which said the images were among those taken by her former husband and presented during his trial as evidence.
Prokhoris, the author, said she had given "full responsibility" for the promotional campaign to the publisher, according to French news agency AFP.

AFP said the back-cover blurb on the book asks readers to "think freely" about the notion of coercive control, which Prokhoris describes as "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy" that is "fundamentally ambiguous" and, she says, involves "each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way."

"There are two types of violence that have been committed," Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM. "There is, on the one hand, the fact that intimate images of her were sent without her consent in the context of purely commercial communication, and then there is a book that calls into question her status as a victim."
"It is a clear violation of the law, and she does not intend to let it go unchallenged," he said.

title: Istanbul lioness never existed, Turkish officials say after search
summary: A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal didn't exist.
story: Istanbul — A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal didn't exist.

Istanbul's governor mobilized teams of animal welfare experts, police and army commandos in the hunt for the lioness after it was "identified" — even releasing two videos of the animal prowling around the upscale neighborhood of Uskumrukoy.
"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.
Residents were warned to stay home, and the roughly 20 square mile Belgrade Forest to the north of Istanbul was sealed off.
By Monday evening, however, officials backtracked and said in a statement new images had been examined that showed the animal was "not a lion or any other large cat species."

"The area has been scanned from the air with a drone equipped with thermal cameras and from the ground by our teams," the statement said. "Baiting was also carried out and motion-sensor camera traps used."
"Fieldwork has not yielded any concrete evidence of a lion being present in the area."

The abrupt change left many bewildered, wondering what animal could have been mistaken for a lioness, with some suggesting it was a large dog. Others posted mocking videos of domestic cats on social media, asking if it was the lioness.
Even after the governor's office statement, media outlets published another video of an animal emerging from bushes and asked readers if it could be a lion.

title: Man with Alzheimer's found alive after 11 days lost in jungle
summary: Rescue workers said the man survived in the jungle by eating berries, drinking water from natural sources and making bedlike structures with the leaves of acai palms.
story: An elderly man with Alzheimer's disease who survived 11 days on his own in the Amazon rainforest is currently recovering at a hospital in the Brazilian city of Macapa, as rescue workers reveal more details about his surprising ordeal.

Janarino Ferreira dos Santos, 74, was rescued by park rangers and volunteers on Friday in a thick patch of rainforest about 6 miles from Macapa in northeastern Brazil. Rescue workers said Dos Santos was able to survive in the jungle by eating berries, drinking water from natural sources and making bedlike structures with the leaves of acai palms, where he could rest for the night.
"When he was younger he had worked in the rainforest, so he knew how to get around," said Aniel Cardoso, a park ranger who helped find dos Santos.

Cardoso and a group of volunteers who joined the search for dos Santos on Friday said they were able to find the man after they identified his footprints and realized he had been walking around in circles. As they tracked dos Santos' footprints, the rescuers came across a bed made from acai leaves that looked like it was at least four days old. Later, they came across a second bed with leaves that seemed to have been taken down from a palm tree that same morning.
"That's when we realized he could be alive, and that he could be close," Cardoso said. The rescuers found dos Santos in a thick patch of the forest, sitting down barefoot and wearing only underwear.
"He wasn't able to talk, he was no longer walking and he was very thirsty," Cardoso said.

The search, which started a day after the man went missing, brought together family members, volunteers and public safety teams, who faced difficult conditions in the forest. Firefighters and specialized teams used ground searches, helicopter and drone overflights as well as thermal cameras to look for signs of the missing man.

After nine days of searching and no news of dos Santos emerged, his granddaughter Sara Montes urged firefighters to keep looking for him. In a video posted on Instagram, she said they planned to suspend the search on Sunday, November 22.
"Don't forget about us. Don't forget about Grandpa," she pleaded.

Getting dos Santos out of the forest proved challenging as dense vegetation, flooded areas and swampy grounds prevented him from walking unaided, so rescuers improvised a stretcher using ropes and carried him through the difficult terrain.
A video posted on the G1 news site shows several men carrying him through the forest on the makeshift stretcher.
Cardoso said the man had walked out of his home on the edge of the rainforest while his relatives were visiting a neighbor.

He said that finding dos Santos was "very gratifying" because two months ago, another man had gone missing in the rainforest near Macapa, but had already died by the time he was found by rescue workers.
"This time, thank God, we were able to deliver this citizen alive," Cardoso said.
The dramatic rescue comes just over a week after a 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.

title: Pope Francis had visions of devil, "gates of hell," diary reveals
summary: Pope Francis suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-2022 linked to temptations to exercise power omnipotently, his diary reveals, adding that he overcame it by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.
story: Vatican City — Pope Francis saw the "gates of hell" when he realized the depths of the clergy sexual abuse scandal and experienced mystical visions of the devil throughout his ministry, according to excerpts of his personal diary published by the Vatican on Tuesday.

"The Private Diary of Pope Francis" also reveals the Argentine pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis in 2021-2022, connected to his own temptations to exercise power omnipotently. He overcame the crisis by entrusting himself entirely to God's mercy.

The book, being released globally in several languages, offers a deeply personal and almost voyeuristic view into the mind and heart of Francis, revealing his innermost fears, insecurities, dreams and temptations that he kept hidden from the world. It shows him as incredibly hard on himself, lamenting his own sense of worthlessness and shame, and his utter trust in God to lead him, even from the depths of despair.

The book was curated by one of Francis' closest aides, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, the Argentine theologian who heads the Vatican's doctrine office. Fernández is listed as the author, as his comments contextualize Francis' diary entries.

Fernández expressed concern to Francis' successor, Leo XIV, that the book would be "left forgotten in some storage," and was permitted to publish passages, noting that "the spiritual concerns present in his (Francis') heart are very clear and can do us good."

Written in a leather-bound calendar used as a notebook, it starts in 1992, when Jorge Mario Bergoglio was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. It continues through his time as cardinal archbishop of the Argentine capital and finally pope. The last entry is Aug. 18, 2024. He died in April 2025 at the age of 88 after 12 years as pontiff.
Francis, the devil and a disastrous Chile trip

The most moving sections are Francis' revelations of his own spiritual torments and what he described as encounters with the devil - visceral, tangible, seemingly terrifying encounters. Two occurred when he was in Buenos Aires, and the third after his disastrous 2018 trip to Chile.

"A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. 'Now I've gotten everything I wanted,'" Francis quoted the devil as saying in a Jan. 24, 2021, entry. "Just as I can't forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice."

During the January 2018 Chile trip, Francis created an uproar for discrediting victims of Chile's most notorious abuser. After journalists, including from The Associated Press, challenged him during the in-flight news conference returning home, Francis commissioned an investigation and realized that the victims were right, that he was wrong and had been misled by the Chilean hierarchy.

"Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane," Francis would write later. "I became aware of how serious the problem was. ... It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Francis wrote on June 7, 2018, a few months after he returned, that he "saw the entrance to hell. Pagan seduction in full force" in the Chile scandal.

In July and August of 2018, as he dealt with the fallout, he wrote: "What shame and evil this has brought on the church!" and "Once more the gates of hell. ... May holiness and conversion abound in the midst of so many scandals."
Spiritual crisis followed Vatican financial scandal, introspection
But Francis' spiritual crisis wouldn't come until 2021.
The book dates the onset of the crisis to Jan. 24, 2021. The day before, Francis canceled several upcoming public appearances due to what the Vatican said was a resurgence of his sciatica.

Fernández reveals, however, that Francis was suffering from "insupportable" pain from an intestinal problem that, in July 2021, would land Francis in the hospital for 10 days for surgery to remove 13 inches of his colon.
In January 2021, while the world was still in the throes of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Vatican was in utter upheaval over a massive financial investigation that Francis had authorized.

A few months earlier, in September 2020, Francis had fired a onetime close collaborator, Cardinal Angelo Becciu, convinced Becciu had embezzled money from the Holy See. The scandal - and Francis' belief that a web of corruption had engulfed the Vatican's secretariat of state - led to an unprecedented Vatican investigation and years of legal proceedings through which Francis sought to show his willingness to crack down on financial misconduct.

The trial resulted in some convictions, including against Becciu, but much of prosecutors' theory of a vast conspiracy of corruption was thrown out. The appeals process is ongoing, with Francis' own role in the investigation a key question for the defense.

There is no mention of the trial in Fernández's text, though he hints at it by revealing Francis' later musings that the 2021-2022 spiritual crisis was "mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation."

In the end, Fernández writes that the crisis was primarily related to Francis' exercise of power, the temptation to omnipotence and belief that he was above the world. It's a vice Francis admitted to publicly in 2013, in his first interview as pope, when he acknowledged a tendency to wield power in an "authoritarian" way.

It is significant that Francis was tormented by something his critics often faulted him for: an authoritarian, go-it-alone governing style in an absolute monarch and supreme leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
For Francis, the temptation to omnipotence was the devil tempting him to "reductive curiosity," or believing he alone could solve everyone's problems, and essentially thinking of himself as God.
Moving on from the crisis

By Dec. 30, 2022, Francis had apparently overcome the crisis, by entrusting himself to God. Fernández writes that by then, Francis realized that what began on Jan. 24, 2021, "was a powerful invitation from the Lord to become aware of an accumulation of interior darkness that he had to overcome so he could be free."

Fernández notes that the final two major teaching documents of Francis' life, a 2023 text on confidence in God's merciful love, and a 2024 encyclical on Christ's human and divine love, are deeply spiritual texts borne out of the crisis. They differ in tone and content from the texts often associated with his pontificate.
While the book reveals some of Francis' innermost thoughts, Fernández says Francis wrote his most confidential thoughts in an indecipherable code, which is not reproduced.
The reader is also left wondering what Fernández left out of his selection of diary entries, and what more context he could have provided as one of Francis' most trusted advisers.

Fernández writes that the diary includes hardly any information about church matters, and is truly a spiritual repository. He said he omitted entries affecting third parties, though he does include some of Francis' personal musings, including about then-Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV: "A great pastor, a generous missionary and an irreproachable man."
Fernández said Francis had shown him the diary during one of their meetings and told him, "From this, you will all see," essentially entrusting the writings to him after his death.
Fernández said he mentioned the writings to Leo a few weeks after his election.
"I added that I wished to study these materials — to make them known and interpret the exact meaning of their contents," Fernández wrote. "The Holy Father showed intense interest."
The posthumous publication of popes' innermost spiritual musings is not unusual.

Pope John XXIII's autobiography, "Journal of a Soul," was published by his secretary in 1960. St. John Paul II had wanted his personal notes burned after his death, but his secretary defied his wishes and had the writings published in 2014.

title: Search on for lioness seen roaming Istanbul's outskirts
summary: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials say.
story: Istanbul — Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upscale neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul's European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.
"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search, which was focused on the wooded area. A drone was being used as well, the Anadolu state news agency reported.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search.

"I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it," he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. "While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie (police)."
Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

The search sparked numerous memes on social media, French news agency AFP noted, including one widely shared image showing a lioness sitting outside a gate with the logo of Besiktas FC, one of Istanbul's three major football clubs (soccer teams).

"The lion being sought is under our protection ... it will be tamed and handed over on Monday evening," read a social media post in a Besiktas fan account, referring to the lion being the the symbol of Galatasaray, the club's fierce rivals.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65; bandmates pay emotional tribute

Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died of prostate cancer at the age of 65, Fox News Digital confirmed.
Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates.
"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family.

"He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."

title: John F Kennedy Jr search commander says Ted Kennedy made one strict demand after divers found nephew’s body
summary: New book "The Last Flight" details the 1999 search off Martha's Vineyard where John F. Kennedy Jr.'s body was recovered with his wife and her sister.
story: Captain W. Russell Webster and Theresa M. Webster, authors of "The Last Flight," detail the five-day search for John F. Kennedy Jr. and his family's specific recovery requests.

In the agonizing days following the 1999 plane crash that killed John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and her sister Lauren Bessette, Sen. Ted Kennedy issued a strict, emotional mandate to the federal crews racing to recover their bodies: All three would be brought to the surface together.

Retired U.S. Coast Guard Capt. W. Russell Webster, who spearheaded the search efforts, co-wrote "The Last Flight" with his wife, maritime historian Theresa Mitchell Webster. The book chronicles the massive recovery mission after Kennedy's single-engine plane crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Martha's Vineyard.
Navy divers recovered all three bodies on July 21, 1999 — five days after the plane went down off Martha's Vineyard.
LAST PERSON TO SEE JFK JR. ALIVE REVEALS CHILLING PREMONITION ABOUT HIS FATAL FLIGHT THAT NIGHT

John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy (pictured here) and her sister Lauren Bessette died on July 16, 1999, when the small plane Kennedy was piloting crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Martha’s Vineyard. They are the subjects of a new book, "The Last Flight," written by Capt. W. Russell Webster and Theresa M. Webster. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"It became more complicated to ensure that his family's wishes were followed," Webster told Fox News Digital about the senator. "It was complicated because, normally, when bodies are recovered, they're recovered individually. He insisted that his nephew not be recovered as a priority. That was difficult, not only during the later body recovery, but also very early on when John F. Kennedy Jr. was found outside the airplane."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The Last Flight: The Untold Story of the Search for JFK Jr. and the Race Against the Atlantic" is available now. (Harper Select)
"There was a sense of urgency, driven primarily by the family doctor to have the divers go back down and retrieve him," said Webster.
John F. Kennedy Jr. and his wife Carolyn walk with their dog on Jan. 1, 1997, in New York City. (Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images)

In the book, Webster wrote, "Senator Kennedy was adamant that Navy divers bring up John, Carolyn and Lauren at the exact same time in a single salvage basket. Even though his staffers initially pushed for JFK Jr. to be raised first because his body was outside the wreckage while the women were trapped inside, the senator insisted they be recovered together, so his nephew would not be perceived as receiving special treatment, even in death."
WATCH: JOHN F. KENNEDY JR. RECOVERY COMMANDER RECOUNTS 5-DAY SEARCH MISSION
Webster wrote that the divers were racing against time. "Walking the Atlantic floor stirs up silt, further compromising low visibility," he wrote.

The divers quickly found Kennedy's Piper Saratoga. There was no roof on the plane, and the windows were missing, "having been blown out from the impact." Kennedy Jr. was on his side on the ocean floor near the wreckage.
Where John Kennedy Jr. kept his Piper Saratoga airplane. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"Senator Kennedy insisted that the bodies be raised together at the same time," Mitchell Webster told Fox News Digital. "So, the Navy on the USS Grasp, has what's called a basket. It's a large metal piece with sides for the divers to hang onto. The platform on which they stood in that basket was large enough for them to put three bodies on it. So, they were raised together, and no preferential treatment was shown to JFK Jr."
A Coast Guard helicopter hovering over the ocean during the search for John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn and her sister Lauren. (Steve Liss/Getty Images)
"His uncle, from what we've been told and from what Russ had observed, was extremely respectful of the process and extremely grateful, as was his family, to the people doing the work."
The Bessette sisters were found together inside the upside-down fuselage, still strapped into their seats.
Carolyn Bessette Kennedy poses for a picture at the Annual Fundraising Gala March 9, 1999, at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City. (Evan Agostini/Liaison/Getty Images)

The book describes Kennedy as a constant, protective presence who remained beside his nephew and the Bessette sisters. Once the remains were transferred onto a 55-foot Coast Guard vessel, Kennedy and his sons boarded with them. During the transit, with a Navy chaplain in attendance, the senator invited the Coast Guard crew to join his family in prayer.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Sen. Ted Kennedy is briefed by Lt. Cmdr. Eric Anderson aboard the USS Grasp, on July 21, 1999, during the recovery of the victims. (US Navy Supervisor of Salvage)

When the boat reached shore, Kennedy overruled an aide who wanted to delay unloading until more relatives arrived. He insisted the caskets be brought straight to the waiting hearses. He stepped in to help carry them.
Ted Kennedy gives his nephew John Kennedy Jr. a piggyback ride down the ski slopes in Stowe, Vermont, one Easter weekend. (Bettmann Archive)

"He obviously never left their sides," said Webster. "After everything was done, he and his wife visited my command at Woods Hole and recognized everybody. He took pictures with everybody, gave out cookies and brownies. It was a very human experience."

A Coast Guard ship, carrying Sen. Ted Kennedy and his son, Congressman Patrick Kennedy, on Gay Head, as they head to the USS Grasp, which recovered the body of John F. Kennedy Jr. (Stephen Jaffe/AFP via Getty Images)

In retrieving the bodies, the crew wasn't just worried about beating the elements. There were also potential looters. Webster said they were driven by a very real fear that "treasure hunters" or commercial fishermen would stumble upon the wreckage first and steal personal items to profit off the tragedy.
"Massachusetts State Police Divers assisting in the Kennedy search had to contend with dive operations in waters recently chummed for a local shark tournament," read the book. (Harper Select)

"I think it certainly was a motivation, the potential for not only treasure hunters, but also for fishermen," said Webster. "This was an active fishing area, and we knew we were driven by the fact, not only by the priority given to us, but also with the knowledge that leaving the wreckage and leaving the victims behind was an unacceptable outcome."
Coast Guard Lt. j.g. Tiffany Drumm, Rear Adm. Richard Larrabee and Navy Cmdr. Jeff Pauls are briefed by Lt. Cmdr. Eric Anderson aboard the USS Grasp on July 21, 1999. (US Navy Supervisor of Salvage)
It was one fisherman in those active waters who unknowingly became a key witness to the tragedy.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
A television technician holds up the official handout map of the search and rescue area off Martha's Vineyard, before a press conference. (John Mottern/AFP via Getty Images)

Just before 9:40 p.m. on July 16, 1999, Pittsburgh attorney Victor Pribanic was casting his line for striped bass off Squibnocket Point on the southwestern tip of Martha's Vineyard. A loud, jarring sound echoed across the dark Atlantic. He turned toward the open ocean, saw nothing in the haze and went back to fishing. Pribanic was unaware that he had just heard the final moments of Kennedy's plane.
"It wasn't an explosion. It was a boom," said Webster. "The impact was grave, and it was severe. They likely just went down 116 feet."
A grainy side-scan sonar (SSS) image of John F. Kennedy Jr.'s airplane at a depth of 116 feet in the Atlantic Ocean, 7.25 miles southwest of Martha’s Vineyard. (NOAA)
Looking back, Webster said he was proud of his crew's commitment to duty in retrieving Kennedy's beloved nephew and his family, even as a heavy sadness settled over everyone involved.
John F. Kennedy, Jr. gives his wife Carolyn a kiss on the cheek during the annual White House Correspondents dinner on May 1, 1999, in Washington, D.C. (Tyler Mallory/Liaison/Getty Images)

"I remember feeling exhaustion," said Webster. "I believe I had just laid down for no more than an hour after not sleeping since I got the original call. It was a mixed feeling, a feeling of profound grief and a feeling of profound happiness.

"I worked with a number of families that we could never save their loved ones or find their remains so that they could celebrate their lives in ceremonies. For me, it was a dichotomy of feelings. One was, 'Oh my God, we found them as a team.' And the other was, 'Yes, they're really dead.'"
WATCH: AVIATION EXPERT EXPLAINS JFK JR.'S FINAL FLIGHT RISKS

Ultimately, the National Transportation Safety Board determined the crash was caused by spatial disorientation. Though Kennedy Jr. had recently passed his written instrument exam, he was not yet certified to fly solely using his cockpit instruments. Just weeks before the crash, a certified flight instructor had noted in his record that he was not ready for instrument conditions.
Jackie Kennedy Onassis stands with her son John F. Kennedy Jr., who graduated from Phillips Academy at Andover. Daughter Caroline and Sen. Edward M. Kennedy were also present. (Bettmann Archive)
"What was clear to me was that in those final miles, he had transitioned into an instrument-rated flight that he was not prepared for," Webster said.

title: Christina Ricci admits Cher is 'still mad at me' decades after one mistake ended 'Mermaids' bond

story: Christina Ricci says her "Mermaids" costar Cher still holds a grudge against her. (Getty Images)

Nearly four decades after playing mother and daughter in the 1990 classic "Mermaids," Christina Ricci revealed that her off-screen relationship with Cher has been rocky — all because of an unreturned voicemail from when Ricci was 19.

Despite the decades-long silent treatment, Ricci holds no ill will — and even took Cher's side in the standoff, noting how supportive the Oscar winner had been to her as a child actor on set.
