"And a judge has to scrutinize that and say, 'Well, oh, okay, I agree in this case. There is enough here. There's enough smoke here that there may be fire. And you have the court's permission to do the investigation that you need to do.'"

title: 'Grave concerns' mount as Army moves to restart DC helicopter training after deadly 2025 crash
summary: Rep. Don Beyer says the Army contacted the FAA to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport, but the FAA says no request arrived.
story: President Donald Trump addresses the FAA ground stop and broader technology disruptions, calling the nation’s air traffic control system outdated. Responding to Fox News' Aishah Hasnie, Trump says air travel remains safe and outlines his request for $50 billion from the Senate to upgrade the system.
Criticism is mounting among experts concerned with the U.S. Army's "risky" plan to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport following a deadly midair collision in 2025.

The Army released a plan and told select members of Congress it wants to restart helicopter test flights near DCA — just a few miles from the Pentagon — as soon as Dec. 1, 2026. Backlash immediately ensued.
Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., asserted on X he has "grave concerns about the decision to resume training flights before the NTSB’s safety recommendations have been fully implemented."

A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital that it "has not received a formal request to resume military helicopter flights around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA)."
"Approval from the agency is required before any training in the area can restart," the spokesperson added.
FAA, NTSB INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF SAFETY PROTOCOL INVOLVING TRUMP, MARINE ONE
Rep. Don Beyer Jr., D-Va., attends a protest in Washington. (Tom Williams/Getty Images)

A U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with American Airlines Flight 5342 in January 2025, killing all 67 people aboard both aircrafts. The FAA subsequently halted military helicopter training flights in the area in May 2025 after another Black Hawk helicopter flew too close to DCA, forcing air traffic controllers to reroute some commercial flights.

In a March 14, 2025, statement the FAA said it was "permanently closing [helicopter] Route 4 between Hains Point and the Wilson Bridge and evaluating alternative helicopter routes as recommended by the NTSB."

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., on Monday wrote in an X post that the Army told his office it had reached out to the FAA regarding its request to resume training flights and is currently "awaiting a response."
"Army officials assured my office that no flights will take place unless they are approved by the FAA," Beyer stated.
His office did not expand on specific concerns when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
An anonymous Army spokesperson told Politico on Monday "there is intent to resume flights," acknowledging that the move would require approval from the FAA.
TRUMP HELICOPTER’S RADIO WARNINGS WENT UNHEARD BEFORE CLOSE CALL WITH PASSENGER JET, REPORT SAYS

A piece of wreckage is lifted from the water onto a salvage vessel near the site in the Potomac River of a midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter, at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Feb. 4, 2025, in Arlington, Virginia. (AP)
The DOT referred Fox News Digital to the FAA when reached for comment.

"Members of the investigative team and I were briefed on the Army’s plans to begin the initial phase of a return to helicopter flights to the Pentagon through airspace near DCA as soon as December 1st," NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy told Fox News Digital.

"It is our understanding that the FAA has yet to receive a formal request for these flights. We have not seen the Army’s concept of operations and look forward to reviewing it once it is formally submitted to the FAA for evaluation."
FAA UNVEILS NEW AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLER HIRING PLAN AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS ‘CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED’
When reached for comment on Tuesday, the Department of War referred Fox News Digital to the Army. The Army did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
Resuming helicopter training flights near DCA could pose "major" safety concerns, according to Randy Klatt, flight safety officer at the Foundation for Aviation Safety (FAS).

"Yes, [there are] major concerns considering that no entity — the airlines, DCA, FAA, or the Army — took any proactive action on the thousands of loss-of-separation incidents that preceded the midair collision. Helicopter Route 4 was a trap as designed, yet it was in use regularly until disaster struck," Klatt told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. "Knowing this does not instill any confidence that the resumption of Army training flights will be done safely and in close coordination with the FAA."
"There has been no mention of reopening Helicopter Route 4 but for the above reasons FAS would strongly oppose such an action," he added.
The air traffic control tower after the American Airlines crash at the Reagan National Airport on Feb. 3, 2025, in Arlington, Virginia. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Heritage Foundation senior research fellow and retired U.S. Navy Capt. Brent Sadler warned Fox News Digital that there is little justification to restart training flights "or even routine flights" in the DCA area.
"Interference to commercial [air] traffic remains a risk," Sadler explained. "Training flights would be better served in a lower activity area at least from commercial civilian air traffic."
"There is little reason to rationalize training flights or even routine flights in proximity to DCA," Sadler continued.

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge from 2020 against incoming House Dem
summary: LaKesha Womack settled a 2019 Budget Car Rental bill for a Toyota Corolla she never returned, allowing prosecutors to drop the felony charge.
story: Incoming Democratic congresswoman LaKesha Womack says she never received court notices for being wanted for a felony after failing to return a rental car on time during a period of homelessness. (Credit: YouTube/Annie Dance)
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Nearly two weeks after she was declared the winner in the Nov. 3 election, flipping a Republican-held seat, a North Carolina Democrat settled a 2019 rental car bill for a car she did not return, allowing prosecutors to drop a felony charge.

Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer B. Merriweather III, a fellow Democrat, dropped the case that featured a court summons served to Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., at a campaign event Oct. 11, more than six years after the Jan. 14, 2020 summons was secured by prosecutors.
Womack said she did not know she was wanted for a felony because she was homeless at the time and not able to receive mail. She paid off the rental car company as part of an agreement last week.
DEMOCRAT WHO TOPPLED GOP INCUMBENT WILL HEAD TO COURT ON FELONY CHARGE JUST DAYS AFTER ELECTION UPSET

Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., poses for a portrait after Congressional freshmen of the 120th Congress participated in a group photograph on the steps of the House of Representatives at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. – just two days after appearing in court on a felony summons and just days before paying the settlement for an unreturned rental car. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"On November 16, 2026, this office was informed of an agreement reached between Defendant Womack and the rental dealer," Merriweather's DA office wrote in a statement Tuesday. "In the days that followed, we were able to confirm that the victim rental corporation received a sum of money from the Defendant equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation.

"In a subsequent phone call with a prosecutor, representatives for the victim rental corporation said explicitly that the corporation did not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved."

Womack first appeared in court on the summons one week after being declared a future U.S. House member, and nearly seven years after the summons was issued. The rental car agreement was from Oct. 11, 2019, according to the district attorney, and the car was seized by local law enforcement on Dec. 4, 2019.

Womack said she did not receive the official felony court summons until Oct. 11, 2026 — less than a month before the midterm elections — when an officer personally handed her the paperwork at a campaign event.
DEMOCRAT HOUSE CANDIDATE HIT WITH FELONY SUMMONS AT CAMPAIGN EVENT

Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., used her battle with diabetes, a hospital stay, single motherhood and homelessness in her campaign to flip a Republican House seat in the once-red state of North Carolina. (LaKesha Womack Facebook)
Womack has spoken publicly about being homeless without a permanent mailing address after moving back to Charlotte in 2016 to work on the Hillary Clinton campaign.

"I was struggling," she said in an October video posted to Facebook. "I was struggled so bad that there were days that I wanted to end my life – that I did not think I was strong enough to push forward.

"At one point, I had a rental car, and I did not return the rental car on time. I did not know that they had filed a case against me, because, again, I was homeless and I had no place to receive mail, so I didn't get any notification about it."
She added she was "going to figure out how much money do y'all need" to settle. That happened after her first court appearance, according to the district attorney's office's news release.
Fox News Digital reached out to Womack's campaign for comment, but they did not immediately respond.
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., was just a one-term House member, having served in the North Carolina State House from 2003 to 2025, including five terms as state House speaker from 2015. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Just a week prior, Womack defeated incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., by roughly two points in the race to represent North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. She had rebuked campaign attack ads from friends of Moore targeting her late in the race, calling "the timing of my court date (one full week after Election Day) especially frustrating" and saying diabetes, an intensive car visit, single motherhood and homelessness contributed to her delinquency.

"I have experienced some incredibly difficult chapters in my life, including a serious medical emergency that required hospitalization in intensive care," Womack told WBTV-3 just days before the election. "As a single mother living with type 1 Diabetes, that experience was frightening, overwhelming and life-changing. Like millions of Americans, I learned firsthand how quickly an unexpected medical crisis can disrupt your health, financial stability, and ability to provide for your family."

The charge, felony failure to return hired property, stemmed from a 2019 Toyota Corolla with an estimated value of $20,000 that Womack rented from Budget Car Rental on Aug. 27, 2019, according to prosecutors and court records. Womack renewed the agreement twice, with the final rental period beginning Oct. 7, 2019, before local law enforcement recovered the vehicle and returned it to the company Dec. 4, 2019.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., went from Election Day to a felony court summons a week earlier this month and now heads to her swearing in to Congress in early January. (Getty Images)

Womack’s attorney, Harold Cogdell Jr., told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that his client had been "unaware a criminal summons had issued" for nearly seven years and moved quickly to settle the balance once notified. Cogdell noted that the Corolla was returned undamaged 41 days before the criminal charge was filed.
The felony became a central attack line in the closing stretch of the race, with Republican ads warning voters against electing a "felony defendant."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"How is she going to be an advocate for our community when she can't manage her own personal affairs?" Moore's campaign told Fox News Digital last month. "As an attorney for over 30 years, I think everyone should be held to the same standard of justice, and this situation is no different. Free legal advice: When the rental agreement ends, so does your right to keep the car."
Fox News Digital's Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Marco Rubio's 2028 stock surges among House Republicans as Trump insiders split on Vance
summary: House Republicans are pushing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to launch a 2028 presidential run, calling him the GOP's unifier after midterm losses.
story: Hurt examines the speculation surrounding Trump's potential successor, the political futures of Vance and Rubio and what the president's comments could mean for the Republican Party's leadership heading into 2028.
As Republicans continue to pick up the pieces from their 2026 midterm losses, one Trump administration official is catching some GOP lawmakers' eyes as the party's next great hope.

"[Secretary of State Marco Rubio] is the whole package. He's intelligent, charismatic, level-headed, cool-tempered and very knowledgeable about the issues and eloquent in explaining them," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "I think there is a lot of interest from Republicans in seeing him explore a run."

Indeed, multiple House Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital said they and their colleagues are pushing Rubio to run for president in 2028. The Cabinet official himself has publicly dismissed any talk about his future political plans, but his name is on the rise among Republicans who have said the party needs to pivot from the issues that cost them votes in November.
HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN'

"Now that we lost majorities, we can't push policy, so we will have to do better at communicating," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital on election night. "I am all in for Marco. He can be a unifier."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio holds his end-of-year press conference at the State Department in Washington, D.C., Dec. 19, 2025. (Kevin Mohatt/Reuters)
They're notable comments coming from the Indiana Republican, who was among the founding members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028
Rubio has long been held up as a potential 2028 contender, despite a previous unsuccessful White House bid in 2016.

He and Vice President JD Vance have been regarded as the top contenders for the GOP nomination, but it's Rubio's name that has come up in conversations among House Republicans, Fox News Digital was told.
GOP MIDTERM BLOODBATH EXPOSES CRACKS IN VANCE'S 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS

"A number of my colleagues, unsolicited by me — they come up with me, knowing that I'm on board, [from] Miami, et cetera — and said that they'd want to support him, that they would support him if he ran," Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. " And it's not just a few. There's a number, a pretty good number, that have told me that."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks at the Pnyx hill, where ancient Athenians held democratic assemblies, with the ancient Parthenon temple atop the Acropolis seen in the background, in Athens on Oct. 7, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein/AFP via Getty Images)

Gimenez said he supported Rubio even before the election. The same goes for Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., who told Fox News Digital he's been openly backing his fellow Florida Republican for two months.
"And I think the affirmation that I'm getting from talking to people is overwhelming," Haridopolos said.

"He is not only understanding what's happening today, but our place in history. And I think his inspirational story, his parents coming from Cuba and living the opportunity that is America, and inspiring people that anything is possible is the uplifting message we need."
SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM

Both Haridopolos and Malliotakis pointed to Rubio's recent speech in Greece calling for the renewal of Western civilization as an example of his presidential possibility. Those remarks, set in Athens, were widely lauded for their scenic backdrop of the Acropolis at sunset.
And Malliotakis, who is half Cuban herself, said Rubio could "reach" Hispanic voters who largely turned away from the GOP in November.
LATINO VOTERS SWING BACK TO DEMOCRATS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS: POLL
"The potential for him to be the first Hispanic president is huge for our party and the country," she said.
President Donald Trump reacts as he speaks to the media as he arrives at Glasgow Prestwick Airport on July 25, 2025, in Prestwick, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
But within the administration itself, it appears no clear successor has emerged.
One source familiar with talks told Fox News Digital that Trump administration staffers were "about 50/50" when asked if they favored Vance or Rubio.
"I think it’s pretty split," one administration official said. "I don’t think the president really knows. I think if you asked him today, he’d say Rubio."
"50/50 feels right to me," a second administration official said.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly referred Fox News Digital to President Donald Trump’s previous comments on the matter.

Over the weekend, Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that Vance and Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" when asked who he would like to see run on the Republican and Democratic tickets ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment but did not hear back by press time.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Trump's Nvidia power play opens Pandora's box Democrats could weaponize, analyst warns
summary: Eric Schiffer says Trump's push to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opens a Pandora's box Democrats may exploit, but national security won.
story: Eric Schiffer, CEO of Reputation Management Consultants Inc., believes Democrats are engaging in double-sided messaging by attacking Trump’s efforts to reinstate Jensen Huang.

The Trump administration’s efforts to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia have set a new bar for shaping a private corporation, according to Eric Schiffer, chairman and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, a crisis management and brand protection firm.
"Trump came in to really give a second life to Jensen, where he would have been dead," Schiffer told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

Schiffer said the intervention has opened a kind of Pandora’s box that Democrats may seek to exploit to benefit ideological allies in the private sector. Still, he said the national security interests underpinning Trump’s efforts to intervene on behalf of Huang fall within the responsibilities of the presidency.
JENSEN HUANG'S NVIDIA RETURN SENDS CHINA A CLEAR MESSAGE: THE AI RACE IS ON

Jensen Huang apologized to Nvidia employees for being unfaithful to his wife, saying his actions hurt her and their children and that "there is no excuse for what I did." (Soeren Stache/picture alliance/Getty Images)
Asked whether he believes Democrats may use the moment as a precedent to tip the scales in favor of ideological allies down the road, Schiffer said he sees that possibility in the cards.
"I think that, of course, they would have that capability. I think that that is a risk," Schiffer said.
But Schiffer said the justification would likely depend on the circumstances.
"If the Democrats had a similar situation or it's a leading organization that is so critical to both national security and the economy, then it would make sense," Schiffer said.

"However, if the Democrats — and perhaps the future president that might be a Democrat — is empowering a crony … then I think they're going to be open to significant criticism. And I think that there would be pushback on behalf of the American public," he added.
"This is very unique and different in my opinion."
CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science during a summit at the U.S. Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, D.C., Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters/Evan Vucci)

Nvidia's board decided to bring back Huang as CEO after he resigned earlier this month following reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence identified Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover.

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News that President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance worked over the weekend to reinstate Huang after they received security briefings and became convinced that Huang did not present a national security threat in his role as CEO.
In recent days, Vance worked with figures in Silicon Valley and executives at Nvidia to urge the board to reinstate him, the source said.

Democrats have blasted Trump's involvement, calling it presidential overreach. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, noted that Trump owns Nvidia stock. Trump holds between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, according to reporting from The Washington Post and its review of Trump's disclosures.
"We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," Garcia said in a statement.
U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-Calif., echoed Garcia's criticisms.
"We will not allow America’s national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," Jeffries wrote in a press release on Monday.

Despite those criticisms from Democrats, Schiffer believes the nation’s security interests prevailed through Trump’s decision, arguing that Nvidia's central role in U.S. competition with China made Huang’s return a matter the president could not ignore.

"[In] the office of the presidency, you know, there's the duty to ensure that the United States continues to be strong geopolitically and certainly from a national security perspective. The move to help Jensen accomplishes those," Schiffer said.
"That's part of what a good leader and a strong leader should be doing."
TO BEAT CHINA ON AI, WASHINGTON MUST FIRST EARN AMERICANS' TRUST
President Donald Trump speaks with Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center Nov. 19, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

Apart from its reasoning for the administration's intervention, Schiffer pointed out that Trump had only used soft power to encourage Huang's return, a far cry from forcing Nvidia into its decision through any formal use of the presidency.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"This was not a situation where the government came in under some military policy and tried to take control of Nvidia," Schiffer said. "This was the lightest form of power."

The White House and the Office of the Vice President did not immediately respond to requests for comment about whether they shared concerns about Democrats using political power to intervene in the private sector in future administrations or whether the administration had created a new precedent for corporate intervention.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'
summary: Kroger faces backlash over cutting 3,000 U.S. jobs while recruiting for a new Bangalore hub, as critics accuse the grocer of offshoring American roles.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Theo Wold, former White House Deputy Assistant for Domestic Policy under Trump, about the controversy surrounding Kroger’s move to offshore jobs.

Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising new positions overseas in India.

The controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year plan it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029.

While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the company is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices.

"‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do,’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners."
KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF
A customer shops for eggs at a grocery store on March 12, 2025, in Chicago, Illinois. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Wold said situations like this need to "start to be an honest conversation about penalizing businesses that take jobs and send them overseas."
Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) responded on X by saying, "Hire American."
"This insanity has to stop," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson posted on X. "Reshore ALL US companies. We’re rapidly becoming India, and I didn’t serve 20 years defending that!"
FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS
A Kroger grocery store in Covington, Kentucky, on Sunday, June 2, 2024. (Jeffrey Dean/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Kroger says these cuts are to ‘lower prices,’" workforce intelligence researcher Amanda Goodall wrote on X. "Classic. Do you think we will see lower prices at the grocery stores? I'm not holding my breath. I'm not a boycott person... but... damn. "

In a statement, a Kroger spokesperson said the notifications "are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology." Kroger declined to answer questions regarding how many U.S. roles are being shifted to its new Bangalore capability center, the projected headcount in India or which departments were most affected.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A young man shopping for groceries at the grocery store. (iStock)

The first wave of layoff notices went out to corporate employees last week, marking the initial phase of an overhaul announced in October by CEO Greg Foran that will pare Kroger’s white-collar workforce from roughly 8,200 to 5,200. Frontline store and warehouse employees are not targeted by the cuts.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
In an October internal memo announcing the 3,000-role reduction, Foran pointed to expanding artificial intelligence and workflow automation as a central driver for trimming corporate overhead.

At the same time, job boards have listed nearly 30 corporate openings for Kroger’s new Global Capability Center in Bangalore across finance, supply chain, real estate and data analytics. Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley previously told investors the overseas capability center would deliver modest savings in 2026 before generating more substantial cost reductions in 2027 and 2028.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Senate GOP takes risky bet on Dems as holiday shutdown deadline looms: 'It's a gamble'
summary: Senate Republicans are betting on Senate Democrats to avert another government shutdown as Democrats aim to use funding to end the eight-month Iran war.
story: Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt discusses House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries refusing to rule out another government shutdown to force an end to the Iran conflict on ‘America Reports.’
Congress is nearing the deadline to avert a government shutdown, and Senate Republicans are taking a leap of faith as the clock ticks: trusting Senate Democrats to dodge a holiday disaster.

When the upper chamber returns on Nov. 30, there will be just shy of two weeks for both sides to reach an agreement to thwart another partisan closure. At the center of the issue is the Iran war: Democrats intend to use the government’s purse strings to bring the eight-month conflict to an end.

Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. They have, for now, pressed pause on ramming those tax dollars through the party-line budget reconciliation process, and instead are opening the door to work with Democrats.
DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

There’s history here: Senate Democrats have twice now ushered in a government shutdown. And though Republicans agreed behind closed doors to move forward with their counterparts, they know it’s a leap in the dark.
"Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.
Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., was seen during a series of Senate votes at the U.S. Capitol on June 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I mean, obviously, if it's party-line, when you look at the House side, you know, we got members not showing up," he continued. "So, either way, it's a gamble. It’s a toss-up whether we try to do [appropriations] or reconciliation."
There is a middle ground beginning to form, however.

Senate Democrats are aligning behind a plan that would fund several of the GOP’s and administration’s defense priorities, particularly refilling dwindling munitions stocks that have taken a hit from the war.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has been working with a small group of Senate Democrats to produce a plan, said that while they want funding prohibitions for the war, there are some exceptions, like "defense of U.S. troops if the president seeks an authorization, evacuation of U.S. personnel."
SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER
Those exceptions would likely ride on a short-term continuing resolution (CR) that would keep the government open into early next year.

He acknowledged that it was a give-and-take with Republicans, given that they do want up to $350 billion in emergency supplemental funding for the war and Pentagon, and that some limited agreements on guardrails for Iran war funding could be used as a bargaining chip for broader funding through the emergency package.

"I think there's a pretty wide recognition on both sides of the aisle that some of the munitions replacement money is needed pretty soon," Kaine said. "It's not like it produces weaponry soon, but you kind of have to start it soon."
MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., arrives for a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on June 2, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Others in the caucus, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are firm in their position that the war must end.
"This is an illegal, unconstitutional and horrific war," Sanders told Fox News Digital. "I want that — the American people want to see it ended as soon as possible."
And Republicans are all too familiar with the recent history of record-shattering shutdown after record-shattering shutdown.
Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital that, boiled down, the issue was about "supporting our troops and investing in our military."

"I would think the Democrats would want to support that," Banks said. "I find it baffling that they're not willing to. So I hope they'll come to the table in the interest of keeping America safe and supporting our military."

Turning to the normal government funding process, or at least using a CR, instead of reconciliation could pay off for Republicans down the line, too, when Democrats take control of the Senate next year.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., balked at Democrats’ recent history of shutdowns and told Fox News Digital that "if you always assume the worst-case scenario, the worst-case scenario is always gonna happen."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He argued that Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and appropriators should be given a chance "to say, look, we know we have areas of controversy, but some of this … spending is very, very important."
"At least try that, because then you're laying the groundwork for maybe some bipartisan regular order appropriations next year if you go down this path," Tillis said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been keyed into the ongoing negotiations, and said that there was "some interest, as you know, probably on our side" in striking a deal with the Democrats.
When asked if it was a proposal President Donald Trump could support, Thune said, "I hope so."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Tuberville suggests Texans 'flee the woke-show' for Alabama after blue wave midterm elections
summary: Alabama Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville is inviting Texas residents and businesses to "flee the woke-show" for his state after Democrats swept every statewide race in Texas.
story: Alabama Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville invited Texans and businesses to relocate to his state, urging conservatives to "flee the woke-show" following recent Democratic election victories in the Lone Star State.

Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is set to become the state's next governor in January, invited Texas residents and businesses to "flee the woke-show" and move to Alabama after historic Democratic gains in the Lone Star State during the midterm elections earlier this month.
"To any red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas… Alabama is open for business," Tuberville, a Republican, wrote Monday on X.
Tuberville was responding to a video shared by Libs of TikTok, an account run by a conservative influencer, that appears to show an event hosted by Equality Texas, a pro-LGBTQ+ advocacy group.
DAN PATRICK CONCEDES TEXAS 'TURNED PURPLE' AFTER DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC BLUE WAVE
Alabama Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville invited Texas residents and businesses to "flee the woke-show" and move to Alabama. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Texas is Black. Texas is gay. Texas is trans. Texas is indigenous. Texas is lesbian. Texas is all of us," the speaker is heard saying in the clip.
"Never, never forget that the 'T' in Texas stands for trans," the speaker continued.
This comes after Democrats swept statewide races in Texas and flipped the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat and the Texas House, while Republicans managed to maintain control of the Texas Senate.
TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

Tuberville's invitation comes after Democrats swept statewide races in Texas and flipped the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat and the Texas House. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Gov. Greg Abbott, who was vying for a fourth term, lost in his re-election bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick lost his re-election to Democrat Vikki Goodwin and Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico, contributing to huge Democratic gains in the state and across the country.

Democrats won every statewide race in Texas, bringing an end to decades of Republican control in contests that had once been considered sure bets for the GOP and leaving U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz as the only Republican holding statewide elected office.
With those key victories, Texas will be under Democratic control for the first time in more than three decades.
Democrats won every statewide race in Texas, bringing an end to decades of Republican control. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Patrick acknowledged that Texas has "turned purple," while Cruz described the elections as a "blue tsunami."
Equality Texas endorsed Hinojosa, Talarico and other Democratic candidates down the ballot in the Lone Star State.
"We're looking cautiously optimistic to see what can be accomplished in this new legislative landscape," the group said earlier this month following the elections.

title: California prosecutors, victim advocates challenge Newsom's mass death sentence commutation
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom defended commuting 548 death sentences, but victims' advocates and a district attorney call the move morally offensive.
story: Victim advocates and California prosecutors are pushing back against Gov. Gavin Newsom’s blanket commutation of all 548 death row sentences, arguing the move overrides the will of voters, bypasses individual case reviews and could eventually open a legal pathway to freedom for convicted killers.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom justified his blanket commutation of 548 death sentences to life without parole by arguing that reviewing cases individually would create "two classes of murder victims," a rationale victims' advocates and at least one district attorney called "morally offensive. "
Modoc County District Attorney Nina Salarno said Newsom's sweeping action denied the loved ones of murder victims any voice in the clemency process.

"I found it really offensive as a victim myself, and [for] my other victims," Salarno told Fox News Digital from Washington, D. C., where she and fellow advocates met with President Donald Trump this week. "There should be individual scrutiny. The individual victims should have a voice. And that's what he has avoided by doing a blanket commutation."
CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks on March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
"The blanket commutation on a moral level as a victim I find very offensive, but I find the whole thing offensive to our entire rule of law," she added.

Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, a nonprofit that advocates for stricter laws against violent offenders, noted that California voters have repeatedly upheld the death penalty at the ballot box, including approving a 2016 measure aimed at speeding up executions.

"Here's a guy who throws rocks about kings and protests throughout the streets," Padilla said, referring to Newsom's past criticisms of Trump. "I will promise you, this is a move that is looked at and viewed as a king. He is trampling on the voters."

On Monday, Trump vowed to direct the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers and expedite federal executions as victims’ relatives spoke out at the Justice Department against Newsom's order.

Lieutenant Sam Robinson, a public information officer at San Quentin State Prison, knocks on the door to the East Block for condemned prisoners during a media tour of California's Death Row in San Quentin, Calif., on Dec. 29, 2015. (Stephen Lam/Reuters)
SLAIN FIREFIGHTER'S MOTHER PLEADS WITH TRUMP TO INTERVENE AFTER NEWSOM STOPS KILLER'S DEATH SENTENCE

"Gavin Newsom and the radical left look at these heinous acts, and their sympathy is not for the children and their parents, but for the monsters who extinguished innocent young lives," Trump said. "He stood with the murderers and child slayers."
Justice for crime victims shouldn't be a partisan issue, Padilla said.
"Whether you're a Democrat or a Republican, you take politics out of this," he said. "The president of the United States stood up and sounded the alarm. And I hope the country hears it."
Newsom's office referred Fox News Digital to news release from Monday featuring victims and survivors who support his decision.

President Donald Trump approaches, Gloria Vega, daughter of murdered Palm Springs police officer Jose "Gil" Vega, at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 23, 2026, as he criticizes California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his decision to commute the death sentences of 548 prisoners. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION

"As a member of the clergy, I believe that all life is sacred. I also believe in the possibility of redemption. Because of this, I oppose the death penalty," said Rabbi Suzanne Singer, the sister of Michele Reiner and sister-in-law of famed film director Rob Reiner, who were both stabbed to death in December 2025 inside their Los Angeles home.

"As a civilized nation, it is barbaric that we still subject people to die at the hands of the state. I am so grateful to Governor Newsom for commuting the death sentences that have been imposed in our state. This is true proof of his moral character."

On Nov. 16, a coalition of roughly 30 county district attorneys, law enforcement groups, victims' rights advocates and grieving families filed a petition with the California Supreme Court seeking to halt Newsom's commutations.
MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

Salarno argued that the governor's move disrespects the jurors and judges who endured months-long capital trials. Even though California has not carried out an execution since 2006, Padilla noted that the death sentence itself provides essential legal validation and finality for grieving families, a loss he knows firsthand.

"The fact of the matter is the law is the law," Padilla said. "It's like changing the innings in a baseball game, changing from nine to seven retroactively, going back [and] going, 'I know you won that game, but we're going to make it seven innings and now you lost.'"
CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

The fight is also deeply personal for Salarno, whose older sister, Catina Rose Salarno, was murdered in 1979 on her first day at the University of the Pacific by her former high school boyfriend, Steven Burns. Following the tragedy, Salarno's mother, Harriet, founded Crime Victims United.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Look, my sister's never coming back, and I understand that," Padilla added. "But I have to accept that she was murdered, like these families have to accept that their loved ones were. And we have to trust the justice system. And now it's been taken away from them. And that's where I think the real issue comes."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: ICE nabs illegal immigrant days after he claims $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery prize
summary: ICE sources say Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an El Salvador man with a 2014 deportation order, ran from officers in East Boston before his arrest.
story: Federal immigration officers arrested Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales in East Boston after a brief foot chase. The arrest came days after he claimed a $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery prize.
A man who smiled for a Massachusetts State Lottery photo with a $1 million check was arrested by federal immigration officers days later after a brief foot chase in East Boston.
Three ICE sources told Fox News that Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal immigrant from El Salvador, ran when officers moved in to arrest him early Tuesday but was quickly caught.
Multiple officers’ body cameras captured the encounter, the sources said.
ICE ARRESTS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF RAPE, MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES AFTER RELEASE FROM MARYLAND JAIL

Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales holds a ceremonial $1 million check dated Nov. 18, 2026. The Massachusetts State Lottery said he bought the winning ticket at a market in East Boston. (Massachusetts State Lottery via Facebook)
Velasquez-Morales had been wanted by ICE under a final deportation order issued in April 2014, the sources said.
He crossed the U.S. border illegally near Roma, Texas, in 2013, according to the sources.
MASSACHUSETTS SUES TRUMP ADMIN TO STOP ICE'S COURTHOUSE ARRESTS: 'UNNECESSARY FEAR'
Velasquez-Morales had been wanted by ICE under a final deportation order issued in April 2014. (Dept. of Homeland Security/ICE, File)
The Massachusetts State Lottery awarded Velasquez-Morales the $1 million prize Nov. 18, and posted a photo on Facebook three days later showing him holding the oversized check.
The lottery said he bought The Lottery's winning "$2,000,000 50X Cashword" $10 scratch ticket at a market in East Boston, the same neighborhood where ICE arrested him.
Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales is shown in ICE custody after his arrest in East Boston, Mass., on Tuesday, six days after he won a $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery prize. (ICE Boston)
The Massachusetts State Lottery says anyone 18 or older can buy a ticket from a licensed retailer. The governor appoints two members of the five-member commission that oversees the lottery.

Fox News Digital reached out to Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey’s office and the lottery for comment.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Kilmar Ábrego García lands in Spain, ending deportation battle with Trump administration
summary: Kilmar Ábrego García voluntarily left the United States for Spain on Tuesday to avoid forced deportation, according to DHS, capping a months-long legal battle with ICE.
story: Kilmar Abrego Garcia lands in Madrid, Spain, after leaving the United States voluntarily amid a deportation fight.

Kilmar Ábrego García, the illegal immigrant from El Salvador whose case became a flashpoint for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies, landed in Spain on Wednesday after agreeing to leave the United States.
Ábrego García departed Tuesday for Madrid on a commercial flight and was swarmed with supporters and journalists after touching down and making his way through the airport.

His voluntary departure ends his battle with the Trump administration that began last year with his initial deportation over allegations that he was a member of the MS-13 gang. He ultimately plans to make his way to Mexico, The New York Times reported, citing his attorneys.
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of Ábrego García's lawyers, said in a statement late Tuesday that this is a "temporary departure" for his client, who has left the U.S. as a "free man."
TRUMP’S SPECIAL STRATEGY TO DEPORT ILLEGALS GIVES HIM ANOTHER TOOL FOR ENFORCEMENT

Kilmar Ábrego García, the El Salvadoran national that the Trump administration has tried to deport for nearly two years, is swarmed by reporters after landing in Madrid, Spain, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Oscar Del Pozo / AFP via Getty Images)

"Mr. Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
The White House celebrated Ábrego García leaving the U.S., maintaining that he is a gang member and a criminal.

"The American people can be thankful this Thanksgiving that this MS-13 gang member, human trafficker, serial domestic abuser, and child predator can no longer terrorize American citizens," said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. "This Salvadoran man chose to self-deport to Spain — a country that has been wrecked by open-border policies. Good riddance."
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that he was "delighted" that Ábrego García would be on his way to Spain the next day.
Karoline Leavitt, formerly the White House press secretary, also weighed in, saying that Ábrego García leaving the country has "vindicated" the Trump administration.

"This was an individual who illegally entered our country, who has a very long and deep criminal record, by the way, and deserves and needs to be deported," Leavitt told Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy on Wednesday. "Kudos to the president, the Department of Homeland Security and Stephen Miller, who have been adamant about what's doing what's right."

A federal judge in Maryland ordered Ábrego García to leave the U.S. by Tuesday, according to two sources familiar with the matter. That order remains under seal, and the exact terms of his release were not immediately clear.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) emphasized that Ábrego García did not receive any financial incentives through the Trump administration's voluntary self-deportation program, which offers migrants travel assistance and financial support to leave the country.

"To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives," DHS posted on X. "He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man who was deported to El Salvador earlier this year, and his wife Jennifer Vasquez Sura, left, arrive for a check-in at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office in Baltimore, Maryland, on Monday, Aug. 25, 2025. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
DHS also rejected descriptions of Ábrego García as a Maryland resident.

"Kilmar Abrego Garcia is not and will never be a Maryland Man—he is a criminal illegal alien from El Salvador and was a public safety threat to American citizens. He is not coming back, despite the efforts of sanctuary politicians who spent massive amounts of time and money defending this low-life," the department said.

The move comes after sustained efforts by the Trump administration to remove Ábrego García, who entered the U.S. illegally more than a decade ago. At one point during the legal proceedings, federal authorities sought to deport him to several African nations, one of them being Liberia.

Ábrego García had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when immigration authorities detained him in March 2025. He was subsequently deported to El Salvador in error and held in the Central American nation's maximum-security CECOT prison despite a standing court order barring his removal there due to the risk of gang persecution.
MIKE DAVIS: KILMAR ABREGO GARCIA, THE DEMOCRATS' PATRON SAINT OF HUMAN TRAFFICK

Kilmar Ábrego García, right, and his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, attend a prayer vigil before he enters a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office Aug. 25, 2025, in Baltimore. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Democrats rallied around him despite his suspected ties to the MS-13 gang.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag. Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who visited Ábrego García while detained in El Salvador.

"While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation," Van Hollen added. "I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution."
Kilmar Ábrego García and his wife, Jennifer, are seen outside the ICE Field Office in Baltimore on August 25, 2025. (Breanne Deppisch/Fox News Digital)

Federal officials eventually returned him to the U.S. to face human smuggling charges from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. He pleaded not guilty to the charges, which a judge later dismissed.

Throughout the legal fight, the administration has claimed that Ábrego García was a gang member and pointed to a 2021 protective order his wife had filed against him over domestic violence allegations.

title: Obama judge's Omar warrant unsealing directly contradicts his own decision in Trump case, DOJ says
summary: Justice Department lawyers say Judge James Boasberg contradicted his ruling by unsealing search warrant records in Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. case.
story: Former Acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the newly unsealed search warrant records revealing a decades-long federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.

Government lawyers argue unsealing documents related to the warrant used to search the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is at odds with a ruling made by the same Obama-appointed federal judge in a high-profile case against President Donald Trump.

Lawyers for the Justice Department pleaded in the filings with Judge James Boasberg, who has frequently found himself at odds with the Trump administration, not to unseal search warrant materials in the Omar case due to the ongoing nature of the investigation,.
The DOJ also argued it has not yet finished executing that search warrant.

Still, Boasberg ordered last week the redacted documents to be released. The DOJ submitted their redacted and the materials were made public Monday night. The only document Boasberg ordered to remain sealed was the government's affidavit presented to a magistrate court judge in order to secure the search warrant.

James Boasberg, incoming chief judge of the US District Court, in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, March 13, 2023. Boasberg, who starts a seven-year term as chief judge on March 17, will oversee the court's secret grand jury proceedings, including pending and future legal fights related to Special Counsel Jack Smith’s probes of Trump, among other duties. mong other duties. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty)
'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT

"Just a few years ago, Chief Judge Boasberg ruled that search warrant proceedings and related documents should not be made open to the public while an investigation is ongoing," the DOJ said in an emergency ex parte brief in opposition to the unsealing.
"The Chief Judge was merely echoing many other courts—like the D.C. Circuit, the Ninth Circuit, the Fourth Circuit, and others when he said that," the brief continued.

The case to which the DOJ referred — where Boasberg ruled that search warrant documents should remain under seal during active investigations — was none other than Special Counsel Jack Smith's probe into Trump for alleged election interference after his 2020 presidential loss, and for the alleged retention of classified documents.
Trump was indicted in both of those investigations. All the charges were eventually dropped.
Judge James Boasberg, President Donald Trump (Valerie Plesch, Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
ILHAN OMAR RECORDS SHOW JUDGE, DOJ OFFICIALS DEBATING BEFORE RAID OF HOME

In that case, like the Omar case, media organizations sought to unseal a warrant related to the search. Specifically, the press wanted to view a warrant obtained by Smith related to Twitter's records associated with Trump's account, @realDonaldTrump.
Boasberg's tune was much different in that case, when, like in the Omar case, the government asked him to keep the warrant under seal due to the ongoing nature of the case.
Notably, Trump had already been indicted when Boasberg ruled that the records needed to remain sealed while Omar has not been indicted.
"Ultimately, the undeniable need to protect an ongoing criminal investigation tips the balance toward the Government’s request to continue sealing," Boasberg wrote in his Nov. 29, 2023 ruling.
The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the apparent u-turn from the judge.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is denying that federal agents have told her what she is under investigation for and speaks to Fox News Digital about the status of her items that were seized after her Washington, D.C., home was raided Oct. 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz)

In the Omar case, government lawyers said they weren't opposed to releasing the documents at an appropriate future date, but did not want them unsealed while the case is ongoing. Boasberg didn't find that argument compelling.
But in the case against Trump, he did.
"There may yet come a time when press access becomes appropriate, but at present the Application is a premature bid for sensitive information pertaining to an active investigation," he wrote in 2023.
Throughout his 2023 ruling in favor of the government's bid to keep the warrant in the Trump case sealed, Boasberg continually noted the government's ability to keep warrants under seal.
ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES

He said in a second instance: "When it comes to an active investigation, the Government 'has always been able to restrict access to warrant materials by requesting a sealing order, which courts have granted freely upon a showing that a given criminal investigation requires secrecy,'" Boasberg's ruling said.
In response to the media's claim that the First Amendment should be a deciding factor in unsealing the Trump warrant, Boasberg disagreed.

"The historical practice is somewhat muddled, but it suggests that the First Amendment does not open search warrants and related documents to public examination when an investigation is ongoing. Search-warrant applications traditionally have been filed ex parte and thus out of the public’s view."

The DOJ confirmed in a brief statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday that the characterization that Boasberg contradicted himself in unsealing the Omar documents "is accurate and a point we have made in our court filings."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One issue distinguishing Boasberg's ruling in the 2023 Trump case from the Omar case is the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which shields lawmakers from certain government intrusions into their legislative work.

In the Omar case, the Justice Department argued that searching her home did not involve those protections. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh disagreed and required safeguards for potentially privileged materials.

Boasberg later questioned why the legal arguments over those constitutional protections should remain sealed when sensitive investigative details could be redacted. He nevertheless agreed to keep the government's warrant affidavit sealed to protect the ongoing investigation.

Boasberg has also faced scrutiny over investigative secrecy during the Biden-era Arctic Frost probe, when he signed nondisclosure orders tied to subpoenas for Republican lawmakers' phone records. Unlike the Omar and Trump rulings, those orders restricted telecommunications companies from revealing the subpoenas rather than deciding whether court documents should be made public. Court officials have said Boasberg may not have known lawmakers' records were involved.
The District Court for the District of Columbia declined to comment. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia did not return a request for comment.

Omar's home was raided in the early morning hours of Oct. 12, 2026. Fox News Digital confirmed that the investigators are probing whether Omar or her father fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork, though the full scope of the investigation remains under wraps.

The unsealing of last night's documents revealed that investigators are seeking evidence dating back as far as 1980, and that investigators believe Omar committed "crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump pauses turkey pardon to salute US troops guarding Strait of Hormuz: 'Watch over and protect'
summary: President Donald Trump paused the White House turkey pardon to thank U.S. troops enforcing what he called the greatest naval blockade against Iran.
story: President Donald Trump thanked U.S. service members enforcing the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz during Tuesday’s annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony, asserting no Iranian ships have gotten through and vowing Tehran will never obtain a nuclear weapon.

President Donald Trump paused Tuesday's annual White House Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony to offer a special tribute and thanks to U.S. service members defending the Strait of Hormuz and enforcing a naval blockade against Iran.

Speaking from the White House South Lawn during the 79th National Thanksgiving Turkey presentation, Trump thanked American troops deployed overseas and praised those working to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"We want to say a special thank you to them, the people that are guarding the strait know or the blockade we call it," Trump said. "It’s a blockade, the greatest naval blockade in history."
TRUMP DARES IRAN TO BREACH US PORT BLOCKADE AS TEHRAN REPORTEDLY READIES 14 OIL TANKERS

President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Trump asserted that the U.S. maritime cordon has stopped every Iranian vessel from passing through since its establishment, save for a brief pause earlier in the standoff.

"Not one Iranian ship has gotten through to the blockade since we established it, other than we had a little moratorium. And we learned that you can’t trust them," Trump said. "But not one ship from Iran has gotten through. Our naval blockade is the most incredible naval blockade, probably in the history of the world. It’s amazing."
IRANIAN ‘GHOST FLEET’ FILMED EVADING US BLOCKADE EN ROUTE TO CHINA, UANI SAYS

President Donald Trump grants a presidential pardon to Freedom during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Trump also contended that U.S. forces have severely degraded Iran's conventional military capabilities and restored oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to levels higher than before the conflict began.
The U.S. naval blockade targeting vessels entering and leaving Iranian ports began in April amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis and resumed in July following a temporary pause.
Before returning to the holiday ceremony, Trump offered a Thanksgiving prayer for deployed U.S. troops and expressed pride in the country.

President Donald Trump, center, pardons Freedom the turkey as, from left, Deans Gap Farm co-owner Scott Rightsell, National Turkey Federation chairwoman Christy Puffenbarger, first lady Melania Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., look on during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"And we send them all our best wishes, Thanksgiving, and is very special. It’s a very special time for me for a lot of reasons," Trump said. "And I ask God to watch over and protect all of our military and all of our people. I’m so proud of our people, and I’m so proud to be your president because we’ve never had a time like this."

Following his remarks, Trump pardoned this year's National Thanksgiving Turkeys, Freedom and Feathers — though Feathers briefly ran into the bushes during the presentation — before sending them to retire at Texas A&M University.

title: Kamala Harris' former political mentor and boyfriend delivers stinging warning about 2028 comeback
summary: Willie Brown says Kamala Harris is "not a communicator" and doesn't want her to run in 2028, as Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom eye the Democratic primary.
story: Tyrus and Ryan return for another round of News or Noise on Planet Tyrus, putting bizarre studies, viral animal headlines, and Kamala Harris’s brutal 2028 straw poll numbers to the test. Can Tyrus spot the real news from Ryan’s fabricated headlines, including a shameless New York Giants Super Bowl trap?
Willie Brown, a longtime California Democrat and a power broker in the state party, said former Vice President Kamala Harris lacks the communication skills needed to run for president again in 2028.
"She’s not a communicator," Brown said in an interview with Tara Palmeri, an independent journalist.
"No Baptist preacher flavor in her soul," he added.
Although Harris remains one of the country’s most recognizable Democratic figures, Brown’s skepticism comes from a longtime political ally and casts doubt on her potential candidacy.
DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028

Kamala Harris, former vice president and 2024 presidential candidate, speaks with Al Sharpton during the National Action Network (NAN) Convention in New York, April 10, 2026. (Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo)
"I’m sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don’t want her to run," Brown said.
"She’s reached the highest electoral level for any woman in America," he added, referring to her post as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

Brown, who once served as San Francisco mayor and California state Assembly speaker, has a long history with Harris. Early in her career, he appointed her to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board and then the Medical Assistance Commission.
The two were also romantically involved between 1994 and 1995.
Brown, in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed, openly discussed their relationship and his role in her political career in an article titled, "Sure, I dated Kamala Harris. So what? "
GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS

Former Mayor, Willie Brown laughs with District Attorney Kamala Harris at the reception before the rededication ceremony for Twenty-First Century Academy in 2005. (Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)
"Yes, we dated. It was more than 20 years ago. Yes, I may have influenced her career by appointing her to two state commissions when I was Assembly speaker," Brown wrote.

"And I certainly helped with her first race for district attorney in San Francisco. I have also helped the careers of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Sen. Dianne Feinstein and a host of other politicians," he added.
Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital about Brown’s comments about her prospects for 2028.
Several other Democrats have already hinted at their own interest in a 2028 bid, crowding the potential field.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a top progressive in the House of Representatives, has hinted at a run. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has said he is "inclined" to run, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to decide on a presidential bid at the beginning of the new year.
DEMOCRATS DEBATE KAMALA HARRIS 2028 RUN AS SURROGATE SAYS PARTY WANTS TO 'MOVE ON' FROM 2024 LOSS

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris both said in separate media interviews that they're keeping their options open for potential 2028 presidential runs. (Patrick T. Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

title: Can hackers still read Gmail after a password change?
summary: Remus Stealer malware developers claim Gmail access survives a password change, but Google says the attack targets infected devices, not a Gmail flaw.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You change your Gmail password after noticing something suspicious. You sign out of unfamiliar devices and figure your account should be safe again. But what if someone could still read your Gmail after a password change? That's the unsettling claim behind Remus Stealer, a malware service being marketed to cybercriminals. Its developers claim they can keep accessing Gmail messages even after someone resets their password and revokes existing sessions.

However, security researchers have not independently verified those claims, and Google disputes the suggestion that the malware exploits a Gmail security flaw. The company says this type of attack targets infected devices rather than Gmail itself. Google also warns that changing your password may not solve the problem if malware remains active on your computer. Here's what the investigation uncovered and how to protect your inbox.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED
A screenshot from the Remus malware dashboard shows a Pinterest verification email that criminals claim they can access through a compromised Gmail account. (Hudson Rock)
Hackers claim their malware can keep reading Gmail

Security researchers at Hudson Rock examined promotional materials for Remus Stealer, a type of malware designed to collect sensitive information from infected computers. In a November 9 report, the company described a new feature advertised in version 1.3.9 of the malware. The developers claim it allows criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from their control dashboard. The promotional screenshots show lists of emails and individual messages. There's also a "Mail" option connected to records of infected devices. According to the developers, criminals can retrieve email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

The developers make an even more concerning claim. They say changing a Google password or revoking existing sessions won't necessarily stop someone from accessing the mailbox. They also advertise a way to share mailbox access with other criminals through links. Think about what that could mean if the claims prove true. Someone with access to your Gmail could potentially read private conversations or collect password reset messages for other accounts. However, these claims come from the people selling the malware. Independent researchers have yet to demonstrate that the feature works as advertised.
What security researchers actually discovered

Hudson Rock contacted the malware developer and spoke with someone who claimed to have used the Gmail feature. That person said they could still access an inbox after closing the browser, resetting a session and changing the Google account password. The developer also described a technique involving browser memory but didn't provide enough technical information to verify it. There are important limits to the investigation.

Hudson Rock did not reverse engineer the feature or conduct controlled testing after a complete account recovery. Researchers also couldn't independently verify the customer's claims. Most importantly, the investigation never established that criminals could retrieve newly arriving emails after someone had properly secured their Google account. The screenshots demonstrate that the service advertises a Gmail-reading interface. They don't prove that Remus can defeat Google's protections after a full recovery. There's also no evidence in the report of a previously unknown Gmail security vulnerability.

Researchers also could not rule out other explanations, including incomplete session revocation, previously collected messages or unauthorized access that remained active through another route. Without controlled testing, there's no way to confirm exactly how the advertised feature operates.
NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH
The Remus malware dashboard displays a Gmail inbox, although researchers have not verified claims that access continues after a complete account recovery. (Hudson Rock)
Google responds to the Gmail malware claims

We reached out to Google about the research, and the company rejected the suggestion that the reported activity involved a vulnerability in Gmail. A Google spokesperson said: "Attacks involving infostealer malware that target session tokens on personal devices are not new, and there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here. We routinely upgrade our built-in defenses to protect users against session theft and automatically secure accounts when we detect suspicious activity. Users can invalidate stolen sessions by removing malware from the affected device and revoking active sessions via g.co/mydevices."

Google explained that this kind of attack targets infected personal devices rather than exploiting Gmail itself. The company also highlighted something especially important for anyone recovering from malware. If the infection remains on a computer when someone resets their password, the malware could capture the new login session. That means a fresh password alone may not solve the problem. Google recommends removing the malware before signing back in on the affected device. From a separate, trusted device, you should also change your password, revoke suspicious sessions through Google's device activity page at myaccount.google.com/device-activity and review your account using Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. The infected computer should remain disconnected until the threat has been removed.

The company says it regularly strengthens its defenses against stolen sessions. Those protections include frequent cookie rotation and additional authentication checks when someone attempts sensitive account changes. Google also highlighted Device Bound Session Credentials, a Chrome security technology designed to make stolen session cookies harder to reuse on another device. This protection applies to supported Chrome sessions, with availability depending on the platform and service. These protections help reduce the risk of account theft, although they don't eliminate every possible malware attack.
Why hackers may access Gmail without your password

You probably open Gmail every day without typing your password. That's because your browser remembers that you've already signed in. Behind the scenes, browsers and applications use session cookies or authentication tokens to maintain access to accounts. These digital credentials help keep you signed in without repeatedly entering your password. Unfortunately, criminals know how valuable that information can be. Infostealer malware can target stored authentication data on an infected computer. If an attacker obtains a valid session, they may be able to access an account without entering the password again. That can also undermine the protection you'd normally expect from two-step verification because the legitimate account holder has already completed the sign-in process.

However, a stolen session doesn't automatically give someone unlimited access. Google can invalidate sessions, and some sensitive actions require additional verification. Google's documentation explains that changing a password generally revokes OAuth access and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions, although certain exceptions apply. Google also notes that password changes sign people out of most devices, but some trusted devices and third-party connections may remain signed in. Those exceptions do not prove that Remus uses any of these methods. The concern with an infected computer is that malware may capture fresh authentication information when you sign in again. That's why securing the computer and reviewing account access are essential parts of recovery.
Warning signs someone may be accessing your Gmail

An unfamiliar Google security alert deserves attention, especially if you haven't signed in from a new device. You should also investigate password reset messages you never requested. These can indicate that someone is attempting to access another account connected to your email address, although an unexpected reset message alone doesn't prove an account has been compromised.

Other warning signs include missing messages or people telling you they received strange emails from your address. Check your Sent folder for messages you didn't write. You might also discover forwarding rules or account recovery settings you don't remember changing. If something looks suspicious, open your Google account directly rather than following a link in an unexpected message.
Infostealer malware can steal login session information from an infected computer, potentially allowing hackers to access Gmail without entering a password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to protect your Gmail from malware and hackers

If you suspect that someone has accessed your Gmail, take action promptly. The goal is to secure your account while preventing malware from stealing fresh login information. Google emphasizes that removing the infection and revoking compromised sessions are both essential. You can begin securing your account from a trusted device while keeping the suspected infected computer offline.
If you believe your computer has been infected, disconnect it from the internet. Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing your important accounts.

Run strong antivirus software to detect and remove infostealer malware.Follow the security software's instructions to quarantine or remove detected threats.Update your operating system and browser once the device is safe to reconnect.Consider reinstalling your operating system if you cannot confidently remove the infection.

If you suspect that malware stole your login information, change your password promptly and make sure the infected computer cannot capture another session. Do not sign back into Google on the suspected infected computer until you have removed the malware.
