If you've already changed your password while malware was still running, make sure the infected device has been cleaned or remains offline, then change your password again from a trusted device and review active sessions once more.

A criminal who gains access to your Gmail may change settings so incoming messages get forwarded to another email address. That could allow someone to receive copies of new messages even after you change your password. Google requires verification when someone adds a new forwarding address, but you should still check for forwarding that may have been configured without your knowledge.

On your computer, open Chrome > click the three-dot menu in the upper-right corner > Settings > Privacy and security > Security > under Safe Browsing, select Enhanced protection.Consider Google's Advanced Protection Program if you face a higher risk of targeted cyberattacks. To enroll, visit Google's Advanced Protection page > click Get started > sign in to your Google Account if prompted > follow the on-screen instructions to enroll using a passkey or compatible security key.

Turn on 2-Step Verification (2FA) if you haven't already enabled it. To set it up, visit your Google Account at myaccount.google.com/ > Security & sign-in > under How you sign in to Google, select Turn on 2-Step Verification > follow the on-screen instructions to complete setup
Set up a passkey through your Google account for stronger protection against password phishing.

Enable Enhanced Safe Browsing in Chrome to help identify dangerous websites and malicious downloads. On your computer, open Chrome > click the three-dot menu in the upper-right corner > Settings > Privacy and security > Security > under Safe Browsing, select Enhanced protection.

Consider Google's Advanced Protection Program if you face a higher risk of targeted cyberattacks. To enroll, visit Google's Advanced Protection page > click Get started > sign in to your Google Account if prompted > follow the on-screen instructions to enroll using a passkey or compatible security key.

Passkeys offer stronger sign-in security, but they cannot remove an existing infection or automatically prevent theft of an already authenticated session. Google's Advanced Protection Program adds stricter account safeguards, including tighter restrictions on third-party access.

Remember how many online services use your email address for account recovery. If criminals accessed your mailbox, they may have seen verification messages from other services. Review important accounts for unfamiliar activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected password changes or security alerts.

If you reused your Google password anywhere else, change those passwords too. Use unique credentials for every important account, and consider a password manager to keep track of them. For additional protection, my CyberGuy article on identity thieves who don't need your password explains other ways criminals try to get around traditional account security.
Kurt's key takeaways

For years, changing your password has been one of the first things I've recommended when an online account gets compromised. I still believe that's essential. But this investigation highlights something many people overlook. If malware is running on your computer, it may be able to steal fresh login information after you've changed your password. What concerns me is how much of our digital lives depend on a single Gmail account. Think about the personal messages sitting in your inbox and the accounts that rely on your email for password recovery.

Someone who gains access could potentially create problems well beyond your inbox. Google's response makes an important distinction. This is a threat involving malware on infected devices, not a newly demonstrated vulnerability in Gmail. We should also remember that the most alarming claims about this malware have yet to be independently verified. There's a big difference between what criminals advertise and what security researchers can actually demonstrate.

My advice is to take account security seriously without panicking over an unproven claim. Keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices and pay attention to suspicious account activity. If you suspect an infection, make sure the malware has been removed before trusting a fresh login. Then change your password from a trusted device and revoke any suspicious sessions. Those extra steps can help prevent someone from regaining access to your account.

title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
summary: Palmer Luckey says SLAB, his floating industrial city, would last 1,000 years, hosting metal processing and oil refining beyond California rules.
story: Palmer Luckey wants to move American industry offshore to escape state and local regulations. His ambitious SLAB project raises big questions about the future of manufacturing in the U.S.

How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions.

The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS
Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries, speaks at Los Angeles Air Force Base in California in August 2026. (Christopher Kim/U.S. Space Force)
What is Palmer Luckey's 1,000-year floating city?

Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB. In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years.

The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top.
AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Floating homes made from shipping containers in Copenhagen, Denmark, offer a real-world example of construction on water, although Palmer Luckey's proposed SLAB industrial city would be far larger. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why Palmer Luckey wants to move American industry offshore

Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining. He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."

His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore.
How much money is behind SLAB?

Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform.

Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well.
Can a floating city really escape U.S. regulations?

This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements.
Could an ocean city really last 1,000 years?

Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water.

That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal.
The Marco Polo offshore oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico illustrates the scale of industrial operations at sea and the engineering challenges they face. (GuavaTrain/Wikimedia Commons)
Why this floating city could send a message to California

California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land?

Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen.
Kurt's key takeaways

I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. For more on this story and our discussion about the future of American innovation, listen to The CyberGuy Report Podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/.

title: What United Airlines banning AI agents from booking flights means for your travel plans
summary: United Airlines is blocking unauthorized AI travel agents from its booking systems, warning that automated purchases could put MileagePlus miles at risk.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the threat of rogue artificial intelligence agents targeting bank accounts. Knutsson shares safety tips to protect personal finances from unauthorized transactions and addresses AI-enabled romance scams, detailing a case where a woman was defrauded of $10,000 by a scammer posing as Jon Bon Jovi.

Wouldn't it be nice to tell an AI assistant to find the cheapest flight to your destination and book your favorite seat while you do something else? That kind of convenience is getting closer. But United Airlines wants to make sure an unauthorized AI assistant never gets that far.

The airline is restricting third-party AI agents from accessing its booking systems without permission. United says these tools could expose sensitive customer information and make purchases travelers never intended to authorize. The concern also extends to MileagePlus accounts, where an automated mistake could put valuable airline miles at risk.

The decision comes as AI assistants become increasingly capable of taking action on our behalf. While that sounds convenient, United is raising questions about how much control we should give software over our travel plans. Here's where United draws the line and what you need to know before letting AI handle your next flight booking.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

FORMER ANTHROPIC SECURITY LEADER WARNS AI AGENTS ARE BECOMING TOO AUTONOMOUS FOR HUMANS TO KEEP THEM IN CHECK
United Airlines is restricting unauthorized AI agents from accessing its booking systems, citing concerns about customer security and unwanted transactions. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
Why United Airlines is blocking AI agents

On Nov. 11, United Airlines published an official news release titled United Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents. The airline explained that protecting customer information and account security prompted the restrictions. According to United, sharing account credentials with personal AI assistants can expose sensitive information. The airline also warned that automated actions might lead to unwanted purchases or changes to existing reservations. Then there's the issue of frequent flyer miles. United specifically mentioned the possibility that an AI assistant could use MileagePlus miles without the traveler intending that redemption.

To address those concerns, United is restricting unauthorized personal AI agents from accessing its digital platforms. The rules also reach travel agencies and booking services that might use automated AI tools to access United's systems. United says it is updating its policies to support these restrictions. The airline also plans to continue evaluating how personal AI assistants interact with its services.
What exactly is an AI travel agent?

You may already use AI to research vacation destinations or figure out which airport is closest to your hotel. An AI travel agent takes that technology further by performing tasks for you. For example, you could ask an AI assistant to find a flight under $400 that arrives before dinner. Instead of simply recommending flights, an AI agent might search booking systems and attempt to complete the reservation. Some agents can also interact with websites using a browser. That means they may be able to enter personal information and complete steps that normally require you to click through a booking process.

The convenience is easy to understand. However, granting an AI assistant access to your airline account can also give it the ability to make changes you never intended. For more on what these assistants can do, see our article on eight seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.
United says AI agents could create airline safety problems

United's concerns go beyond account security. The airline also warns that automated AI activity could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. Consider what happens when you check in for a flight. Airlines require travelers to acknowledge important safety information, including whether their bags contain prohibited hazardous materials.

United specifically points to the requirement for a person to confirm that baggage contains no banned substances, such as explosives. An AI assistant handling check-in could potentially bypass that acknowledgment. After all, how would an AI assistant know what you actually packed in your suitcase? United has identified this as a potential regulatory concern. The airline has not established that every AI-assisted check-in violates federal law.
Could United cancel a flight booked by an AI agent?

This may be the biggest concern for travelers experimenting with automated booking tools. United revised its Contract of Carriage on Nov. 11. The updated rules prohibit AI agents from making or modifying tickets and purchasing airline products or services.

The contract also identifies reservations made or changed through AI agents as subject to cancellation without advance notice. The definition of an AI agent includes automated tools even when a traveler supervises or approves their actions. However, there is an important exception for existing reservations.

United says bookings made by AI agents before Nov. 11, will not be canceled under the new restriction. The airline recommends reviewing those reservations to confirm that they were properly booked and ticketed. If you previously used an AI assistant to arrange United travel, open the United app or website and verify your itinerary. Check that your ticket was actually issued rather than assuming a booking confirmation means everything is complete. You can review the airline's published rules in its Contract of Carriage at united.com/en/us/fly/contract-of-carriage.html.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Travelers can still manage flights through United's website and app, but unauthorized third-party AI agents face new restrictions on accessing the airline's systems. (Robert Alexander/Getty Images)
Can you still use AI to plan a United Airlines trip?

Yes, although United has established limits on how outside AI tools can interact with its systems. You can still ask an AI chatbot for general travel advice or help creating an itinerary. United's guidance allows AI-assisted research and trip planning as long as the tool does not access United's website or app. However, an unauthorized AI agent cannot search United's website or app on your behalf. The restriction also covers automated purchasing and reservation management. That means an AI-powered browser feature that automatically searches United's website could fall under the restriction, even if it never buys a ticket.

United says assistive technology for travelers with disabilities remains unaffected. Traditional travel booking services can also continue operating through permitted channels. The restriction specifically addresses unauthorized AI agents, including those used by travel agencies. According to United's published guidance, the airline does not currently work with any third-party AI agents under this policy.
Southwest Airlines is taking a different approach to AI

While United is putting restrictions in place, Southwest Airlines is exploring a different approach. On Oct. 6, Southwest announced a ChatGPT integration. The feature allows you to discover destinations and shop for Southwest flights directly through ChatGPT. However, Southwest's integration still directs you to the airline's website to complete purchases. The company describes the arrangement as an early step toward broader AI-powered booking capabilities.

That approach gives Southwest a way to use AI for flight discovery while maintaining control over the final transaction. United is taking a more restrictive position on outside AI assistants. The airline says it will continue evaluating the technology as it develops.
How to protect your United Airlines bookings and miles

If you normally book flights through United's website or app, you can continue doing so. You can also use permitted travel booking services. However, if you've started experimenting with AI assistants that make purchases or manage accounts on your behalf, United's restrictions deserve your attention. An AI agent with access to your airline account could potentially reach sensitive travel information. Depending on its permissions, it might also make purchases you never intended to authorize. Here are a few ways to protect yourself.

Avoid giving third-party AI assistants your MileagePlus password or other sensitive login information. If you've already shared your credentials with an AI agent, United recommends changing your password immediately. You should also remove any saved login details from the AI service. Consider using a password manager to create and securely store a strong, unique password for your airline account. This can help protect your account if a password you use elsewhere gets exposed in a data breach.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices from malware and malicious links designed to steal login credentials. This is especially important if you use travel booking websites or receive airline confirmation emails. While antivirus protection won't stop an AI assistant from making an unauthorized reservation, it can help prevent cybercriminals from gaining access to your MileagePlus account. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Use United's official website or app, or a booking provider operating under United's rules. United currently does not work with third-party AI agents under this policy. Even if an AI assistant offers to complete a reservation with your approval, that does not necessarily make the transaction permissible.
UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’
United warns that giving AI agents access to customer accounts could expose sensitive information and potentially put valuable MileagePlus miles at risk. (iStock)

Review your MileagePlus balance for unexpected activity. If you notice a redemption or purchase you don't recognize, secure your account immediately. Contact United through its official website or app to report the activity and request assistance.

Check your booking confirmation and make sure United has issued your ticket. If an AI assistant arranged your travel before Nov. 11, verify the reservation directly with the airline. United says those earlier bookings will not be canceled under the new restriction.

AI can still help you plan a trip using general information without accessing United's systems. However, complete your flight purchases and reservation changes yourself through permitted channels. That way, you can review what you're buying without risking a prohibited AI-agent transaction.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why United is concerned. I've spent enough time searching for flights to appreciate the idea of handing that job over to AI. Let the assistant find me a great fare and save me the hassle of comparing a dozen options. I'm all for that. But the moment it starts making purchases or accessing my airline miles, I want to know exactly what it's doing.

I recently spoke with travel expert Katy Nastro, who discovered that someone had stolen 50,000 miles from her American Airlines account. Her experience had nothing to do with AI agents, but it reminded me how much value we keep in these loyalty programs. I certainly wouldn't want an automated mistake putting those rewards at risk.

At the same time, I do wonder whether security is the only concern driving United's decision. Airlines have spent years building direct relationships with travelers. AI agents could change how we compare fares and choose which airline gets our business. I would hate to see useful technology held back simply because it gives you more control over the shopping process. United says it will keep evaluating these tools, and I hope that eventually leads to a secure way to book flights using AI. Until then, I'm happy to let AI help find my next trip. I'll take care of the booking myself.

title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
summary: Apple's macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds new Mac security controls for AI agents, letting you pick specific protected folders instead of granting Full Disk Access.
story: Reviewing your Mac's privacy settings can help you identify apps with unnecessary access to your personal files and revoke permissions you no longer need. (REUTERS/Norbert von der Groeben)

Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected?

That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended.

Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Apple's new Mac security controls are designed to give people more control over how much personal information AI agents can access. (Annette Riedl/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Why AI agents are raising new Mac security concerns

AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps.

Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step.
What Apple is changing in macOS 27.3

Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working.

Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing.

One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose.

For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods.

Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions.
Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf.
MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR
Apple's new macOS 27.3 permissions let Mac owners choose specific folders an app can access instead of granting Full Disk Access. (Getty Images)
Why Apple is tightening AI agent security now

Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported.

These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions.
One important catch with Apple's new Mac security controls

There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward.

That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate.
How to check which apps have access to your Mac
You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available.
Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS.

Click the Apple menu in the upper-left corner of your screen.Select System Settings.Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar.Scroll down and select Full Disk Access.Review the apps listed and look for anything you no longer recognize or need.Return to Privacy & Security and select Files & Folders to review access to protected locations.Check Accessibility and Automation to see which apps have permission to control parts of your Mac or interact with other applications.
Click the Apple menu in the upper-left corner of your screen.
Select System Settings.
Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar.
Scroll down and select Full Disk Access.
Review the apps listed and look for anything you no longer recognize or need.
Return to Privacy & Security and select Files & Folders to review access to protected locations.
Check Accessibility and Automation to see which apps have permission to control parts of your Mac or interact with other applications.

If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs.

Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
Tips to protect your privacy when using AI agents on a Mac
You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure.

When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access.

If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information.

Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes.

Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy.

An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use.

If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer.
Kurt's key takeaways

I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update.

Would you trust an AI assistant with unrestricted access to your Mac if it could save you hours of work, or does the thought of software reading your private information cross a line? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Google AI smartwatch could flag high blood pressure
summary: Google's AI used smartwatch sensors to spot hypertension without a blood pressure cuff, but the Nature study found it missed about 1 in 3 cases.
story: Eko Health co-founder and CEO Connor Landgraf discusses how their AI-powered stethoscope is revolutionizing cardiac care and improving patient outcomes. This innovative device amplifies heart and lung sounds, analyzes them in real-time and detects early signs of heart disease and arrhythmias in just 15 seconds. The technology offers physicians consistent, reliable insights, enhancing early diagnosis and intervention.

When was the last time you checked your blood pressure? If you're like a lot of people, it probably happened during your last doctor's appointment. And if you feel perfectly healthy, you may not give it another thought. That's what makes high blood pressure so concerning. You can have it for years without noticing anything wrong.

Now, Google researchers are exploring a way to uncover that hidden danger using something many of us already wear on our wrists. In a new study recently published in Nature, researchers demonstrated an artificial intelligence system that can identify signs of hypertension using standard smartwatch sensors. It works in the background without requiring calibration with a traditional blood pressure cuff.

The technology uses sensors that already exist in consumer smartwatches. That could make early detection much more accessible. However, the research also reveals a limitation that anyone relying on a smartwatch for health information should understand.

SMARTWATCH AFIB ALERT SENDS DAD TO ER BEFORE HEART SURGERY
Google's Health Guardian feature tracks blood pressure trends over time and can flag potentially elevated levels without providing actual blood pressure readings. (Google)
How Google AI detects high blood pressure using a smartwatch
Your smartwatch already knows quite a bit about your body. It can track your heart rate throughout the day. Depending on the model, it may also detect irregular heart rhythms.

Google's new AI takes the information collected by those sensors and looks for signs of something harder to detect: ongoing high blood pressure. According to Google Research, the system analyzes two types of sensor data.

The first sensor uses light to detect changes in blood volume beneath your skin. It's the same basic technology many watches use to monitor your pulse. The second sensor measures movement. Researchers found that it can also capture incredibly small vibrations caused by your heart pumping blood. You wouldn't notice those vibrations. However, the AI can analyze them alongside your pulse patterns to look for signs associated with hypertension.

The system collects information over multiple days. It then combines those patterns with your height to estimate the likelihood of sustained high blood pressure. Unlike a traditional monitor, the smartwatch doesn't produce a reading such as 120 over 80. Instead, it looks for signs that your blood pressure may be consistently elevated. What's interesting is that you wouldn't have to do anything differently. You could go about your day while your smartwatch quietly looks for potential warning signs.
Google's smartwatch AI study reveals promising results

Google worked with researchers from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School to develop and test the system. First, researchers trained the underlying AI using nearly 500,000 hours of smartwatch sensor data collected from 2,109 consenting participants. They then evaluated the hypertension detection system in a clinical study involving 196 participants across five U.S. locations. None of those participants had known cardiovascular disease or were taking blood pressure medication.

During the study, participants wore a consumer smartwatch for seven days. Researchers compared the AI's findings with results from 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. That medical test uses a cuff to measure blood pressure repeatedly throughout the day and night. Doctors use it to help confirm hypertension.
During initial screening, the results showed:

65.8% sensitivity: The AI correctly identified nearly two-thirds of participants who had hypertension.90% specificity: The system correctly classified 90% of participants who did not have hypertension.80.6% positive predictive value: Among participants the AI flagged as having hypertension, about four out of five actually had the condition.
65.8% sensitivity: The AI correctly identified nearly two-thirds of participants who had hypertension.
90% specificity: The system correctly classified 90% of participants who did not have hypertension.
80.6% positive predictive value: Among participants the AI flagged as having hypertension, about four out of five actually had the condition.

For comparison, initial blood pressure screenings performed in medical offices identified 55.3% of participants with hypertension in the study. That's an encouraging result. However, the difference between the smartwatch and office screening was not statistically significant, according to a Nature Portfolio summary of the findings. There's another number worth paying attention to.
The AI missed roughly one in three participants who had hypertension during initial screening.
That's a number worth paying attention to. After all, we're talking about a condition that can lead to a heart attack or stroke, often without any warning signs.

Researchers also looked at a smaller group of 48 people who had elevated blood pressure readings during their initial doctor's visit. In that group, the AI correctly identified 78.4% of those with ongoing hypertension. It also correctly ruled out the condition in 90.9% of those who didn't have it. Those results are encouraging, but there's still work to do. Google needs to test the technology on more people before we can know how reliably it can detect high blood pressure.
MICROSOFT AI BEATS DOCTORS IN SIMULATED DIAGNOSIS TEST

Google's AI analyzes pulse patterns and tiny vibrations from the heart using smartwatch sensors to identify possible signs of high blood pressure. (Andreswd via Getty; Justin Chin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Can your Pixel Watch detect high blood pressure today?

Here's where things get interesting for people who already own a Google smartwatch. Google introduced its Health Guardian features in September 2026. Among them is a blood pressure trends feature available through the Google Health app.

According to Google's September announcement, blood pressure trends are available at no additional subscription cost on eligible Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 devices. Availability depends on your region.

The feature analyzes pulse and movement patterns over time. Then, it provides a monthly assessment of whether your blood pressure trend appears high. Google says these existing Health Guardian capabilities are informed by clinical research, including work connected to its newly published findings. However, there's an important difference between the experimental system described in Nature and the feature available on your watch today.

The existing Pixel Watch feature is intended for general wellness. Google specifically says it cannot diagnose hypertension or serve as a medical screening tool. It also cannot tell you your actual systolic or diastolic blood pressure numbers. According to Google's support documentation, the feature provides a monthly trend assessment such as "High" or "Not high."

And a "Not high" result doesn't guarantee your blood pressure is normal. Google also warns users against relying on these estimates to change medications or treatment plans. Meanwhile, the newly published research remains exploratory. Google has not announced that the experimental hypertension screening system will become a commercial diagnostic feature.
Apple Watch already offers hypertension alerts

Google has some competition in this area. Apple has already introduced FDA-cleared hypertension notifications for compatible Apple Watch models. As we previously reported in Apple Watch gets FDA-approved hypertension alerts, the feature looks for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure. It uses information gathered by the watch's optical heart sensor over 30-day periods.

The feature supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later models, along with Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later models, subject to software and regional availability. If the watch detects concerning patterns, it can notify you. However, Apple also makes clear that the feature cannot diagnose hypertension. And it may miss cases. Apple recommends checking your blood pressure with a traditional cuff and discussing the results with a healthcare professional if you receive an alert.

So, while Apple and Google are approaching this technology differently, the current guidance remains clear. A smartwatch alert can give you useful information, but you still need an accurate blood pressure measurement.
Why detecting high blood pressure earlier could save lives

High blood pressure has earned the nickname "silent killer" for a reason. According to the World Health Organization, more than one billion adults worldwide live with hypertension. Many have no idea they have it.

Meanwhile, untreated high blood pressure can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of a heart attack or stroke. Younger adults can be particularly vulnerable to missed diagnoses because they may feel healthy and see little reason to get checked. Now, consider what could happen if a smartwatch noticed concerning patterns before someone developed symptoms.

That person might decide to schedule an appointment and have their blood pressure checked. If doctors confirm hypertension, earlier treatment could help reduce the risk of complications. Of course, researchers still need to determine whether smartwatch-based screening actually improves diagnosis rates and long-term health outcomes.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

Smartwatches can alert users to possible signs of high blood pressure and encourage them to check their readings with a traditional cuff and discuss the results with their doctor. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What should you do if your smartwatch flags high blood pressure?

If your smartwatch warns you about possible high blood pressure, don't ignore it. But don't assume the watch has diagnosed you, either. The next step is to check your blood pressure using a validated upper-arm cuff.

The American Heart Association recommends automatic upper-arm monitors for home measurements because they provide more reliable readings than typical wrist or finger monitors. If you're using Google's blood pressure trends feature and receive a "High" result, Google recommends checking your blood pressure twice a day for seven days and sharing those readings with your doctor.

Make sure you follow your monitor's instructions and use the correct cuff size. Also, keep an eye on how you're feeling. If you experience emergency warning signs such as chest pain or difficulty breathing, seek immediate medical attention rather than waiting for another smartwatch assessment.

And remember, even if your watch never sends an alert, you should continue getting your blood pressure checked. For another way to track your readings, see our article on how to monitor blood pressure with your Apple Watch using a compatible blood pressure monitor.
The biggest challenge Google's smartwatch AI still faces

One of my biggest questions about this technology comes down to how much confidence people will place in the results. Let's say your smartwatch tells you everything looks normal. Would you still bother checking your blood pressure? That's where the research raises an important concern.

In Google's initial screening study, the AI missed a meaningful number of people who actually had hypertension. And while the results compared favorably with initial office screening, the study was relatively small. Researchers will need more evidence before the technology can become a dependable part of routine medical screening.

Google's findings suggest that everyday wearables could eventually help identify people who might otherwise go undiagnosed. For now, though, a reliable blood pressure cuff and a conversation with your doctor remain essential.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like where Google is going with this. Most of us probably don't think about our blood pressure until we're sitting in a doctor's office with a cuff around our arm. So the idea that a smartwatch could spot a potential problem before we even know something's wrong is pretty exciting. But there's one number in this study that concerns me. The AI missed roughly one in three people who actually had high blood pressure. That's a lot, especially when you consider the serious health risks involved. I think this technology has tremendous potential, and I'm looking forward to seeing how Google improves it. But for now, I wouldn't rely on my smartwatch to tell me whether my blood pressure is normal. I'd still want to check it with a traditional cuff.

title: FBI warns AI hackers can breach systems in under 3 hours
summary: The FBI warns the ARTEX AI hacking tool can give criminals privileged access in under three hours, targeting Microsoft 365 and financial firms.
story: James Gagliano, retired FBI supervisory special agent, warns about the rising threat of artificial intelligence in global cyberattacks. This follows a string of disruptive tech outages impacting major financial institutions including Chase and Bank of America.

Your bank could spend millions protecting its computer systems. Your employer might have an entire cybersecurity team watching for suspicious activity. Yet hackers now have an AI-powered tool that can help them break into some organizations in less than three hours.

The FBI is warning that criminals are using the ARTEX AI hacking tool to automate cyberattacks against businesses around the world. Some attacks have moved from initial targeting to powerful administrator-level access in under three hours. That leaves companies very little time to recognize an attack and stop it.

If hackers reach a business that stores your personal information, you could end up dealing with the consequences. Here's how ARTEX works, why the FBI is concerned and what you can do to protect yourself.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
Strong passwords and multifactor authentication can help protect your personal accounts if criminals obtain sensitive information through a company data breach. (Pornyot Palilai via Getty Images)
What is the ARTEX AI hacking tool?

ARTEX started as a legitimate penetration testing framework. Cybersecurity professionals use these tools to find weaknesses in computer systems before criminals discover them. However, hackers have found ways to turn ARTEX against organizations without permission. The framework uses artificial intelligence to handle tasks that previously required significant hacking expertise. It can search for security weaknesses and attempt to exploit them. Once inside a system, ARTEX can work toward gaining higher levels of access and extracting sensitive information. What makes ARTEX particularly concerning is its ability to operate with limited human involvement. Attackers can give the software instructions, then let AI agents carry out much of the work automatically.

ARTEX also connects to external AI models, including OpenAI's GPT and Anthropic's Claude. It supports DeepSeek and several other models. These integrations allow the framework to process instructions and automate complicated hacking operations. Their availability does not mean the AI companies are directing the attacks. According to the FBI, the technology allows criminals with relatively little technical knowledge to launch sophisticated attacks against multiple organizations simultaneously.
FBI warns ARTEX hackers can gain access in under 3 hours

In a November 13, 2026, security advisory, the FBI warned that criminals have used ARTEX in cyberattacks since at least August 2026. The agency identified campaigns targeting financial institutions and healthcare organizations. Government agencies and technology companies have also appeared among the targets. The speed of these attacks is especially troubling. According to the FBI, some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. That means hackers obtained powerful permissions that could allow them to make changes inside compromised systems.

ARTEX can also identify weaknesses in systems that companies sometimes overlook. These include employee portals and older business applications. Criminals may exploit vulnerable third-party connections to reach organizations with stronger security. Although automated attacks can trigger security alerts, their speed creates another challenge. A company's security team might detect suspicious activity only after criminals have already gained access.
How hackers used ARTEX to attack Microsoft 365

One of the clearest examples involves Microsoft 365, the service millions of employees rely on for work email and company files. In October 2026, hackers exploited compromised application credentials associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup. The service, formerly known as SkyKick Cloud Backup, helps businesses back up Microsoft 365 information. Here's why that attack is so concerning. The compromised applications already had permission to access customer environments. Hackers took advantage of those existing permissions to authenticate without needing an employee to sign in. In an October 21 investigation, Microsoft attributed the campaign to a China-state-aligned hacking group it tracks as Storm-0940.

The group used ARTEX to speed up its operations and attempt access to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments. Cybersecurity company Huntress reported unauthorized sign-ins across at least 162 customer environments during its initial investigation. However, the number of environments targeted does not represent the number where criminals stole information. Microsoft specifically warned that successful authentication does not automatically mean customer data was accessed or taken. The attack also did not result from a vulnerability in Microsoft's own systems or services. Hackers exploited permissions associated with a trusted third-party application. For businesses, that's a serious concern. Employees could have strong passwords and multifactor authentication enabled, yet criminals might still gain access through a compromised application the company already trusts.
ARTEX cyberattacks have already exposed personal information

The Microsoft 365 incident represents only part of the FBI's warning. In South Korea, hackers used ARTEX in attacks against financial institutions. Those attacks exposed personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people, according to the FBI.

In a separate investigation, South Korean authorities arrested seven suspects connected to attacks against more than 90 organizations. Police said the group stole approximately 8.2 million data records, with ARTEX reportedly used in many of the attacks. Researchers have also identified a separate international cyberespionage campaign.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked hacking group known as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The campaign compromised at least nine organizations. The AI agents helped criminals identify vulnerabilities and obtain credentials. When one attack method failed, the software could attempt another approach. These incidents show how quickly AI-assisted hacking has expanded from individual targets to coordinated attacks against organizations around the world.
Why the ARTEX warning should concern you

You probably have never heard of ARTEX before now. But the businesses you depend on could become targets. Think about the information your employer keeps on file. It may include your Social Security number and banking details for direct deposit. Your healthcare provider holds sensitive medical information, while financial institutions maintain records connected to your identity. If criminals steal information from those organizations, they could use it to attempt identity theft or target you with convincing scams. A hacker who obtains your email address and details about your employer could create a phishing message that looks legitimate. A message mentioning a company you actually do business with may be harder to recognize as fraudulent.

There's another concern. Your personal information could be exposed through a company you barely remember giving it to. The FBI has not warned that ARTEX automatically compromises personal phones or home computers. Its advisory focuses on attacks against organizations and the systems they operate. Still, you don't have to be the direct target of a cyberattack to feel its effects.
NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH
The FBI warns that hackers using the ARTEX AI hacking tool can gain privileged access to company systems in under three hours. (Craig Hudson For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Why removing ARTEX from GitHub hasn't stopped the attacks

The original ARTEX developer released the framework publicly in July 2026. After reports emerged that criminals were abusing it, the developer removed the original GitHub repository on October 8. However, the software remains available through archived copies and modified versions. The FBI also identified a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles. That figure refers to accessible framework interfaces, rather than 1,600 confirmed criminal operations. Removing the original project did little to eliminate copies already circulating online.
How to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks
While companies are responsible for securing their systems, you can still take steps to protect your personal information and limit the damage if a business you trust gets hacked.

If criminals steal login credentials from one organization, they may test those credentials against other accounts. Reusing passwords makes that easier. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A reputable password manager can generate secure passwords and store them for you. Start with your primary email account because criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services.

Multifactor authentication adds another security check when someone tries to sign in to your account. Enable it for your email and financial services whenever available. Choose a passkey or authenticator app when supported. Passkeys can provide stronger protection against phishing than traditional passwords. Keep in mind that these protections cannot prevent every attack. The ConnectWise incident involved compromised application credentials rather than someone entering an employee's password.

You may have granted third-party applications permission to access your Google or Microsoft account without thinking much about it. Review those connections periodically. Remove permissions for unfamiliar services or applications you no longer need. For personal Microsoft accounts, visit account.microsoft.com. For Google accounts, review your connected apps through myaccount.google.com. Look for unfamiliar sign-ins while you're there. If something seems suspicious, secure the account and revoke any sessions you don't recognize. For work accounts, contact your IT department before changing business application permissions.

Cybercriminals often use major security incidents to create convincing phishing messages. You might receive an email claiming your bank was hacked and asking you to verify your password. Another message could direct you to a fake account recovery page. Avoid clicking unexpected links or opening unfamiliar attachments. Instead, visit the company's official website or open its app directly to check for alerts. Never share verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if the person claims to work for your bank.

Install security updates on your computer and phone. These updates frequently address vulnerabilities criminals could exploit. Strong antivirus software with real-time protection can also help identify malicious downloads and suspicious programs. Some security tools offer additional protection against phishing websites. However, antivirus software on your personal computer cannot prevent criminals from compromising a company's cloud systems. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

Check your financial accounts regularly and enable transaction alerts. These notifications can help you spot unauthorized activity quickly. Review your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or credit inquiries. You can request free reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If your Social Security number has been exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze is free and can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using your identity. A freeze will not prevent fraud involving accounts that are already open, so continue monitoring those accounts.
VISA, MASTERCARD AND JPMORGAN CUSTOMER DATA LEAKED

ARTEX uses artificial intelligence to automate cyberattacks, allowing criminals to identify security weaknesses and attempt to break into multiple organizations at once. (Philip Dulian/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Know what to do if your information is exposed
If a company notifies you about a breach, find out exactly what information was compromised. Then take action based on the type of data involved.

Change exposed passwords immediately. Update any other accounts where you reused the same password.Secure your email account. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions.Contact your bank if financial information was exposed. Ask whether your accounts need additional protection.Consider a credit freeze. This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen.Watch for follow-up scams. Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing.Report identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan if someone has misused your personal information.
Change exposed passwords immediately. Update any other accounts where you reused the same password.
Secure your email account. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions.
Contact your bank if financial information was exposed. Ask whether your accounts need additional protection.
Consider a credit freeze. This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen.
Watch for follow-up scams. Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing.
Report identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan if someone has misused your personal information.
You can also report suspected internet crime to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/.
Kurt's key takeaways

A backup service is supposed to help protect a company's information. In the ConnectWise attack, hackers abused that trusted connection to gain access to customer systems. That's especially concerning because employees could have followed every security recommendation and still been exposed through a service their company depended on. The speed of these AI-powered attacks also worries me. Three hours gives security teams very little time to stop criminals who know exactly where they're going. I think companies need to take a much harder look at the outside applications they trust and how quickly they can detect unauthorized access. For you, the best approach is to secure your own accounts and pay attention when a company reports a breach. You shouldn't have to become a cybersecurity expert to feel confident that businesses are protecting your information.

If AI-powered hackers can gain privileged access to company systems in less than three hours, do you still trust businesses to protect your personal information, or should companies face tougher consequences when that information gets exposed? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: FDA clears tiny surgical robot to remove bladder tumors
summary: The FDA-authorized Virtuoso Endoscopy System uses needle-sized robotic arms to remove bladder tumors intact, helping pathologists assess detrusor muscle.
story: CEO of Sellas Life Sciences Angelos Stergiou explains how AI is revolutionizing medicine by enabling precision medicine in cancer treatment.

If a doctor finds a tumor in your bladder, you want to know what you're dealing with. Is it cancer? Has it reached the bladder muscle? The tissue removed during surgery helps answer those questions. Now, a tiny surgical robot could give doctors a clearer view of what's happening inside the bladder.

The FDA has authorized the Virtuoso Endoscopy System, developed by Nashville-based Virtuoso Surgical. It uses two needle-sized robotic arms to remove bladder lesions through the urethra, without cutting through the skin. The technology allows surgeons to remove many tumors in one piece, potentially giving pathologists better tissue samples to examine. This new approach to robotic bladder tumor removal could help doctors make more informed treatment decisions.

WOULD YOU TRUST A TINY DENTAL ROBOT?
The FDA-authorized Virtuoso Endoscopy System uses two miniature robotic arms to help surgeons remove bladder lesions through the urethra without external incisions. (Virtuoso Surgical)
How robotic bladder tumor removal works

The Virtuoso Endoscopy System uses a narrow medical instrument called a rigid endoscope, which enters the bladder through the urethra. At the tip are two miniature robotic arms made from a flexible metal alloy called nitinol. A surgeon controls both arms from a console. One arm lifts and holds the tumor while the other carefully separates it from the tissue underneath. This gives the surgeon two-handed control inside a very small space.

The technique is called en bloc resection, which means removing a tumor in one piece. Surgeons can already perform this procedure using conventional instruments, but it can be technically demanding. Virtuoso designed its system to make that approach easier to perform. The robot also relies entirely on the surgeon's movements. Unlike some autonomous surgical robots being tested in research settings, Virtuoso does not make surgical decisions or operate independently.
Why removing bladder tumors in one piece could help

Bladder cancer affects thousands of Americans every year. The American Cancer Society estimates that approximately 84,530 people in the United States will receive a bladder cancer diagnosis in 2026. One of the most common procedures for evaluating and removing bladder tumors is called transurethral resection of bladder tumor, or TURBT. During conventional TURBT, surgeons often remove tumors in smaller fragments. While effective for many patients, that approach can disrupt the tissue's original structure. As a result, pathologists may have a harder time determining how deeply cancer has grown. That's particularly important when it comes to the bladder's muscle layer, called the detrusor muscle. Doctors need to know whether cancer has reached this muscle because that can change the recommended treatment.

Removing a lesion intact may preserve more of the information pathologists need. It can also allow them to examine the tissue around the tumor more clearly. Dr. Duke Herrell, a urologic surgeon and CEO of Virtuoso Surgical, explained the potential benefit in the company's FDA announcement. "Removing a tumor intact can provide a better tissue specimen, which supports clearer diagnosis and staging," Herrell said. For patients, a more complete tissue sample could help their medical team determine the next steps with greater confidence.
Early results show promise for the tiny surgical robot

Virtuoso has already tested the system in human patients, and the early clinical findings are encouraging. In the first 20 patients enrolled in the company-sponsored VIABLE study at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, 94% of removed lesions contained detrusor muscle. That exceeded the study's predefined performance goal of 60%. Researchers also reported that surgical margins could be evaluated in 93% of malignant lesions. Surgical margins are the edges of the removed tissue. Examining them can help doctors assess whether cancer cells extend to the edge of the sample. However, being able to evaluate a margin does not necessarily mean it is free of cancer. The company reported no adverse events during the operations.

There are important limitations to these findings. The study involved a small number of patients at one medical center. The previously published first phase of the same VIABLE study involved six patients and recorded two postoperative adverse events. One patient experienced temporary urinary retention, while another developed a chest infection later linked to a separate esophageal tumor. The company also compared its results with previously published research on conventional bladder tumor removal.

However, the Virtuoso study did not directly compare the robot against traditional instruments in a randomized trial. Researchers still need larger studies to determine whether the system improves long-term outcomes or reduces the need for additional procedures.
BRAIN TUMOR FOUND DURING PREVENTIVE SCAN PUTS FULL-BODY MRIS BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT
The Virtuoso Surgical control console allows surgeons to independently guide two tiny robotic arms during bladder tumor removal procedures. (Virtuoso Surgical)
What the FDA authorized for bladder tumor surgery

The FDA granted De Novo authorization for the Virtuoso Endoscopy System on Oct. 30, 2026. The company publicly announced the decision on Nov. 10. The authorization establishes a new FDA classification for robotic surgical instruments that operate through an endoscope inside the body. Specifically, the system is authorized to remove bladder lesions in adult patients and obtain tissue samples, including bladder muscle, to assist in diagnosing bladder cancer.

The decision follows the FDA's September 2025 Breakthrough Device Designation for the system. That earlier designation recognized the technology's potential and allowed the company to receive additional regulatory guidance during development. However, the new authorization does not establish that the robot improves survival rates or prevents cancer from returning. The system must also be operated by trained surgeons in an operating room.
When will hospitals start using this surgical robot?

Virtuoso Surgical plans a limited U.S. launch in 2027, starting with leading urology centers. The company has not announced which hospitals will receive the system first. That means patients may have to wait before the technology becomes available at their local hospital. Questions also remain about pricing and insurance coverage.

Virtuoso is exploring other potential applications for its miniature robotic instruments, including procedures involving the lungs. However, those uses remain experimental and have not received FDA authorization. For now, the company's focus is bladder surgery, where better tissue samples could help doctors evaluate cancer more accurately.

Virtuoso Surgical's miniature instruments, shown next to a penny for scale, are designed to remove bladder lesions in one piece, potentially improving cancer diagnosis and staging. (Virtuoso Surgical)
What this means to you

If you or someone you love is facing bladder cancer, this technology could eventually provide another surgical option. Its miniature robotic arms may help doctors obtain more complete tissue samples during the initial procedure. However, availability will be limited at first, and the early results still need confirmation in larger studies. The robot's FDA authorization also does not guarantee better results for every patient.

If you're discussing bladder tumor surgery with a urologist, ask whether en bloc resection might be appropriate for your situation. You should also ask how the surgeon plans to obtain enough tissue to determine whether cancer has reached the bladder muscle. Those answers can help you understand your options before surgery.
Kurt's key takeaways

When you're facing a possible cancer diagnosis, getting accurate answers as early as possible can make a real difference. That's what I like about this technology. Virtuoso's tiny robotic arms could help surgeons collect better tissue samples without taking control away from the medical professional performing the operation. It's also encouraging to see the FDA authorize a system designed for such a specific surgical challenge. Still, 20 patients represent a very small study, and I want to see how this robot performs in larger trials before getting too excited about its potential. If the results hold up, this could become a valuable addition to the tools doctors use to diagnose bladder cancer.

title: What really happens when you need help restoring your identity
summary: Identity theft restoration involves credit freezes, fraud alerts and disputing fraudulent records. Here's how the recovery process works, step by step.
story: Morgan Wright, former State Department antiterror advisor, joins the broadcast to analyze a massive cybersecurity breach affecting Chase, Visa and Mastercard. Wright explains how customer data was exposed in the leak and outlines critical safety measures individuals must take to protect their financial information amid a period of unprecedented global technology turmoil.
Identity theft restoration takes more than one phone call. It often means securing accounts, documenting fraudulent activity and working with several companies to correct inaccurate records.

The term "identity restoration" can sound complicated until you suddenly need it. Maybe someone opened a credit card in your name, took over your bank account or used your personal information to get medical care. Now you're dealing with unfamiliar charges, paperwork and companies that all seem to have different requirements.

Fortunately, knowing what happens during recovery can make the process easier to manage. Here's how identity restoration typically works, what you may need to do yourself and where professional help can make a difference.
