title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
summary: Former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warns AI voice cloning scams could trick families into losing thousands of dollars this holiday season.
story: Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real communications from fake ones.

A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.
"Everybody's on edge," Brown said.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
The more details a scam includes, the more likely it is built from your publicly available data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.
"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.
AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

Former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and increasingly difficult for Americans to recognize. (Fox News Digital)
AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.
Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.
"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.
"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.
As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Scammers may impersonate major delivery companies during the holiday shopping season, sending fraudulent messages claiming packages cannot be delivered without additional payment. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.
"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.
Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.
AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warned holiday shoppers to be cautious of suspicious delivery notifications appearing to come from UPS, FedEx or the U.S. Postal Service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone, over the computer is stop, think and then independently verify," he added.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: What to know
summary: For the first time in its history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled due to weather, shifting to Saturday amid a forecast of high winds.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss recent airport disruptions due to severe weather and technological glitches. He also guides viewers on how to handle any delays or frustrations during the holiday travel weekend.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed ahead of an expected nor'easter in New York City, marking the first time the parade has been rescheduled due to weather.
The parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday due to a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain, according to The Associated Press.
All the balloons that were filled up on Wednesday will be deflated and returned to New Jersey for storage until Saturday.

"With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day and in close partnership with our city partners, the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will now march on Saturday, November 28th," Macy's Thanksgiving Parade Executive Producer Will Coss told reporters.
WORST AIRPORTS FOR THANKSGIVING TRAVEL CHAOS RANKED AS MAJOR US HUBS TOP LIST
A Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade float on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City Nov. 25, 2026. (Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)
Coss noted that organizers have spent two years preparing for Saturday's event.
Spectators typically watch workers fill up the balloons the night before the parade, but there won't be an "inflation night" on Friday, he said.
"It's the only inflation we support here in New York City," Mayor Zohran Mamdani joked.
Macy's was working with school bands from outside the city who were in town so they could perform in Saturday's parade, Coss said.
"It will be spectacular. I promise you. It will be the parade that we set out to deliver, so I look forward to sharing it with everyone," he said.
A view of the Bluey balloon during the 2022 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on November 24, 2022 in New York City.  (Michael Loccisano/Getty Images)
A Thanksgiving storm is expected to hit New York City and the tri-state area with heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in some places expected.

An area of low pressure developing off the Southeast coast will push northward into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast beginning Wednesday night. The storm is expected to intensify through Thanksgiving Day before clearing out on Friday, according to the FOX Forecast Center and the National Weather Service.
The iconic parade draws thousands of spectators along the 2½-mile route, which begins in Manhattan's Upper West Side to Herald Square on 34th Street, the site of the Macy's department store.
The Charlie Brown balloon during the 90th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Nov. 24, 2016, in New York City. (WireImage)
Mamdani said the parade is part of the city's iconic culture, but that public safety could not be compromised.

"I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," he said. "Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets, and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences."
"Yet safety has to come first," he added.
The Tom Turkey float makes its way down Central Park West to kick off the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, Thursday, Nov. 27, 2025, in New York.  (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/AP Photo)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Along the route, there will be an expanded police presence, and "the NYPD is fully prepared for an event of this magnitude, just as they have been prepared for the 99 parades that preceded this," said NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Parents of 5-year-old boy killed in Oregon school shooting seek court order against teen gunman's mother
summary: Parents of 5-year-old Rhoam Summer asked an Oregon court to force the shooter's mother to release shotgun records and preserve his online activity.
story: Newly released 911 audio captures the call from Kaylub Giamanco, the hero dad who took down a gunman at Oregon’s Silver Rail Elementary School. (Credit: Deschutes County District Attorneys office)

The parents of a 5-year-old boy killed in last month's shooting at an Oregon elementary school are asking a judge to compel the teenage gunman's mother to turn over records detailing how she acquired the shotgun used in the attack and to preserve his online activity before potential evidence disappears.

Lillian and Kelik Summer, the parents of kindergartner Rhoam Summer, filed the pre-suit discovery petition Monday in Deschutes County Circuit Court against Shauntai Nickerson, the mother of 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II.

The filing comes ahead of a planned wrongful death lawsuit over the Oct. 15 rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where John fatally shot three children and a teacher inside a special education classroom before being killed by an armed parent.
Rhoam, who had been in kindergarten for six weeks, is cited in the petition as the youngest person ever killed in a deliberate mass school shooting in the U.S.
HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children shot and killed at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. (AP; Bend Police Department)

Tim Williams, an attorney representing the Summers, told Fox News Digital that law enforcement informed the family it is reviewing "thousands of pages of communication" involving John and "the underbelly of society," which investigators described as "fans of school and mass shootings."

Williams said police also indicated that at least one person who communicated with John has been contacted by investigators and "intimated" that one or more artificial intelligence platforms may have been used in planning the attack.

"Because criminal liability is much more narrowly focused than civil liability, we are concerned that, without such letters, some of the evidence may not have been gathered by law enforcement, and thus will be lost to time and processes," Williams said, explaining the petition seeks to identify potential defendants so preservation notices can be sent immediately.
911 CALL CAPTURES HERO DAD’S BRAVERY BEFORE HE TOOK DOWN OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL GUNMAN
Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Oct. 16, 2026, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)

Citing public reports that Nickerson bought a Maverick 88 12-gauge shotgun around her son's birthday in August and gave it to him as a gift, the petition seeks a limited deposition, firearm purchase records, gun-related communications and access to John's social media, gaming and AI accounts.

The filing also notes John had not attended school since Nov. 25, 2025, and lists his estate, Bend-La Pine Schools, the unidentified gun seller and any online platforms or users who assisted him as potential defendants.
Flowers and candles are placed at a makeshift memorial at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Oct. 16, 2026, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Nickerson's attorney, David Glenn, told the Summers' lawyers she will not voluntarily produce the records, according to the filing.
Fox News Digital reached out to Bend-La Pine Schools for comment and did not immediately receive a response.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Lindsay Clancy retrial moves forward as state's highest court denies prosecutors' request to pause murder case
summary: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court denied prosecutors' bid to pause Lindsay Clancy's murder case as her double jeopardy appeal is considered.
story: Legal clashes erupted in Plymouth, Massachusetts, when defense attorney Kevin Reddington argued there was no evidence Lindsay Clancy killed her three children. Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham countered that the evidence is voluminous.
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court rejected prosecutors' request to delay Lindsay Clancy's murder retrial while it considers a double jeopardy appeal filed by her defense attorneys.

Prosecutors with the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office filed a motion Monday seeking to pause proceedings in Clancy's murder case, arguing it would be "ambitious" to expect the state's highest court to resolve her double jeopardy appeal before jury selection begins March 29. Clancy is accused of strangling her three young children to death.
"The full Court will presumably determine whether such a retrial will violate the defendant’s double jeopardy rights," Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnsen wrote.
"As such, it makes little sense to move forward with proceedings intended to bring the defendant to a trial, where this Court may ultimately decide that a retrial is barred by double jeopardy."
LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS ASK COURT TO DELAY HER RETRIAL IN CHILDREN'S STRANGLINGS

Lindsay Clancy and her attorney, Kevin Reddington, attend a status hearing for the Clancy case at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Sept. 29, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
The motion was denied without explanation by Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court justices.
Clancy's lawyers, Kevin Reddington and Martin Weinberg, opposed the motion, stating in a reply to the state's motion that "she wants to keep her trial date."
LINDSAY CLANCY TO BE RETRIED FOR MURDER IN KILLING OF THREE CHILDREN
READ THE MOTION:

Clancy, 36, faces murder charges in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan — all under age 6, who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict, ending in an 11-1 divide.
SEND US A TIP
Lindsay Clancy looks on as jurors enter the courtroom during Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Sept. 4, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Prosecutors argued a stay would "forego any additional expense and effort" in preparations, while Clancy's lawyers said, "The cost of a stay would fall on Ms. Clancy, who is held without bail."
PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL

Judge William Sullivan indicated he was going to declare a mistrial before changing course and giving Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney one hour to appeal as the jurors in the case indicated they were unable to reach a verdict Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

In her appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, Clancy's attorneys argued that Sullivan unnecessarily declared a mistrial and that forcing her to stand trial again would violate her constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
The legal battle comes while another major change hovers over Clancy's case. Sullivan is preparing to retire in June 2027 when he reaches Massachusetts' mandatory judicial retirement age of 70.
MICHAEL RUIZ: LINDSAY CLANCY SCORES 'LITTLE WIN,' BUT APPEAL COULD 'UNRAVEL' FUTURE TRIALS, RETIRED JUDGE SAYS
Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts judge and legal scholar, previously told Fox News Digital he thought the request was reasonable.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The prosecution's position is probably based on the difficulty of deciding a full bench appeal and getting ready for trial No. 2 so quickly," Lu said.
"I see this as a reasonable request, and the parties have not even publicly stated, after setting the actual trial date, that they will really be ready."

title: Autonomous AI agents are giving everyday hackers ‘nation-state’ firepower, cyber expert reveals
summary: Cybersecurity expert John Walsh of IGEL says AI gives individuals the power to disrupt critical infrastructure once held only by nation-states.
story: Individual hackers equipped with AI now have the same cyber-disrupting capabilities that were previously only held by large nation states, John Walsh, the senior vice president at the Germany-based software company IGEL, told Fox News Digital.

While the recent string of headline-grabbing service outages across critical U.S. sectors may not be the result of a coordinated cyberattack, governments and companies across the globe still face a reality in which individuals have the same power to disrupt that was once only held by large nation-states, cybersecurity expert John Walsh explained.

"AI and the fact that it enables organizations that wouldn't have, let's say, financial resources that a nation-state might have to really invest in a specific type of attack methodology to go after some specific resource or objective, AI definitely enables them," Walsh, the senior vice president at the Germany-based software company IGEL, told Fox News Digital.

Since Microsoft's high-profile service outage on Nov. 12, numerous corporations and government agencies have suffered network-related service disruptions. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for just the second time since 9/11 on Nov. 13, citing a faulty router replacement flooding the telecommunications network.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
Several other critical industries and sectors, including major U.S. banks and the National Security Agency, have also been hit by major network disruptions in the ensuing days.
Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
However, the White House and several prominent cabinet members have repeatedly denied seeing any evidence that the events are the result of a coordinated cyberattack on the U.S.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

"We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here. And we can be fairly confident in that because we know those things exist, and we’ve been looking for them in the past," Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, told Fox Business on Nov. 17.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio concurred with Clayton's assessment.
SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS

"We are not under systemic attack…Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cybercriminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country…The American people should have confidence in that," Rubio said during a press conference in the Philippines the same day.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a press conference on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 22, 2026. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
In lieu of a coordinated cyberattack arranged by a foreign adversary such as Iran or North Korea, Walsh offered a counter hypothesis.
FBI WARNS AI HACKERS CAN BREACH SYSTEMS IN UNDER 3 HOURS
"The ability to attack is significantly lower cost than the cost of defending, [so] we create an asymmetry...in the advantage of the attacker," Walsh explained.

"In the past, these types of attacks that were persistent would look for things, try to identify opportunities to take advantage of, and there was typically, you know, an iterative process, if you will, where there were humans in the loop and making changes. And now that essentially all happens instantaneously without the need for the AI attacker to reach back. So I think, yeah, I think that it's quite possible that some of the things we're beginning to see are certainly related to that, and we're going to see more of that," he told Fox News Digital.
THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE
Walsh also concurred with Rubio and Clayton's assessment regarding the lack of evidence pointing to a coordinated assault.
John Walsh, senior vice president and chief technology officer at IGEL (Fox News)

Rather, he posited, much of the disruption is coming from critical industries recognizing vulnerabilities that could be exploited by AI-assisted hackers. Those disruptions, due to the increasingly centralized and interconnected digital world, may naturally cause ripple effects throughout linked systems.
DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
"What we're seeing is more of a common architectural concern," Walsh explained.

"It really is related in a way that we've spent decades connecting these legacy systems with modern applications. We've implemented cloud services, networks to improve efficiencies. And so we've created a lot of dependencies, and not just dependencies within the organization," Walsh told Fox News Digital.
Those dependencies extend to large financial institutions, which Walsh also explained are highly interconnected.

"It wouldn't be unusual that an event that might affect one financial institution might create transaction relations, related issues or other things, and other organizations that are in the process of clearing transactions and so on with these large, large infrastructures," he said.
A Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
Walsh's recommended defense strategy is to build resiliency within the architecture of the nation's critical digital infrastructure.

"The big issue that really we're beginning to, as a community, recognize that it's about resilience. It's about the architecture's ability to operate through events, and the systems have to isolate the events. They've got to protect what the essential services are," Walsh said.
Besides working with silo networks and identifying users accessing those networks, there are also hardware fixes that chipmakers like Apple and Intel can implement.
Walsh explained that chipmakers can install a cryptographic signature into their chips called a trusted platform module, or TPM.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"These are actual in the silicon cryptographic mechanisms so that you can latch on to those as the software and pass that what we'll call ‘root of trust’ up," he said.

title: Pre-Thanksgiving flight to Chicago disrupted when unruly passenger rushes toward airplane door
summary: An American Airlines flight to Chicago diverted to Phoenix, Arizona, after an unruly passenger allegedly tried to pry open an aircraft door mid-flight.
story: A Chicago-bound American Airlines flight diverted to Phoenix after a passenger allegedly tried to manipulate a cabin door. Crew and passengers restrained him ( Credit: Facebook / Sean Bennett).

A Chicago-bound American Airlines flight had to divert to Phoenix, Arizona, on Wednesday, after an unruly passenger allegedly attempted to pry open an aircraft door, the Federal Aviation Administration confirmed.

The flight landed safely at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport around 1 a.m. local time Wednesday, Nov. 25, after the crew reported a passenger disturbance on board, the FAA told Fox News Digital in a statement.

The flight, which originated in San Diego, once again headed for its destination of Chicago O’Hare International Airport after the unruly passenger was removed, according to the FAA and American Airlines.

"American Airlines flight 1494 diverted to Phoenix (PHX) due to a disruptive customer. Upon arrival, law enforcement met the aircraft and assisted with deplaning the customer before the flight continued to its destination," the airline told Fox News Digital in a statement.

title: Army detonates nearly 5 tons of lead azide at Iowa ammunition plant
summary: Two explosions were heard near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday as the U.S. Army detonated 68 barrels of degraded lead azide — a move officials said was necessary to prevent a spontaneous blast.
story: Drone video captured smoke rising from the site of the ammunition plant in Middleton, Iowa, where the U.S. Army detonated tons of lead azide on Wednesday. (Credit: WeatherVaultMedia / James Wilson)
After multiple delays and a federal court intervention, the U.S. Army has detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa.
Two explosions could be heard in the vicinity of the site at around 9 a.m. local time (10 a.m. ET), according to a video feed.
"Great job by the Army, and others, in Iowa!!! President DJT," President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social of the operation.

Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley said in a press conference after the explosion that "all the lead azide barrels were definitively removed," adding that there were no secondary explosions, notable dust kick-outs or infrastructure damage.

"I believe, absolutely, that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," said Shirley, the commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command.
The US Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026.  (Reuters/Jim Urquhart)
US ARMY MAKES PREPARATIONS AHEAD OF LEAD AZIDE STOCKPILE DETONATION IN IOWA
As of 5:30 p.m. ET, none of the EPA's live air monitors in the expected plume path have detected any lead in their readings.

The U.S. Army announced on X at 6:31 p.m. ET that FEMA has issued an all-clear around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, adding that Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA) maps indicate zero airborne lead detection following the morning's controlled detonation. Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, with results to be released once complete, the Army said.

A senior official within the Trump administration told Fox News that the planned explosion "exceeded all expectations" and that "maximum mitigation" was achieved. That was followed up by a short Truth Social post from President Donald Trump himself, in which he said early reports showed mitigation efforts had been successful.

About 15 minutes after the explosion was heard, Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe confirmed that it had taken place. He said there were not any detectable traces of lead in the air headed toward his state following the detonation.
Updated Army maps had projected the blast's plume could drift southwest into the northeastern corner of Kehoe's state.

"Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained," Kehoe wrote in a social media post.
Barrels of unstable lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant ahead of a planned controlled detonation Wednesday. (U.S. Army)
CONTROLLED IOWA MUNITIONS DETONATION BETTER THAN ‘WORST-CASE SCENARIO,’ ACTING ARMY SECRETARY SAYS

Ahead of the blast, residents and environmental advocates had warned that detonating the bomb-making materials at the plant risked blanketing the surrounding community in toxic lead dust. To prevent this, the Army built extensive barriers and deployed specialized gels to absorb the fallout.
Maj. Gen. Shirley also credited aqueous foam barriers with helping to contain the blast.
After the detonation, FEMA said that residents within 20 miles of the blast site who have not evacuated "should continue to shelter in place" and follow EPA safety guidance.
FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton told Fox News there was a "sigh of relief" at the Army's command center following the explosion, which he said was likely effective at containing lead particles.

"From what we see now, it doesn't appear that there's a big lead plume that was in the projection models," Hamilton said, adding that the Army's mitigation efforts to contain the blast "were very, very successful."

U.S. Army personnel prepare for the detonation of a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the U.S. Army Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026, in this screengrab from a handout video. (U.S. Army/Handout via Reuters)
US ARMY TO PROCEED WITH IOWA DETONATION OF DEGRADED BOMB MATERIALS: ‘A CONSENSUS DECISION’

Hamilton said that in the coming days and weeks, various federal agencies will be taking air and soil samples, while officials with the Department of Agriculture will visit nearby farms to carry out impact assessments.
Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the situation in Iowa resulting in the Army deciding to detonate the degraded stockpile began with the Obama administration in 2009.

"I think we have to remember that this was a problem, the can had been kicked down the road. If you go back to 2009 under the Obama administration, we stored this highly unstable stuff with no real plan for how to move it, no real plan for how to neutralize it. When I say we, I mean, the Obama administration, the United States government did this back in 2009," Vance said.

Rob Sand, Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, echoed what federal officials have said so far about lead dispersal being limited and thanked those on the ground who worked to make sure the detonation was "as safe as possible."

"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," Sand added. "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared. There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did. And any Iowans who have been impacted in any way must be taken care of fully, right away."

Officials with the Army and other federal agencies had agreed that a controlled detonation of the 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly volatile explosive material, was safer and far preferable than a spontaneous explosion.

Such a blast, officials said, was possible at any moment because the lead azide had crystallized. The crystals are extremely sensitive to heat, shock and friction, and officials warned that freezing temperatures — like those that hit Middletown on Wednesday — could further destabilize the material and trigger an explosion.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

ATF Director Robert Cekada said the lead azide was first brought to the munitions plant in Middletown at some point in 2009, right around the time the U.S. military was beginning to phase out the combustible material due to its extreme volatility.
The Army discovered that the lead azide had begun to crystallize during a routine inspection in March, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle has said.

The Army initially considered hiring a private firm to neutralize the explosives using chemicals, as well as options for thermal treatment or relocation. However, officials determined that opening the unstable barrels to add chemicals risked triggering an immediate explosion, leading them to pursue a controlled detonation instead.
On Nov. 13, the EPA granted an emergency permit authorizing a detonation through February 11, 2027.
After the Army set a date for Nov. 20, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club sued the EPA, which put the detonation plans on hold.
Trump ordered the Army not to proceed without court approval, which it got on Monday, when the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted its stay.

story: Sheridan Gorman's parents speak with Fox News Digital about their daughter's beloved holiday traditions, the empty seat at their Thanksgiving table and the memories they cherish as they face their first holiday without her.

EXCLUSIVE: The parents of an 18-year-old college student allegedly killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago are preparing for their first Thanksgiving without their daughter, as they grapple with an empty seat at the table and what they believe to be missed opportunities to prevent her death.

In an emotional Zoom interview with Fox News Digital, Sheridan Gorman's parents, Thomas and Jessica Gorman, remembered their daughter's love for the holidays while saying they're frustrated over what they believe were several missed opportunities by Chicago authorities to arrest the illegal immigrant accused of killing her.

Jose Medina-Medina, 25, was arrested after he allegedly killed Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student, on March 19. According to the Department of Homeland Security, he illegally entered the U.S. from Venezuela in 2023, when he was apprehended but released into the country by the Biden administration. He has pleaded not guilty to murder, attempted murder, aggravated assault, aggravated discharge of a firearm and illegal possession of a weapon.
ANGEL FAMILIES PLEAD WITH LEADERS TO 'CHOOSE' AMERICAN CHILDREN OVER PROTECTING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS
Sheridan Gorman, 18, whose parents are preparing for their first Thanksgiving without her, was accepted into a Vanderbilt University internship program just two days before her death. (Thomas Gorman)
"Our dogs actually still sit in her bedroom window every day waiting for her to come home. It's been over seven months and that's where they are all day, just waiting."

The Gormans said Sheridan's favorite Thanksgiving tradition was making apple pie. This year, her parents will continue that tradition without her, and said they plan to leave an empty seat at the dinner table.

"We're going to share an apple pie together and try to start, I guess, some new memories," Sheridan's father said. "As hard as it is without her, it's definitely going to be an empty seat at the table."
Sheridan's mother said the family usually gathers around the Thanksgiving table to share what they're thankful for, but this year will be different.
"I guess this year for us, it's going to be gratitude and grief at the same time," she said. "I think we're thankful that we had 18 years with her. The grief part is I wish we had so many more."
SHERIDAN GORMAN'S PARENTS SAY PROTECTING CHILDREN FROM FAILED IMMIGRATION POLICIES ISN'T A ONE-PARTY FIGHT
Close up of Sheridan Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student who was fatally shot near campus. (Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

BIDEN BORDER OFFICIALS RELEASED ALLEGED KILLER OF CHICAGO STUDENT 'DUE TO LACK OF SPACE,' DOCUMENTS SHOW

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Spivey family lawyer says no evidence points to 'stand your ground' shooting victim firing first
summary: Scott Spivey's family attorney says audio evidence undercuts claims the insurance adjuster fired first in the 2023 road rage shooting in South Carolina.
story: Witness testimony and 911 audio indicate Scott Spivey did not fire first in a deadly South Carolina road rage shooting that left him dead in 2023, according to his family's attorney. Three years later, two men face murder charges.

The South Carolina attorney representing the family of an insurance adjuster killed in a 2023 road rage shooting says there is "no physical evidence" that the 33-year-old Scott Spivey shot first, as his accused killers have alleged in court.

"I think we have the eyewitness testimony of Frank McMurrough, who says that that did not happen," said Mark Tinsley, who represents Spivey's family in an ongoing wrongful death lawsuit against two men who were charged with murder last week. "We believe that we have audio forensic evidence that supports that that didn't happen, and I think that we'll present that at trial."

Spivey died in what Tinsley has described in court documents as "a hail of gunfire" on Sept. 9, 2023, after pulling over on Camp Swamp Road, nine miles from where he first encountered defendants Charles "Weldon" Boyd, 35, and Kenneth "Bradley" Williams, 37, on Highway 9.
MICHAEL RUIZ: 911 CALL REVEALS CHASE BEFORE DISPUTED 'STAND YOUR GROUND' SHOOTING, 'HE'S TRYING TO RUN'

South Carolina attorney Mark Tinsley in court representing the family of Mallory Beach, a teen killed in a drunken boating crash involving Paul Murdaugh, the son of disgraced former attorney Alex Murdaugh. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

There were no criminal charges in the case for more than three years, after the two initially claimed self-defense and said Spivey had pulled a gun on them first in what had initially been deemed a "stand your ground" shooting. A civil judge later ruled that Boyd and Williams were not eligible for "stand your ground" immunity.
In a 911 call that Boyd placed during the chase, he told the dispatcher that Spivey opened fire first.
GOT A TIP?

But Tinsley, who questioned that the case could have ever involved a "stand your ground" claim given the highway distance traveled by Boyd and Spivey's trucks, said that in addition to the witness testimony, audio evidence undercuts the idea that Spivey could have fired first.
"Had the weapon been fired, [the sounds of gunshots] would have been captured," Tinsley said. "They weren't captured because it didn't happen."
Scott Spivey was killed on September 9, 2023, during a road-rage incident that occurred on Camp Swamp Road in the Loris area of Horry County, South Carolina. (Obtained by Fox News)
'STAND YOUR GROUND' CLAIM FALTERS IN ROAD RAGE KILLING AS MEN CHARGED WITH MURDER, EX-COPS FACE ACCUSATIONS

O'Bryan Martin, Williams' attorney, told Fox News Digital McMurrough has said he saw Spivey raising a firearm and that the autopsy indicates his arm had been raised when he was struck by at least one bullet.
"There's no evidence he didn't fire first, either," he said.
A single casing was found outside Spivey's truck, he said, with more recovered inside the cab.

"When he collapsed, the slide on his gun was locked back on an empty magazine, so he had fired every round, and the pathologist testified at the immunity hearing that the location and angle of the wound mean his arm had to be raised when he was hit," he added.

Charles "Weldon" Boyd and Kenneth "Bradley" Williams appear in court during a hearing on a wrongful death lawsuit from the family of Scott Spivey. They were indicted on murder charges last week. (Keith Allen Jacobs/Pool)
SECRET TAPES SINK SHOOTER'S DEFENSE IN SCOTT SPIVEY ROAD RAGE KILLING

Indictments were announced last week against Boyd, Williams and two former Horry County police officials, onetime deputy chief Brandon Strickland, 43, and a 49-year-old ex-sergeant named Paul Damon Vescovi.

Charges against Boyd and Williams include murder and weapons offenses. Strickland and Vescovi have been accused of official misconduct and obstruction of justice. And Boyd and Strickland, who spoke on the phone dozens of times after the shooting, face additional conspiracy charges.

Strickland allegedly told Boyd he'd be taken care of and that the right people were responding to the scene, and Vescovi is accused of coaching Boyd and Williams at the scene on how to act in front of bodycams.

Former Horry County Deputy Police Chief Brandon Strickland is pictured in uniform. He was arraigned Thursday on conspiracy and obstruction of justice charges in connection with a road rage shooting that resulted in murder charges against two other men — which was initially deemed self-defense. (Horry County Police Department)

Strickland's attorney, Bert von Herrmann, said he looked forward to presenting his client's defense in front of a judge, noting that the defense is not allowed to present evidence or witnesses to the grand jury.

"We respect the findings of the grand jury," he told Fox News Digital. "However, we recognize the indictment stems from the untested state's presentation to the jury to meet the lowest standard known in criminal law."

And Brad Richardson, who represents Vescovi, said he had not yet received discovery and that while the case has received attention in the news and on social media, there may be more information forthcoming.
"We’re gonna depend on the jury looking at everything, not just what certain sides have chosen to present in the light they want to present it," he said. "It's still very early."

title: Invasive Burmese pythons push farther north into Florida as hunters race to stop ecological devastation
summary: Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years, and now, experts warn they've been spotted further north.
story: COLLIER COUNTY, Fla. – Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years. Now, experts warn they are making their way farther north.

Hard freezes were once thought to limit Burmese pythons to South Florida, but researchers have documented the invasive snakes sheltering and sometimes breeding in burrows, which can protect them from cold temperatures.

"First of all, they're following the food," said Amy Siewe, professional python hunter and guide. "But they are also stealing gopher, tortoise burrows and armadillo burrows. And that's how they're staying warm during those colder nights in Florida that they typically wouldn't be able to survive."

For Siewe, python hunting is a full-time job. Known as the "Python Huntress," she left behind a 13-year real estate career in 2019 after discovering Florida's Burmese python problem, turning her lifelong passion for snakes and reptiles into a new purpose.
BEAR SWIPES HUNTER'S DEER BEFORE HE GETS A CHANCE TO CLIMB OUT OF HIS TREE STAND TO RETRIEVE IT
Amy Siewe holds an invasive Burmese python. (Amy Siewe / pythonhuntress.com)

"They eat 98% of the mammals in parts of the Everglades," said Siewe. "So they're really devastating our ecosystem. So we need to do everything we can to get them out of our ecosystem to save the native wildlife. But also, you know, we don't even know what type of damage this is going to do to our ecosystem in the years to come."

Siewe's husband, Dave, and her puppy, Dixie, like to get in on the action, too. Fox News Multimedia Reporter Amy Galo joined them on a hunt through the Everglades in Collier County, getting a firsthand look at what it takes to find the invasive snakes.
Python hunter Amy Siewe searches for pythons while standing on her truck's snake deck. (Amy Galo)

"She's (Dixie's) really just telling us where they are. And when she finds one, she says her indication," said Siewe as Dixie searched through the brush. "So then I go in. Well, once she sits, Dave calls her off, and I go verify that there's a python."
Siewe searches for pythons in the Everglades several times a week, even leading guided hunts.

"We've got our snake deck here," said Siewe. "It's a platform on the truck that just gives us a little bit of height so we can see the pythons easier in the grass and in the water and things like that."
Amy Siewe's dog, Dixie, is trained to search for invasive Burmese pythons. (Amy Galo)
Conservative estimates place the population of Burmese pythons in the Greater Everglades region in the tens of thousands. An exact count is difficult because these snakes are masters of camouflage.
According to Siewe, they spend roughly 85% of their time lying still in often inaccessible areas.
"We are always happy catching one, like I always want to catch one more," said Siewe. "There are a lot of times we go out and you don't catch any. That's just the nature of the python."
AGGRESSIVE TURKEYS ARE HARASSING PEOPLE ACROSS THE BOSTON AREA JUST DAYS BEFORE THANKSGIVING
More than 23,000 Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. But recently, the snakes have also been spotted farther north.
Amy Siewe and Dixie search through the long grass in the Florida Everglades. (Amy Galo)

"There are two different populations. One in Brevard and also up in Charlotte County," said Siewe. "But based on what we know, the scientists think that those are separate events. So that is not an extension of the colony down here (in the Everglades) that has been established for years."
Once a breeding population becomes established, eradication is extremely difficult.

"The problem with the pythons is that you don't even know that they're there until it's way beyond your control," explained Siewe. "These guys spend 85% of their time not moving. And so, when we find one python, there could be up to a thousand more that we're not seeing."
Siewe added, "They lay eggs, you know, 20 to 40 eggs a year. Sometimes the big ones can lay over 100. So it's just, it's a never-ending cycle."

That is why researchers emphasize early detection and public education to try to prevent additional releases of captive invasive snakes.

title: PETA protesters interrupt Rockettes' Christmas performance at Radio City Music Hall over use of live animals
summary: PETA activists rushed the stage at Radio City Music Hall's "Christmas Spectacular," protesting the use of live camels, sheep and donkeys in the Nativity scenes.
story: Three PETA activists interrupted a performance of the Radio City Music Hall "Christmas Spectacular" in New York, holding up signs and chanting to protest the show's use of live camels, sheep and donkeys in its Nativity scene.
A trio of PETA activists crashed the Rockettes' performance at Radio City Music Hall in New York City on Tuesday in protest of the Christmas show's use of live animals in the Nativity scenes.

The protesters disrupted Radio City Music Hall’s "Christmas Spectacular" because of the camels, sheep and donkeys used in the Nativity scenes. PETA said the animals were offstage during the demonstration against the "shameful" Nativity scenes that the group argues "exploited" the animals.
During the demonstration, the activists rushed on stage with signs reading "Radio City: End Animal Acts Now!" and chanting the same message.
"No more animals on stage!" one protester shouted as she ran up on stage in front of the performers, according to footage shared by PETA.
ANIMAL RIGHTS ACTIVIST ATTACKS NYC HORSE CARRIAGE DRIVER WITH SKATEBOARD DURING TIRADE, UNION SAYS
The activists rushed on stage with signs reading "Radio City: End Animal Acts Now!" (PETA)
"Keep the camels and donkeys out of the performance!" another screamed.
"Take the cruelty out of Christmas!" a third yelled.
The three demonstrators were swiftly removed from the stage and hauled out by security.
PETA said it took issue with the show subjecting the live animals to flashing lights and loud noises, including fireworks and cheering crowds.

"Unlike the Rockettes, the camels, sheep, and donkeys exploited for the Christmas Spectacular didn’t sign up for bright lights, roaring crowds, and the chaos of the stage, which can be confusing and downright terrifying for them," PETA President Tracy Reiman said in a statement.
The three demonstrators were swiftly removed from the stage and hauled out by security. (PETA)

"PETA is calling on Radio City Music Hall to listen to the growing chorus demanding that it stop exploiting animals as living set pieces and let talented human performers or clever stagecraft steal the show," Reiman continued.

The animal rights group also claimed that the animals used in the performance undergo stressful transport and are confined backstage, including some reportedly kept in the basement, when they are not performing during the show’s months-long run every winter.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Radio City Music Hall said PETA "deliberately attempted to disrupt today’s performance, endangering our performers and interfering with the experience of our guests."
"We have zero tolerance for this behavior and will pursue all available legal action against anyone who engages in such conduct," the statement continued.
HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY
The protesters disrupted Radio City Music Hall’s "Christmas Spectacular" because of the camels, sheep and donkeys used in the Nativity scenes. (PETA)
The disruption during Tuesday's show was PETA's latest attempt to pressure Radio City into ending the use of live animals for shows.
Nearly 40,000 PETA supporters have called on Chase, Lexus, SpotHero and Verizon to end their sponsorships for the show until it stops using live animals.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Earlier this year, PETA sent a letter to the show’s director and choreographer, offering to fund a crafted life-size camel puppet if Radio City Music Hall agrees to retire the live animals from its Nativity scene, citing Broadway’s "The Lion King" as evidence that stagecraft can captivate audiences without forcing animals to perform.

title: Man arrested after bystanders stop alleged rape attempt inside popular fast-food restaurant's restroom
summary: Matthew Lewellen, 39, is held on $200,000 bail after his alleged attack in the women's restroom at an In-N-Out Burger in Vancouver, Washington, police say.
story: Bystanders intervened after hearing screams from a women's restroom at an In-N-Out Burger in Vancouver, Washington, where police say a man was choking a woman.

A 39-year-old Washington state man is being held on $200,000 bail after bystanders intervened to stop an alleged attack inside the women's restroom at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Vancouver, Washington, police and jail records show.

Matthew Lewellen was booked into the Clark County Jail on suspicion of first-degree attempted rape, second-degree assault by strangulation, unlawful imprisonment and indecent liberties, according to a news release Monday from the Vancouver Police Department and online jail records.
Officers responded around 1:50 p.m. Sunday to a disturbance report at the restaurant, police said.
OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO
Witnesses reportedly heard screaming coming from inside the women's restroom of the In-N-Out Burger. (iStock)
Witnesses heard screaming coming from inside the women's restroom, prompting several bystanders to run inside, where they reportedly saw a man choking a woman, according to the release.

According to a probable cause affidavit obtained by People, the woman told police she had gone into the restroom to check her teeth in the mirror when Lewellen allegedly opened the door, stared at her, walked inside and grabbed her from behind in a chokehold while groping her body.
Her husband ran in after hearing her scream and pulled Lewellen off her before bystanders detained him inside the bathroom until officers arrived, police and People reported.
SUSPECT IN ALLEGED RAPE OF LSU STUDENT KILLED BY CAR FIGHTS TO KEEP MOM’S WARNING TEXTS OUT OF DECEMBER TRIAL
Officers responded to a disturbance report at the restaurant Sunday afternoon, police said. (Stephen M. Katz/South Florida Sun-Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, File)
The woman did not suffer serious injuries, police said. Investigators determined the man had also attempted to sexually assault the woman, and police confirmed the two did not know each other.
A witness also told investigators Lewellen had been standing outside the restroom with his arms crossed "scoping it out" for about 20 minutes before the alleged attack, according to People.
A witness also told investigators that the suspect had allegedly been standing outside the restroom. (iStock)
In the affidavit, police wrote that Lewellen told officers "he knew it was wrong, but felt like she was the girl for him," and said "the voices in his head told him to do it," People reported.

Lewellen is scheduled to appear in Clark County Superior Court on Nov. 30, jail records show.
A representative for In-N-Out Burger did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Florida AG calls for doctor to lose medical license over 149 alleged illegal abortions
summary: Florida's attorney general is pushing to revoke a North Miami Beach doctor's medical license, citing suspected violations of the Heartbeat Protection Act.
story: Florida AG James Uthmeier calls for revoking Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite’s medical license, citing at least 149 alleged illegal abortions. (Credit: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier)

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is pushing to strip a North Miami Beach doctor of his medical license over at least 149 suspected illegal abortions, a number he says could rise to 180 as the investigation continues.

Uthmeier said in a video posted by his office on X that preliminary reports from state health officials indicate Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite allegedly performed the procedures between June 2024 and September 2026.
He said some may have been late-term abortions and called on the Florida Board of Medicine to revoke Braithwaite’s license.
DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier during a news conference. He is calling for a Miami doctor to lose his medical license over alleged illegal abortions. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, File)
"A medical license is not a license to break the law," Uthmeier said.

Uthmeier cited Florida’s Heartbeat Protection Act and said none of the cases fell under the exceptions he outlined for medical emergencies or victims of rape, incest or human trafficking. He said each alleged violation amounts to a third-degree felony.
"My office is investigating this conduct, and we will follow the facts wherever they lead," Uthmeier said. "And we will prosecute doctors who ignore our laws."

Noah Brandt, executive vice president of the anti-abortion group Live Action, told Fox News Digital that Braithwaite should lose his medical license for good and face prosecution if investigators confirm the allegations.

"If these allegations are true, at least 149 innocent preborn children were killed in direct violation of Florida law, and each of those children deserves justice," Brandt said. "The killing of innocent human beings, including through abortion, should be illegal, and the fundamental human rights of every person, born and preborn, must be protected under the law."
‘YOU’RE FIRED’: NEARLY 40 PRO-LIFE GROUPS URGE TRUMP ADMIN TO CUT OFF PLANNED PARENTHOOD FUNDS
Women & Teens Healthcare in North Miami Beach, Fla., where Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite serves as medical director, according to his professional biography. (Google Maps)
Brandt said Braithwaite should be "prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law" if the allegations are proven.
He also praised Uthmeier for "his commitment to enforcing Florida’s pro-life laws and setting an example for attorneys general across the country."

Florida state Rep. Taylor Yarkosky backed Uthmeier in a reply on X, calling the alleged conduct "the Devil at work" and thanking the attorney general "for upholding the law in Florida, and mostly for protecting the lives of the unborn!"
Uthmeier did not say whether any charges had been filed or how far along the pregnancies were in the cases he described as potentially late-term.

A woman hands a pamphlet to a person outside of Women & Teens Healthcare, a clinic that provides abortion services in North Miami Beach, Fla. (Josh Ritchie for The Washington Post via Getty Images, File)
Braithwaite is a board-certified obstetrician and gynecologist who serves as medical director of Women & Teens Healthcare in North Miami Beach, according to his professional biography.

The Florida Department of Health lists his medical license as active and confirms his certification in obstetrics and gynecology.
Fox News Digital reached out to Braithwaite’s office for comment.

title: All 6 passengers found dead inside wreckage of plane off Mississippi coast
summary: All six passengers aboard the Cessna 210 Centurion that went down roughly 2 miles northeast of Horn Island, Mississippi, have been found dead, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
story: The plane was reportedly heading from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, when it went down southwest of Pascagoula with four adults and two children on board.

All six people aboard a small plane that crashed off the Mississippi Gulf Coast were found dead Wednesday morning, bringing a search-and-rescue operation to a tragic end, according to the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG).
The USCG and partner agencies concluded their search after divers located the remains of all six people inside the aircraft's fuselage approximately 2 miles northeast of Horn Island, Mississippi.

The victims' identities have not been released, but earlier authorities said they were searching for four adults and two boys between the ages of 8 and 12, according to local outlets WDSU and WLOX, citing the USCG.
The Cessna 210 aircraft went down Tuesday afternoon, prompting a multi-agency search. It was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when it crashed, the outlets reported.
BODY WASHED ASHORE IN OREGON IDENTIFIED AS FORMER CITY COUNCILOR MISSING SINCE SEPTEMBER PLANE CRASH
U.S. Coast Guard rescue crews are conducting a search operation off the Mississippi Gulf Coast Tuesday after a plane carrying six people went down. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

"This is a heartbreaking outcome, and our deepest sympathies are with the families and loved ones who are facing an unimaginable loss," Cmdr. Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard Sector Mobile search and rescue mission coordinator, said in a statement.

"While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families," Blount added.
Coast Guard watchstanders in Mobile received a report from air traffic control at approximately 3:45 p.m. Tuesday that contact had been lost with the aircraft.
FLORIDA LEARJET CRASH 911 CALLERS REPORT HEARING ‘BOMB’ AS PLANE CARRYING YOUNG FAMILY PLUNGES NEAR BUSY ROAD
In a Tuesday post on X, the U.S. Coast Guard Heartland said the plane went down off the Mississippi Gulf Coast.

"[USCG] rescue crews are searching for a downed Cessna 210 Centurion aircraft with 6 people, 2 mi NE of Horn Island, Mississippi, after [USCG] watchstanders in Mobile received a report from [the Federal Aviation Administration], Tuesday," the U.S. Coast Guard Heartland said.
A Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital the plane went down southwest of Pascagoula, Mississippi, at about 3:30 p.m. local time.
A Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital the plane went down southwest of Pascagoula, Miss., at about 3:30 p.m. local time. (iStock)
The aircraft was traveling from New Orleans Lakefront Airport to Page Field in Fort Myers, Florida, when it dropped off FAA radar around 3:45 p.m., WLOX reported.
FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK
The FAA confirmed it will investigate. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, File)
By 5:40 p.m., Coast Guard crews told WLOX they had located several pieces of wreckage, including the cabin, a life raft and three life jackets, though none of the passengers had been found.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asks federal judge to halt execution
summary: Former U.S. Army Maj. Nidal Hasan filed a federal court motion Tuesday seeking to delay next week's scheduled execution at Fort Hood while he challenges his sentence.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin looks at the history of the firing squad being used in the United States and debates over the plan to stream Nidal Hasan’s execution on ‘Special Report.’

Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army officer slated to be executed next week for the 2009 murder of 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, has asked a federal judge to halt the execution while he mounts a legal challenge to his sentence.

The motion, filed in civilian court with the American Civil Liberties Union and the ACLU of Kansas acting as standby counsel, seeks a stay so Hasan can file a habeas corpus petition challenging the constitutionality of his death sentence.
Hasan remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE
Nidal Hasan has been sentenced to death for the mass shooting at Fort Hood. (Getty Images)

"There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss. But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system," said Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, in a statement Tuesday.

"Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case," the statement continued. "We urge the court to stop the government from bypassing Mr. Hasan’s due process rights in its rush to carry out this execution."
Hasan is scheduled to be executed by an Army firing squad on Dec. 3 at the same Texas military installation where he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others.
He was convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The execution would be the U.S. military's first in more than six decades.
SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’
President Donald Trump approved execution by Army firing squad for Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood attack, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced Monday. (Reuters)

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire inside a medical processing building at Fort Hood —an attack he said was motivated by opposition to the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Now 56, Hasan uses a wheelchair after being left partially paralyzed when police officers shot him during his arrest nearly 17 years ago.
Plans surrounding the execution drew national controversy weeks ago after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially proposed livestreaming the firing squad.

That proposal drew criticism across the political spectrum, with opponents warning a broadcast would fulfill Hasan's desire for martyrdom. President Donald Trump announced in October that the execution would not be livestreamed.

Meanwhile, the Army on Tuesday rejected appeals from three survivors of the 2009 shooting who had asked to witness the execution. Officials ruled that because the three were not physically wounded by gunfire, they were not considered direct victims under military execution regulations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Retired Col. Kathy Platoni, who would have served as Hasan's supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal.
"I would desperately like to attend," Platoni said from her home in Ohio. "To look Hasan in the eye and say, ‘You didn’t get me.'"

title: Benjamin Franklin impersonator appears in shackles and full costume after Boston arrest
summary: Timothy Kingman, 66, appeared in Boston Municipal Court dressed as Benjamin Franklin a day after his arrest on Hanover Street during a warrant sweep.
story: Courtroom video shows Boston tour guide Timothy Kingman, 66, in his Benjamin Franklin costume Tuesday, a day after police arrested him on shoplifting and assault and battery warrants. A judge released him without requiring bail. (Credit: Pool)
A Benjamin Franklin impersonator walked into a Massachusetts courtroom dressed as the Founding Father one day after police arrested him in the same getup.
Courtroom video shows Timothy Kingman, 66, appearing before a judge Tuesday in Boston Municipal Court after spending the night in jail.
Kingman has made his living giving tours of Boston as Franklin for six years, his attorney, Nicholas Santiago, told the judge, according to CBS News Boston.
"It takes guts. He’s committed. He wears the outfit," Santiago said, according to the outlet.
ALLEGED 'MIME' STALKER STRIPPED TO UNDERWEAR, COVERED HIMSELF IN COOKING OIL: OFFICIALS
Timothy Kingman, 66, appears in Boston Municipal Court dressed as Benjamin Franklin on Tuesday, a day after his arrest. (Pool)
A not guilty plea was entered on Kingman’s behalf in the assault and battery case.
The prosecutor said the case stemmed from an alleged altercation March 2 in downtown Boston and asked the judge to set bail at $500, CBS News Boston reported.
Santiago told the court that the police report indicated the other man appeared to knock a phone out of Kingman’s hand before the altercation.
FLORIDA WOMAN ROCKING 'RETIRED DRUG DEALER' T-SHIRT GOT ARRESTED ON, YOU GUESSED IT, SEVERAL DRUG CHARGES
Timothy Kingman appears in costume in Boston Municipal Court on Tuesday. A not guilty plea was entered on his behalf in the assault and battery case. (Pool)
The attorney said Kingman needed physical therapy for a shoulder injury and went to the hospital for a thumb injury. He said the police report listed no injuries to the other man.
Santiago said the incident allegedly stemmed from alcohol issues, and told the judge Kingman had been sober for eight months.
"He wants to continue to work, he wants to continue to strengthen his roots with the community," Santiago said.
A wide courtroom shot shows Kingman in the full Benjamin Franklin costume he wears to give tours of Boston. A judge released him without requiring him to post bail in either case. (Pool)
The judge released Kingman without requiring him to post bail and set a Jan. 13 pretrial hearing in both cases.
The judge ordered him to stay away from and have no contact with the man in the assault case and to stay away from the location involved in the shoplifting case.
The judge also granted a protective order.
Boston police said officers spotted Kingman on Hanover Street during a downtown warrant sweep Monday afternoon.

They recognized him and discovered two outstanding warrants, one on charges of shoplifting and one on charges of assault and battery.
Officers arrested him a short distance away and booked him into the Nashua Street Jail.

title: Florida official addresses 'misimpression' about teen son's fatal campsite shooting
summary: Florida official Joe Vinson says whoever fatally shot his 19-year-old son inside a tent near Blackwater River aimed deliberately and "laughed" while fleeing.
story: Escambia County Commissioner Joe Vinson is speaking out to correct what he calls a "misimpression" around the fatal shooting of his 19-year-old son, Wash.

A newly elected Florida official is speaking out to correct what he called a "misimpression" about the fatal shooting of his 19-year-old son during a weekend camping trip, alleging whoever fired the shots aimed deliberately at an occupied sandbar and "laughed as they drove away."

In an Instagram post Tuesday, Escambia County Commissioner Joe Vinson mourned his son, Carey Washington Vinson, who was known as "Wash," while sharing new details about the Sunday night shooting along the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle.

"I need to correct a misimpression you might have gotten about the shooting," Joe Vinson said. "This was not a freak hunting accident — not someone firing carelessly in the dark. It was not a ‘stray bullet’ that killed our Wash."
According to Joe Vinson, the shooter or shooters stood on the opposite riverbank, close enough to see the group's campfire and hear them talking, and aimed at the occupied campsite.

They fired shot after shot with malicious intent, and after a pause when the panicked campers screamed ‘stop,’ they fired another volley, then laughed as they drove away."
Law enforcement officials have provided few details about the shooting.

First responders were dispatched to the Blackwater River area Sunday after a 911 call. Deputies found the 19-year-old inside his tent with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead, according to the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office.

In a Facebook update Tuesday, the Sheriff's Office issued an urgent plea for witnesses, asking anyone who saw suspicious activity near Deaton Bridge Road and Boat Ramp Road on Sunday to come forward.

"Santa Rosa County, we need your assistance," the Sheriff's Office wrote. "Investigators continue to work diligently to identify those involved in the fatal shooting of Carey Vinson on November 22, 2026, and determine the circumstances that led to this tragic loss of life.

"Our thoughts and prayers remain with the Vinson family during this incredibly difficult time. The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office remains committed to conducting a thorough investigation and bringing those responsible to justice."

Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, first announced the tragedy on Monday, writing that his family was "shocked and heartbroken about our sweet boy."

In his follow-up tribute, Joe Vinson remembered his son as a "sweet, thoughtful young man" and a history major at Florida State University who loved tabletop games, played Beethoven on the piano and Jeff Buckley on guitar and had just been accepted to a summer study-abroad program in Valencia, Spain.

I can’t believe I’ll never feel his hugs again, or hear him bickering with his siblings. I can’t believe any of this. Every impatient moment, every unkind word, I will gladly take them back if you would just come back to us," Joe Vinson wrote.
Joe Vinson urged anyone with information to contact the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office at 850-983-1190 or Crime Stoppers at 850-437-STOP.

title: FAA issues ground delay at Chicago O'Hare due to 'equipment outage'
summary: An equipment outage prompted the FAA to issue a Tuesday afternoon ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, delaying flights until at least 4:15 p.m.
story: FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble reports on the FAA issuing a ground-stop for some flights departing to Chicago O'Hare International Airport amid Thanksgiving holiday travel on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop Tuesday at Chicago O'Hare International Airport due to an "equipment outage," during what is anticipated to be a heavy Thanksgiving travel rush before changing it to a brief ground delay.

The FAA reported the ground stop just after 3 p.m. local time Tuesday. The ground stop was expected to be lifted by 4:15 p.m., according to local reports. The ground delay was canceled around 5 p.m. local time.
"Due to EQUIPMENT / OUTAGE, departure traffic destined to Chicago OHare International Airport, Chicago, IL (ORD) is currently experiencing delays averaging 47 minutes," the FAA website states.
TRAVELERS CLASH OVER WHETHER CRUISE LINES SHOULD ALLOW DOGS AND CATS ON BOARD OR NOT

Chicago O'Hare International Airport was the subject of a brief ground stop on Tuesday because of an equipment outage, the second ground stop in as many days.   (Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The FAA identified the issue as an outage involving equipment used to track aircraft and vehicles on the airport surface, Fox 32 reported.

"The FAA is no longer under a ground stop at Chicago O’Hare International Airport but is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment," the agency said.
The agency did not say what caused the outage. The issue was limited to O’Hare, and it does not impact all flights nor affect any other airports or FAA systems, the FAA said.
Ground Stop issued for equipment outage at Chicago O’Hare Airport in Illinois. (Photo by KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI / AFP via Getty Images)

The initial advisory listed a delay of up to 42 minutes for flights covered by the ground stop, Fox 32 reported. In a separate status update, the FAA reported arrival delays of 15 minutes or less for flights already in the air.
The advisory did not specify what equipment was affected. Tuesday’s ground stop followed a separate one at the same airport on Monday morning because of staffing issues.
Flight delays and cancellations have been at the forefront of the minds of travelers, given what happened on Nov. 13, when every plane was grounded as part of a massive nationwide ground stop.

title: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic service outage
summary: Microsoft declared a "Code Red" after a historic 24-hour outage hit most of its 420 to 450 million users that wa blamed on a Windows scalability defect.
story: FOX Business correspondent Grady Trimble and former CISA Executive Director Bridget Bean join ‘The Faulkner Focus’ to examine the widespread fallout from a major global Microsoft outage that disrupted essential services, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot.
Tech giant Microsoft declared a "Code Red" alert recently, signaling an urgent effort to address the historic 24-hour outage that downed its core products between Nov. 12-13.

The outage, which brought down the majority of Microsoft's core products, "affected most" of Microsoft's users, according to the company's post-incident report. The company's total user base is between 420 million and 450 million people, according to financial disclosures.
"Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in an email to employees Friday obtained by Reuters.
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
The incident also marked the most customer-impacting event in Microsoft's history, Henderson told employees.
The Microsoft campus in Mountain View, Calif., Jan. 26, 2026. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Microsoft blamed the outage on a previously undetected scalability defect within the Windows operating system.
SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS
"Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson wrote.
Microsoft employees exchanged over 11,000 messages during the crisis in an effort to diagnose the issue, Microsoft Corporate Vice President Amanda Silver told employees in a memo Monday.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

Silver also detailed the nature of the "Code Red" rapid response, explaining that the mobilization would involve five work streams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms.

She added that, in the event of a future situation of a similar nature, the company is working on a target to be able to restore service to users within one hour. The company will also work on deploying AI agents to help with quicker diagnosis in the future.
LAWMAKERS WARN AMERICANS OF VULNERABLE SYSTEMS AMID STREAK OF OUTAGES: 'SOMETHING IS GOING ON'
An estimate from the Anderson Economic Group approximated that the outage cost the global economy roughly $7 billion in lost productivity value.
A computer user utilizing Microsoft's M365 business suite (Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Henderson, in another memo, told employees that urgent patches to Microsoft's flagship M365 suite took too long to deploy.

"In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

An error message is shown when trying to access Microsoft's Outlook Nov. 12, 2026, in Chicago. Microsoft reported a widespread outage that left users unable to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft services. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital contacted Microsoft for further comment.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Fox News Digital that Alexander Florentino-Maldonado, a Honduran national, was released from custody seven times in 2026, including on five occasions when ICE had lodged immigration detainers.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH BRUTAL SLAYING ONE DAY AFTER CALIFORNIA JUDGE RELEASED HIM: DHS

Alexander Florentino-Maldonado, a 27-year-old Honduran national, was arrested by NYPD officers on Saturday morning in connection with the fatal beating of 62-year-old Jin Yu inside her Chinatown apartment. (DHS)
